parties:
Abdul Mumin alias Tanu Miah ------ Appellant (in all the appeals)
Vs.
Mahfujur Rahman and others ------ Respondents (in C.a. No 85 of 1998)
Pervejur Rahman and others ------ Respondents (in C.a. No 86 of 1998)
Riajur Rahman and others ------ Respondents (in C.a. No 87 of 1998)
Salimur Rahman and others ------ Respondents (in C.a. No 88 of 1998)
Selima Rahman and others ------ Respondents (in Ca. No 89 of 1998)
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin, J :- These appeals, by leave, are against the order dated June 30, 1997 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division passed in Civil Order Nos. 3230, 3231, 3232, 3233 and 3234 of 1997 rejecting the 5 revisional applications summarily. The revisional applications were filed against the judgment and order dated 10.4.1996 of the 1st Court of Additional District Judge, Sylhet, passed in Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 76, 77, 78, 79 and 80 of 1994 allowing the same upon reversing the judgment and order dated August 31,1994 in Miscellaneous Case (Preemption) Nos. 179, 180, 181, 182, and 183 of 1989 allowing the same. The Miscellaneous Cases were filed under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 seeking pre-emption in respect of the sale by 5 different kabalas dated 5.9.1988. The claim of pre-emption was made on the assertion that by inheritance the pre-emptors the co-sharer of the land of lot Nos. 2183 and 2184 of khatian No. 450. 

 2. The pre-emptor claimed to have inherited the land of khatian No. 450 from his father late Abdul Mogni and uncle Abdul Ghani who died leaving only daughter, Respondent No. 2 Panda Begum. It was the case of the pre-emptor that Panda Begum as co-sharer of the Khatian in question sold parcels of land by five registered kabalas dated September 5, 1988 to Mehfzur Rahman, the Respondent No.1 in each of the appeal. It was also averred by the pre-emptor that a suit for partition, partition Suit No. 111 of 1988, is pending before the 2nd Court of Joint District Judge, Sylhet as regard the land of khatian No. 450 filed by one of the co-sharers by name Abdul karim. 

 3. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed upon assertion that there was amicable partition of the land of khatian in question amongst the co-sharers and the pre-emptor and other co-sharers of the khatian had separated their jamas and have recorded their names in respect of their respective saham got by amicable partition in separate khatians, that the pre-emptor in respect of his share separated the jams and has got his name recorded in khatian No. 450/2 and as such pre-emptor ceased to be the co-sharer of the land of the case khatian. The preemptees, contended that they had effected improvement of the disputed land. 

 4. The trial Court allowed the prayer for pm emption on the finding that the pre-emptor and the seller opposite party are co-sharers of the khatian and that preemptees failed to establish there had been partition of the land of khatian by the decree of the Court or by a registered deed of partition. The trial Court also held that the Miscellaneous Cases were not barred by limitation and further held that opening of khatian No. 450/1 and 450/2 do not establish that the jama of the khatian No. 450 was separated. The trial Court while allowing the prayer for preemption awarded Compensation of Tk. 1,00,000/- to the pre-emptees. On appeal the judgment and order of the trial Court was reversed and the Miscellaneous Cases were dismissed. The appellate Court held that upon amicable partition amongst the co-sharers the pre-emptor splitting fame got his name recorded in khatian No. 450/2 and as such pre-emptor was not entitled to pre-empt the sale held on September 5, 1988. 

 5. Thereupon the pre-emptor moved the High Court Divisions in revisional jurisdiction. The High Court Division by common order, as stated hereinabove, rejected the revisional applications summarily upon observing "Since in the instant Cases the holding in question has been separated or sub divided upon opening a new khatian at the instance of the pre-emptor, the preemptor ceased to be a co-sharers in the holding in question". 

 7. The learned Counsel for the appellant, in all the appeals, submitted that amicable partition of the land of the khatian No. 450 alleged by the preemptees being not partition in the eye of law and thus there being no ceasing of co-share ship in the land of the khatian by the so called amicable partition the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court were in error in holding that pre-emptor ceased to be a co-sharer of the land of libation No. 450 and as such he was not entitled to seek preemption in respect of the purchase made by the preemptees. The learned counsel also submitted that in fact by the opening of khatian No. 450/1 and 450/2 in the name of the heirs of late Abdul Mogni and the pre-emptor there was no separation of jams or sub division of the holding as contemplated by section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, rather the same were updating of the record of right i.e khatian No. 450 as per provision of Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 . The teamed Counsel continued since there was no legal partition i.e partition by metes and bounds by the decree of the Court or by a registered instilment of partition and consequent thereupon there was no separation of title of the recorded tenants of khatian No. 450 and as by amicable partition title is not separated but only possession is separated and it being the case of the pre-emptees that there was a amicable partition amongst the co-sharers of the khatina no.450 and as thereby there had been no separation of title the High Court Division as well as the appellate Court below were in error in holding that pre-emptor ceased to be a co sharer in respect of the land of khatian No. 450 and consequent thereupon in rejecting the prayer for preemption, that ratio decadent of the decision reported in 35 DIR(AD) 230 being that by a legal partition co-sharer of a holding ceases to be co-sharer of the original holding and in the instant case there being no legal partition, rather partition suit being pending, the High Court Division and the lower appellate Court were in error in rejecting the prayer for pre-emption upon holding that the pre-emptor ceased to be a Co sharer in the background of the assertion made by the preemptees that there had been amicable partition of the land of khatian No. 450 amongst the co-sharers and that in the light of the amicable partition the pre-import got his share recorded in khatian No. 450/2, that the ratio dividend of the decision reported in 35 DLR(AD) 338 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. 

 8. The learned Counsel for the Respondent No.1 submitted that the very fact of opening of khatian No. 450/1 clearly shows that after amicable partition amongst the co-sharers of khatian No, 450 the heirs of late Abdul Mogni got the aforesaid khatina opened in their names in respect of the land inherited from their father and their late uncle, Abdul Gani and that opening of the said khatian No. 450/1 and later on opening of khatian No. 450/2 in the name of the preemptor as there has been ceasing of co share ship of the heirs of late Abdul Mogni in respect of the land of khatian No. 450 the High Court Division and the Court of appeal below were quite correct in rejecting the prayer for pre-emption upon arriving at the finding that the pre-emptor ceased to be the co-sharer in respect of the land of khatian No. 450. The learned Counsel also submitted that after opening of the new khatian in the name of the pre-emptor he is claiming the land separately from the land recorded in khatian No. 450/1 and that in the light of amicable partition separate Municipal holding has been opened in respect of the land of respective co-sharers. he also submitted that the contention of the pre-emptor that since there was no legal partition or that there was no partition by registered instrument and consequently there having no partition of the land 0f khatian No. 450 in the eye of law and that a suit the partition is being pending and as such the High Court Division and the appellate Court were not correct in holding that pre-emptor ceased to be a co sharer is no merit since the fact of opening of khatian No. 450/1 as clearly manifest there has been a partition among the co-sharers of the khatian No.450 and that the said partition was given effect by opening of the aforesaid khatian and as such as in fact there had been partition of the land of khatian No. 450 the High Court Division and the appellate Court below were quite correct in rejecting the prayer for pre-emption on the finding that pre-emptor ceased to be the co-sharer. 

 12. Facts of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230, in short, are that the land of C.S Khatina No. 214 was owned by Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Chowdhurani Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 for partition and by the decree passed in the suit Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik got sham and Rangubala Chowdhurani got share. Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik sold his share to Nafisa Khatun by the sale deed dated 19.7.1952 and thus she became the co sharer of Rangubala. Rangubala Chowdhurani created a lease in respect of her Share in favour of Ayesha Khatun by a registered lease deed dated 23.12.1953. Nafisa Khatun sold her share to the Respondent No.1 (preemptor) by the sale deed dated 18.4.1972 . Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant (preemptees) by a registered sale deed dated 10.9.1973. This sale was sought to be pre-empted claiming to be the co-sharer of the holding primarily on the plea that on the acquisition of rent receiving interest under raiyat being up graded to raiyat and thereupon only one S.A. khatian having been prepared recording the names of the persons who acquired interest in the land of C.S. khatian No. 214. 

 13. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed contending that seller Ayesha khatun (Respondent No. 2) was not a co sharer in the tenancy, because the land of the tenure was partitioned by the decree in Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 between Akshoy Kumar and Rangubala and that a separate tenancy was created in favour of the Respondent No.2 by Rangbala by granting permanent lease reserving to herself annual rent of Tk.1/- and that Ayesha Khatun paid the rent to the lessor till the rent receiving interest was acquired by the Government. It was also the case of the preemptees that S.A. khatian was not correctly prepared because neither preemptor (Respondent No.1) nor his vendor was co sharer of Respondent No.2 and that he (preemptees) after purchase applied for mutation of his name and accordingly his name was mutated in the S.A. khatian and the jama was separated. The trial Court allowed the prayer for pre-emption and the appeal by the pre-emptees was dismissed preempted went on revision before the High Court Division but did not have the desired result. 

 Facts of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 1 338, in short, are that pre-emption was sought in respect of an auction sale in Certificate Case No. 408 of 1967-1968 clamming to be the co-sharers by purchase of the land of plot No. 107 and 87 of Khatian No. 14 from recorded tenant H.E. Percival by the kabala dated 29.12.1965. It was the case of the preemptors that their names were mutated in khatian No.14. It may be mentioned H.E. Percival was the owner of the land of khatian Nos. 14,18,20, and 24. plot No.108 originally was listed in khatian No.14 . At one stage of the certificate proceeding the land of the aforesaid 4 khatian were amalgamated in khatian No.18 comprising plot Nos. 108, 116, 117, 119 and 121 and finally in the certificate   case land of khatian No.18 was put to auction and the same was purchased by the preemptees. 

 18. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed contending, inter alia, that though the pre-emptors were co-sharers of khatian No .14 but they ceased to be the co sharers of the said khatian while the different plots of khatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24, as owned and possessed by H.E. Percival were amalgamated and consolidated in one khatian, namely khatian No.18, land of which was sold in auction and where in the preemptors were not co-sharers of the certificate debtor. 

 20. The Appellate Division by majority decision restored the judgment of the trial Court holding that although at one point of time the pre-emptors were the co-sharers of the khatian No. 14 by purchasing land of plot Nos. 107 and 87 and plot No. 108 was in the said khatian, but when the land of the different Khatians, i.e khatian Nos. 18, 20, 24 as well as the land of plot No. 108 of Madan No. 14 was consolidated in one khatian i.e . in khatian No. 18, the pre-emptors ceased to be the co-sharers of the recorded tenant RE Percival in respect of the land of khatian No.18. Pre-emptors prayer for pre-emption was riot allowed since on the consolidation and amalgamation of the land of H.E. Percival in a new khatian i.e. khatian No. 18, the preemptors ceased to be the co-sharers of the recorded tenant of the said khatian. So it is seen that a tenant though at one time was the co-sharer in a particular tenancy alms, with the co-sharer in a particular tenancy along with the person who acquired interest subsequently in the land of the tenancy, but when the land of the original tenant or tenants of the said holding wherein purchaser-tenant(s) has no right, is listed in a different khatian and thus leaving the land of the tenant (s) who became the co-sharer in the tenancy either by purchases or by some other mode(s) in the old tenancy them exists no co-share-reship in respect of the land so listed in two (2) different khatians and as such prayer for pre-emption by one of the recorded tenant of the original tenancy is not available in respect of the land of the new tenancy or khatian and vice-versa. 

 21. It may be mentioned the second point in the leave was left undiscussed. The admitted position in the instant case is that appellant's predecessor Abdul Mogni and appellant's uncle, Abdul Ghani along with others were the tenants of khatian No. 450. It is the case of the preemptor appellant that his uncle Abdul Ghani died leaving no male issue and as such Abdul Ghani and for that matter his heirs also inherited the property of Abdul Mogni along with his daughter. It is seen from the materials on record that heirs of Abdul Mogni some time in 1985 upon splitting up jams separated their share whatever they had in plot Nos. 2180-2184 of khatian No. 450 by opening new khatian No. 450/1 and that later on upon splitting up the jama the appellant in the year 1995 separated Iris share in plot Nos. 2183 and 2184 of khatian No. 450/1 by opening new khatian no. 450/2. 

 22. It is the case of the preemptees-respondent that there has been a amicable partition of the land of khatian No. 450 between the heirs of Abdul Ghani and Abdul Gani. As against this it was the contention of the appellant that there was no partition by metes and bounds amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani. In the background of the aforesaid contention of the appellant it has been submitted by the learned Counsel for the pre-emptor appellant that in the absence of a 'legal partition' that is partition by Metes and bounds through a decree of a court, and in the absence of any partition by any legal installment of partition there had been no separation of title, as such pre-emption sought by the appellant was very much available and that amicable partition is no partition in the eye of law. 

 24. In the instant case it was contended from the side of the preemptees-respondent that there was amicable partition of the land of khatian No. 450 amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gain. This contention appears to be correct in the background of the fact of the opening of khatian No. 450/1 in the name of the heirs of Abdul Mogni. In the aforesaid state of the matter it is seen that jointness of possession of the land of khatian No. 450 among the hens of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani ceased. The preemptees purchased the land of khatian No.450 from the heirs of Abdul Gain. The preemptor prior to the transaction under pre-emption got opened separate Khatian, khatian No. 450/2, taking out his share from the land of Khatian No. 450/1. In our opinion in the afore state of the matter there being to jointness of possession between the pre-emptor and the preemptees in respect of the land of khatian No. 450 and jointness of possession or co-sharer ship in the land transferred being the requirement for seeking pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land and the said legal requirement being absent in the instant case, pre-emptor's prayer for pre-emption is not legally available to him. 

 25. The finding of the trial court that by the disputed alleged separation of jama the pre-emptor in view of his inheritance from his uncle retained his status as a co-sharer in the land of khatian No. 450 appears to be not well funded in that no material has been brought is record to establish that khatian No. 450/1 in the name of heirs of Abdul Mogni was opened only in respect of the property they inherited from Abdul Mogni or in other words in the khatian No. 450/1 property inherited from Abdul Gani was not listed. 

 26. As the law is now settled that pre-emption under Section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act can be sought for by a person who is a co -sharer of the land sought to be preempted. It has already been mentioned Abdul Mogni's heirs taking out the land whatever they inherited from Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani in the land of khatian No.450 got recorded their share in khatian No. 450/1 with new jama on in other words upon splitting up of the original jama and this step of Abdul Mogni's heirs reflects that whatever quantity of land they got by inheritance in the land recorded in khatian No.450 and were possessing got the same recorded in the new khatian i.e khatian No. 450/1. This shows said step was taken by the heirs of Abdul Mogni by the Division/partition amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani of the land whatever they had in the said khatian. In the background of the partition/division heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani brought to an end of joint possession of the land inherited by them in khatian No. 450. It is also seen that later on the appellant whatever share he acquired in the property of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani he got said share recorded in a new khatian i.e khatian No. 450/2 with a new jama. This shows that whatever quantity of property he got from his father and also from Abdul Ghani he got that quantity of property recoded in khatian No. 450/2. This fact demonstrates that he is in possession of the property recoded in khatian No. 450/2 and thus he ceased to be a co possessor or joint possessor of the property of khatian No. 450. The very fact of opening of khatian by the appellant in his name shows that he is in exclusive possession of the land of his share in plot Nos. 2183 and 2184. On the opening of new khatian No. 450/1 in the names of the heirs of Abdul Mogni comprising the land of aforesaid two plots and some other plots inherited by them from Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani and later on upon opening of the khatian No. 450/2 comprising the share of appellant in plot Nos. 2183 and 2184. in other words in respect of the share which he had in the land of khatian No. 450/1, he ceased to be a co-sharer in the land of khatian No. 450, or in other words in respect of the land whatever left in the share of heirs (s) of Abdul Ghani in khatian No. 450. Thus the appellant being not the recorded tenant of khatian No. 450 and that being not the co-sharer of the land as recorded in khatian No. 450 or in other words appellant being the tenant of the tenancy as in khatian No. 450/2 and consequently not being the co-sharer of the tenancy or the land as in khatian No.450 as such was not entitled to seek preemption of the land sought to e preempted since the land so sought of be preempted is of khatian No.450. The jointeness of possession amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Ghani in respect of the land on khatian No.450 has been served by the fact of opening of khation No. 450/1 in the name of the heirs of Abdul Mogni in respect of the land which they inherited from Abdul Mogni and Abdul gani. The opening of new khatian in their names by the heirs of Abdul Mogul shows that they are in specific possession of the land of the plots listed in the said khatian and further opening of khatian No. 450/2 with separate jama comprising land of plot Nos. 2183 and 2184 by the appellant in his name in respect of the quantity of land he got by inheritance out of the land of khatian No. 450/1 shows that he is in specific possession of the land of the plots listed in the said khatian. 

 27. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that opening of khatian No. 450/1 and khatian No.450/2 are not in fact separation of jama or creation of new tenancy with separate jama upon splitting up of tenancy of khatian No. 450, but in fact is correction of record of right making the same up to date as contemplates by section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or in other words the learned Counsel wants to say that there is more mutation of the names of the heirs of Abdul Mogni. The Submission no made is not well founded in that had the steps that were taken by the heirs of Abdul Mogni were in fact making the record of right upto date there was no earthly reason for starting a new khatian with different jama i.e khatian No. 450 /1 in the name of the heirs of Abdul Mogni and later on khatian No. 450/ 2 in the name of the appellant, In our opinion mutation of the names because of transfer or inheritance would be certainly noting down the names of the transferee (s) or the names of the heir (s) of original recorded tenant (s) in the record of right as stands at that particular moment and that not to open a separate khatian with separate jama as in the instant case has happened, It is also seen from the I record that heirs of Abdul Mogni paid rent as  against the khatian No. 450 /1. This fact shows that heirs of Abdul Mogni ceased to be the tenants of khatian No. 450. 

 28. In the background of the materials on record and the discussions made hereinabove it is seen that jointness of possession of the land of khatian No. 450 amongst the heirs of Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani ceased on the opening of a khatian No. 450/1 by the heirs of Abdul Mogni in respect of the land they got by inheritance   from Abdul Mogni and Abdul Gani and that later on upon the opening of khatian No. 450/2 in the name of the appellant and as in respect of non agricultural land pre-emption is available only to a non-agriculture tenant who is a co-sharer of the land so transferred i.e co-sharership in the land transferred is the sole criterion for the purpose of seeking pre-emption when a part of the non-agricultural land held by a on-agricultural tenant is Transferred to a stranger i.e a person who is not a co-sharer tenant in the land to transferred and as in the instant case it is seen that appellant is not a co-sharer tenant in the land sought to pre-empted, as such he is not entitled to seek pre emption of the land transferred by the heir of Abdul Ghani to the preemptees.

parties:
Rokeya Begum ------ Appellant
Vs.
Md Nurul Absar and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Pre-emption was sought under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in respect of 381/2 decimals of land in each of the Miscellaneous cases. The land sought to be pre-empted was transferred by two kabalas dated June 25, 1988. 

 6. The prayer for pre-emption was opposed by filing written objections stating, amongst others, that the prayer for pre-emption sought under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintainable since the land being within the Chittagong Municipality is non-agricultural land, that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer of the holding since the jama has been separated by the pre-emptor as well as by the pre-emptees, that pre-emptor is not a contiguous land holder in respect of the land sought to be pre-empted since there is a pathway separating the land sought to be pre-empted from the land owned by the pre-emptor, that the land sought to be pre-empted being non-agricultural land claim of pre-emption on the claim of being contiguous land owner is not available to the pre-emptor. 

 7. The trial Court by separate judgments of the same date allowed the Miscellaneous Cases upon holding that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the holding, that the Miscellaneous Case Nos.1134 of 1986-87 and 561 of 1986-87, on the basis whereof jama is claimed to have been separated by the pre-emptor, were not filed by him and notices of the said Miscellaneous Cases were not served on the co-sharers of the jama and, as such, there was no separation of jama in the eye of law and consequently, the pre-emptor remained co-sharer of the jama. The trial Court also held that order in Mutation Case No. 550 of 1988-89 by which pre-emptees are said to have separated the jama was obtained during pendency of the Miscellaneous Cases and no notice of the said Miscellaneous Case was served on the co-sharers of the holding. The trial Court further held that although the land is within the municipal area, but the said land being agricultural land there no bar for the pre-emptor to have the relief sought in the Miscellaneous Cases and that no evidence was brought on record by the pre-emptees to establish that brick built 3' width 'ail' is a municipal road and that there was no amicable partition of ejmali land and the land of the jama was not partitioned by the decree of the Court. The trial Court also found that the Miscellaneous Cases were not bad for defect of parties or barred by limitation. Finally, the trial Court allowed Miscellaneous Cases upon placing reliance on the decision in the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114 wherein it has been observed that merely for wrong mentioning of the provision of law in the cause title of the petition seeking pre-emption, the petitioner should not be denied the relief sought since by converting the application so filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act same could be given as it was proved that the pre-emptor is entitled to seek pre-emption and to get the relief prayed for in the Miscellaneous Case and it was not necessary to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title. 

 9. The appeal, i.e.- Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991, filed against the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 315 of 1988 was allowed by the High Court Division by the judgment and order dated November 15, 1993 upon observing, amongst others, that the Miscellaneous Cases for separation of jama were not filed by the pre-emptor and that the notices of the Miscellaneous Cases were not served on the co-sharers and, as such, it cannot be found for certainty that the jama was separated, that pre-emptor was competent to seek preemption as co-sharer of the jama but since she has sought pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in respect of the land which is non-agricultural land being within the Chittagong Municipality the Miscellaneous case was not maintainable and that no application seeking amendment was filed for converting to a case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act. The High Court Division also rejected the prayer for pre-emption on the ground of contiguity upon observing that "As there is a pathway in between the lands it cannot be found that the petitioner has land contiguous to the case land," 

 10. The other Appeal i.e. Miscellaneous Appeal No. 134 of 1991, filed against the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 314 of 1988 was also allowed by the High Court Division on January 26, 1994 on the finding that the 'ail' or pathway separates the case land from the land of the pre-emptor and, as such, pre-emptor is not a contiguous land owner of the case land and consequently, his claim of pre-emption on that score is not available to him and the land being within the Chittagong Municipality is not an agricultural land and, as such, prayer for pre-emption made by filing application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not available and the Miscellaneous case filed seeking pre-emption was not maintainable since there was separation of jama and that the separation so made was acted upon by payment of rent, and the 'same was tried to be established by the pre-emptees showing payment of rent of the separated jama and that "Though there is nothing on record to show at whose instance the Mutation Case was started the fact remains that the order of separation of the jama has been passed and the Dakhilas Exhibit H proved the payment of rent" and that genuineness of that Exhibit H was not challenged by the pre-emptor and that though notices of the Mutation case was not served on the co-sharers but the fact remains that rent was paid in respect of the jama so separated and "When the order has been acted upon on payment of rent the plea that no notice has been served on the respondent for separation of the jama cannot be sustained. Further, it appears that immediately after the knowing of the separation of the jama no appeal has been preferred against the order passed by the Revenue Officer indicating also that the separation of the jama has been accepted. The mere fact that notice of the mutation proceeding has not been served on the respondent cannot defeat the final order passed by the Revenue Officer when on the basis of that a separate Khatian was opened and rents paid by the petitioner-respondent. The non-filing of the petition for mutation and non-production of the service return of the notice cannot be a ground to ignore the final order of mutation due to the fact that the same has been acted upon as before" and that as the jama was separated the pre-emptor ceased to be a co-sharer of the holding for getting a pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act. 

 11. It may be mentioned in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 314 of 1991 the learned Advocate of the pre-emptor-respondent filed an application seeking conversion of the petition filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to a petition under section 24 of the Non Agricultural and Tenancy Act, but the same was rejected on the finding that the application so filed was neither verified, nor supported by affidavit and, as such, cannot be considered a petition for amendment of plaint of Miscellaneous case. 

 12. Leave was granted to consider the Submissions that the High Court. Division committed an error of law in holding that pre-emption could not be allowed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act without amendment of the application for pre-emption filed tinder section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act pursuant to a proper application by the pre-emptors to that end and that the findings about the separation of the holding concerned in both the pre-emption cases being contradictory to each other as given in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991 and First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 134 of 1991 requires reconsideration and re-conciliation. 

 13. The land sought to be pre-empted is undisputedly within the Chittagong Municipality and, as such, the pre-emptor (appellant in both the appeals) was required to seek preemption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act, but petition seeking pre-emption was filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, as it appears since the land sought to be pre-empted was described in the kabalas as "কৃষি নাল জমি ". Be that as it may, it appears from the judgment of the High Court Division that the said Division rejected the prayer for pre-emption, amongst others, that the petition seeking preemption was filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that no proper application seeking amendment to convert the petition so filed to a petition under section 24 of the Non Agricultural and Tenancy Act was filed. 

 19. The learned Counsel for the appellant upon referring to the case of Md Jabed Ali and others vs Rakhal Chandra Mondal and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309 has submitted that in view of the provision in section 117(1)(c) an order of the Revenue Officer separating holding would be valid only when the same is made in conformity with the provision of the said section of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act i.e. there must be an application from one or more co-sharer tenants seeking separation of holding and that an order of separation of holding shall have to be made upon serving reasonable notice "to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter". 

 20. The learned Counsel submits that the High Court Division found that it was established before the Court that application in Miscellaneous Case No. 1134 of 1986-87 or Miscellaneous Case No. 561 of 1986-87 was not filed by the pre-emptor and that notices of the said Miscellaneous Cases were not served on the co-sharers of the holding and that it was also not established that Mutation Case No. 550 of 1988-89 was filed by the pre-emptees and that notice of the same was not served on the pre-emptor and pre-emptee as well as on the other co-sharers of the holding and thus as there was no separation of holding the High Court Division was in error in reversing the judgment and order of the trial Court allowing pre-emption on the finding that pre-emptor is a co-sharer. It may be mentioned in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1991 High Court Division reversed judgment of the trial Court on the sole ground that the land sought to be pre-empted is within the municipality and consequently, being nonagricultural land pre-emption application filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not maintainable. 

 23. The learned Counsel for the respondent in support of his contention that pre-emptor was not entitled to the relief sought for since there was separation of the jama and consequent thereupon new khatians were opened and rent was paid and thus fact of separation of jama being a concluded one or, in other words, there was ceasing of co-sharership the High Court Division was quite legal in reversing the judgment of the trial Court allowing preemption has referred to the case of Md Khairullah Bhuiyan vs. Haji Nurul Alam Chowdhury reported in 35 DLR (AD) 338 wherein it has been observed "The term 'separation' is not a legal term like amalgamation" or 'subdivision’; it is not used in section 116 or 117, but nevertheless, it denotes, in general sense, separation of a share from a joint tenancy, and, as such, 'separation' necessarily means subdivision of a joint tenancy and falls under, and is governed by clause (c) of section 117. Effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all Co-sharers who, after separation, cease to be co-sharers of the original holding and the case of Fatema Bibi vs Sree Manik Lal Somaddar reported in 50 DLR (AD) 97 and also has referred to the case of SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 wherein this Division noticed a Full Bench of the Dhaka High Court had held by majority decision that the two terms that 'nonagricultural land' and 'holding' are synonymous carrying the same meaning, but this Division held 'nonagricultural land' used in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is not synonymous with the word 'holding' as used in SAT Act. The decision in the case reported in 50 DLR (AD) 97 in the background of the facts and circumstances as well as point came up consideration is an authority for the case therein decided. We have already found that there was no legal separation of jama or holding as per provision of section 117(c) and the first proviso thereto and, as such, there was no ceasing of co-sharership either of the holding or land. 

 24. In reply to the aforesaid contention, the learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is available to one or more co-sharer tenants of nonagricultural land in case of transfer of a portion or share of the non-agricultural land. It can hardly be disputed that pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is available to one or more co-sharer tenants of non-agricultural land when a portion or share of the non-agricultural land is transferred to a stranger, or, in other words, who is not a co-sharer of the land so transferred. The submission so made in the background of the language of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is of merit since the provision of said section of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act is explicit to the extent that for raising claim of pre-emption under the said provision the pre-emptor shall have to be co-sharer of the land transferred. 

 26. The learned Counsel for the pre-emptee-respondents also submitted since sufficient time had passed from the time of filing the Miscellaneous Cases upon mentioning wrong provision of law and by such passage of time right has accrued to the pre-emptees, as such, at this stage of the matter upon resorting to the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act relief sought by way of pre-emption will not be an equitable and justifiable one since in case of allowing the pre-emption the pre-emptees will be deprived of their vested right and in support of the aforesaid submission has referred to the case of Abdur Rabban vs Aminul Hoque Sowdagar and another reported in 43 DLR (AD) 19 wherein it has been observed with the passage of time, question of limitation and accrual of vested rights step in and the High Court Division correctly rejected the application for amendment of the plaint. It may be observed the aforesaid observation has been made in the background of the facts and circumstances of the said case and the facts and circumstances which were present in the aforesaid case are absent in the instant case since relief in the light of the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act was very much available to the pre-emptor from the very date of filing of the petition seeking pre-emption. The learned Counsel has also referred to the case of Ahmed Hossain and others vs. Basharat Ali and others reported in 32 DLR (AD) 54 wherein it has been observed "A citizen's right to deal with his property freely, in view of the special statutory provision, bears a clog, that is, subject to right of pre-emption. The statutory provision providing such a right curtailing owner's right to deal with property must be construed very strictly". It is true that in considering the prayer for pre-emption Court is to construe strictly the provision of law as to right of pre-emption. In the instant case from the material on record it is clearly seen that pre-emptor is entitled to the relief sought, but the same has been dis-allowed by the High Court Division on mere technicality in that in the application seeking pre-emption provision of law which was mentioned was not the one which ought to have been mentioned as well as upon contradictory finding as to separation of holding. We have already observed that in a situation of the first category if the Court is satisfied that the relief sought is available then because of mis-description of law in the cause title the relief should not be denied, rather Court is required to grant the relief. The second category is not legally sustainable.

Ramzan Mia and others
Vs.
Idu Mia and others
with
Idu Mia and others
Vs.
Raman Mia and others
full_judgment:
3. Plaintiffs' case in title suit no.37 of 1985 is that Abdul Gani Khalifa was the original owner of the suit land on whose death, Sk. Jummon, Mohiuddin, Idu, Karim, Joygun Bibi and Belaton Bibi became the owners of the suit land. The said Abdul Gani Khalifa settled the suit land in favour of Abdul Hakim, the predecessor of the plaintiffs on yearly rental basis, who constructed a dwelling house on the suit land. After the death of Abdul Gani Khalifa, Abdul Hakim executed a kabuliyat in Chaitra, 1348 B.S. in favour of said Sk. Jummon and others for a period of 11 years. Abdul Hakim mutated his name in the Municipal holding, paid rent to the Municipality and also paid rent to the Government and continued such possession till the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, came into operation. In 1955 Abdul Hakim died and the plaintiffs continue such possession as of right. On 8.2.84, the defendants served a. notice upon them under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act demanding them to vacate possession of the suit land, which cast cloud in their title in the suit land. 

 8. It is admitted by the parties that Abdul Gani Khalifa was the original owner of the suit land who granted settlement of the suit land in favour of Abdul Hakim. It is also admitted fact that after the death of Abdul Gani Khalifa, Abdul Hakim executed a registered kabuliyat on 8th Chaitra, 1348 B. S. in favour of Sk. Jummon and others binding himself as tenant to pay yearly rent of Tk.3/= for 11 years in respect of the suit land. In the plaint there is positive averments that Abdul Hakim took settlement of the suit land and .thereafter he raised constructions in the suit land. In the written statement, the defendants have not denied the said facts, rather in paragraph 13(kha), they have admitted that Abdul Hakim gave lease of the land and not the premises with land. In such admitted position of the case, there is no dispute that Abdul Gani Khalifa gave lease of non-agricultural land to Abdul Hakim and the plaintiffs Predecessor Abdul Hakim was non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of Sub-section(5) of Section 2 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, which provides: 

 In the plaint there is clear averment to the effect that the land was settled in favour of Abdul Hakim by Abdul Gani Khalifa. On a perusal of the said Kabuliyat ext 2, there is no dispute that the plaintiffs' predecessor was given "Miras settlement" of non-agricultural land for 11 years from before 22.3.42. Before the expiry of said period of 11 years, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force on 20th October 1949. It is an admitted fact that the "Miras settlement" of the suit land was granted at an annual rental of Tk.3/-. 

 10. The tenancy of Abdul Hakim was created under the provisions of the Bengal Non Agricultural Tenancy (Temporary Provisions) Act 1940, which tenancy was neither heritable nor transferable. The said Act, 1940 was repealed on 20.10.49 and the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force on and from that date. Though the defendants claim that the plaintiffs surrendered possession, but they failed to prove such claim, rather it has been established from the pleadings as well as from the evidence on record that from before the date of execution of the kubutiyat, ext-2. Abdul Hakim had been in possession of the suit land in the same capacity for more than 12 years. Rights of a tenant of Non-Agricultural land were recognised under section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, the relevant provision runs thus:- 

 (2) if the non-agricultural land comprised in any tenancy which has been or is created after the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act; 1882 (IV of 1882), has been held for a period of not less than twelve years without any lease in writing, or 

 (i) the tenant holding the non-agricultural land comprised in such tenancy shall not be ejected by his landlord from such land except on the ground that he has used such land in a manner which renders it unfit for use for any of the purposes specified in section 4; 

 (ii) subject to the provisions of section 91 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, (E.B. Act XXVIII of 1951), the interest of the tenant in the non-agricultural land comprised in such tenancy shall, in the case where such tenant dies intestate in respect of such interest, be transmitted by inheritance in the same manner as his other immovable property. 

 11. In view of the nature of settlement as given to Abdul Hakim "Mirash Bandubasta" of the suit land, followed by continuous possession over 12 years, by raising constructions such settlement, falls into one such class under section 7(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. The tenancy in question was created prior to 22.3.42 which continued on 20.10.49 when Act XXIII of 1949 came into force and in view of section 89A of the said Act, the plaintiffs acquired an interest to continue such possession as of right which is protected from eviction. The interest of Abdul Hakim in the suit land in such tenancy has been transmitted by inheritance to the plaintiffs on the death of Abdul Hakim under clause (II) of sub-section (5) of Section 7. 

 13. The Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was amended by Ordinance No. IX of 1967, wherein certain chapters and sections of the said Act were repealed and section 26A was inserted prohibiting sub-letting of tenancy, which provides:- 

 "26A(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant shall sub-let the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms or conditions whatsoever. 

 (2) If any tenancy or any part of a tenancy is sub-let, in contravention of the provision of sub-section(1), the interest of the non-agricultural tenant in the tenancy or in that part of the tenancy, as the case may be, shall be extinguished, and the tenancy or the part of the tenancy shall vest in the Government from the date of such sub-letting free from all encumbrances. 

 " This provision is almost similar to section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The intention of the legislature in inserting this provision and deletion of certain provisions is clear. The rights of the landlord of non-agricultural land which they had, even after the acquisition of rent receiving interest has been curtailed, on and from the date of promulgation of ordinance No. IX of 1967. There cannot be any new lease of non-agricultural land from the date of promulgation of the said ordinance. The expression "subletting" connotes the creation of a sub-ordinate tenancy or under raiyat, under which the sub-lessee would but for a special contract be liable to pay rent for that land to a person other than the Government. The purpose of inserting this section appears to be that since after the acquisition of the interest of rent receivers by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the rent receivers were themselves to retain certain classes of retainable khas land as tenants directly under the Government, they should not be allowed to create further sub-tenancies under them. I am therefore, of the view that the plaintiffs status became tenants under th6 Government after section 26A, came into force. Considering this aspect of the matter, Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan finds difficult to oppose the rule. He however, feebly argues that the court of appeal below was justified in dismissing the suit. 

 15. The court of appeal below misconstrued Ext. 2, the kabuliyat and held that the said deed being an unilateral deed," Abdul Hakim was a lessee under the defendants and not tenant in the suit land and that as no bilateral lease deed was executed, the said kabuliyat is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. The court of appeal below further held that Abdul Hakim was not a yearly tenant, who acquired no status as "tenant" under the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act. The court of appeal below totally misread ext.2 wherein there is specific recitals to the effect that the tenancy would be heritable, which was created at a yearly rental of Tk.3/=. The court of appeal below also did not consider section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, under which provision if the landlord allows the tenant to erect pucca structures in the tenanted land such tenancy will be heritable. It may be pointed out here that Abdul Hakim raised construction in the suit land is not disputed by the defendants. In view of such facts, though the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendants, I am of the opinion that such record will not stand on the way in getting a decree by the plaintiffs in the suit since the plaintiffs have acquired a heritable, non-eject able right in the suit land particularly when the said S.A. record which was prepared after 1960, after the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force. I am further of the view that the plaintiffs have acquired a right which cannot be said anything less than title in the suit land. The court of appeal below upon misconstruction of Ext. 2, the Kabuliyat held that Abdul Hakim was given lease of the suit land by Kabuliyat ext.2 which is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. This decision of the court of appeal below is an error occasioning failure of justice In that view of the matter, the learned Assistant Judge was justified in finding title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and has rightly decreed the suit.

parties:
Kajemuddin Miah (Md) ------ Petitioner
vs
Bangladesh and other ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
3. The petitioner has given a short background of the law relating to diluvion land alluvion of lands By the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act No. XXVIII of 1951) the rent-receivers intervening between the Government and the actual occupants of the said land were abolished and such occupants became tenants directly under the Government, subject to a ceiling as to the maximum area of land which a tenant could hold. No substantial charge with regard to this law as to accretion or reformation in situ was brought about by this enactment excepting the law of accretion (which was so long regulated by the provisions of Bengal Regulation XXI of 1825) was made in section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The provisions relating to abatement of rent due to diluvion of some land of the tenancy and subsistence of the tenant's title in respect of such land, similar to those contained in section 86(A) of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 provides for abatement of rent on account of diluvion and re-entry into lands which re-appear, Time to time the law relating to the tenant's fight on his diluviated land were passed. On 13-7-1994 the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Act, 1994 (Act No. 15 of 1994) was promulgated substituting in place of the old section 86 with regard to abatement of rent on account of diluvion and determination of right in land reappearing on account of alluvion. By the said Act the right, title and interest of the original tenant or his successor-in-interest would subsist in the lands of a holding or portion thereof during the period of loss by diluvion if such lands re-appeared in situ within thirty years of their loss instead of 20 years. The respondent No. 1 by the impugned order as contained in letter No ML/S-9-24/94-764/1(40) dated 29-11-1994 issued to all the Deputy Commissioners of the districts containing guidelines for implementation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1994 and directing them to take necessary steps for processing the diluvion and reformation of land. By the said impugned order it was directed that all land already diluviated and alluviated shall vest in the Government as the said Act dated 13th July, 1994 was prospective and not retrospective. The petitioner is aggrieved by the circular because it is not in accordance with the State Acquisition and Tenancy (amendment) Act of 1994 and by the said circular his subsisting right on the lands diluviated in 1991 and 1992 in the district of Faridpur and in Dohar Police Station, District Dhaka has been taken away, and is therefore, constrained to file this writ petition challenging the validity of the impugned order (Annexure 'D'). 

 4. The question before us is, whether the petitioners right on his lands diluviated in 1991 and 1992 subsists under the State Acquisition and Tenancy (amendment) Act, 1994. It may be convenient to quote the relevant portion of the laws passed at different times with regard to the abatement of rent, right, title and interest of the owner on diluvion and alluvion of his land. By the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the rent was abated and the right, title and interest of the owner to diluvion subsisted for 20 years under section 86 of the said Act which reads as follows: 

 Section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was amended by President's Order No.135 of 1972. The rent abated. The right, title and interest of tenant extinguished whether loss was due to diluvion before or after commencement of said order. The relevant portion of the Bangladesh State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (4th Amendment) Order 1972 President's Order No. 135 of 1972. President Order No. 135 of 1972 by Article 2 provided as follows: 

 2. In the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB XXVIII of 1951), hereinafter referred to as the said Act for section 86 the following shall be substituted, namely: 

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successors-in-interest shall be extinguished in such lands or a portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. 

 5. By Ordinance LXI of 1975 section 86 (4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was further amended. By this amendment it provides that in making the settlement of any land vested in the Government under sub-section(3), preference would be given to the person or his successors-in-interest who, immediately before loss by diluvion, was owner of such land, subject to the condition that if the land re-appears within 20 years. 

 "In the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Act XXVIII of 1951) in section 86, for sub-section (4) the following shall be substituted, namely, "(1) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Act, in making settlement of any land vested in Government under sub section (3), preference shall be given to the person or his successor-in-interest who, immediately before loss by diluvion, was owner of such land, subject to the condition that such land or portion thereof reappears within twenty years from the date of such loss:" 

 6. Lastly, by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (Amendment) Act 1994 (Act XV of 1994) section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was again amended whereby the rent abated The right, title and interest of the owner subsists for 30 years. It provided for the right of Collector to possess the land immediately upon reappearance and publication of notice, survey, map and allotment to tenant, the amendment of section 86 by Act XV of 1994 reads as follows: 

 7. The petitioner's case is that by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1994 (Act XV of 1995) the right, title and interest in his land lost by diluvion in 1991 and 1992 has been restored and on its re-appearance he is entitled to get its allotment subject to ceiling imposed by the Act as tenant of the land. If the impugned order is not interfered with his right of ownership which has been restored by the Act, 1994 will be taken away. It is submitted that the respondent has misconstrued both the provisions of President's Order No. 135 of 1972 and the Act of 1994 which amended section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act of 1950. The respondent has illegally notified that the State Acquisition and Tenancy Amendment Act, 1994 is effective from 13th July, 1994 that the right, title and interest of all lands which had diluviated or alluviated prior to that date i.e. 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the said Act of 1994 will be applicable only to dilluvion and alluvion of land after 13th July, 1994 i.e. the Act is retrospective and not re-prospective. It may be convenient to quote the impugned order Annexure 'D' to see whether it has been passed in accordance with law. 

 The State Acquisition & Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1994 

 8. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents has defended the impugned order as being in accordance with law. He argued that the Act of 1994 was not retrospective as was specifically provided in President's Order 135 of 1972. Because if was not made re-Prospective the lands which had diluviated and alluviated prior to 13th July, 1994 would be recorded in Khas Khatian. He particularly relied on the amendment made to section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 by which the right, title and interest of the land vested in the Government. He argued since the right, title and interest of the tenant extinguished by diluvion under President's Order No. 135 of 1972 the right, title and interest vested with the Government. As such, the right of the Government could not be substituted under sub-section (2) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 as amended by Act (XV of 1994,) because it was not given retrospective effect. The right, title and interest in land which vested in the Government on diluvion by amendment of the Act under President's Order No. 135 of 1972 was not taken away, The learned Deputy Attorney-General has submitted that the land vested absolutely in the Government at point of diluvion under the President's Order 1972. In this connection we may refer to the amendment made by the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 in respect of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 with regard to abatement of rent by diluvion and extinguishment of right, title and interest of the tenant thereto. Sub-section (2) of Ordinance 2 of the Order relates to the extinguishment of the right, title and interest of the tenant by diluvion. This sub-section does not say that on diluvion the tenant's right, title and interest shall vest in the government, Clause 3 of Article 2 of the said Order says about vesting in the Government and this clause (3) says all lands lost by diluvion under sub-section (2) which re-appeared before the date of commencement of the said order but in respect of which the right of the tenant whose land was lost on his successors-in-interest to re- possession was not recognised or declared by a competent authority or court under any law for the time being in force and also all lands, so lost by diluvion under the said sub-section, which may re-appear on or after the said date shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances and shall be at its disposal (our emphasis) It is clear from this clause 3 that although by clause 2 of the article the right, title and interest of the tenant is extinguished on diluvion the right, title and interest will vest in the Government in respect of such diluviated land on its re-appearance. Therefore, we are not in agreement with the statement made by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the diluviated land vest absolutely in the Government at the point of diluvion. The Government can claim title and interest in the land diluviated after re-appearance. It cannot claim vesting under the said order while the land remains diliuviated By sub-section (2) of section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by Act XV of 1994 the right, title and interest of the original tenant or his successors-in-interest shall subsist in the lands of a holding on operation thereof during the period of loss by diluvion if such lands re-appear in situ within thirty years of their loss It would only follow that the land which were in diluvion prior to 13th July, 1994 the right of the original tenant or his successors in those lands would continue if the land re-appear in situ within 30 years. The Government can only claim such of these lands in diluvion which had re-appeared prior to 13th July, 1994 under the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 but cannot claim such right in respect of lands which is still is diluvion. Therefore, the impugned order in respect of land which re-appeared (alluviated) prior to 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the Act XV of 1994 was not applicable to such lands. We find that the impugned order 'Annexure D' to the extent giving a direction that all lands diluviated prior to 13th July, 1994 will vest in the Government and that the Act XV of 1994 was not applicable to such lands in diluvion to be illegal and without lawful authority.

parties:
Syed Sad Ali ------ Petitioner
vs
Bidhan Chandra Dev and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The case of the pre-emptor petitioner Syed Sad Ali, in short, is that he instituted a case for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act being Preemption case No. 4 of 1987 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Moulavibazar contending, inter alia, that the case property (shop) along with other lands belonged to the. predecessor in interest of proforma opposite parties Nos. 7-20; out of the aforesaid reported a quantum of land measuring 0.07 acres was transferred by registered kabala dated 4-9-83 to the predecessor-in-interest of opposite party Nos. 10-12 namely, Azadur Rahman, Syed Sad Ali and his full brothers namely, opposite party Nos. 4-6 and ever since the petitioner and his brothers (opposite party Nos. 4-6) have been owning and possessing the same and after their purchase they completed the construction work of the shop which at the relevant time was under construction; that the case land is a shop of the pre-emptor petitioner which he acquired earlier by purchase from opposite party Nos. 7 and 8 M Serajul Islam and Md Nazrul Islam. The said Serajul Islam and Nurul Islam transferred the case shop to opposite party No. 1 Bidhan Chandra Dev on the 1st of Ashar 1392 BS corresponding to 16-6-85 and the said deed was registered on 11-9-86 without serving any notice to the petitioner who is a co-sharer to the holding; that having been aware of the transfer the petitioner procured a certified copy of the kabala dated 11-9-86 and tiled an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 4. The learned Subordinate Judge, Moulavibazar by judgment and order dated 29-11-93 allowed pre-emption holding, inter alia, that admittedly the pre-emptor petitioner is a co-sharer by purchase to the holding and the pre-emptee opposite party is a stranger to the said holding and that the case having been filed within the statutory period of limitation the petitioner is entitled to have the case land pre-empted. Having felt aggrieved by the said judgment and order the pre-emptee preferred Misc. Appeal No. 3 of 1994 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Moulavibazar which on transfer was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, Molavibazar who by the impugned judgment and order dated 23-9-95 allowed the appeal by setting aside the judgment and order of the trial Court holding, inter alia, that the pre-emptor petitioner Syed Sad Ali though a co-sharer of the holding he is not a co-sharer of the land (shop) transferred and, as such, he is not entitled to pre-empt the case shop. The learned Subordinate Judge relied on a decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 in the case of SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and others in which case their Lordships departed from the view taken in the case of Manindra Chandra Ghose vs Mujibul Islam reported in 12 DLR 785 which view was endorsed by Mr Sekander Ali, J and concurred by Mr Murshed, J holding that the petitioner appellant (pre-emptor) being co-sharer in the tenancy were also co-sharer in the land which is the subject matter of the pre-emption case. In the 35 DLR case Ruhul Islam, J held according to Hasan, J the words non-agricultural land means a piece of land in joint possession and enjoyment without partition which may form a tenancy or a portion of a tenancy. The learned Judge explained that this interpretation will not throw the land open to unlimited number of persons but to persons who are co-sharer tenants under the same landlord in respect of the undivided land, though such co-sharer tenants may be co-sharer tenants of the tenancy. In the instant case it is found that the case land is demarcated by a boundary wall as per admission made by PW 1 the pre-emptor Syed Sad All himself. The joma remained unaltered. No separate holding was opened by any of the co-sharers and although allegedly there was an amicable partition between the co-sharer that did not ipso facto split up the joma. 

 5. In the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act were elaborately discussed. The expression co-sharer in the land transferred used in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was held to be much narrower and limited in its scope and extent. Under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor has to be a co-sharer not only in the holding transferred but also a co-sharer in the land transferred. In the instant case the pre-emptor though a co sharer in the joma was not a co-sharer in the land (i.e. shop) transferred to opposite party No.1 Bidhan Chandra Dev because of the fact that the shop transferred is well demarcated as per admission of the pre-emptor himself. 

 6. Syed Dastagir Hossain, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the case reported in 35 DLR has no manner of application in the instant case firstly, because there being no partition by metes and bounds between the co-sharer and the holding not having been split up, the pre-emptor did not cease to be a co-sharer of the holding and that the expression co-sharer in the tenancy and co-sharer in the land transferred are synonymous and in that view of the matter the petitioner is competent to maintain this petition for pre-emption as he has filed the application for pre-emption within the prescribed time in compliance with all the legal formalities required under the law. Mr Hossain further submits that there has been no splitting up of the joma in accordance with the provision of section 117(1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On the other hand Mr Nirmalendu Dev, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee opposite party submits that the appellate Court has pronounced a correct judgment by setting aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge allowing pre-emption. In support of his contention Mr. Deb has referred to the provision of section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act with special emphasis on the expression "co-sharer to the land transferred" unlike the expression appearing in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which is a co-sharer in the tenancy or holding. Mr Deb relied on the decision in the case of SM Basiruddin Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another reported' in 35 DLR SAD) 230 wherein their Lordships took different view from that taken by Sekander Ali, J and concurred by Murshed, J that the expression co-sharer in the holding and co-sharer in the land transferred is synonymous but in the case reported in 35 DLR their Lordships held that the legislature consciously used the expression non-agricultural land in section 24 instead of using the expression tenancy or holding as used in section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This was done with the purpose of limiting the number of applicants by making it available only to the co-sharers of the land and not of the tenancy, so that distribution among all the co-sharers may not make the land unfit for the purpose for which it was taken and it was observed by Ruhul Islam J. So, according to me, the words non-agricultural land means a piece of land in joint possession and enjoyment without partition which may form the tenancy or a portion of tenancy. This interpretation will not throw the land open to the unlimited number of persons but to persons who are co sharer tenants under the same landlord in respect of undivided land though such co-sharer tenants may be co-sharer tenants of the tenancy. 

 7. In the reported case, the case land appertaining to a permanent tenure stood recorded in CS. Khatian No. 214 under Mouza Shahar Dacca, owned by Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani, Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca for partition and by the decree passed in the suit Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik got one-third ((1/3)) share while Rangubala got the remaining two-tbird ((2/3)) share. One Nafisa Khatun by purchasing the interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik became co-sharer of Rangubala. Rangubala created a lease in respect of the 2/3rd share for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 in favour of Ayesha Khatun. Respondent No. 2 Nafisa Khatun sold her interest to respondent No. 1 by registered sale deed dated 18-4-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered sale deed dated 10-9-73. Against this sale respondent No. 1 filed the application for pre-emption. The appellant contested the case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 was not a co-sharer in the tenancy, because the land of the tenure was partitioned by the decree in Title suit No. 126 of 1946 between Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani; and that a separate tenancy was created in favour of Ayesha Khatun by Rangubala by granting permanent lease for 99 years reserving for herself annual rent of Taka 1/-; and that Ayesha Khatun paid rent of Taka 1.00 to the lessor Rangubala till the rent receiving interest was acquired by the Government. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed pre-emption against the appellant and the appeal was dismissed. Thereafter the appellant moved the High Court Division in revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and being unsuccessful moved this court and obtained leave from this court to appeal from the judgment of the High Court Division and their Lordships having considered the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act allowed the appeal with costs and the order allowing pre-emption was set aside and thus the application for pre-emption was dismissed.

caseno: Second Appeal No.468 of 1974 with Civil Rule No. 401(s) of 1991
parties:
Mander Sheikh and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Sultan Ali Molla and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Relevant facts are summarized as follows: Plaintiffs filed the aforesaid title suit for a declaration of title and confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of khas possession of the suit land on the allegations that they as benamdar of the judgment-debtors auction purchased a jote which included 5.33 acres of tenanted land under Khatian No. 99 standing in the names of Panchy Sheikh, Kamaruddin Sheikh i.e. the father of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and Ramjan i.e. the father of the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 in Rent Execution Case No.1035 of 1930 arising out of Rent Suit No. 607 of 1930 on 20-1-1931 and took delivery of possession thereof on 2-5-1931 after having annulled the encumbrance namely, the said under-tenancy by service of notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Father of defendant Nos.1 and 2 late Kamaruddin Sheikh having admitted annulment of the said under-tenancy took fresh settlement of some of the said under tenancy by executing kabuliayat. But due to mistake 2.30 acres of land of the said under-tenancy was wrongly recorded in the names of the defendants during SA settlement and by taking advantage of such wrong recording the defendants threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession from the said land on 21st Chaitra 1373 BS. Hence the plaintiffs were constrained to file the suit. 

 3. Defendants contested the suit by filing a written statement asserting that their under-tenancy was never annulled and they were all along in possession. The defendants denied that late Kamaruddin or Samajuddin ever executed any Kabuliyat admitting annulment of their under tenancy or taking over Khas possession of the same by the plaintiffs stating that if there was any Kabuliyat by Kamaruddin that must have been manufactured for the purpose of the case. The defendants further asserted that since there was no annulment of the under-tenancy in question the suit land was recorded in the name of the predecessors-in-interest of the defendants during the petty and revisional settlement that took place after the purported auction-sale. Subsequently the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendants during the SA settlement. 

 4. Both the trial Court as well as the first appellate Court below decreed the suit on the finding that the plaintiffs succeeded in proving the service of notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act annulling the under-tenancy in question and that they were in possession of the suit land holding that although the plaintiffs could not prove the service of notice of annulment of the under-tenancy in question in terms of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act by producing any paper, but admission of late Kamaruddin i.e. the father of the defendants Nos.1 and 2 and Mominuddin i.e. the defendant No.6 (not an under-tenant) and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 sufficiently proved service of notice. Being aggrieved the defendants preferred this Second Appeal. 

 5. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, the learned Advocate for the appellants, submits that both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below earred in law in holding that the plaintiffs as auction-purchasers annulled the under tenancy in question by serving notice on the under-tenants in terms of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, although they (plaintiffs) failed to prove the service of notice as required in law. Learned Advocate also submits that the courts below also erred in law in failing to appreciate that since the plaintiffs as benamdars of the judgment-debtors were debarred under section 173 of the Bengal Tenancy Act from auction purchasing the suit land no notice under section 167 of the Act was served by the Court which held the auction-sale. 

 7. The moot question requiring determination is whether the respondents succeeded in proving the annulment of the encumbrance, namely, the under-tenure of the appellants, by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The question whether notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act was duly served in this case is a question of law. Hence the concurrent finding of the Courts below on this point is liable to be interfered with by this Court in case such finding is bad in law. 

 8. A sale in execution of a rent decree will ipso facto cancel an encumbrance. Until an encumbrance namely, the under-tenancy, as in this case, is annulled by notice as required under section 167 of the Bengali Tenancy Act the under-tenancy subsists vide AIR (1929) Cal. 392. If an auction-purchaser in a rent sale desires to exercise his power of annulment of any encumbrance he is required to strictly comply with the requirements of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act as regards service of notice and such notice must be served within one year from the date of confirmation of sale or from the date of knowledge thereof whichever date is later. 

 10. Purchaser is under obligation to show that the notice under section 167 has been served in the manner provided under this section, namely, that he made an application to the Court or the revenue officer in writing requesting him to serve on the encumbrancer a notice declaring that the encumbrance is annulled. Notice of annulment is to be served in the manner provided for the service of summons under Order 5, rules 11 and 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure as required by the Rules framed by the Government under sections 189 and 190 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The case of Ananda Gopal vs Nafar Chandra reported in 18 CWN (PC) 259 is an authority on this point. The purchaser must prove service of notice by the production of the person who served it or by any other means recognized by law vide 7 CLJ 262. Even the entries in the order-sheet of the Court which caused the notice to be served on the application of the purchaser are not the prime evidence against the encumbrance that the notice was served. 

 11. In the instant case, respondents have admittedly failed to produce any paper in support of service of notice under section 167of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The finding of the Courts below, particularly the appellate Court below that service of such notice as well as possession of the suit land by the respondents have been proved by admission of the appellant Nos.1 and 2 and their father late Kamaruddin and also by admission of defendant No.6 Mominuddin is erratic and perverse being contrary to law and evidence. The decision reported in 37 DLR 126 is not applicable in the present case as the facts are distinguishable. The defendant No.6 is not an under-tenant but apparently a camp-follower of the respondents and accordingly, he deposed as PW 2 stating in his evidence that notice was served in his presence. Such admission by defendant No.6 cannot be a proof of service of notice as contemplated under Section 167. 

 12. Respondents are admittedly the benamdars of the judgment-debtors. Section 173 of the Bengal Tenancy Act debars the judgment-debtors as well as their benamdars from purchasing any defaulting tenure. A judgment debtor or his benamdar purchasing the defaulting tenure, even if the sale is allowed to stand, is not entitled to annul the encumbrance. The case of Fakir Chander Dutt and others vs Ram Kumar Chatterji reported in 8 CWN (PC) 721 is referred to in this connection. Since the service of notice under section 167 in this case has not been proved as proscribed by law the encumbrance in question still subsists. Accordingly, the finding of possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs by the Courts below is not sustainable in law. Therefore, the contention that the plaintiffs have acquired title by adverse possession is not acceptable.

parties:
Ramisunnessa Bibi and another ------ Petitioners
VS
Soleman Molla and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
By this Rule the defendants opposite parties were called upon to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 16.6.92 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Bagerhat in Title Suit No. 355 of 1969 dismissing the same should not be set aside. 

 2. The short facts giving rise to this Rule are, that the plaintiff petitioner filed the said suit for ejectment of the defendants opposite parties on the ground that Sirajuddin Mollah, the predecessor of the said opposite parties, was, monthly tenant under them and he became defaulter and violated the terms of tenancy agreement.
