The case of the petitioners is that they purchased the suit lands along with other lands and building from Rashik Lal Dey, one of the co-sharers of the property belonging to a partnership firm known as Laxmi Bhandar, by a registered deed dated 23.5.63. The original defendant Sirajuddin Mollah became a tenant under them who by admitting the petitioners as the title holder and his landlords executed tenancy agreement and paid rent by obtaining rent receipt after putting his thumb impression on the counterfoil of the same from the month of Falgoon 1368 BS to Jaistha 1370 BS at the previous rate fixed by the vendor of the petitioners. After some time the said defendant tenant stopped paying rent and filed a Title Suit No. 105 of 1968 and obtained an order of injunction and against the said order of temporary injunction the petitioners filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 100 of 1968 and the appellate Court came to the finding that the petitioners acquired a right in the suit property and directed the defendant to pay rent to the petitioners. The further case of the plaintiffs petitioners was that the story of defendant's purchase of the suit land from one Shorat Babu and his brother Surendra Nath Biswas by a kabala dated 8.6.70 is false and collusive. The defendant now being defaulter tenants are liable to be ejected and hence the suit. 

 3. The original defendant No. 1 Sirajuddin Mollah, died after filing the written statement and thereafter his substituted heirs and the minors who are being represented by the court's guardian contested the suit by filing separate written statements-and denied the allegations of the plaint. Their main contention was that their predecessor Sirajuddin Mollah was never a tenant under the plaintiffs and it was also denied that their predecessor did not obtain any rent receipts by putting his LTI on the said counter for. It was further contended that the original defendant Sirajuddin filed Title Suit No.105 of 1968 against the plaintiff petitioners and obtained a temporary injunction and the plaintiffs petitioners preferred a Miscellaneous appeal against the said order of injunction and the said appeal was dismissed. It was further contended that the suit property along with other lands belonged to a joint business firm known as Laxmi Bhandar. About 40/50 years back the said original defendant was inducted as tenant in the suit property by the person in charge of the said property. Thereafter Nalini Kanti Biswas, son of Ashutush Biswas, having acquired the suit property measuring 18-1/2 decimals by way of amicable partition amongst his brother and other co-sharers by a kabala dated 27.7.69 and delivered possession to him and since then the defendants acquired title. It was further contended that one Abdul Majid Advocate was appointed a receiver in connection with different suits as between the share holder of the said firm named Laxmi Bhandar. The said Abdul Mojid used to realise the house rent from the said predecessor of the defendants. It was alleged that the husband of the plaintiff No. 1 in collusion with the said Abdul Mojid might have fabricated the papers by obtaining the impression of Sirajuddin taking advantage of his being an illiterate and simple person. The alleged thumb impression might have been taken by deceitful means and for which the said opposite parties are not bound by it. It was contended that the movable and immovable properties by Laxmi Bhandar were not partitioned by metes and bounds at any time and, as such, one of the share holders of the said business firm named Santosh Kumar Howlader filed partition suit No. 38 of 1972 at Khulna which is still pending. The defendants are possessing some portion of the suit land by themselves and other portion was let out to tenants and thereby they possessed the entire suit property as owners and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 6. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that Sirajuddin Mollah, the predecessor of the defendants opposite parties, was a monthly tenant of the suit land and the building under the petitioners by executing the unregistered deed of monthly tenancy agreement (Bhara Nama) Ext. 2 dated 1st. Ashar 1370 BS and on payment of rent by Ext. 1 the counterfoil of the rent receipt. In order to prove the said tenancy, the LTI of Late Sirajuddin appearing in those documents were compared by the hand writing expert who found those LTI tallied with specimen LTI obtained for the proof in the said title suit No. 41 of 1972 as renumbered from the said original Title suit No.105 of 1968 filed by the said original defendant against the petitioners for temporary injunction. In view of proof of tenancy of said Sirajuddin, the present defendants opposite parties are estopped from denying the monthly tenancy of Sirajuddin under the provisions of section 116 of the Evidence Act, the learned Assistant Judge having not applied his judicial mind in to considering that the plaintiffs petitioners proved the tenancy of the said original defendants, committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision causing failure of justice. 

 7. Secondly, it has been submitted by Mr. Rahim that once a tenant is always a tenant and tenancy being heritable the defendants opposite parties are also the tenants under the plaintiffs since the plaintiffs acquired their title in the suit property by virtue of the registered kabala of 1963 and the admission said Sirajuddin being a tenant under the plaintiffs as proved by the recital of Bharanama Ext. 2 is binding upon the defendant opposite parties, as such, the learned court below committed error of law in not considering the said Ext. 2 in its proper perspective which has resulted in an error in decision causing failure of justice. 

 8. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the plaintiffs' kabala is of 1963 and the defendants' kabala is of dated 27.7.69 in respect of the same property clearly shows that the defendant till before their kabala of 1969 for about 6 years did not deny nor challenge the plaintiffs' right and title as landlord of the suit premises and they created kabala after the institution of the suit on 22.5.69 and the defendants' kabala being of a later date is hit by the doctrine of lis pendens under section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act and the learned Assistant Judge committed error of law in not holding that the plaintiffs had prima facie title in view of the evidence on record and admission of the original defendant that the plaintiffs were his landlord and this has resulted in an error in the decision causing failure of justice. 

 9. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has further submitted that the heirs of the original tenant Sirajuddin are estopped from setting up an independent title by the alleged subsequent purchase of the suit property after the filing of the plaintiffs' suit and the learned Assistant Judge thus failed to consider that suit for determination of tenancy was filed two months before the alleged title of the defendants in respect to the suit land and, as such, the plaintiffs were not obliged to file a suit for declaration of their title and recovery of possession and it is good enough for them to file a mere suit for establishment of tenancy right of said Sirajuddin, the predecessor of the defendants opposite parties at that time and, as such, the learned Assistant Judge failed to consider the aspect of the matter and thereby committed error of law in finding that the plaintiffs' suit is not maintainable, is wrong and the same cannot be sustained in law. It has been further submitted by Mr. Rahim that the learned court below has travelled beyond the scope of the instant suit and unnecessarily embarked upon investigation on the question of title of the defendant without confining himself to the issue as to whether the plaintiff has been able to establish the tenancy of the defendants in the suit property. 

 10. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendants opposite parties, on the other hand, contended that the predecessor of the defendants was never a tenant under the petitioners and both the parties claim the self same property by registered kabalas and in such view of the matter plaintiffs' suit for ejectment of the tenant without a suit for declaration of title is not maintainable and the learned court below rightly passed the impugned judgment and decree upon proper consideration of materials on record. It has been further submitted by Mr. Majumder that the alleged execution of Ext.2 (Bharanama) by Sirajuddin and the thumb impressions appearing therein and in the alleged counterfoil of the rent receipt are fabricated and those were obtained by fraudulent means and, as such the defendants are not bound by the recital of the said Ext. 2. Mr. Majumder has further submitted that the original defendant Sirajuddin Molla denied his being a monthly tenant under the plaintiffs and alleged that a fraud has been practised in the matter of obtaining his left hand thumb impressions in the said Exts. 1 and 2 and thereafter filed Title Suit No. 105 of 1968 against the plaintiffs and obtained an order of injunction and the said suit being re-numbered as Title Suit No. 41 of 1972 is still pending and, as such, the present opposite parties cannot be estopped from asserting their own right and title in the suit property and the learned Assistant Judge has rightly observed that there exists a doubt regarding the validity of the said documents Exts. 1 and 2. 

 11. From the above submissions of the learned Advocates of the parties the points that call for determination in this case is whether the original defendant Sirajuddin Mollah was a tenant under the plaintiffs and secondly, whether the plaintiffs' suit as framed is maintainable. 

 12. I have heard the learned Advocates at length and perused the records. The whole argument of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties was that once a tenancy is denied by a tenant claiming an independent title in the self same property, the petitioners ought to have filed a full fledged suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. Repelling the above contention, Mr. Rahim has rightly argued that parties' right is to be determined at a time when the suit is instituted or when a course of action arises. In elaborating this point Mr. Rahim has pointed out that the plaintiffs' claim in suit property by way of purchase on 29.3.63 and the original defendant who was already in the suit land as tenant of the ex-owner, executed a tenancy agreement Ext. 2 with the petitioners on and from 1st Ashar 1370 BS that is, from the year 1963, and he also paid rent for some time admitting the petitioners (plaintiffs) as his landlord. The fact remains that the original defendants had no title whatsoever at that time. 

 13. It appears from the record that plaintiff-petitioners purchased the suit land from one Rashik Lal who was one of the co-sharers of the property belonging to a partnership firm named Laxmi Bhandar. The plaintiffs claim that original defendant Sirajuddin Mollah was their tenant but subsequently the payment of rent to them and then the dispute arose between the plaintiffs and the original defendant Sirajuddin Mollah who denied the right and title of the plaintiff petitioners. The said Sirajuddin Mollah brought a Title Suit No.105 of 1968 denying the right, title of the plaintiffs and prayed for an order of injunction restraining the plaintiffs petitioners not to disturb their possession and the suit was heard and the learned court concerned granted injunction in favour of the original defendant Serajuddin Mollah. Against the said order of injunction the petitioners filed Miscellaneous Appeal and though the appeal was dismissed the court directed the said defendants to pay rent to the plaintiffs. The said Title Suit No.105 of 1968 of the defendants was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 41 of 1972 which is still pending. It further appears from the record that the plaintiffs in order to prove the tenancy of the original defendant Serajuddin Mollah, filed counterfoil of the rent receipt Ext. 1 and Bharanama Ext. 2 and also filed their documents of title Ext. 5 (Ka) and in that suit they prayed for proving the left hand thumb impression of Serajuddin Mollah appearing in the said exhibits 1 and 2 by hand writing expert and for that purpose Serajuddin Mollah gave some specimen thumb impressions in court. It appears from the report of the hand writing expert that he compared the specimen thumb impressions with his thumb impressions appearing in said exhibits 1 and 2. The hand writing expert found that the LTI in Exts. 1 and 2 tallied with the specimen thumb impressions of Serajuddin Mollah. It further appears that Serajuddin Mollah admitted the petitioners as his landlord and agreed to pay the enhanced rent of Taka 75.00 in consideration of the improvement made in the suit properties by the petitioners, Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder tried to argue that the defendants opposite parties denied the tenancy under the plaintiffs and alleged that the LTI in the said exhibits 1 and 2 have been taken by practising fraud as Serajuddin was illiterate and a man of simple nature. Be that as it may, the report of the hand writing expert was accepted without any objection and was marked as Ext. 20. But the learned court below did not at all consider this aspect in the proper perspective and came to an abrupt finding to the affect that: 

 14. This finding is wrong because there are LTIs of Serajuddin Mollah in the said agreement Ext. 2 and in the counterfoil of rent receipt Ext.1 were tallied with the specimen thumb impressions for Sirajuddin Mollah and it was neither denied by him nor the report of the hand writing expert was challenged and, as such, the monthly tenancy of Serajuddin under the plaintiffs has been proved. When the tenancy of Serajuddin was prima facie found by the court of law in the earlier suit, the said tenant became defaulter then the plaintiffs petitioners filed the instant suit for his ejectment but the said defendant having died his legal heirs that is, the present defendants opposite parties, contested the instant suit and the learned court below failed to consider that the plaintiffs claim the suit land by purchase on 25.3.63 and suit was filed on 22.5.69 for ejectment of the tenants when there was no existence of the defendants' title in the self same suit property by way of purchase from a different co-sharer on 27.7.69. It shows that the plaintiffs' suit for determination of the tenancy was filed two months before the alleged title of the defendants and, in such circumstances, I am of the opinion that plaintiffs were not obliged to file a suit for declaration, rather the defendants who ought to have filed such suit for declaration by virtue of their subsequent title in the property, but they have not done so. Accordingly, I find that the suit for ejectment filed by the plaintiffs petitioners is quite maintainable in the above facts and circumstances of the case and accordingly, I find substance in the conception of Mr. Abdur Rahim that once a tenancy has been established the tenant must vacate first and then he can claim independent title. In this connection a reference may be made to a decision cited by Mr. Rahim in the case of Hajee Abdus Sattar vs. Mahiuddin and others reported in 6 BCR(AD) 71. I have gone through the said decision and the principle enunciated therein is applicable in the instant case as their Lordships held in the following language; "The estoppel as described in this Section is known as tenant's estoppel or estoppel by contract. This estoppel is founded upon a contract between the tenant and the landlord. It provides that when a person enters into possession of immovable property as a tenant of another person then neither he nor anybody claiming through him shall be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to deny the landlord's title, however defective that title might be. This necessarily implies that in case the tenant sets up a claim of title in himself he shall first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken it." 

 16. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate of the opposite parties, made a strong emphasis on the question that there are circumstances which proved that a fraud was practised upon the predecessor of the opposite parties in the matter of obtaining his thumb impression in the said Exts. 1 and 2, It is a settled principle of law that he who alleges fraud must prove it. Mr. Mihir Kanti Majumder could not place any material before me to find that any fraud has been practised by the petitioners in obtaining the LTI of said Serajuddin appearing in the said exhibits 1 and 2. I therefore, find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate as to the allegation of fraud and find that the said Ext. 1 and Ext. 2 are genuine documents to prove the tenancy of Serajuddin and that the same were legally proved by the plaintiffs and supported by the hand writing expert. In such view of the matter, there is no cogent reason to hold the said Serajuddin Mollah was not a tenant under the plaintiffs. Since tenancy is heritable and the present defendant opposite parties being the heirs of the said original tenant they are also deemed to be the tenants under the petitioners, 

 17. It appears from the record that there are various civil litigations including a partition suit between the alleged original co-sharers of the properties of the said business firm and ending in the court of law. It is not desirable for me to go into all those disputed questions of title. 

 18. On perusal of the impugned judgment, it appears that the learned court below, instead of confining itself to the question as to whether the plaintiffs have been able to prove the tenancy right of the original tenant defendant Serajuddin Mollah and whether the instant suit as framed is maintainable or not, unnecessarily embarked upon investigating and raising question of the defendants' title, and thereby misdirected itself in properly deciding the real issue in the suit and failed to apply his judicial mind. Accordingly I find it a legal infirmity in the impugned judgment and decree and the same is liable to be set aside. 

 19. In view of the above discussion I find that plaintiffs suit is maintainable in law. As the present defendants opposite parties stepped in to the shoes of the original tenant they arc also tenants under the petitioners until they could establish their independent title in the self same property by subsequent purchase. Since the present defendant opposite parties defaulted to pay the rent to the petitioners they are also defaulters and they are liable to be evicted. In view of the proposition of law as enunciated by the Appellate Division in the aforesaid decision, the opposite parties must surrender possession to the petitioners firstly and then they may seek remedy to establish their title in the property by subsequent purchase from a different co-owner,
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed J.R. Mudassir Hussain

parties:
Mokbul Hossain Khondker ------ Petitioner 
vs.
Jaheda Khatoon ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
The petitioner Md. Mukbul Hosain Khandkar was a defendant in the said SCC Suit No. 24 of 1982 instituted by the opposite party Mst. Jahada Khatun as plaintiff for eviction of the petitioner from the suit land and for a decree for Taka 360.00 being arrear rent for the term. The case of the opposite party as plaintiff in the aforesaid suit was that she took lease of the land of dag No. 1414 consisting 28 decimals of land appertaining to khatian No. 125 of Sutrapur Mouza, Police Station Kotwali, District Bogra on. 28.11.55 by a registered deed under the care and initiative of her husband M. Rafiq Khan and constructed some stalls by wood and CI sheets and proposed to give them on rent to the people and called it Rafiq Khan Market. The defendant petitioner entered into a registered tenancy agreement with the opposite party plaintiff on 6.10.65 to be effective for 5 years from 1.11.65. It was stipulated in the tenancy agreement that the defendant petitioner would pay monthly rent in the first week of the following month. It was further stipulated that the defendant petitioner would not sub-let the premises or make any pucca construction. Later it was also agreed that if the plaintiff opposite party wished to make pucca construction she should let it be known to defendant petitioner and if such construction was undertaken the defendant petitioner would continue to remain a tenant on the same of the registered agreement. Towards the end of 1970 the plaintiffs’ husband purchased bricks worth Taka 90,000.00 and 50 cubit feet of sand and kept it in open space next to the market for construction. It was contended that defendant petitioner was habitual defaulter in payment of rent. He did not pay the rent in time and sometimes kept 2/3 month’s rent arrear and paid rent only on persuasion. The defendant paid rent till February, 1971. In 1971 the said Rafiq Khan Market was set on fire and parts of some of the stalls including that occupied by the petitioner were destroyed. The plaintiff opposite party's husband was a member of political party Muslim League and in 1971 he was Secretary of Bogra Peace Committee. He was a candidate for membership of parliament. Being afraid of his life after the liberation of Bangladesh he went into hiding at different places at different times. Taking advantages of his absence the defendant petitioner with the building materials left by the plaintiff opposite party, without approval, constructed a two-storied building which was depicted in the sketch map as No.9 on the ground floor, 9/1 on the 1st floor and 13 on the ground follow and 13/1 on the 1st floor, After a general amnesty was declared by the Government of Bangladesh in 1974 the plaintiffs husband returned to his place of residence and wanted to know from the defendant under what authority he had constructed the pucca building and demanded rent. But the defendant avoided the plaintiff on some pretext or other. The defendant being a habitual defaulter the plaintiff opposite party served notice through his lawyer under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and demanded vacant possession of the premises by 31st December, 1991 which was refused by the defendant petitioner. In the circumstances, the plaintiff opposite party was constrained to file an eviction suit under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and claimed 3 years' arrear rent. It was contended by the plaintiff opposite party that he remained busy and because of financial constraint he could not file the suit earlier. The defendant petitioner contested the suit by filing a written statement. It was, inter alia, contended by the defendant petitioner that the relationship of landlord and tenant did not exist between the plaintiff opposite party and the defendant petitioner and, therefore, the SCC Suit was not maintainable. After denying the material allegation of the plaintiff the defendant petitioner stated that the suit premises originally belonged to one Akram Hossain Tarafdar. The premises having remained vacant and fallow for a long time a market in the name of Badruddin New Market was started in the western side of the premises. After partition of the Sub-continent business in Bogra town developed and moveable shops made of tin and wood were created on both sides of the road near the suit premises. On promulgation of Martial Law in 1958 the moveable’s stalls were removed from both sides of the road. In the meantime the plaintiff claimed title over the suit premises and the shop owners approached the plaintiff to carry on their business which was allowed by the plaintiffs’ husband and accordingly, the owners of the stalls created their respective shops and carried on business. It was claimed by the defendant that the suit plot 15/14 was vacant and so he constructed a stall there and carried on cloth business. Actually the said suit plot became a market and in the beginning of October, 1965 the husband of the plaintiff demanded from the defendant and one Afzal Hossain Pramanik and other owners of the stalls for written permission to use the premises in order to avoid future complication. It was agreed that for permission to use the shops they would pay Taka 2.00 per foot as licence fee for the respective shops. Accordingly, an agreement to this effect was entered into and registered. It was stated the agreement was not written according to the agreement nor it was read out to the defendant. It was claimed that the plaintiffs’ husband managed to write the agreement according to his wishes and got it registered. It was later discovered by the defendant that the registered agreement was not a licence agreement for use but was tenancy agreement. In fact the agreement was to be a licence agreement. It was further stated that in 1969 some of the users of the stalls namely, Munsur Rahman, Zahirul Islam, Nasiruddin were purchased by the defendant. Stall No.6 was sold by defendant petitioner to defendant Muslimuddin Khondker who carried on cloth business there. Subsequently this was also purchased by the defendant and these stalls are as deposited in the map. Stalls Nos. 9 & 9/1, 13 & 13/1 belonging to one Matius Rahman were claimed to have been purchased by the defendant. These stalls were set on fire in 1971 by the Pakistan Army which were completely destroyed as a result of which the possession of the premises of the plaintiff opposite party came to end. After the emergence of Bangladesh the Government directed the defendants and others to carry on their usual business, In the meantime, the suit land was declared as abandoned property and the Management Committee of the abandoned property verbally directed the owners of the stalls to construct shops at their own costs and continue their business. Accordingly, the owners constructed shops in 1972 and have been in possession of their respective shops. In these circumstances it was stated by the defendant petitioner that the plaintiff opposite party had no right, title or interest in the suit premises. The property was abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. 

 6. It has been submitted on behalf of the petitioner that he did not accept the plaintiff as his landlord after the expiry of the agreement dated 1.1 1.65, that he has built two sets of shops on the aforesaid suit land after the original stall was gutted by fire by the Pakistan Army, that he has not accepted the plaintiff either orally or by written document as his landlord after the liberation of Bangladesh when he built the aforementioned shops. It was submitted that the original agreement having expired in November, 1970 and there being no proof of renewal the landlord and tenant relationship ended. It is also contended that the original shops taken on tenancy in 1975 having been completely destroyed by fire set by Pakistan Army in 1971 the tenancy was frustrated. It has been argued that the see Judge misconceived the provision of holding over and wrongly found relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties on misconception of aforesaid principle of law. The see Judge failed to notice that on expiry of original lease agreement and the destruction of the stall by fire there was no evidence on record to hold that the landlord accepted the rent from the defendant or asserted to his continuing in the original shop as tenant. 

 7. The plaintiff opposite party by evidence passed Ext 1 which is a registered deed of settlement signed on 19.11.55 and registered on 28.11.55. This deed of permanent settlement was made in favour of the plaintiff opposite party. Her name was recorded in Mr. RR Khatian which was proved by Ext. VI Exts.5 (d) to 5(ka) showed payment of revenue. The holding tax receipts were proved by Ext. 5 to 5(c). The defendant in his cross-examination admitted the plaintiff to be the owner of the suit premises. It is on evidence that the see court was satisfied that the plaintiff had proved his right, title and interest in the suit land. The se court then next considered whether the defendant was a tenant of the plaintiff or not. He found from Ext. 8 which is a registered lease deed dated 8.10.65 whereby the defendant by signing the same accepted the plaintiff as the owner and agreed to pay rent on the basis of the agreement. The see court was, therefore satisfied that the defendant was undoubtedly a tenant of the plaintiff. It was further found that rent receipts were issued by the defendant in favour of the plaintiff which are marked Exts.4, 4(a) 4(b) & (c). It was found from evidence that the defendant continued to pay rent to the plaintiff until February 1971. The se court was, therefore, satisfied that there could not be any question that there did not exist a landlord-tenant relationship between the plaintiff and the defendants. The next question that SC Court took up was whether the defendant petitioner was a habitual defaulter or not. It was the case of the plaintiff that the defendant continued to pay rent up to February, 1971 but did not pay the rent in time as stipulated in the agreement. After operation of Bangladesh the plaintiff went into hiding and after general amnesty was declared by the Government he returned to his home in 1974 and demanded arrear rent from the defendant which was refused. The plaintiff therefore, served notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act to deliver vacant possession of the suit premises by December, 1981 and hand over the possession of the same to the plaintiff. As the defendant did not pay the arrear rent nor vacated the premises the plaintiff filed the present suit. As a part of the arrear rent became barred by limitation, the plaintiff claimed 36 month’s rent from 1979 to 1981 at the rate of Taka 10.00 per month which is Taka 360.00. The SC Court having believed Ext. 9 which was the deed of tenancy and the rent receipt Ext. 4 it was satisfied that the suit was maintainable in its present form in the SC Court. The SC Court further held that the defendant had admitted that the plaintiff was her landlord, and thereafter the tenant could not raise question of plaintiffs’ title and for this the court relied on the case reported in 36 DLR (AD) 93. The SC Court found that it was admitted that the stall was gutted by fire when the Pakistan army set fire to the stalls in 1971. The defendants had argued that as the subject matter of the tenancy was completely destroyed the tenant-landlord relationship ended with it. However, the SC Court held that although the stall was destroyed by fire it was agreed that if the plaintiff constructed new pucca building the old tenancy would continue and the defendant would continue to pay the rent on old terms of the written agreement. Having made such an agreement the SC Court held that the defendant could say that the tenancy had come to an end because the stalls were destroyed by fire. That there was an oral agreement was stated in the plaint. In cross examination PW.2 stated that the plaintiff told him that there was an oral agreement. The SCC Judge further held that according to section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, so long as the tenant does not leave or abandon the premises after it is destroyed by fire, the relationship of landlord and tenant is not destroyed. In the instant case the defendant did not hand over the premises to the plaintiff. Thereafter the landlord-tenant relationship was not broken simply on the ground that the premises was destroyed by fire It was also found by the SC Court that the plaintiff was a Bangladeshi national and that his property could be declared abandoned under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Further, that the suit premises was an abandoned property, was not notified in the Gazette as required under law and then on the representation made by the plaintiff the relevant authority held that it was not an abandoned property. The SC Court then discussed the evidence of PW 3 who deposed that the suit premises and other stalls were constructed by the plaintiff and that the evidence of PW 3 was corroborated by PWs 4 and 5. Court had no reason to disbelieve their evidence as the defendant did not have any evidence to contradict them. Thus relying on the evidence of the PW 5 the court believed that the stalls were originally constructed by the plaintiff and did not believe story of the defendant that the stalls were moved across the road by the defendant. PW 4 Saiful Islam also stated that he had seen the plaintiff to take and keep the bricks and sand next to the suit premises and PW 6 Abdul Majid deposed that he supplied the bricks to the plaintiff from his own brick field. Placing reliance on these evidence the court found the claim of the defendant that he had later constructed the pucca stall with his bricks, sand and cement after the original stalls were gutted by fire to be false. It was stated by the defendant that after emergence of Bangladesh one Matiur Rahman along with others constructed pucca buildings. Matiur Rahman who carried on business in the suit stall Nos. 13/1 died. Upon his death his wife and sons continued business and on 30.4.77 sold the stall to Ataur Rahman Talukder from whom the defendant purchased the suit stalls by deed on 17.11.77 in the name of his son Rafiqul Islam and carried on business. The court below held that since the defendant and others who carried on business in the suit premises had no title or interest they could not claim the suit property nor transfer them. 

 8. It was submitted that the original agreement having expired in 1970 and there being no proof that there was renewal of the said agreement, the landlord tenancy relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant ended. The mere expiry of a registered lease deed will not bring an end to the tenancy. Thus, if the tenant continues to occupy the premises and the landlord continues to receive rent after the expiry such tenancy is a tenancy by holding over. In the instant case it is the case of the plaintiff that the tenant petitioner continued to pay rent which was accepted by the landlord till February, 1971. The SC Court had found that the tenant petitioner had paid rent to the plaintiff until February 1971 and therefore, the assertion that the tenancy ended in November, 1970 with the completion of 5 years cannot be accepted. There is nothing to show that the tenant after the expiry of the lease period of 5 years did not continue as a tenant or refused to accept the plaintiff as his landlord. 

 "Tenant's continuous possession with landlord's assent creates an implied contract constituting a tenancy by holding over. Such a tenancy cannot be created by tenant's continuance of possession alone-there must also be the assent of the landlord, which may be expressed or implied. It may be evidenced by acceptance of rent or by other circumstances. Where the lessor dissents there cannot be any holding over. Absence of dissent will not necessarily imply assent, but from the tenant's continuous possession for a long period, without contrary indication from the landlord may constitute an implied assent. Implied assent is a question of fact inferable from the length of possession and other circumstances excluding an inference of landlord's dissent". 

 10. I have said that in the instant case after the expiry of the registered agreement in February, 1970 there is no evidence that the tenant dissented or that the plaintiff did not give assent to the tenancy, In the circumstances it cannot be said that with the expiry of the lease after 5 years the relationship of landlord and tenant ceased to exist between the plaintiff and the defendants. A similar view was taken in the case of Nakul Das Mridha vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 1986 BLD 331 where it was held that: 

 Holding over means retaining possession It does not necessarily create any tenancy after the expiration of the stipulated term. The common law rule is that if a lessee remains in possession after the expiry of the terms, he is tenant by sufferance. A distinction is however, made between a tenant continuing in possession after the determination of the lease with the consent of the landlord, and the tenant remaining so without his consent. In common law the former is called a tenant holding over or a tenant at-will and the latter is called a tenant by sufferance. " 

 In the instant case we have seen that there has been no dissent either by the tenant or by the landlord on the expiry of the written agreement and therefore, the tenancy continued by holding over. 

 11. It was next submitted that the lease premises having been gutted by fire and the suit premises being completely destroyed the tenancy between the plaintiff and the defendant petitioner came to an and as it rendered the tenancy agreement void. 

 12. Mr. SR Paul, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has argued at length that under section 56 of the Contract Act the tenancy between the plaintiff and the defendant was frustrated as the whole suit property was completely destroyed. In this connection he has relied on the case of Azizur Rahman & others vs. Abdus Sakur and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 195. In that case several cases were referred to and discussed. While discussing whether the doctrine of frustration as embodied in section 56 of the Contract Act is applicable to leases of immovable property the Appellate Division discussed the case of Khitish Chandra Mondal VS. Shiba Rani Debi and others reported in AIR 1950 Cal. 441. In that case the plaintiff erected a thatched shed and which was rented out to a monthly tenant was burnt by fire. The tenant raised another structure on the land in spite of the landlord's protest and claimed to be a tenant. It was held: 

 (3) that under the tenancy B had no right to raise structures of his own, treating the lease as the lease of the land only." 

 After considering these decisions among others the Appellate Division in Azizur Rahman's case held; that the doctrine of frustration as embodied in section 56 of the Contract Act is applicable to leases of immovable property. In that case the subject matter of the tenancy was destroyed by fire. The said premises however, remained vacant and in possession of the plaintiffs. The defendant appellant in collusion with each other and ignoring plaintiffs and also lawyer's notice wrongfully constructed new huts and houses on the premises and refused to deliver possession of the land. The landlord plaintiff instituted suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession after removal or the structures by the defendant. The contention of the defendant, inter alia, was that some kutcha houses were only partly damaged by fire which were repaired by the defendant and made habitable and, therefore, there was no extinction of the subject matter of tenancy due to conflagration as alleged by the plaintiff. The Appellate Division held that frustration in the present case was apparent from the facts proved and, therefore, the defendant appellant's contention failed. 

 14. Mr. SR Paul has argued that the instant case was similar in that the subject matter of the tenancy having been completely destroyed by the Pakistan Army by setting fire to it the tenancy was frustrated and the plaintiff, therefore, could not file the present suit under the Rent Control Ordinance for eviction of the defendant petitioner as no landlord-tenant relationship existed between them. 

 It has been argued that in the instant case that as the suit premise was completely destroyed by fire it became impossible for either party to act under the tenancy agreement. Therefore, it is a question of fact whether it became impossible by reason of some event (in present case the suit premise being gutted by fire) to do the act under the contract. 

 16. Keeping this in mind, let us now see whether as a result of the suit premise being gutted by fire it did become impossible for the parties to perform their act under the tenancy. Admittedly the suit premise was gutted by fire by the Pakistan Army in 1971. It is also admitted that the tenant defendants did not leave the premises or hand over possession of the suit premises to the plaintiff landlord. Puce a shops were construed and the tenant continued to do business an usual. Although the defendant has claimed that his construction was made by him from bricks, cement and both at his own cost, the evidence is otherwise. I have seen while narrating the judgment of the SC Court that PW 4 Saiful Islam had deposed that he had seen the plaintiff keep cement and bricks and sand on the vacant land next to the suit premises in 1970 prior to the destruction and demolition of the suit premises. These materials were brought by the plaintiff with the intention to construct pucca building on the suit land in place of the tin shed. PW.6 deposed that the bricks were supplied to the plaintiff from his own brick field. It is also in evidence that it was agreed between the plaintiff landlord and the defendant tenant that in the event of the plaintiff making pucca construction the defendants would continue to occupy the premises as a tenant on the old terms and conditions. Therefore, although the old huts were destroyed by fire, by subsequent construction of pucca building and continuous occupation of the premises by the defendant it appears to me that the tenancy was not completely frustrated making the parties impossible to act under the agreement. It is true that the tenant did not pay any rent to the landlord after the suit premises were destroyed but the mere non-payment of rent does not mean that the tenancy had come to an end. The plaintiff had accepted the defendant to be his tenant and there is no evidence that there was dissent from either parties I have already said that there was finding by the SC Court that there was an oral agreement that in the event of construction of pucca shops the tenant would continue to occupy the premises as a tenant on the same terms and condition therefore from the facts and circumstances discussed above, I find that the tenancy had not been completely frustrated as a result of the fire but continued with the construction of pucca house as per oral agreement. 

 17. In the facts and circumstances, I find that if would not be just and reasonable not to hold the parties any longer to the terms of the contract i.e. the tenancy agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant. As the contract could be still performed in substance it cannot be said that the agreement had become impossible of performance within the meaning of section 56 of the Contract Act.

caseno: Appeal From Original Order No. 109 and 110 1984.with Civil Rule No. 298 (FM) of 1984. and Civil Rule No. 297 (FM) of 1984
parties:
Sagir Ahmed and ors ------ Appellant 
vs.
Dclwar Hossain and ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Facts are that the appellant-petitioners No. 1 and 2 filed two Miscellaneous Cases under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the property described in the schedules. Opposite party Nos. 1 to 8 namely, Delwar Hossain and others are the purchasers. Opposite party No.9 is the seller and Opposite party Nos. 10-21 are the other co-sharers of the holding. The case of the petitioner pre-emptors, who are father, son and daughter, is that the properties mentioned in C.S. Khatian No. 12223 appertaining to Mouza Sahar Dhaka originally belonged to one Parbati Charan Datta Kabiraj in raiyatijote right. He died leaving one widow Khiroda Sundari and 4 sons, Profullah Chandra Datta Kabiraj, Pizus Kiran Datta Kabiraj, Pran Goura Datta Kabiraj and Khitish Chandra Datta Kabiraj. Khiroda Sundari died leaving those 4 sons where after Khitish Chandra Datta Kabiraj transferred his entire interest in the suit property to his other three brothers. The three other brothers there sifter transferred their entire interest in the said to one Moulvi Yahayia Bawani who again transferred the same to opposite party Nos. 9.10 and 11 and Mujibur Rahman who are 4 brothers by executing a registered sale deed dated 6.1.1959 and delivered possession. The 4 brothers having gone into possession continued to possess the entire property so purchased from Bawani and during the S.A. and R.S. operation the name of the four brothers have been correctly recorded in Khatian No. 895 and 1708 respectively and the brothers, though separated the property amicably amongst them for convenience, continue to remain in ejmali in payment of rent as the tenancy remained one. When that was the position one of the brother namely, Habibur Rahmar., opposite party No. 10 transferred part of his share in the land of the holding together with the structures standing thereon to appellant-petitioner No. 1 namely, Sagir Ahmed by two registered sale deeds dated 22.3.1982 and 23.3.1982 and also transferred in favour of petitioner No.2 Reaz Ahmed minor son of petitioner No. 1 some other portion of the holding by two registered sale deeds dated 19.3.1982 and 20.3.1982 and delivered possession of the same to the appellants-petitioners. The petitioners' case is that they thus remained co-sharers in the case holding with other co-sharers namely, Habibur Rahman Matiur Rahman and Mozaffar Rahman. It was their further case that opposite party No. 22 wife of Sagir also purchased the remaining share of Habibur Rahman by separate sale deed and got delivery of possession of the purchased land. When that was the case Matiur Rahman one of the other brothers Opposite party No. 9 of the Misc. Case No. 327 of 1983 transferred his entire interest in the holding to opposite party Nos. 1-8 by registered sale deed dated 26.3.1982 for a consideration of Tk. 6,00,000/-. In the same way Mozaffar Rahman, the other brother transferred his entire interest in the holding to opposite party Nos. 1-6 by a registered sale deed dated 31.3.1982 for a consideration of Tk. 6,00,000/-. It is the appellants-petitioners' case that the two brothers transferred their respective properties without giving any notice to the petitioners though the petitioners are co-sharers in 'the case holding. The petitioners came to know of it long afterwards and after depositing the consideration money along with the statutory compensation then prayed for pre-emption. 

 3. The cases were contested by opposite party Nos. 1-8 by filing two similar written objection in both the cases denying the material allegations made therein contending that the petitioners are not co-sharers in the lands sought to be pre-empted. It is the case of the opposite party Nos. 1-8 that the four brothers namely, Matiur Rahman, Majibur Rahman, Habibur Rahman and Muzaffar Rahman became owners of holding No. 221 and 221/1 now holding Nos. 56 and 57 at Mitford Road, Dhaka by purchase. After the said purchased, one of the brothers, who had other ejmali properties also in the District Bogra along with the brothers filed a suit being Title Suit No.161 of 1981 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Bogra for partition of their ejmali property including the case holding. The said suit was decreed on com- promise on 1.12.1981 in terms of the solenama in the preliminary. form: As per direction of the said decree, the case holding was partitioned as per map and four separate blocks were created in blue print in pursuance of which Majibur Rahman obtained Block No. 1, Habibur Rahman obtained block No. 2, Matiur Rahman obtained Block No. 3 and Muzaffar Rahman obtained block No.4 and by that they accepted the partition map between the parties and the parties went into possession of the respective saham each having a compact plot of land and building separately. Thereafter the partition map was readjusted for convenience of possession and blocks Nos. 1-4 were readjusted, according to which Matiur Rahman got 'C' block, Muzaffar Rahman got 'D' block. When that was the position, opposite party Nos. 1-8 purchased block Nos. 'C' and 'D' from Matiur Rahman and Muzaffar Rahman and possession of those blocks were delivered to opposite party Nos. 1 and 8 by their vendors by raising pucca boundary wall in between the land. Thereafter Md. Habibur Rahman, vendor of the appellant-petitioners ceased to become co-sharers of Matiur Rahman and Muzaffar Rahman, vendors of the opposite party Nos. 1 to 8. It is the further case that the petitioners-appellants also separated their jama and paid rent separately by opening a khatian as also the opposite parties and that the opposite party Nos. 1-8 are owners of separate land and holding having no jointers .of the tenancy and as such they being not co-sharers, they are not entitled to pre-empt. In the court below the parties fought out the suit on specific issues. After a consideration of the pleadings of the parties the evidence on record the court below came to a finding that as the property had been partitioned among the brothers, each brothers having a separate possession and the appellant-petitioner Sagir Ahmed after purchase having separated his jama paying rent separately creating two separate tenancy, the petitioners-appellants arc no longer co-tenant in the case holding and in that view of the matter the court held that the petitioners are not entitled to pre-empt the case land and in holding so the court has referred to the principle enunciated in 35 DLR (AD) page 230. As against that the appellants-petitioners have preferred these appeals which are heard together and disposed of by this one judgment. 

 5. Mr. Gholam Rabbani, the learned Advocate who argued the case at length for the appellant having taken us through the judgment and the various exhibits, has submitted that the court below erred if law in not holding that what the four brothers has was an amicable partition for convenience and not a partition by metes and bounds when in fact there was no final decree in that partition suit, for the partition to take any legal effect. He has further submit- ted that the court below erred in not holding that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 161 of 1982 being not a final decree and not admissible in evidence for want of stamp papers, the decree proved nothing and hence the finding of fact arrived at on a consideration of the inadmissible evidence, can not be sustained in law. It is his further case that the appellant-petitioner remained co-sharers in the tenancy and unless the tenancy is separated the co-tenant would be a co-sharer and the decision referred to in 32 DLR (AD) has no application in the fact and circumstances of the instant case. Mr. Gholam Rabbani the learned Advocate having referred to certain exhibits on record and to the deposition of Sagir before the court below, submitted that there are assertion made by the appellant that he had not supplied the names of the other co-sharers in his petition for separation of jama and no notice were in fact served upon the co-sharer and this having been corroborated by the testimony on record the court ought to have held that the separation of jama or tenancy behind the back of other co-sharers had no basis in the eye of law and, therefore, they remained co-sharers in tenancy inspite of the separation of the jama which was illegal. In support of this contention he has referred to the decision reported in 33 DLR(AD) page 323 and 12 DLR (Dhaka) at page 785 and 17 DLR (Dhaka) page 77. 

 6. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate, arguing the case for the opposite parties has submitted that the decree passed in the title suit for partition was in fact a final decree with a direction to separate the specific possession as already effected by the parties on compromise as evidenced by Exhibit- H dated 30.11.80 on which the decree was passed on 1.12.81 and the parties having acted on it and having partitioned the properties on the basis of the said mutual partition it cannot be said that there was no partition in law. He further stated that there is evidence on record that the brothers were possessing the property separately and distinctly and that Sagir Ahmed, the appellant No.1 being in possession of the distinct portion of the holding under his vendor and paying rent only to that brother as his landlord should not be allowed to say that his vendor and landlord was a co-sharer with others. It is the further contention of the learned Advocate that Sagir himself separated his tenancy and against that separation of jam a no appeal was preferred and the tenant having paid in a separate jama his specific amount of the rent, the said matter cannot be agitated now before this court on appeal.In support of this contention he has referred to certain decision to which we shall advert at the relevant portion of the judgment. Mr. Habibul Islam lastly submits that the principle enunciated by the Appellate Division in S.M. Basiruddin case reported in XXXV DLR (AD) at page 230 is the law in this field and it is that in case of non-Agricultural tenancy it is the factum of separate possession of the co-owners of the holding which is relevant and not the tenancy and that inspite of one tenancy, the possessors having possessed separately it cannot be said that one is a co-sharer to the other. 

 7. In the instant case when one looks at the petition for pre-emption one would find that the averment made initially before the court, asking for pre-emption was that the four brothers were in separate possession for their convenience but there was no separation of the tenancy but there is no averment to the effect that there was no final partition decree and no Partition according to law and hence the court at the first instance had to frame issues relevant to the averment made in the petition and it was to the effect whether the petitioners are co-sharers of the case land and whether the tenancy had been separated. The parties in fact fought out the suit on this two specific issues and that being the position we would limit ourselves within these two issues to find out whether the court below had committed any error of law in arriving at a finding of fact regarding those two issues. 

 9. It has been argued by the appellants that there was no separation of the tenancy and in case of both a Non-Agricultural Tenant and a tenant under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is the co-tenancy of the holding which would determine the status of a tenant as a co-sharer and not possession by amicable partition. In support of that he has referred to certain decisions. 

 10. This brings us to the case of S.M. Basiruddin Vs. Zahurul Islam Choudhury and another reported in 35 D.L.R. (AD) page 230. In that case the court had to consider whether the expression such as "non-agricultural land" appearing in the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act and the expression "holding" appearing in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are synonymous, carrying the same meaning for the application of the principle which is applicable to agricultural land that partition alone would not extinguish co-tenancy and the right of pre-emption. It was held by the Appellate Division in that case under report that those two expressions are not synonymous but arc distinct expressions which were used consciously by the legislature. Their Lord-ships of the Appellate Division, having reiterated the principle of law that the right of preemption is not extinguished by mere partition but by a partition of the tenancy itself, had held that the legislature in the case of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, maintained a distinction between the expression "Non-Agricultural land" and "holding" with a purpose which may be to limit the number of applicants for pre-emption of non-agricultural land by making it available only to the co-sharer in the land and not to the co-sharer in the tenancy. It was held, at para 34, thus:- 

 "In my opinion the respondent not being co-sharer in the case land transferred though they may be co-sharer in the tenancy, the right of pre-emption did not accrue in their favour" and after finding so it was held that the application for pre-emption must fail. 

 11. The court of first instance however on evidence on record found that there was in fact a separation of tenancy when it was the case of the petitioner that no notice of that proceeding were served upon others. Against that it was argued that the matter having not been taken on appeal before the appropriate authority, the said matter can not be agitated here in appeal before this court. The learned advocate has referred to a decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 309 in support. There is substance in this contention and it need be considered in the affirmative but here we do not have to consider that as we find that the principle enunciated by the Appellate Division in Basiruddin's case reported in 35 DLR(AD) would be relevant in the instant case and that being so the question of joint tenancy-would be irrelevant.

parties:
Hajee Abdus Sattar ----- Appellant.
vs
Mahiuddin and other ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. The suit land is a Chandina-bhiti with a construction thereon in Maijdee town. One Gagan Ali was admittedly its owner in possession. In fact, he had only the possessory right therein. Case of the plaintiff-appellant is that Gagan Ali sold the premises to him by a registered sale-deed dated 8 December 1953 (Exhibit 1) and delivered possession to him. Thereafter, he possessed it by inducting different tenants, one Hashmatullah (PW 4) being one such tenant. After the tenancy of Hashmatullah was terminated the appellant inducted into the premises as tenant one Kala Miah by a registered Agreement dated 31 August 1964 corresponding to 15 Bhadra 1371 BS (Exhibit 3). Kala Miah continued his tenancy on payment of rent till his death and on his death his sons and other heirs. Who are the main defendants in this suit, held over possession as tenants but they defaulted in payment of rent. The appellant therefore, filed the suit namely OC Suit No. 886 of 1973, in the First Court of Munsif, Noakhali, for realization of arrears of rent from January 1972 to October 1973 at the rate of RS 45/- per month and also for eviction of the defendant tenants on whom notice of eviction was already served under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 5. Mr Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate for the appellant, has seriously assailed the decision of the learned Single Judge, particularly his interference in revision with the finding of facts arrived at by the lower Appellate Court on the question whether the respondents were tenants by holding-over' under the appellant. The learned Advocate has criticised the learned Single Judge for, what he terms, illegally rejecting the appellant's documentary evidence including a clear admission of the respondent that he was a tenant under the appellant and also for the view taken by the learned Single Judge that in the absence of satisfactory proof of payment of rent the respondent was not a tenant of the appellant whose registered instruments including the registered Lease Agreement have been arbitrarily rejected. The learned Advocate contends that in view of creation of the tenancy in favour of Kala Mia, father of the respondent, the latter was estoppel from questioning the appellant's title under section 116 of the Evidence Act. 

 116. No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant, shall, during the continuance of the tenancy, be permitted to deny that the landlord of such tenant had, at the beginning of the tenancy, a title to such immovable property; and no person who came upon any immovable property by the license of the person in possession thereof shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time when such license was given." 

 The estoppels as described in this section are known as tenant's estoppels or estoppel by contract. This estoppel is founded upon a contract between the tenant and the landlord. It provides that when a person enters into possession of immovable property as a tenant of another person the neither he nor anybody claiming through his shall be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to deny the landlord's title however defective that title might be. This necessarily implies that in case the tenant sets up a claim of title in himself he shall first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken it. This principle of law has been nicely expounded by Jessel MP in Re Siringer's Estate, page 384 LR 6 Ch 9 in the following works: 

 Sometimes it is found that after entering into possession as a tenant a person, from some motive, defaults in the payment of rent and when the question of eviction is raised he takes the plea that he is not a tenant for there is no evidence that he ever paid rent to the landlord. Such a device cannot carry him anywhere in view of the basic principle that once he is found to have entered into possession as tenant non-payment of rent shall not be interpreted as non-existence of the tenancy. Payment of rent is one among many other proofs of a tenancy. Mere non-payment of rent does not terminate the tenancy or make the possession of the tenant adverse to the landlord, as has been rightly held in the case of JM Singh vs Baldeo Singh, 49 IA 299. This position is based on the footing that once relation of landlord and tenant is established it is presumed to continue, and the burden of proving that it has ceased is on the person who alleges it to have ceased. Section 116 in express language precludes the tenant from questioning his landlord's title during the continuance of the tenancy: this section however does not debar him from doing so after it is shown by him that the landlord's title has been lost or extinguished since then. But if he himself claims title he must first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken the lease. Again, if the landlord determines the tenancy on any ground but the tenant continues to stay on still the tenant will be stopped from questioning the landlord's title unless he restores possession to the landlord who had put him into possession. 

 7. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocates for the respondent does not dispute this proposition of law particularly when the question has finally been decided by the Privy Council in the case of Currimbhoy & Co vs Creet, AIR 1933 (PC) 29. But his contention is that in the instant case the appellant filed to prove that the respondent was his tenant by holding over or that his father Kala Mia, had been a tenant under the appellant; on the contrary, he contends, evidence has been led by the respondent to show that he had got possession of the land by purchase in his own name and by his own right and that his father was not a tenant of the appellant, that he did not inherit it on his father's death and, as such, there was no question of holding over. This argument clearly takes us back to the disputed facts between the parties, whether Kala Mia was a tenant under the appellant and, if so, whether Kala Mia's heirs including defendant, respondent No. 1 continued in the tenancy. Since these question had been decided finally by the appellate Court they could not be reopened and reagitated in revision unless it is shown that the findings had not been made on due consideration of all material evidence according to established principles of assessment of evidence. As such, the evidence both oral and documentary requires to be reviewed. 

 8. Registered Agreement Exhibit 3 is the evidence of creation of a tenancy by the appellant in favour of Kala Mia at a monthly rent of Taka 45. The learned Single Judge has observed that through this exhibit is a registered Agreement. It does not by itself prove the tenancy. What appears to be meant by this observation is that the Agreement even if genuine might not have been acted upon. The respondent questioned the execution of the Agreement and also alleged that it was not acted upon. So far as the execution is concerned, besides PW 1 (the appellant), PW 5 a Deed- writer has deposed that he had written this Agreement, which was executed in his presence. As to whether it was acted upon, besides the evidence of PW 1, there is the evidence of a number of witnesses including PWs 2, 3 and 4 PW2 is Kala Mia's son-in-law, that is, he is brother-in-law of the respondent (defendant No-1); he has supported the appellant's case that Kala Mia was a tenant under the appellant and resided in the house carrying on cloth- business there. Evidence of PW 2 was sought to be discarded on the ground that he married a stepsister of defendant No.1 and as such he is hostile to him. But there is no evidence whatever that there was any clash of interest or enmity between defendant No.1 and PW 2; and if there were any strained relationship between them, it appears, it is due to the fact that PW 2, through a relation, came to the Court to depose against his disclosing the truth and not supporting his claim of rival title by the unregistered Agreement (Exhibit Ka) which has been challenged by the appellant to be antedated PW 3 is an independent witness. He is a practicing lawyer having residence near the suit premises. He claims to know both the parties. He has stated that the premises belonged to the appellant who possessed it through different tenants and that he saw Kala Mia possessing it as a tenant of the appellant PW 4, Hashmatullah, says that the possessed the premises as tenant of the appellant before the structure was destroyed by fire, that is, prior to Kala Mia's tenancy. On consideration of evidence the lower Appellate Court held that the Agreement, Exhibit 3, was not only genuine but it was acted upon. Case of the respondent (Kala Mia's son) is that his father did not take the tenancy, but he himself purchased the premises from one Mohammadullah who is DW 2 Mohammadullah's evidence is that he sold it to the respondent by the unregistered Agreement, Exhibit (Ka" as already stated on 2-6-64, that is, about three months earlier than Kala Mia's registered Agreement, Exhibit. If Exhibit 'Ka' is relied upon, the we find two tenants simultaneously for the same premises, one is the father and the other is the son Case of the appellant is that Exhibit Ka is a fraudulent and antedated document. Even if it were not fraudulent and antedated, still the broad fact remains that under this Agreement no interest passed to Kala Mia's son unless it is shown that Mohammadullah had any right, title or interest in the premises himself. Mohammadullah claims title from Gagan Ali Bepari, but there is no paper to show that Gagan Ali Bepari had transferred the premises to Mohammadullah. Secondly, Gagan Ali Bepari could not have made such transfer in 1964 as he had already transferred his entire interest in the premises to the appellant by an earlier registered Sale-deed 8-12-53, Exhibit 1. The claim of the respondent that he purchased it from Mohammadullah is negative by Exhibit 1 read with the supporting oral evidence. Evidence of Mohammadullah has been challenged on another ground; his elder brother PW 4 Hashmatullah has deposed that he had taken lease of the premises from the appellant as a month to month tenant by a registered Agreement dated 13-6-55 (Exhibit 3A) and continued their till the structure was gut- ted by fire in 1964. He has further deposed that Mohammadullah, his younger brother, was at that time a mere student. Thus it appears that Mohammadullah, respondent's vendor, was not even a tenant in the premises but his elder brother was the tenant. To avoid that question of validity of the alleged transfer of the property by Mohammadullah to him, the respondent went to the extent of denying the genuineness of appellant's title under, Exhibit 1, the registered sale-deed and it has been argued that this Sale-deed was either fraudulent or it was not acted upon. To counter this contention evidence, both oral and documentary, has been led by the appellant. It is that after the purchase under Exhibit 1, and when Hashmatullah was a tenant, the premises was sold in auction for recovery of some public dues and it is the appellant who got the sale set aside. In this connection the appellant filed an order of the Board of Revenue setting aside the sale at his instance. That order is Exhibit 5 dated 30 January. 160. PW 3, the lawyer, has supported the appellant's case saying that he was engaged by the appellant in the proceedings for setting aside the auction sale under Exhibit 5 the learned Single Judge has observed that this document got no direct bearing on the issue in question. If the tenancy of Kala Mia is in question, this document is not so much relevant, but if the appellant-land-lord's title is challenged, this document is very much relevant. We therefore find that the respondent with a view to boosting up his story of purchase from Mohammadullah, who was nobody to make any such transfer, raised out of motive the dispute about the appellant's original title under Exhibit 1, by the registered sale-deed, executed by Gagan Ali Bepari. Curiously enough, it is Gagan Ali Bepari from whom Mohammadullah claims title by oral purchase at a subsequent- date. In the circumstances, the appellate Court's finding that both Exhibits 1 and 3 are genuine documents and were acted upon is a finding based on proper consideration of evidence and as such this finding was not open for re-opening in the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. 

 9. Mr Asrarul Hossain has laid considerable stress on Exhibits 4 and 4(a) which purportedly contain an admission of the respondent (defendant No.1) that he was a tenant under the appellant. These exhibits are certified copies of two applications of the respondent to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) praying for settlement to the suit-premises from the Government, the ultimate owner. Both the appellant and the respondent (defendant No.1) prayed for settlement from the Government in 1973 where upon two separate cases were started which ended ultimately in favour of the appellant, obviously in view of the appellant's possessory right from Gagan Ali Bepari for a long time. The question raised here, however, is not as to who got the settlement from the Government, in both these applications, Exhibits. 4 and 4(a), filed about six years after his father Kala Mia's death, the respondent (defendant No.1) stated that he was a tenant of the appellant, Haji Abdus Sattar, who by misrepresentation had created the tenancy though he had no title, that because of this defect of title, he was offering himself as a candidate for settlement in view of the fact that he had been running a cloth-shop in the premises for a long time. This is a clear admission and it estoppel him from denying the appellant's title in the premises. To wriggle out of this tight comer, he has contended that the documents exhibits 4 & 4(a) are not correct copies of his applications to the Revenue Authorities. The learned Single Judge has observed that these copies of the applications were not legally proved, that they are private documents and further that attention of the respondent was not drawn to the statement contained in these supplications, and as such the question of binding him with the statement therein does not arise. This observation, we find, got no legal or factual basis. For these are certified copies of applications to the Additional Deputy Commissioner for settlement, who after necessary endorsement, incorporated them into the record of the Settlement Case and issued certified copies thereof in accordance with law the originals of the applications cannot be produced or obtained by anybody unless a Court calls for them. These certified copies were filed as exhibits in this suit in presence of respondent who them raised objection, but the Court ignoring his objection marked them as exhibits 4 and 4(a). Again, while deposing in Court as DW 1 he himself drew his attention to these documents stating in his examination-in-chief that these were not true copies his applications to the Additional Deputy Commissioner. In the circumstances, there was no necessity for drawing his further attention to them during cross-examination. As to the authenticity of these certified copies, the respondent did not apply to the Court to lodge in complaint under section 195 CrPC against the appellant on a charge of forgery who produced or filed in evidence these documents in a judicial proceeding Such a complaint may be filed under section 195 (1) (c) CrPC even now if the respondent dares to move the Court for that purpose. These documents issued and certified to be true copies by an authorised officer of the Government are admissible in evidence. The statement contained therein as described above is an admission within the meaning of section 20 of the Evidence Act and the respondent is bound by his admission that he was a tenant of the appellant who allegedly got no valid title to the premises. 

 10. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate for the respondent, has tried to make out a case of total non-payment of rent and has contended that in the absence of reliable evidence that rent was ever paid to the appellant it cannot he said that any tenancy was created or the Agreement Exhibit 3, purportedly creating the tenancy was acted upon. Evidence in this connection is that Kala Mia paid rent so long be was alive and after his death his heirs, the defendants, became irregular in payment of rent and ultimately stopped it. PW 2 has stated that Kala Mia during his life-time had engaged him to AD-14 look after his cloth-shop and to pay rent for the premises and that the respondent paid rent for 14 months at a time by Exhibit 6. He has also deposed that he had been authorised in writing by his father in-law to act as his Assistant in the cloth-business (Exhibit 13). These two documents have been seriously challenged as fabrication for the purpose of the suit, PW 2 has, of course, denied the suggestion as to fabrication of Exhibits. 6 and 13; but the payment of rent for 14 months at a time and non-production of any receipts for payment of rent for the earlier period create suspicion in the genuineness of the receipt Exhibit 6. But I have already observed at the beginning that mere non-payment of rent does not snap landlord and tenant relationship and that non-payment of rent will not enable a tenant to question landlord's title unless he discontinues the tenancy and restores possession to the landlord. If mere non-payment of rent is taken as proof of non-existence of landlord and tenant relationship grave consequences will follow, for an unscrupulous tenant upon entering a premise as a tenant will deliberately as a convenient time. Mr TH Khan has contended that there is no evidence of the respondents holding over and that if the evidence as to payment of rent by Exhibit 6 is rejected no tenancy under the appellant exists. Answer to this contention is contained in the principle enunciated already in paragraph 6 above. It is that once a tenancy is created, it will be presumed that it is continuing, unless it is shown that it has ceased. The tenancy was created in favour of Kala Mia on whose death his heirs (including defendant No.1) continued to possess the premises. This is "holding over." For without Kala Mia's tenancy they could not have entered upon possession particularly when the claim of independent title by purchase has fallen through. They say that they did not pay any rent to the appellant but such non- payment of rent hardly improves their case, for the tenancy continues even if payment of rent is not made. 

 11. Lastly Mr TH Khan has drawn our attention to our decision in the case of Abdus Sattar vs Suresh Chandra Das, 32 DLR (AD) 170 and has contended that a monthly tenancy is not heritable. In that case it was observed: 

 "A tenancy-at-will is determinable at the will of either landlord or tenant and is a personal relation between the original landlord or tenant and is determined by the death of either of them." 

 It is obvious that such a tenancy is not heritable in the sense that on the death of a tenant his heirs are not under any legal obligation to pay rent to the landlord or to continue the tenancy, in the same way, as the landlord is not bound to keep the lease alive. Both the parties are at liberty to discontinue the tenancy. If the heirs of late tenant continue to stay on, but do not pay rent they shall not be permitted to say that the landlord has no title and in case they themselves claim title they must first of all restore possession to the land-lord an act which has not been done in this case. As such they have been rightly held to be tenants by holding over.
