parties:
Haji Aklema Khatun and another ------- Appellant
Vs.
Shah Alam and ors ------- Respondent
full_judgment:
4. The defendants filed written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable and raised several other objections as to valuation, court fee etc. They further alleged that the suit was not maintainable in the absence of a prayer for recovery of khas possession. The defendants contended that the plaintiffs acquired no title in the suit property on the basis of the so-called oral gift which is an afterthought and concocted with ulterior motive for illegal gains. They further contended that section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 is a bar to the accrual of title to the plaintiffs in the suit property in the absence of a registered written instrument of conveyance. They further contended that even if the gift was genuine as contemplated under Mohammaden Law no title did pass upon the plaintiffs in the absence of a registered written instrument of gift. They, however, stoutly denied the story of the alleged oral gift and contended that the application before the Income Tax Authority for clearance certificate is a manipulated affair. They contended that Abdur Rahman Chowdhury died without making any gift and that the defendants being consanguine paternal uncles of the donor (sons of the consanguine brothers of the grandfather of deceased Abdur Rahman Chowdhury) are entitled to 6 annas share by inheritance under the Mohammaden Law. But the plaintiffs have set up the case of verbal gift to defeat the claim of these defendants in the disputed property and that the suit ought to be dismissed and the succession certificate should be granted to the defendants. The facts relating to the succession case need not be stated separately since the defendants defence in this suit is their case as petitioners in the succession certificate case. This suit was tried analogously along with the said Succession Certificate Case. 

 5. The learned Subordinate Judge after framing necessary issues and on consideration of materials and evidence on record decreed the suit. On appeal the suit was remanded; mainly on the ground that the defendants had no opportunity to file additional written statement against the belated amendment of the plaint and to examine the witnesses with a view to controvert the genuineness of the documents by handwriting expert if the defendants so desired. In the order of remand it was further directed that both the suit and the Succession Certificate should be heard analogously as before. After remand the learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit. Tie learned Subordinate Judge held that the alleged story of gift of the suit property by Abdur Rahman Chowdhury in favour of the plaintiffs is absolutely false and concocted. The learned Subordinate Judge disbelieved the witnesses of plaintiffs and its acceptance and the delivery documents with respect to the suit property. He also found that there was no delivery of possession of the suit property by the donor to the plaintiffs. The learned Subordinate Judge also held that section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 is a bar to. the passing of title by oral gift in favour of the plaintiffs, even if the story of alleged gift taken to be a true one. He also found that the Transfer of Property Act being a Central Law and the provision of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act being special law on matters of the transfer of property, Non Agricultural Tenancy Act would prevail over the provision of Transfer of Property Act. He also held that in view of provisions of section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, by the alleged transfer of suit property by oral gift, the plaintiffs did not acquire any title to the property. Upon these, finding the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit and allowed the Succession Certificate Case. This appeal is directed against the aforesaid decision of the learned Subordinate Judge. 

 6. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr. Md. Shafiqur Rahman, learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the plaintiff appellants and Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan with Mr. Md. Bazlur Rahman, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the defendants respondents. The learned Advocate for the appellants firstly contended that the court below was wrong in not considering that all the witnesses to a transaction are not supposed to see, note and remember all the facts and aspects relating to the same in the same way and slight variation and deviation amongst the witnesses in stating the facts do not render the evidence adduced by the witnesses to be untrue. He has also submitted that the witnesses of the plaintiffs have proved the oral declaration of gift as oral gift and the handing over of documents relating to the gift and the acceptance of the gift by the donees and these evidences of the witnesses could not be impeached at all with regard to the main ingredients necessary to prove a gift. He has submitted that the trial court was wrong in observing that the plaintiffs did not state anything in their deposition about deli very of possession of the suit property inasmuch as delivery of title deeds of tenanted premises is an act sufficient to constitute delivery of possession. He has also submitted that even if the trial court disbelieved the genuineness of Ext. 5, the fact of handing over the lease deed and letter of extension of tenancy by the donor at the time of gift proved that the gift was completed and effective in law. He has also submitted that the trial Court failed to consider the purport and effect of the evidence of P.Ws. 5, 6 and 8 and was wrong in not relying upon their evidence in deciding the issue as to genuineness of gift. He has also submitted that the court below erred in law in holding that sec. 23(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act rendered the personal law of Mohammadans and section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act nugatory and ineffective. He has also submitted that the provisions of section 23(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 was repugnant and/or inconsistent with the provision of section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act and as such it did not affect oral gift by a Mohammadan. 

 12. Next witness for the plaintiffs is P.W. 9 Shamsul Huda. He has corroborated the evidence of other witnesses with regard to the declaration of gift to the plaintiffs in his presence and in presence of other witnesses. He stated that the gift was made in presence of the witnesses and the sale deed dated 29-12-60 and the agreement for monthly tenancy between the donor and May & Baker and letter from the May & Baker extending the tenancy were handed over to the donees. Ho also stated that May and Baker made correspondence with the plaintiffs but, did not make any payment of rent without any indemnity bond. He further stated that the plaintiffs. however, took all steps for payment of municipal tax and filing of appeal against enhancement of taxes, etc. through him. He proved certain municipal papers and certain copies of letters written by his wife to the Municipality. He stated that he obtained Income-Tax Form and submitted application for Income Tax clearance certificate Ext. 1 signed by Haji Abdur Rahman Choudhury on 21-12-68. He also stated that chalan was also received from Income Tax Authority for payment of gift tax. He also stated since his marriage in May 1956 he never saw the defendant on visiting and in familiar terms with the donor's house. He stated in his cross examination that May & Baker and Co. paid rent of the disputed house upto November, 1969 and this was paid on 2nd or 3rd December, 1968 when the donor was alive and thereafter no payment was made after that by them. He denied the suggestion that the story of heba was got up and entirely false one. He also denied that the Income Tax papers and Municipal papers were procured after the death of his father-in-law by ante-dating them. These are all the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs besides several documentary evidence which they have produced in support of their case. 

 16. In the background of the evidence let us consider whether Haji Abdur Rahman Choudhury made declaration of oral gift in presence of the witnesses as alleged and whether the said gift was accepted by the plaintiffs and delivery of possession of the disputed property was given. In this connection it may be mentioned that the disputed property is in possession of the tenant under an agreement of tenancy. It is in evidence that the plaintiff No. 1 is the widow and plaintiff No. 2 is the only daughter and only issue of late Abdur Rahman Choudhury. It appears that late Abdur Rahman Choudhury left no near relation besides the plaintiffs. The defendants are step-brothers of, grandfather of late Abdur Rahman Choudbury. It is not disputed that the defendants are distant agnates and that they would inherit a share of the property left by Abdur Rahman Choudhury if there was no disposition of the suit property by the impugned oral gift. The plaintiffs have filed this suit for declaration of their title on the basis of oral gift. We do not think that the plaintiffs are required to pay ad valorem court fee as they were not seeking recovery of khas possession after establishment of their title. The relief for declaration is competent and as such the suit as framed is maintainable. 

 17. As stated earlier the plaintiffs are the near and dear ones of late Abdur Rahman Choudhury and that the defendants are consanguine paternal uncles in the 4th category of distant kindred under Muslim Law. In our opinion the facts of declaration of gift by the donor and acceptance of the gift by the donees have been well proved by the evidence of P.WS. 1, 2, 3, 4, 8 & 9. It is true that excepting P.Ws. 8 Chairman of the Local Union Council, all other witnesses of the gift are near relations of the donor and the donees. In a transaction like a heba made by the husband in favour of his widow and by father in favour of his only daughter and issue, the person expected to be present and witness the heba would naturally be the near relations. The donor, however, in his wisdom called the chairman of the locality to witness the gift. He has corroborated the evidence of other witnesses with regard to the declaration of the gift, acceptance of the same and delivery of the document relating to the property. We do not find any reason to reject the evidence of P.W.8, the local Chairman who corroborated the evidence of other witnesses. We also find that the plaintiffs being near and dear relations of the donor in the world, it would not be unnatural to make a gift in their favour, affecting inheritance of the defendants who are consanguine paternal uncles and distant kindred under the 14th category under Musalman Law. It is seen in deposition that the material fact with regard to the making of gift and its acceptance by the donees could not be impugned by cross-examination of the witnesses. Serious criticism has been put forward by the defendants about the number of papers and documents handed over during the declaration of gift but the material evidence of the declaration of gift by the donor and the acceptance of the gift by the donees could hardly be impugned in cross-examination. The discrepancy about the number of papers and documents banded over to the donees by the donor as we have discussed earlier would be natural in view of lapse of time that passed between the time when the transaction took place and the witnesses deposed in the Court. It is not natural for the witnesses to remember the details of the transaction at the time of making of the gift witnessed by them with meticulous accuracy. Small discrepancies bring truthfulness in their evidence. With regard to the discrepancies about how many papers were handed over by the donor to the donees at the time of making of the gift it is seen for the evidence that P.Ws. 1 and 2 stated that the donor passed all the documents relating to the disputed property. There is no discrepancy between the evidence of those two witnesses about the handing over of the document of title with respect to the suit property to them by the donor. P.W. 3 stated the donor handed over the title deed of the disputed property and bharanama with May and Baker and Co. to the plaintiffs. P.W. 4 stated some other papers beside the title deed and bharanama were handed over to the plaintiffs as a token of gift P.W. 8 Chairman stated that the donor handed over the title deed and another paper to plaintiff, through the son-in-law, P.W. 9 stated that few other papers besides the title deed were banded over to the donees. This discrepancy with regard to the handing over of some other papers including the lease agreement besides the title deed appear in the evidence of P.Ws. 1 and 2. But the evidence that the title deed with respect to the property was handed over to the donees by the donor is consistent and there is no discrepancy with regard to the handing over of the title deed to the plaintiffs. In our view the discrepancy appearing in the evidence of some of the witnesses with regard to the number of papers and documents banded over to the donees by the donor should not affect or impair the veracity of the evidence with regard to the declaration of gift and its acceptance by the donees. We, therefore, hold that the plaintiffs have proved successfully by cogent evidence the fact of declaration of gift in presence of witnesses and its acceptance by the donees. 

 20. It has been submitted on behalf of the appellants that Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is a Special Law with respect to the incidence of tenancy and it is not a law of transfer, and that even if section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act deals with transfers relating to Non-Agricultural Tenancy land, the provision of Transfer of Property Act, it being a central Law, shall prevail over the provision of section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. He has submitted that the transfer by a gift by a Muslim to a Muslim will be governed by the personal Law of the Muslims. It has been so stated by section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act. He submits that although by virtue of the assent of the Governor-General under sub-section (2) of section 107 of the Government of India Act. Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was a valid legislation but the provision with regard to transfer of Non-Agricultural Tenancy cannot override the provision of general law. For that purpose the provision of Muslim Law relating to transfer shall prevail. In our view Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not a special law of transfer. General law of transfer may be affected by the special law of transfer and in that event the provision of special law will prevail. In our view, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not a special law of Transfer. This is a law with respect to the incidence of tenancy of Non-Agricultural lands and the provisions in section 23 of the Act cannot over-ride the provision of general law relating to the transfer of immovable property, namely, the Transfer of Property Act and for that purpose the provision of Muslim Law. We are, therefore, of the view that with regard to a transfer of immovable property between a Muslim and another Muslim, the Muslim Law relating to gift will be applicable, i.e., an oral transfer by gift in accordance with Muslim Law may be made in the absence of a registered written instrument of gift. 

 21. Mr. M. H. Khondker, the learned Advocate who appeared as amicus curiae on our request to assist the court on the question whether a Muslim can make a valid oral gift in respect of immovable property submitted that section 12 of the Transfer of Property Act having accepted the Rules of Mohammadan Law and the provisions of Transfer of Property Act relating to gift was not affected by the provisions of section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. He has submitted that whether if the provisions of Chapter on gift in. Transfer of Property Act is in conflict with the Mohammadan Law the latter shall prevail. The Transfer of Property Act requires that a gift must be made by a registered instrument. But under the Mohammadan Law a gift of immovable property may be made orally and by delivery of possession. Mr. Khondkar has also submitted that Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act does not apply to a premises with structure and that the transfer of a land and building is not attracted by section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. He has referred to the decision reported in 1968 SC, M. R. 341 and to the case of Abdul Mutate Vs Musammat Rezia Begum reported in 22 D.L.R. (SC) 134. Mr. Fakir Abdul Mannan, learned Advocate, on the other hand, submitted that it is a Non-Agricultural Tenancy and in spite of the building standing therein section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will apply with all force as the tenancy is Non-Agricultural tenancy. tie has referred to the decision of G. Narayana-swami Naidu and others Vs. Inspector of Police," Mayavaram and another reported in A, L R. 1949 (Madras) 307 (Special Bench) and to an unreported decision in Afsaruddin Ahmed Vs. Nahar and others in F. A.. No. 79 of 1963. In our view the provision in section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act prohibiting the transfer of Non-Agricultural Tenancy without registered document shall not apply to gifts of immovable property by a Muslim. A valid gift of immovable property with buildings and structures inter vivos can be made under the Muslim Law by oral gift. In this connection their Lordships of the Privy Council in the case of Mohammad Abul Vs. Fakir Jan an Begum reported in 49 I.A. 195 (209-10) have stated as follows ;

parties:

Vs.
Bangladesh (formerly Province of East Pakistan) & another..........Respondents.
full_judgment:
3. The appellant, thereafter, moved High Court of East Pakistan under Article 6(B) of the Provisional Constitutional Order, 1969 read with Article 98 of the late Constitution of Pakistan for a declaration that the notice asking the appellant to make payment of Rs. 82/26 was without any lawful authority and also for a direction restraining Respondent No. 2 from realising amount in excess Rs. 36/- per year payable under the deed of lease dated 29-6-57. The appellant contended in the said application that the lease in his favour was not a tenancy under any of the provisions of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and that the terms and conditions were exclusively controlled by the deed of lease under which he held the land and that according to the said terms the rent being payable according to the Gregorian Calendar the attempt to realise rent according to Bengli Calender year was absolutely without any lawful authority. 

 7. Mr. M.H. Khandker, the appellant, who has appeared in person, has submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court were wrong in taking the view that he was a tenant under the Govt. in respect of the residential plot of land, leased out to him on the basis of the Indenture of lease dated 29-6-57 by the Governor of East Pakistan for the purpose of assessment of the Development and Relief Tax and Additional Development and Relief Tax under the two East Pakistan enactments referred to above. His contention is that he is a lessee of piece of Govt. Khas land within the meaning of the Transfer of Property Act on the terms and conditions as laid down in the Indenture of lease and that he cannot be taken to be a tenant, as contemplated in the said two Taxing Statutes, which means, according to the appellant, a holder of agricultural land. The appellant has also contended that the term 'tenant' has got a specific connotation in the context of the land law system of the country and generally refers to a holder of agricultural land, as has been contemplated in the definition clause, section 2(17) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, which has been bodily incorporated in section 2(27) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the latter Act having ultimately been repealed and replaced by the Bengal Tenancy Act, and that inasmuch as ordinarily a holder of agricultural land under another person is known as tenant & that of the non-agricultural land is known as lessee, the appellant, who in a lessee of some non-agricultural Govt. Khas land, cannot be brought within the purview of Taxing Statutes in question, which refer to a tenant and not to a lessee. It has been further submitted by Mr. Khandker that the basis of the decision of the learned Judges of the High Court that the appellant is a tenant within the meaning of Taxing Statutes being that he has been described as such in the very Indenture of lease by which lease was created and that the appellant's lease is in effect a lease in perpetuity is absolutely erroneous, as misdescription of the status of a person in a private document cannot alter has legal position and that the lease of the appellant having been created specifically for a term of 99 years cannot be taken to be a lease in perpetuity. 

 . . . 2.(1) There shall be levied and collected by the provincial Government development relief tax from every tenant at the rate of four annas on each rupee of rent payable by him in respect of the land comprised in his tenancy with effect from the 1st day of Baishakh, 1362. Provided that when such land is held free of rent, such development and relief tax shall be levied and collected at the rate of four annas on each rupee of rent that would be assessable on such land on the principles laid down in section 26 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act,1950. 

 "2.(1) There shall be levied and Finance Act, collected by the provincial Government an additional development and relief tax from every tenant at the rate of fifty paisa per acre in respect of the land comprised in his tenancy with effect from the 1st day of Baishakh, 1374. 

 11. Both the taxes were sought to be levied and collected under the terms of the two taxing statutes from "every tenant" at a certain rate on the payable by him or on the area "in respect of the lands comprised in his tenancy". From the manner of the levy and the method of collection of the taxes, as have been provided in the said statutes, it is clear that such a tenant would be one of the lands held under the Government. Tenant has not been defined in any of the said two statutes. According to the well-established rule of statutory construction, every word is to be understood in its plain and natural meaning. If, however, such a word has received a distinctive or technical meaning in the statutes in pari materia i.e., statutes dealing with the same person or thing or class, the aid of such a meaning may be taken for interpreting the word as used in the statute under consideration. 

 In the legal literature, the word "tenant" has acquired a meaning which is substantially definite and precise. The legislative history in respect of the Tenancy Laws of the country also provides a dependable guideline for the proper appreciation of the word. It is also a well-settled rule of construction that the legislative language will be interpreted on the assumption that the legislature, while enacting a particular statute, was aware of the course of legislation and of the existing statutes, where a particular word or words had been given a specific definition or meaning. The rule of construction in this connection has been stated in Craies on Statute law, 6th Edition, at page 141, after referring to the observation made by Lord Shaw of Dunfermline in the case of Lennon Vs. Gibson & Howes Ltd. (1919) A.C. 709 in the following words: 

 "985. General principles. The relation of landlord and tenant was originally one of contract only, but from early times the contract conferred an estate in the land on the tenant without losing all its contractual characteristics. The relation arises as a rule when one party confers on another the right to the exclusive possession of land, mines or buildings, for a time which is either subject to a definite limit originally, as in the case of a lease for terms of years or which, though originally indefinite, can be made subject to a definite limit by either party as in the case of a tenancy from year to year. The interest in the property which remains in the landlord is called the reversion, and, as a rule, there is, incident to it, the right to receive from the tenant payment for the use of the property in the shape of rent." 

 14. It is true that having regard to the historical and socio-political conditions of this country, the laws relating to the lease of agricultural and non-agricultural property have developed here differently. Because of the fact that at the advent of the East India Company in this country towards the middle of the 18th century, when the entire territory which came under their control was agrarian in its nature, the laws which were enacted regarding landlord and tenant were mainly in respect of agricultural lands and until 1882 it does not appear that there were any codified law relating to leases of non-agricultural land. As we have indicated above the tenancy laws connected with agricultural holding have developed stage by stage and the rights and liabilities of the lessors and the lessees of such holding have undergone changes with the changing pattern of the society. There have been charges also in the laws relating to the leases of non-agricultural lands with the increase in the pressure of population in the urban areas of the country. 

 16. In 1859 Rent Act (Central Act X of 1859) re-enacted, with certain modifications, the provisions of the existing law relating to the rights of the raiyats and this Act appears to be the earliest of the comprehensive tenancy legislations to safeguard the interests of the tenants of agricultural land. In the said Act the tenants of agricultural land have been referred mainly as 'raiyats' and in certain provisions they have been referred also as 'under tenants or raiyat'. The next important legislation was the Rent Act (Bengal Act VI of 1862) which was enacted to amend the law relating to the recovery of rent in the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal as contained in Rent Act of 1859. The next Act was also a Bengal Act being Landlord and Tenant Procedure Act (Act VIII of 1869) which was to amend the procedure in suits between the Landlord and Tenants. Although in the title of the Act the general term 'tenant' had been used, the 'tenant' contemplated in the said title was really the raiyat and he had been referred to as to such in the different provisions of the Act. 

 18. In 1885, the Bengal Tenancy was enacted to amend and consolidate certain enactments relating to law of landlord and tenant within the territories under the administration of the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal, and by the said Act all those Acts referred to above, namely, Rent Act, 1859 (Central Act X of 1859), Rent Act, 1862 (Bengal Act VI of 1862) and the Landlord and Tenant Procedure Act, 1869 (Bengal Act VIII of 1869) were repealed. In the district of Sylhet, however, the said Acts remained in force until the enactment in 1936 of the Sylhet Tenancy Act-whereby the provisions similar to those in the Bengal Tenancy Act were brought into force in the said district, which was at that time a part of the province of Assam. 

 19. Although the Bengal Tenancy Act was stated in the preamble to be an amending and consolidating Act relating to landlord and tenant, the provisions of the Act were made applicable only to the case of lease-hold, interest in agricultural land only. The definitions of 'tenant' and 'landlord' as were given in section 3 of the Act were expressed in general terms and it does not appear that they were to be understood in the restricted sense of being applicable only to the holders of agricultural land. The definitions of landlord, rent and tenant as given in clauses (6), (13) and (17) of section 3 are quoted below:— 

 21. Section 4 of the Act, however, purports to confine the operation if the Act to the particular classes of tenants namely, tenants connected with agricultural holdings. The following provisions of the Act clearly indicate the scope of the operation of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Section 4: 

 22. It will thus appear that Mr. Khandker was not correct in his initial assumption on the basis of which he built up the subsequent part of his argument that in the Bengal Tenancy Act the terms "tenant” has been used in the sense of holder of agricultural land. The framers of the Act were very clear in their mind as to the general connotation of the term leant and, therefore, deliberately categorised the tenants connected with agricultural holding as tenure-holder, raiyat or under raiyat for the purpose of application of the provisions of the Act to them. 

 23. Before we deal with the subsequent development of the tenancy laws of the country we shall have to consider another law, namely The Transfer of Property Act which was enacted about 3 years before the enactment of the Bengal Tenancy Act and has some relevance to our present discussion. The Transfer of Property Act (Act IV of 1882) and the provision of Chapter V of the said Act comprising sections 105 to 117 dealing with leases of immovable property have some bearing upon the present question. In these provisions the term 'lease' and other connected terms have been statutorily defined and the rights and liabilities of lessor and lessee have also been clearly laid down. By section 117 of the Act, however, leases of agricultural land have been kept outside the purview of the provisions of this Chapter. But that does not modify or restrict the meaning of the general expressions as have been used in the said chapter. In this context, the provisions of section 105 of the Act, by which "lease" has been defined, section 106, which deals with duration of various leases, and section 117, by which leases of agricultural land have been kept outside the scope of the Act, may be referred to. Lease has been defined in section 105 of the Act in the following manner:— 

 24. This definition indicates that by a lease a subordinate interest is created by a person in favour of another person in respect of some immovable property on condition on payment of premium and/or rent. The fact that the nature of the immovable property, the subject matter of lease, has not been spe-cified indicates that it may be any kind of immovable property, agricultural or non-agricultural. It is true that in this definition section the transferor has not been termed as landlord nor the transferee has been named as tenant but that this relationship, as is created by lease, is the relationship of a landlord and tenant as is evident from the provisions of section 106 in which the manner of termination of various kinds of leases by service of notice at the instance of the lessor hat been prescribed, providing that the notice wilt be, subject to any contract to the contrary, 15 days or 6 months expiring with the end of a month or year of the tenancy as the case may be. This provision clearly indicates that the right which is created by the lease is the right of tenancy. Section 117 by which agricultural tenancy has been kept outside the purview of the Act Hat also been referred as "leases for agricultural purpose." 

 25. From the aforesaid provision of the Act it is clear that the terms, 'lease' and 'tenancy' are cognate terms, implying the same kind of jural relationship. There appears to be absolutely no basis for imagining that 'lease' is a kind of relationship peculiar to non-agricultural land and that the terms 'tenancy' is a kind of expression which is exclusively applicable to only agricultural land. 

 26. It is the contention of Mr. Khandker that by the Indenture of lease a lease of some non-agricultural Govt. Khas land was granted to him by the Provincial Government in consequence whereof he became a lessee under the Government, the lessor, and that the description of his status as a tenant in the said Indenture was misconceived. In support of his contention, that a transaction of lease is to be distinguished from that of tenancy, Mr. Khandker has referred with a good deal of persistence to the definition clauses of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the Transfer of Property Act and have also cited certain decisions which, in our opinion, have rather demonstrated that the distinction between the said two terms, which Mr. Khandker has so strenuously tried to impress upon us, is without any difference. A lessee is, in its ordinary acception, no other then a tenant and the lessor, the landlord, and when such terms have been given any statutory definitions in any enactment they have not departed from meanings. 

 This view of Jenkins, J was approved by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Abhirain Goswami Vs. Shyama Charan Nandi, 36 IA 148; 36 Cal 1003; 14 CWN 1; Raja Kumar Thankur Vs. Mogblal Pandey, LR 44 IA 246; ILR 45 Cal 87; 22 CWN 201 and also Raghu Nath Roy Marwari Vs. Raja Durga Prasad Singh LR 46 IA 158; 23 CWN 914. The view expressed in these judicial authorities as to the characteristics of a lease is in conformity to the definition of the term as has been given in section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. In such a transaction the relationship which is created between the transferor and the transferee of certain immovable property in consideration of periodical payment of what is called rent is essentially that of landlord and tenant and this relationship of landlord and tenant arises independently of the nature of the immovable property, the subject matter of the lease. 

 28. It is pertinent to mention that the provisions of Chapter V of the Transfer of Property Act, which reserve a large scope for settlement of terms by mutual agreement, were for a long time the only legal provisions regulating the rights and liabilities arising out of the leases other than for agricultural purposes. With the gradual change in the socio-economic conditions of the country, there was a consequent increase in the pressure of population in urban and other areas resulting in larger demand for land and houses for purposes other than agriculture. By the time the Second Great War broke out, the necessity for some legislations for regulating the leases of residential houses and non-agricultural land was felt and in consequence certain legislative measures were promulgated for control of rent of certain premises and non-agricultural land and for safeguarding the interests of the tenants of such premises and land. Since the partition of the country, these legislations have gradually taken more comprehensive shape. Now, the leases of premises for residential and non-residential purposes solely on payment of rent are controlled by the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 and the Transfer of Property Act, 1892. So far as the leases of non-agricultural land were concerned, the ultimate specific legislation was the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, which was enacted "to make better provisions relating to the law of landlord and tenant of certain non-agricultural tenancies in East Bengal." Sub-section (2) of section 85 of the Act, however, excludes the non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Government from the operation of the said Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 29. It should be noticed that the lessees of the premises, as contemplated in the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, as well as the lessees of non-agricultural land, as have been dealt in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, have been defined as "tenants" for the purposes of the respective enactment. By such definition of the term in the said Ordinance and Act, it has been given a restricted meaning for the purposes of the said Ordinance and Act. 

 In 1951 a comprehensive legislation was promulgated in East Bengal, which is now Bangladesh, in the shape of The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 30. This Act may be divided into two main divisions in accordance with the subject matter dealt therein: (1) the first one containing parts II and IV of the Act relates to the acquisition of the interests of all rent-receivers and the lands in excess of the maximum limit set down by the Act and (2) the second one comprising part V, of the Act relates to the tenancy laws which are to be operative after the process of acquisition as provided in the earlier parts of the Act has been completed. 

 31. The peculiar feature of the tenancy laws prevalent in this part of the country since the ancient days was a kind to successive sub-infeudation and creation of interests of various grades superimposed upon one and the same piece of land. The main object of the Act, as contained in parts II and IV, was to eliminate all those interests Intervening between the Government and the tenant in actual occupation of the land and to create, throughout the country, one class of tenants directly under the Government, which would be the sole receiver of rent payable by the tenants in respect of the lands comprised in their tenancy, and their rights and liabilities would be regulated by uniform Code of laws. The definition of tenant, as has been given in section 2 (27) of the Act, is in the same language as in the Bengal Tenancy Act and, by providing a definition of land in the Act, it has been made clear that the land comprised in his tenancy may be agricultural or non-agricultural. As we see, 'land' has been defined in section 2(16) of the Act as meaning land cultivated, uncultivated or covered with water at any time of the year and includes benefits to arise out of land, houses or building and all things attached, to the earth of permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth and this definition does not leave any room for doubt that the term "tenant" within the meaning of the Slate Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a generic expression of which tenant of agricultural holding is a species. This view is reinforced by the definition of "Khas land" or "land in Khas possession" as provided in clause (15) of section 2 of the Act which "includes any land let out together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto, otherwise than in perpetuity". That the scope of parts II and IV of the Act relating to acquisition of all rent-receiving interests is wide enough to include such interests connected with non-agricultural land as well as borne out also by the definition of rent-receiver, as provided in clause (23) of Section 2 of the Act which runs thus: 

 33. Part V of the Act incorporating the tenancy laws has come into force on different dates in different areas of the country on repeal of a number of enactments including The Bengal Tenancy Act and The Sylhet Tenancy Act in the respective areas and the rights and liabilities of the tenants which were formerly determined under the relevant repealed enactments are now regulated by the provisions of the said part of the Act. Most of the repealed enactments, no doubt, relate to the rights connected with agricultural land, but the scope of this new Act in respect of the class of tenants dealt therein is manifestly wider than those of the earlier legislations so repealed. This Act, unlike the Bengal Tenancy Actor the Sylhet Tenancy Act, is not confined in its application to the tenancies for agricultural or horticultural purposes only. Both of the main divisions of the Act, dealing with acquisition of superior interests and tenancy rights, as referred to above, purport to cover interests in all kinds or properties, agricultural or non-agricultural. 

 34. Mr. Khandker appears to have accepted the position that the assessee under the two taxing statutes for the purpose of levy of. Development and Relief Tax and Additional Development and Relief Tax are the tenants within the meaning of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but contends that such tenants, as contemplated in State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, are necessarily-tenants of agricultural holding and that the appellant does not belong to the said category. Mr. Khandker is undoubtedly correct in the first part of his contention that the assessee must necessarily be a tenant within the meaning of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. because the said Act was the existing general law dealing with the rights and liabilities of tenants at the time of the enactment of the two taxing statutes and the said statutes which purport to fasten a liability upon the tenants to be assessed to certain taxes do not lay down any special definition of tenant. It may also be noted in this connection that the proviso to Section 2(1) of the Finance Ordinance, 1958, in particular, which makes the principles laid down in Section 26 of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act applicable for the assessment of rent-free land of a tenant for the purpose of levy of the tax imposed by the said Ordinance makes it abundantly clear that the tenant contemplated in the Ordinance is no other than the tenant within the meaning of the said Act. The second part of the contention of the appellant seeking to exclude himself from the said category, however, appears to have no reasonable basis. 

 35. Now, the definition of tenant, as has been given in section 2(27) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act/is in the same language as in the definition of tenant in the Bengal Tenancy Act, which, as we have already noticed, is a kind of general definition without specifying the nature of the land held by such a tenant, agricultural or non-agricultural. If the provisions of the Act are carefully examined, it will be seen that the terms, "tenant" and "raiyat" have been used in the Act for distinct purposes, the former implying the holder of any kind of land and the latter implying the holder of agricultural land only. 

 "81A. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this part, the rights and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under Provincial Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such land under the provisions of this Act, shall, where the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, applied to such land, at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by the provisions of that Act. 

 Provided that, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non agricultural tenant shall sublet the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms and conditions whatsoever and, if any tenancy or any part of a tenancy is sublet in contravention of this provision, the interest of the non-agricultural tenant in the tenancy or in that part of the tenancy, as the case may be shall be extinguished, and the tenancy or the part of the tenancy shall vest in the Provincial Government from the date of such sub-letting free from all encumbrances." 

 37. In section 82, clauses (1) and (2) new definitions of 'bona fide-cultivator' and 'raiyat' have been given for the purposes of the tenancy part of the Act and it has been provided in clause (8) of the said section that the word ‘malik’ should be deemed to have been subs-muted for the word 'raiyat' or 'tenant', wherever they occur in part V in relation to agricultural land. The provisions which have been quoted above clearly contemplate two categories of holders of land, one in case of a lease for agricultural purposes and the other is a general expression without such limitation as to the nature of land. When the Act itself envisages a tenant of a holding without any limitation as to its nature and a raiyat meaning thereby a tenant of agricultural holding, there seems to be no valid reason for taking the view that the tenant as has been mentioned in the taxing statutes under consideration shall be deemed to refer to only tenants of an agricultural holding. 

 38. After part V of the Act has come into force, all raiyats, that is, tenants of agricultural land, have been styled as maliks and their rights and liabilities are regulated, as has been provided in section 81 of the Act, by the provisions of part V of the Act subject to the condition that in case of a lease of any land by the Government for a particular period the rights and liabilities of such a lease to be governed by the terms of the lease. The position of the tenants of non-agricultural lands under the Government has been dealt with in section 81A of the Act, as has been quoted above. According to the said section such tenants have been divided into two categories, namely, (1) those who have become tenants under the Government because of the acquisition of the superior interest of their landlords by the government under the Act and were governed by the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act at the time of the acquisition of the superior rights over the said land, and (2) other non-agricultural tenants. The rights and liabilities of the tenants of the first category would be regulated by the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and those of the second category would be controlled by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act except in the matters relating to determination, enhancement or reduction of rent or sub-letting, which would necessarily be governed by the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 39. It is necessary to refer at this stage to the definition of "non-agricultural tenant" as has been provided in section 2 (17) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which is as follows: 

 40. Learned Judges of the High Court appear to have made some confusion in interpreting the said definition clause and in holding the appellant to be a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of that clause on the view that he was a holder of a lease in perpetuity. The appellant is obviously not a holder of a lease in perpetuity, as the preamble of the Indenture of the lease clearly provides that it is a lease for the specified period of 99 years. Term no 23 (3) (a) of the Indenture does no doubt reserve the right of option for the lessee for the renewal of the lease after the expiry of the specified period of 99 years and in case of exercise of such option the lessor shall have to renew the lease but on such terms, covenants and conditions and for such period as the lessor may determine. There is no doubt that this is not a lease in perpetuity but is one for a fixed period, though a lease in perpetuity is unlike in England, sanctioned under the law of the country, as provided in section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. Although there seems to have been some misapprehension in the said observation of the learned Judges of the High Court in respect of the meaning of non-agricultural tenant, their conclusion that the appellant is a non-agricultural tenant cannot be taken exception to in view of the fact that he having held lands for purposes other than agriculture or horticulture comes under the first part of the said definition clause and being the owner of the buildings standing on such land does not come under the second part of the said clause. According to the said definition, a person who is a tenant in respect of the land as well as the building standing thereon on the basis of a lease which is not perpetual is not a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of the said definition clause and he may be a tenant coming within the purview of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963. According to the definition clause quoted above, only such a person will be a non-agricultural tenant as has constructed the building, if any, in his own right on the land leased out to him by the owner of such land. It is, therefore, abundantly clear that the appellant is a tenant as well as a non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of sub-section (2) of section 81A of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and his rights and liabilities are, according to the said provision, to be governed by the terms of the Indenture of his lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act except in regard to his powers of sub-letting and in matters relating to determination, enhancement and reduction of rent, which shall be regulated according to the provisions, of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, notwithstanding anything contrary thereto in the terms of the lease or elsewhere. There is, therefore, no difficulty in holding that the learned Judges of the High Court were correct in taking the view that the appellant is assessee under the provisions of the two taxing Statutes as have been referred to above. 

 45. There appears to be, however, one irregularity in respect of the demand under challenge. It is to be noticed that the method of payment of rent as has been settled in the a terms of the Indenture of lease is by two half yearly installments payable according to English Calendar year but according to the rules; framed read with section 135 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, rent is payable, according to the Bengali Calendar year. Having regard to the provision of section 81 A, which has been already considered and section 135, which also protects the terms of agreement as contained in the Indenture, the appellant's liability to pay according to the English Calendar year has not been affected. From the provisions of the East Pakistan Ordinance No.LXXXII of 1958 and the East Pakistan Finance Act, 1967 it is clear that the taxes under the said two enactments were to be levied and collected with effect from the first day of the Bengali year whereas the local rate under Article 59 of the Basic Democracies Order is to collected along with the rent of the land, which is payable by the appellant in accordance with the terms of the lease, according to English Calendar Year. The break up of the demand as stated by the respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition shows that annual rent payable by the appellant was split up, for the purpose of showing his liability from the beginning of the Bengali Year. This being contrary to the terms of the Indenture of lease is not permissible. The annual rent as well as the local rate, so far as the appellant is concerned are to be collected according to the English Calendar year. The demand of the annual rent and local rate contrary to the said time schedule was not therefore lawful.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed A.B. Mahmud Husain

parties:
Giri Bala Das ----- Petitioner. 
Vs. 
Basudev Dey and others ----- Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
S. M. Husain, J—This Rule is directed against a judgment of the Lower Appellate Court affirming an order of the Trial Court dismissing the petitioner's application for pre-emption of the suit land under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, XXIII of 1949. The petitioner's application for pre-emption of the suit land was con-tested by the opposite parties as co-sharers alleging that neither the transferee nor the transferee had any right, title and interest the suit land and the question of pre-emption of the basis of the said transfer does not wise. In the impugned transfer under pre-emption one Profullya Kumar Dey was the transferee on his death his right, title and interest if any devolved on this heirs. The alleged transfer took place on 12.8.61 and the present pre-emption case were filed on 21.5.62 Although the pre-emption case was filed beyond the statutory period of four months from the date of the alleged transfer but the courts below concurrently found that the case was filed within four months from the date of the knowidea FA of" the petitioner about the said alleged transfer. However, when the pre-emption case was filed by that time the transferee Profullya Kumar Dey had already died and the heirs of the transferee were accordingly made parties in the preemption case. It appears that one of the heirs of the aforesaid transferee was left out, that is opposite party No. 6 and he was impleaded in the proceeding on 26-9-64, almost after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case. The courts below dismissed the petitioner's pre-emption case holding firstly, that the addition of opposite party No. 6 after 2 years makes the application for pre-emption itself barred by limitation and even if the pre-emption case in allowed against other heirs of the transferee, the same cannot be allowed against opposite party No. 6 since it was barred by limitation and on that account the pre-emption case shall fail since no partial pre-emption can be allowed in favour of other heirs of the said transferee. 

 2. In this Rule 2 questions have been raised by the petitioner, firstly, whether by adding Opp. Party No. 6 after 2 years from the date of the filing of the pre-emption case, the pre-emption case itself becomes barred by limitation and secondly, whether partial pre-emption against other heirs of the said transferee can be allowed in this case. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that under Sub-Section (1) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, if the main application for pre-emption to have been filed within 4 months from the date of the knowledge of the alleged transfer, any subsequent addition of any party would not make the application as barred by limitation. It has been further submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act partial pre-emption has not been prohibited as has been found in the case of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 3. So far as the addition of parties in the present case is concerned opposite party No. 6 being an admitted heir of the aforesaid transferee is not only a necessary but a proper party. In a pre-emption case the proper party is the transferee whose transfer is challenged. The transferee being dead the heirs of the transferee must be held to be the parties in the pre-emption, case. In that view the opposite party No. 6 was one of the proper and necessary party in this pre-emption case and the case itself would have remain  defective for non-joinder of such proper and necessary parties. The question now is whether such joinder of a proper and necessary party after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case shall make the pre-emption case itself, barred by limitation at least as against the aforesaid added party as such. Section 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that the procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be followed, as far as it can be made applicable, in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction. Thus, an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act before a Civil Court is governed the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Sub-rule (5) of rule 10 of Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure provides, that subject to the provisions of section 22 of the Limitation Act, the proceeding as against any person added as defendant shall be demand to have begun only on the service of the summons. Section 22 of the Limitation Act provides that whether after the institution of the suit if a new defendant is added, the suit shall, as regards him, be deemed to have been instituted when he was so made a party, provided that such addition has not been made owing to an assignment or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suite Considering the provisions of section 141 and sub-rule (5) of rule 10 of Order I of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 22 of Limitation Act as aforesaid it clearly appears that in a pre-emption case either under the State Acquisition Act or under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act if a proper and necessary party like an heir of transferee is added as a party to the proceeding evidently after the statutory period of limitation such pre-emption case must be held to be barred by limitation at least against such party added after the period of limitation as such. In the present case it is on admission that when the pre-emption ewe was initially filed, the opposite party No. 6 was already born by then and was a minor heir of the aforesaid transferee and that he was added as such in the pre-emption case after 2 years from the date of the institution of the pre-emption case, long after the statutory .period of limitation. Thus the irresistible conclusion is that this pre-emption case is barred by limitation at least as against the opposite party No. 6. 

 4. The next question is, if the pre-emption case is barred by limitation as against opposite party No. 6 why the same shall not be allowed with regard to the other heirs of the transferee, who were on record admittedly within the period of limitation, that is opposite parties No. 1-4. This question in certainly leads to a vital issue as to whether partial pre-emption is allowed under the law. So far as pre-emption under Section 26 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 96 F of the State Acquisition Act are concerned, there are consistent Judicial pronouncements that partial pre-emption could not be allowed both under the law and equity. Single Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in 38 C.W.N. 654 and 49 CWN 242 and a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 19 DLR 659 held that partial pre-emption was not allowed under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. A Single Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 13 DLR 323, a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 14 DLR 847 and another Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court reported in 28 D.L.R, 400 held that partial pre-emption was not allowed under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act. 

 5. The question still remains as to whether partial pre-emption could still be allowed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, Section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides that one or more co sharers-tenants of the holding, a portion or share which is transferred may apply to the court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. Under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act provides that if a portion or share of a holding of a raiyat is transferred, one or more co-sharers tenants of the holding may apply to the court for the said portion or share to be transferred to him or themselves. Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, provides that if a portion or share of the non-agricultural land held by a non-agricultural tenant is transferred, one or more cashiers tenants of such land may apply to the court for such portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, Thus basically the language of sub section (1) of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, sub-section(1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition Act and sub-section(1) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is almost in the similar language that where if a portion or share of any holding or land is transferred, one or more co-sharers-tenants of such holding or laid may apply to the Court for such portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, Taking into consideration the aforesaid similar .language in the relevant statutes concerned it clearly appears that the provision of pre-emption both under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act and under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act are similar excepting that under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act, all the co-sharers of the holding must be impleaded in the pre-emption case whereas under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act a co-sharer may apply for being added as a party in a pre-emption case, The aforesaid decisions of the Calcutta High Court and Dacca High Court referred to above disallowed partial pre-emption in view of the language imported in sub-section(1) of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and sub-section (I) of section 96 of the State Acquisition Act, The language imported in sub-section (I) of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is also similar to that of the language imported in sub-section (i) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that view, the aforesaid judicial decisions disallowing partial pre-emption under Bengal-Tenancy Act and State Acquisition Act are also applicable in the case of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Partial pre-emption has been disallowed under the Bengal Tenancy Act and State Acquisition Act on equitable ground and for the same reason partial pre-emption should be disallowed under Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. In that view no partial pre-emption can be allowed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, XXIII of 1949.

parties:
Abdul Mannan and others  ------ Appellants.
Vs.
Kulada Ranjan Mowali and others  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.-This appeal is against a judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division, discharging a Rule issued on an application made by the appellants under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order or the Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali, recording abatement of a suit, instituted by the appellants, under section 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972. 

 3. According to the plaintiff's case, as made out in the plaint, the disputed lends appertained to the Estate of Bishweshwar Roy Choudhury, which were diluviated and after the said lands had reappeared as reformation in stu and had become fit for possession. Babu Rajeswar Choudhury, the then executor of the -10/- annas share of the Estate of late Bishweshwar Roy Choudhury settled the said lands with the predecessors of plaintiffs 1 to 42 and plaintiff No. 45 at an annual rent of Tk. 250/- on the basis of a Karsha Kabuliyat dated 1st Jaistha, 1331 B.S. corresponding to May, 1924.  The proprietors of 6/- annas share of the said Estate settled their 6/- annas share of the said lands with some of the defendants at an annual rent of 7k. 75/- on the basis of another Kabuliyat of the sane date, namely, 1st Jaistha, 1331 B.S. which were ultimately sold, and purchased in auction by the landlords, in execution of a decree for rent obtained by them and were then settled in 1344-45 13.S. with the predecessors of some of the plaintiffs on the basis of a Kabuliyat at a rental of Tk. 75. After the rent receiving interests of the previous landlords had been acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the Government has stepped into the shoes of the previous landlords and the plaintiffs have become tenants directly under the Government, in respect of the said lands, some of which had been wrongly recorded in the name of the Government. The Government, however, have had no right, title and interest in the said lands nor any right to dispossess the plaintiffs from any part thereof, which are the lands of their tenancy. 

 5. After the amendment of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 the contesting defendants filed an application for abatement of the suit under the said amended provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. While disposing of the said application by his order dated 24.3.73. the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have gone into the question of the truth or otherwise of the allegations made in the plaint and having held, on the basis of certain papers, that the story of reformation in situ and the induction of the plaintiffs as tenants could not be believed, recorded an order of abatement of the suit in respect of the lands in suit on The basis of the amended provisions of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 7. The High Court Division was moved under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure on behalf of the plaintiffs against the order of abatement made by the learned Subordinate Judge but the learned Judges of the High Court Division affirmed the decision of the Subordinate Judge on holding that the suit had been rightly held to have abated in view of President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 amending the provisions of Sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 8. Special Leave to appeal was granted by the Appellant Division to consider whether the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by the Presidential Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 could be applied in respect of the lands in the instant suit. This appeal, thus, raises an important question as to the interpretation of the amended provisions of the aforesaid two sections of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 10. It should be pointed out at the out-set that the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Judges of the High Court Division were not correct in going into the question as to the truth of the allegations made in the plaint before any evidence had been adduced in deciding the question of abatement of the suit as a preliminary issue. To decide the question of abatement of the suit in the light of the provisions of the newly enacted sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act., the proper procedure which should have been followed was to take the allegations made in the plaint as such and then to see if the relevant provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act were attracted to them. 

 11. The plaint of the suit, out of which the appeal arises, if properly read, would show that the claim of the plaintiffs is based upon an allegation of settlement of the tenancy right in respect of the disputed lauds in their favour by the former proprietors of the estate to which the disputed lands appertained. The said proprietors are alleged to have acquired right to the said lands when they reappeared after division by virtue of their right to reformation in situ and there appears to be no allegation in the plaint relating to accrual of any right of accretion at any stage, requiring the application of section 87 as amended by President's Order Nos. 72 and 137 of 1972 but as the trial Court held that the suit abated in view of the amended section 87, and the learned Judges of the High Court expressed the view that the suit had abated in view of the provisions of both the sections, namely sections 86 and 87, as amended the Appellate Division granted special leave to consider the meaning and scope of both the said two sections amended by the relevant Presidential Orders. 

 The lands gained from the river is or sea by the means above mentioned are a frequent source of contention and affray, and although the law and custom of the country have established rules applicable to such cases, these rules not being generally known, the Court of Justice have sometimes found it default to determine the rights of litigant parties claiming chars or other lands gained in the manner above described. 

 19. The former tenancy law, as incorporated in sections 17 and 18 of the Rent Act 1859, recognized the principle that a tenant was liable to enhancement of rent in case of increment of the area of the land of his tenancy by allusion or otherwise and that similarly a tenant was entitled to abatement of rent in case of diminution of the area of the land of his tenancy by dilution or otherwise. On diluvion a tenant was entitled to reduction of rent in respect of the diluviated property under section 17 of the Act but his title to such property was not affected in any way by such dilution and whenever they said property reappeared he could take back the property in his own right, however long the period of submergence might be. On the repeal of the Rent Act 1859, by the enactment of Bengal Tenancy Act 1885, similar provisions as to abatement and enhancement of rent were made in section 52 of the Act. There were no specific provisions relating to the right of accretion or right to reformation in sue either in the Rent Act of 1889 or The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885. Such matters were regulated by e provisions of Alluvion and diluvion Regulation of 1825 and the principles laid down by the judicial authorities. Some change was effected in 1929 when section 86A was inserted in the Bengal Act by an amendment introduced by Bengal Act IV of 1928, which provided that the tenants' right in the diluviated lands, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, would be deemed to have been surrendered and would be extinguished, if the tenant obtained any abatement in respect of such dilution. This extinction of the right in respect of reformation in situ was dependent on the tenant's obtaining an abatement of rent of such land which was to be deemed, according to the amendment, an act or surrender on his part. It was, however, clearly provided in sub section (2) of this newly inserted section that such extinction of right would not affect the accrual of his right of accretion in respect of the said land if it was available to him under any other law. In 1938 a new section 86A was substituted in place of the aforesaid provision, enlarging the rights of the tenants in certain respects. This new provision provided for automatic abatement of rent in case of the loss of land by delusion, and also ensured the subsistence of the right title and interest of the tenant in the lands lost by such diluvion for a period of 20 years, notwithstanding the abatement of rent of such lands. 

 20. After the partition of the country a big change was effected in 1951 in the land tenure system of the country by the enactment of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 where under all grades of rent-receivers intervening between the Government and the actual occupants of the soil were abolished and such occupants became tenants directly under the Government, subject to a ceiling as to the maximum area of land which a tenant can hold. No substantial change in regard to the law as to accretion or reformation in situ was, however, brought about by this enactment excepting that a specific provision incorporating the law of accretion, which was so long regulated by the provisions of Bengal Regulation XXI of 1825 was made in section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The provisions relating to abatement of rent due to diluvion of some land of the tenancy and subsistence of the tenants' title in respect o such land, similar to those contained in section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act, were incorporated in section 86 of the new Act, Part V of the Act which contains sections 86 and 87 came into force on different dates in different areas of the country on the publication of the Notifications as prescribed under section 79 of the Act and, according to the provisions of section 80 of the Act, on and from the date of coming into force of the said Part in a particular area the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed in the said area. 

 21. On June 28, 1972 the riparian owner's right of accretion which was recognized by the usage and custom of the country, as referred to in the preamble of the Bengal Regulation XI of 1815 and which had enjoyed the sanction of positive legislation for about a century and a half was abrogated by President's Order No. 72 of 1972, which substituted, in place of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, a new Section 87 which is to the following effect; 

 "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being enforce, when any land has been gained by gradual accession, whether from the recess of a river or of the sea, it shall not be considered as an increment to the holding or tenancy to which it may be thus annexed, but shall vest absolutely in the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and shall be at their disposal." 

 22. The aim and object of this amending legislation has not been spelt out in the Presidential Order nor there do any reference in the order to any possible mischief which this legislation intended to remedy. It has been stated in a very brief preamble, as is usual in modern legislation, that "it is expedient to amend the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950" "for the purposes appearing" in the enacting provisions. When the law of accretion was given a legislative shape in Bengal Regulation XI of 1825 the law-making authority explained in a very detailed and comprehensive preamble, which may have been prolix in certain respects but sufficiently expressive of the considerations which weighed with the said authority in making the said legislation. This preamble has been quoted above for the proper appreciation of the nature and background of the right created by the said regulation and the principle underlying it. 

 "(2) The provision of sub-section (1) shall apply to all land so gained whether before or after the 28th June, 1972, but shall not apply to any land so gained before the said date if the right of a Malik to hold such land as an increment to his holding was finally recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Sixth Amendment) Order 1972 	(P.O. No. 137 of 1972), under the law then in force. 

 27. The effect of making the provision of sub-section (1) of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act applicable to any land which may have been gained by accession by the recess of a river or the sea before 28.6.72, as it purported to have been done under President's Order No. 137 of 1972 appears to do away with, in the literal sense of the words used in the amending Presidential Order/ the right which had been acquired by the riparian owner under Bengal Regulation XI of 1825 and, if such accession took place after Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act had come into force, also under section 87 of the Act, as it stood before the enactment of the President's Order No. 72 of 1972. 

 31. The provision of sub-section (1) of section 87 that the land gained by accession shall not be considered as an increment to the holding or tenancy makes it abundantly clear that the said provision is applicable only to the land which has been added to the land of a raiyat or any other tenant and it is not attracted to the case of the land which has been added to the khas land of a proprietor or a tenure-holder. If for the applicability of the aforesaid provision the Legislature conceived of a situation where there were the lands of a tenant as well as those of a proprietor or a tenure-holder, there appears to be absolutely no good reason to exclude the khas land of a proprietor or a tenure-holder from the operation of the said provision and thus to discriminate against those who were not so. The inference seems to be irresistible that, for the application of the said provision, the Legislature was conceiving of a situation where there were no proprietors nor tenure holders but were only tenants and such a situation arose when all the rent receiving interests were acquired by the Government under the provisions of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 24. According to the aforesaid provisions on and from the date specified in the notifications all tenants in respect of the lands of their tenancies, and the rent receivers in respect of their khas lands, became tenants directly under the Government in respect of the said lands. If any land had accreted to the land of the tenants or the khas land of the rent-receivers before the date specified in the said notifications, the said accreted land became a part of their tenancies or khas land, as the case may be, under the law then in force and they became tenants, by virtue of the provisions of clauses (e) and (f) of sub-section (4) of Section 3 of the Act, directly under the Government in respect of the said lands. The right of accretion accruing to the tenants or the rent-receivers in respect of the lands, accreting to the lands of their tenancies of khas lands, was given a new statutory force by the said legislative & provisions and the right so acquired became indefeasible in the sense that it was not dependent for its enforceability on any further recognition or declaration by any authority or court. Since the State Acquisition an Tenancy Act had come into force on 16.5.51, the notifications under section 3 of the Act were issued in respect of certain big rent receivers from time to time as a special measure for acquisition of their interests on or about the 2nd April, 1956 several omnibus notifications under section 3 of the Act purporting to acquire the entire interest of the whole body of the rent-receivers within the province of East Bengle with effect from 14.4.56 were issued, and since 14th April, 1956 all accreted lands, if any, adjoining those of the tenants or rent receivers became parts of their tenancies by virtue of the aforesaid provisions of The State Acquisition on and Tenancy Act. Having regard to the legal consequences flowing from the notifications under section 3 of the Act, as referred to above, no retrospective effect can be given to the provision of sub-section (2) of Section 87 of the Act, in any view of the matter, in most of the cases beyond 14.4.56, as the said provision read with that of sub-section (1) does not purport to extinguish or nullify any right which has been created under the provision of this very statute, of which this newly enacted section 87 is a part. It is significant that in the introductory clause of sub-section (1) of section 87, namely, "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force" there is reference only to ''any other law", but there is no reference to the law as contained in the present Act. It is, therefore, reasonable to conclude that there was never any intention on the part of the legislative authority to extend the retrospectively of section 87 beyond 14.4.56 or such other date as may have been specified in any earlier notifications under section 3(1) of the Act. 

 (2) Each proprietor, tenure holder and other rent receiver, whose interests in any estate, tenure or holding or tenancy or in any part of any estate, tenure or holding or tenancy as the case may be, within the area to which such roll relates, are acquired under this Act, shall with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of such notification in the Official Gazette, be entitled to retain possession of this Act, as a tenant. under the Provincial Government all lands of which he is entitled to retain possession of and holy, subject to the provision of this to, as a to cant, under Provincial Government all lands of which he is entitled to retain possession under Chapter IV and he hall.; to pay rent for such lands to the Provincial Government ; 

 37. There appears to be another limitation to the retrospectively of section 87 of the Act. This section is contained in Part V of the Act, which includes sections 9 to 152 of the Act. We have already noticed that section 79 provides for commencement of the provisions contained in Part V of the Act in different areas on different dates and section 80 provides for repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act along with some other Statutes in the said areas on the commencement of the sad Part therein. It is pertinent to quote section 79 in this connection, which is as follows; 

 "unless (Sic) the right of a Malik to hold such land as an increment to his holding was finally recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (6th Amendment) Order 1972 (President's Order No. 137 of 1972) under the law then in force.
