 40. The use of the term 'Malik" in sub section (2) is also significant. Such term can be used in place of the term 'raiyat' or tenant only after Part V of the Act has come into operation. Section 81 (1) of the Act provides that on and from the date of coming into force of the whole of Part V in any area, there shall be within that area one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, Maliks' and the rights and liabilities of every such land holder shall be regulated by the provisions of this Part, and clause (8) of section 82, which is an interpretation section also provides that on and from the date of coming into force of the whole of this Part in any area, the word 'Malik' shall be deemed to have been substituted for the word 'rayiat' or 'tenant'. The use of the word malik in place of the word 'raiyat' or tenant' in sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act to denote a person whose right to hold the newly added land as accretion to his holding or tenancy might be recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the commencement of President's Order No. 137 of 1972 unmistakably points out that the legislative authority was contemplating a situation in subsection (I) and sub-section (2) of Section 87 Which could arise only after the coming into force of Part V of the Act in the area in which the accreting lands are situated. The retrospectively of the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act cannot therefore be pushed beyond the date of the commencement of Part V of Act in the area where the accretion in question had taken place and it is only such accretion as took place after the coming into force of Part V of the Act to which sub-section (1) read with sub-section (2) of section 87, may apply. The date of the commencement of Part V of the Act in any area must necessarily be a date later than that of the publication of the notification under Section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act in that area. 

 44. We have noticed that all accretions, which took place before the notification under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act, have been statutorily recognized to be the lands appertaining to the tenancies of the riparian owners and the provisions of clause (e) and (f) of Sections 3(4) or items (2) and (4) of section 44 of the Act have clearly conferred the right of tenancy upon the riparian owner in respect of such accredited lands. Any suit etc. which may be brought in respect of such land is not obviously a suit in which the assertion of the claim of right is on the basis of the riparian owner's right of accretion. Such a suit is really on the basis of the statutory right as has been conferred by clauses (e) and (0 of sections 3 (4) or items (2) and (4) of sect ion 44 of the Act and is, there-fore, clearly outside the purview of sub-section (3) of section 37 of the Act. As regards the accretions, which took place after the publication of the notifications under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act but before the coming into force of Part V of the Act, they are also, we have noticed above, beyond the scope of sub-sections (1) and (2) of sections 87 and as such, the rights which accrued to the riparian owners in respect of such accretions have not been affected in any way by the said provisions of section 87. There seems to be no conceivable reason why the legislative authority, while preserving the right of a riparian owner in respect of such accretions under sub-section (1) and (2) would deprive, by sub-section (3) the said owner of the remedy to enforce the said right. Such reading of sub-section (3) would undoubtedly lead to injustice and some absurd consequences, which cannot be the intention of the legislative authority. Sub-section (3) should be read harmoniously with sub-sections (1) and (2) and the land gained or alleged to have been gained from the recess of a river or the sea, as have been contemplated in subsection (3) must be such lands as are within the purview of sub sections (1) and (2) of section 87. It will necessarily be those accredited lands which have appeared as hard soil only after the coming into force of Part V of the Act and the provision as to the and abatement of suits etc. as made in sub-section (3) are attracted in case of those suits etc. where a claim of the right is asserted in respect of such lands. 

 (2) "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successors in interest shall be extinguished in such lands or a portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by dilution took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972 lands or portion thereof within twenty years of their loss by dilution, and be liable to pay the arrears of rent without interest or damage in respect of the land, which has re-appeared, for the period during which it was lost or four years whichever is less; 

 Explanation:-For the purpose of this section, the word "family" shall have the same meaning as in clause (a) of section 151 J, as amended by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order 1972". 

 46. It will appear that the provision of subsection (1) of this new section, which latest to abatement of rent in respect of the land lost by dilution did not bring about any great charge in the law then in force, as this provision is similar to sub-section (I) of the old section as amended by East Pakistan Ordinance No. XXI of 1969 which dispensed with the filing of an application by the tenant to the Revenue Officer for abatement of rent, as was required under the former provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act. This provision is clearly prospective and refers to land which is still subject to delusion. The provision of sub-section (2) which purports to extinguish the title of the tenant to the land which has been lost by delusion, whether before or after the commencement of the President's Order No. 135 of 1972, is also clearly prospective and there is no difficulty as to the construction of the said provision. But the construction of subsection (3) which purports to confer title upon the Government in respect of the lands which were lost by delusion under sub-section (2) but re-appeared before the date of commencement of the Order seems to be fraught with some difficulty, in so far as its real import is concerned. The plain meaning of the said provision seems to be that the lands which were lost by diluvion but have reappeared before the commencement of the Order and also the lands so lost by diluvion which may re-appear on or after the said date shall vest in the Government and shall be at the disposal. So far as the second part of the subsection is concerned, there is no difficulty, but the first part of the sub-section which provides for accrual of right in favour of the Government in respect of the lands which were lost by diluvion but have re appeared before the commencement of the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 does not appear to be consistent with the provision of subsection (2) of the section, which purports to extinguished the title of the tenant to such land as has been lost by diluvion. Subsection (2) does not appear to contemplate a case where the lands which were lost by diluvion before the commencement of the order but have also re-appeared before such commencement does on the other hand, mean that the title of the tenant to the land which is lost to him by diluvion at the time of the commencement of the Order shall be extinguished on such commencement, although the diluvion took place before such commencement. If the diluvion and the loss in consequence thereof have ceased, and the land reappeared before the commencement of the Order there was no discontinuance of his right and it subsisted with all its force. But the first part of subsection (3) which purports to vest such lands on the Government seems to be incongruous to a certain extent, because, by such vesting, the tenant is also correspondingly divested of all his rights by necessary implication, although under sub-section (2) which provides for the extinguishment of the tenants' right, such divestment is not contemplated. However, if sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 86 are read together, it appears that the legislative authority wanted to give a kind of retrospective effect to the provision of subsection (2) although such intention has not been properly expressed in the language used in the said subsection (3) is clear so far as it Oaks to divest, though in-directly a tenant of his title to the land which was once lost by diluvion but reappeared before the commencement of the Order, unless his right to repos session was recognized or declared by a competent authority or court. But the question is, as it was the case of sub-sections (I) and (2) of section 87 whether the lawmaker intended to give the full or limited retrospective effect to the provision of sub-section (3) of section 85 of the Act. 

 50. Now, the provisions of sections 86 and 87 as have been enacted by President's Order Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 are clearly inapplicable to the facts of the suit out of which this appeal arises, inasmuch as there is no assertion in the plaint of the suit of a claim of the right of accretion or reformation in situ in respect of the lands in suit. The allegations made in the plaint are that the lands in suit which formerly appertained to the estate of Bishweswar Roy Chowdhury were lost by diluvion, that the said lands having re-appeared as firm land and become fit for cultivation, the 10/-annas share of the said lands was settled with the predecessors of plaintiffs No. 1 to 42 and plaintiff No. 45 by the proprietors of the said share on the 1st Jaistha, 1331 B S. that is, middle of May, 1924 and the remaining 6/4 as share in the said lands was also settled with some of the plaintiffs and the predecessors of some other plaintiffs in 1345 B.S. i.e. 1938/39. The basis of some of plaintiffs' claim in respect of the 10/- as share of the lands is the settlement granted by the landlords of the said share in May, 1924 and that of some other plaintiffs in respect of the remaining 6/- as share is the settlement granted to the said plaintiff by the landlords of the 6/- as share in 1938/39. There is no recital in the plaint as to accretion in respect of any part of the lands in suit. There are, no doubt, some allegations in the plaint as to diluvion of the land in suit aid subsequent reformation of the said lands but they happened, according to the said allegations, long ago i.e., prior to May 1924. The plaintiffs have prayed in the suit for a declaration of their title which accrued, according to the averment made in the plaints, from the settlement granted by the proprietors, partly in May 1924 and partly in 193 8/39. After the promulgation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in 1961 the rent receiving interests of the plaintiffs' landlords were acquired by the Government on publication of the notification under section 3 and section 43(2) of the Act and the plaintiffs have become tenants directly under the Government by virtue of the provisions of clause (e) and (f) of sub-section (4) of section (3) and items (2) and (4) of section 44 of the Act slur then. The immediate basis of the plaintiffs' claim in the suit, therefore, is the statutory right conferred upon them by section 3(4)(e) and (f) and there-after, under items (2) and (4) of section 44 and the remote basis of the claim may be said to be the settlement granted by the superior land-lords partly in 1924 and partly in 1938-39. But the basis of the plaintiffs' in respect of the lands  in their site after they had been lost by diluvion, and, as such, the present suit cannot be said, in any view of the matter, to be a suit for a claim to repossession of any land lost by diluvion which has re-appeared or is alleged to have reappeared.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed A.B. Mahmud Husain

parties:
Pradhip Das alias Shambhu and others ------- Judgment-debtor-Appellants.
Vs.
Kazal Das Sarma and others ------- Decree-holder-Respondents.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed C.J.: In this appeal by special leave the question is whether, on the death of a monthly tenant judgment-debtor, his heirs can be substituted for the purpose of execution of the decree for ejectment. In order words, whether a monthly tenancy is heritable. In an earlier decision of this Court in the case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Suresh Chandra Das, 32 DLR (171, which was followed in the case of Abdul Latif Vs. Abdul Mannan 1982 BCR, AD, 428, it was held by this Court that a monthly tenancy was not heritable and that the right of a monthly tenant in respect of a premises was his personal right which ceased on his death. Facts leading to this question are given below. 

 2. Respondents-landlords filed Other Suit No.172 of 1976 in the First Court of Munsif, Chittagong for ejectment of their monthly tenant, Sukhendu Bikash Das, on the ground of default in the payment of rent and also of bonafide requirement of the premises by them. The suit was decreed and the decree was upheld upto the High Court Division and thereafter the decree was put into execution by filing Execution Case No. 23 of 1984 against the tenant-judgment-debtor. During the pendency of the Execution Proceeding, the tenant, Sukhendu Das, died whereupon his heirs, who are appellants before us, were substituted. But they challenged the continuation of the Execution Proceeding by an application under section 151 of the Civil PC alleging that the tenancy created in favour of their predecessor, Sukhendu Das, ceased to exist on his death as it was his personal right and, as such, the decree against him became infructuous. Their contention was upheld by the learned Munsif who further held that for ejectment of the appellants a fresh suit was to be filed. But in revision, CR No.131 of 1985, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, held that the decree passed against the original tenant during his life time was perfectly valid and did not become infructuous and further that his heirs, though they did not inherit the tenancy right, were not trespassers either, but they became "tenants by sufferance". The Execution Proceeding was therefore held maintainable. Both the learned Single Judge and the learned Munsif sought support for their respective views from the decision of this Court in the earlier case of Abdus Sattar Vs. Suresh Chandra Das, 32 DLR (AD) 171 as referred to above. 

 3. Mr. SR Pal, learned Counsel, has appeared for the appellants in this case. He has submitted, though half-heartedly, that in view of the decision in the 32 DLR (AD) 171, the relationship of landlord and tenant in this case snapped on the death of the original tenant, Sukhendu Das, that his heirs did not inherit the tenancy and as such they could not have been substituted in the execution proceeding as the tenancy in favour of Sukhendu Das was a personal right which "is not heritable". The learned Counsel has, however, expressed serious doubt about the correctness of the decision in the 32 DLR (AD) 171 case and has submitted that if contention of the appellants in this case is rejected and decision of the learned Single Judge is upheld, the decision of this Court in 32 DLR (AD) 171 that the right of a monthly tenant is not heritable cannot but be reviewed and reconsidered. 

 4. In the earlier case, Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel had appeared for the appellant-landlord, and submitted that a monthly tenancy was heritable. To assist the Court Mr. SR Pal was engaged as amicus curiae in that ease. After hearing both Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed and Mr. SR Pal in that case, this Court rejected Mr. Mahbubuddin Ahmed's contention and held as stated above. In the instant case, Mr. SR Pal his appeared for the appellants-tenants; he has relied upon 32 DLR (AD) 171 decision in the different context. We engaged Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed as amicus curiae in this case. On behalf of the respondents-landlords Mr. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record has appeared to defend the decision of the High Court Division that the Execution Proceeding is quite maintainable. 

 5. As appears, the question before us in this appeal is a question of great public importance. Both Mr. SR Pal and Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed cited before us a great number of decisions including some decisions from the Indian jurisdiction. Mr. Pal, though he defends the High Court Division's decision in this case, has expressed the view that the earlier decision of this Court is not correct and that it has created serious complications in the landlord-tenant relation in respect of monthly tenants. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed has reiterated his earlier stand that the right of a monthly tenant is heritable and that the earlier decision of this Court was not based on correct interpretation of Sections 105 and 106 of the Transfer of Property Act governing "lease of immovable property". Both the learned Counsels have contended that the earlier decision of this Court had resulted from an erroneous view that a lease under section 105, TP Act is quite different from a lease under section 106 of that Act. They contend that a tenancy, whatever may be its duration, is a "lease" and that the right of the tenant is not a personal right but it is survived by, and passes on, to his "legal representatives", as defined in the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963 and also within the meaning of section 2(11) of the CP Code. In a nutshell, the decision in the previous case, in their opinion, needs to be reconsidered. 

 "106. In the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six months' notice expiring with the end of a year of the tenancy; and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen days' notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy " (relevant portion only) 

 This section provides that in the absence of a contract (or local law or usage), a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes "shall be deemed to be" a lease from year to year; and a lease for any other purpose, say for residential purpose, "shall be deemed to be" a lease from "month to month". It is here from which the term 'monthly tenancy' is derived. At to termination of these two kinds of leases, one from "year to year" and the other "from month to month", it has been provided in this section that in the case of the former, it is terminable by six months' notice expiring with the end of the year of the tenancy, and in the case of the latter, it is terminable by fifteen days' notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. On careful consideration of these sections, we find that a 'lease', whatever may be its purpose or duration, is created only under section 105. This section does not say that a lease for an agricultural or manufacturing purpose shall always be a lease from year to year, or a lease for any other purpose shall always be a lease from month to month. In this section a legal fiction has been introduced in the words, "shall be deemed to be", just to fill up the vacuum left in the contract if any, or when there is no contract creating the lease, as to duration of the lease and the manner of its termination. As to a tenancy from month to month, it is provided, it shall be deemed to be terminable by fifteen days notice. This does not necessarily mean that its duration is only one month and that on the expiry of one month it shall cease to exist. A monthly tenancy, if provided in the contract, may continue for months or years together unless it is determined by a notice to quit under this section. In the case of monthly tenancy, the period of which has been fixed in the contract, it shall continue till the expiration of that period which may be one month or one year or several years. Similarly, the period of notice to quit may also vary in terms of the contract, such as, if the contract fixes the period of notice, say, two months, then notice of fifteen days will not be valid. 

 9. In the previous decision of this Court 132 DLR (AD) 171], a clear distinction was made between a lease under section 105 and a lease under section 106 of the TP Act; whereas, these two sections do not appear to say so. In that decision a lease under section 105 was held to be a right in an immovable property but not so a lease under section 106. Upon consideration of section 105 it was observed in para 11 of that decision : "The lease, as defined, no doubt creates an interest in immovable property and the Act also says that it is transferable" We are to see the true character of the lease created under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act." It was further observed in para 13; "Analysing in this way, we find that a relationship is created under this section between the landlord and the tenant which is of a personal nature. The right of occupation of the premises has been given, and this right of occupation from month to month, from its very nature, cannot but be personal and so cannot create an interest in the land as a lease under section 105 does. The right of occupation remains personal with the tenant. The right being personal it ceases with the death of either party and so on the death of the tenant, the tenancy ceases and hence it is not heritable". 

 10. The Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963, in section 2(8), defines "tenant" which expression includes his "legal representative" "as defined in the Civil Procedure Code". A tenant under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance means "any person by whom, or on whose account, rent is payable for any premises and includes a legal representative as defined in the Civil Procedure Code". Furthermore, a person continuing in possession after the termination of a tenancy is also a tenant under this definition. A "legal representative" within the meaning of section 2(11) of the Civil PC means "a person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person, and includes any person who intermeddles with the estate of the deceased and where a party sues or is sued in a representative character the person on whom the estate devolves on the death of the party so suing or sued". A tenant under the Ordinance is same as a lessee under the TP Act and the monthly tenancy is also a lease within the meaning of section 105 TP Act. 'Tenancy' has not been defined in the Ordinance, but it clearly falls within "lease" as described in section 105 TP Act. "Tenancy" relates to "premises" which has been defined in the Ordinance". "Premises" means any building/hut or its part to be left for residential or non-residential purpose and includes garden, out-house and also furniture supplied by landlord. Whereas, lease 'covers all immovable property including a premises'. A legal representative of a person is one who represents his estate on his death. The lease under section 105 TP Act is transfer of a right to enjoy an immovable property. This right to enjoy, by occupation of a premises, which is no doubt an immovable property, is a limited right. Premises Rent Control Ordinance is intended to govern some specific aspects of a monthly tenancy, such as, the procedure for determination of a tenancy, for protecting tenant against unjust or improper eviction and prohibition of increase in the rent by undue means. Section 18 of the Ordinance is relevant for this purpose. Provision of this section shall prevail "notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 or the Contract Act, 1872". The provision is that no order or decree for recovery of possession of a premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent in full and regularly and performs all other conditions of the tenancy. In the previous decision the definition of "legal representative" of a tenant was of course looked into, but it was observed in para 8 that "the definition was inserted in the Ordinance only to emphasize the tenant's liability to pay rent and nothing more and this meaning becomes clear when we advert to the second half of the definition of 'tenant' which says that it also includes a person continuing in possession after the termination of the tenancy". We find it rather difficult to accept this view as correct that 'legal representative' of a deceased tenant will be brought to the scene only to pay rent and not to inherit the deceased tenant's right to hold the tenancy for the purpose of enjoying or occupying the premises. 

 11. A monthly tenancy being a lease within the meaning of section 105, TP Act, it is an interest in an immovable property. It is transfer of an interest in the property as shown in this section. The TP Act does not specifically say that a lease is heritable also, because this Act is not intended to govern the matter of succession to immovable property. But the incidence of heritability is easily discernible from the tenancy being an interest in the property. It is also easily gathered from the fact that a contract, which creates a tenancy is binding upon the parties to the contract as well as upon their heirs, and that, a contract is legally enforceable against parties thereto and their heirs. A tenancy may be created under a statute also; such as, on legal termination of a tenancy, a person continuing in possession and paying rent to the landlord, who accepts it, becomes a statutory tenant. In the instant case, we are not dealing with any statutory tenant. The tenancy in this case is a contractual tenancy. Right in such a tenancy is ordinarily heritable, though this right is limited "to enjoy" and occupy the property only, and the tenant is liable to be ejected either on the expiration of the fixed period, if any, or by notice to quit. 

 12. A number of cases from Indian jurisdiction have been cited before us in order to support the view that a monthly tenancy is heritable though right in the tenancy is limited or partial and the tenant inherits only that right which the original tenant held and nothing more. Among others, the following cases have been considered by us: Rajib Hossain and another Vs. Nowab Unus Khan, AIR 1937 Nagpur, 321; Anwar Ali Bepari Vs. Janakilal Roy Chowdhury, 43 CWN, 797; Smt. Vishnawati Vs. BV Chowdhury, AIR 1970, All. 389; Sau Nakabai Vs. Mahadu Sakharam Adsule and others, AIR 1980 Bom. 208. The then Dhaka High Court also held this view in the case of Gouribala Pal Vs. Kunjalal Saha, 12 DLR 37. The Indian Supreme Court, in the case of Damadilal and others Vs. Parashram and others, AIR 1976 (SC) 2229 considered the question as to heritability of a in contract. There is no dispute that a contractual tenant has an estate or property in the subject-matter of the tenancy and heritability is an incident of the tenancy. It cannot be assumed, however, that with the determination of the tenancy the estate must necessarily disappear and the statute can only preserve his status of irremovability and not the estate he had in the premises in his occupation". 

 13. That a tenancy is an interest in an immovable property was considered from another angle in a Letters-Patent appeal in the case of Ramchandra Annappa Vs. Subraya Timmaya, AIR 1951 Boni. 127. The question there was whether "tenancy right is protected under section 53A of the TP Act." It was contended that the tenancy being merely a transfer of a "partial right in property" viz a right to enjoy the property, it could not be said to be a transfer of property within the meaning of the expression used in section 53A of TP Act. The contention was rejected and it was held that though the right is only to enjoy the property still it is a right and the tenancy is a transfer of immovable property within the meaning of section 53A of the TP Act. 

 14. This Court in the previous decision (32 DLR (AD) 171) took into consideration two concepts of English law of tenancy to support the view that a monthly tenancy creates only "personal right" of the tenant which vanishes with his death. One of the concepts is "tenancy-at-will". Such a tenancy under the English law is created and continues at the mere will of the landlord; it is terminable at any time, without any notice, at the mere will of the landlord; it is also terminable at any time, without any notice at the wish of the tenant. The relation between landlord and tenant under this concept of tenancy is a personal relation between the two and is terminable by the death of either of them. From this point of view, this Court came to the conclusion that a tenancy from month to month is in the nature of the English tenancy of "tenancy-at-will". In our law governing tenancy there is no such concept as "tenancy-at-will" to be terminable at any time and without any notice at the mere wish of either party. Under our law a person may get possessory right in an immovable property by a licence granted by the owner of such property. Such a right is terminable, at any time, at the mere will of the person granting the licence. The person who is granted this right is Galled a "licensee". A licensee is not a tenant; but a tenant from month to month under TP Act is different from a licensee. Taking them at par is found to have led to the erroneous view that a monthly tenant is same as a "tenant-at-will". A tenancy from month to month, as we have already found, dots not mean that it is meant for only one month, at the end of which it ceases to exist, and thereupon, a fresh tenancy is to start. Similar view was taken in the case of Usha Rani Devi Vs. The Research Industries Ltd., 50 CWN, 461. There it has been held that a monthly tenancy is not a tenancy which commences or begins in one month, and on the expiry, a fresh tenancy is created in the following month or months, but is a tenancy for an unstated period, which is, however, determinable by either party by a notice to quit. 

 15. The other English concept, as considered by this Court in the earlier case, is "tenant by sufferance". A tenancy created by sufferance comes into being when, on the lawful termination of a tenancy, the landlord by his own act of negligence, does not take steps to enforce his right of evicting the tenant who therefore continues in possession by landlord's negative permission. Such a tenant by "sufferance" acquires no right in the property which can be transferred or inherited. Nevertheless, such a tenant is not a trespasser either, for neither he nor his predecessor-tenant entered upon the property by wrongful means. In the previous decision a tenant from month to month was thus taken as a synonym of the English "tenant by sufferance". In our law there is no such concept as "tenant by sufferance", who is liable to be evicted at any time and who does not inherit any right in the property. Under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, a tenant may continue in possession even after lawful termination of his tenancy. A lessee may continue in possession of a lease property on its lawful termination if the landlord either expressly or impliedly recognises him as lessee taking rent from him; he is called a tenant by holding over under section 116 of the TP Act. He is not a tenant by sufferance. Death of the original tenant is not a ground for determining the tenancy, nor a person continuing in possession of the tenancy on the death of the original tenant, as found in that decision, is a trespasser either. In such a circumstance, the only basis of his possession is the right of in her now ever limited in scope that right may be. 

 16. In the instant case, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division accepted the contention of the appellants-tenants that they had not inherited the tenancy from their father, the original tenant, but nevertheless, held them to be "tenants by sufferance" as they were not trespassers. This view is erroneous. 

 17. If a monthly tenancy is found to be heritable a question may arise, whether any difficulty will be faced by landlord if a notice to quit is to be served on several persons who may inherit a tenancy right on the death of their predecessor-tenant. We do not think that any such difficulty will arise. For, on the death of the original tenant several heirs may inherit his right, and all of them become co-tenants or joint tenants. All of them may not be in actual occupation of the premises. A notice under section 106 TP Act must be addressed to all the co-tenants, or joint tenants, but service of the notice upon any one of them must be treated as prima facie service upon them all. If none of them is found in the premises the notice may be served upon "one of his family or servants at the premises". If none of them is found at the premises, the notice may be served by affixing it to any conspicuous part of the premises, as specifically laid down in the second paragraph of section 106. We get support to this view from a number of decisions including the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Harihar Banerji Vs. Ramshasi Roy, AIR 1918 (PC) 102. This decision was followed by us in SM Bindubashini Chanda Vs. Al-haj Jahanara Begum, 1982 BCR (AD) 181. 

 18. In conclusion, we find that a tenancy from month to month is a lease which, like any other lease, is contemplated only in section 105 TP Act and that the right therein is heritable and not personal to vanish with the tenant's death. The right on inheritance is same as that of the original tenant and not in any way better or higher than his right. On re-consideration of the previous decision in 32 DLR (AD) 171 case in the light of the materials now placed before us, we find that that decision is not correct. The Execution Proceeding against the appellants in this case is maintainable. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is upheld, though on different grounds as given above. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed without, however, any order as to cost.

parties:
Kamruzzaman Khan ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Shahidul Alam Khan and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
6. Mr. BK Das, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, submits that according to the plaintiff himself, defendant-petitioner was let out with the suit premises on stipulation of payment of Taka 800.00 as monthly rent to be paid on the following month according to Bengali calendar and that later with effect from 1396 BS increased Taka 1000.00 per month and that the defendant paid rent according to Bengali calendar month but the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act (Exhibit 5) was issued on 23-6-1993 asking the defendant to vacate the suit premises within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice in question. He therefore submits that the notice being not given with reference to Bengali calendar month and also being not issued terminating the tenancy with the expiry of Bengali month the said notice is not a valid notice in the eye of law and, as such, in the absence of valid notice, the plaintiff was not entitled to get a decree of ejectment, as sought for, by him against the defendant-petitioner. He then submits that the trial Court without considering this vital legal flaw passed the impugned judgment and, as such, the judgment is liable to be set aside. 

 8. It appears from paragraph 2 of the plaint filed by the plaintiff-opposite party that there was no written agreement between the parties as they happened to be dose relations and that defendant No.1 was inducted as a tenant in the suit premises on condition of payment of monthly rent at the rate of Taka 800.00 'per month to be paid on the following month according to Bengali calendar and that. from 1396 BS rent was increased to Taka 1,000.00 per month and that the defendant paid rent upto Aswin 1399 BS and that the plaintiff being in bonafide requirement of the suit premises and also defendant becoming a defaulter in payment of rent, was requested, to vacate the suit premises and pay arrear rents: From the aforesaid averment it appears that the plaintiff filed the suit against the defendant for his eviction referring to the tenancy made according to Bengali calendar and, as such, repeatedly used Bengali year and Bengali month in the plaint and so by all means it must be held that the tenancy between the plaintiff and the defendant was a tenancy according to Bengali calendar month.It appears that the notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was admittedly issued, on 23-6-1993 and according to plaintiff it was received by the defendant on 4-7-1993. Here again, it appears that the notice does not contain any reference whatsoever to the date according to Bengali calendar. The notice was issued terminating the tenancy within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. On the plaintiffs own showing the notice being received by the defendant on 4-7-1993, it is needless to say, that the defendant was asked to vacate the suit premises within 15 days from 4-7-1993 i.e. by 19-7-1993. It appears from paragraph 4 of the plaint that pursuant to the purport of the notice terminating the tenancy by 19-7-1993, plaintiff on his own showing in the said paragraph 4 of the plaint asked the defendant to vacate the suit premises and hand over possession in favour of the plaintiff and that on the following clay i.e. on 20-7-93 the plaintiff approached the defendant for handing over possession of the suit premises and admittedly, according to the plaintiff, the cause of action thus arose on 20-7-1993 on the failure of the defendant to vacate the suit premises and hand over possession in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party. Learned Advocate appearing' for' the defendant-petitioner seriously challenged the validity of the notice issued under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, Section 106 of the Transfer or Property Act-runs as follows: 

 "106. In the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contrary, a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six month's notice expiring with the end of a year of the tenancy; and a lease of immovable property of any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen day's notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. 

 9. It appears from the above provision that in case of a monthly tenant the tenancy, can be terminated by 15 day's notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. A notice as contemplated by law therefore should be a notice of 15 days expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. In other words, the notice must contemplate the period of expiry of the tenancy with the month of the tenancy. In the Instant case it is already found that the notice was issued on 23-6-1993 which was received by the defendant on 4-7-1993 terminating his tenancy within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice which being received on 4-7-1993 the tenancy thus expired on 19-7-1993 which cannot be regarded to be a notice expiring with the end of a month. Further, it has been provided therein that such notice is to be issued terminating tenancy by 15 day's notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy. On elaborate discussion made above and from the plaint itself it has already been noticed that the tenancy in question in the present suit was according to Bengali Calendar month and the instant notice therefore having no reference to the Bengali Calendar month the notice served upon the defendant cannot be regarded as a notice expiring tenancy with the end of a month of the tenancy. 

 10. Mr. BK Das, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, in this connection referred to the case of Seati Bibi vs Jogendra Nath reported in 57 Indian Clues (IC) 593. A plaintiff sought for ejectment of the defendant serving it notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The defendant raised objection as to issuance of the legal notice. The learned Munsif framed an issue on the point but the learned Munsif came to a finding against the plaintiff on another issue and did not determine this issue. In appeal the learned District Judge upheld the order of the learned Munsif. The case reaching the High Court discussed the facts and found that the notice in question was issued on 28th December 1915. The notice directed defendant to vacate the house by 31-1-1916. The Court below found that the defendant was holding on a monthly tenant terminating on the 26th day of each successive month according to Hindu calendar. This finding being a finding of fact was regarded by the High Court Division to be binding upon him. In view of the discussion made above it appears that in order to be a valid notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act it would be issued terminating tenancy by 15 day's notice expiring firstly with the end of a month and secondly, with the end of a monthly tenancy. Thus the two essential ingredients being not complied with in the instant case while issuing notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, I am of the opinion that the notice is not a valid notice terminating the tenancy of the defendant. 

 "lease of immovable property is created under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act and, as such, statutory notice must be given under section 106 of the Transfer of Properly Act for termination of tenancy. The landlord should comply both with the provisions of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and also with the provisions of the special enactment. The provisions of the Rent Control Ordinance are in addition to this section of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of property Act. There is nothing in the Ordinance which also absolves the landlord to serve a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. Unless the tenancy is determined by giving a notice as contemplated under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act no suit for ejectment of a monthly tenant can be filed."

parties:
Mantu Faraji alias Jamal Faraji and others ------ Petitioners
vs.  
Mahiuddin Khan ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
2. The opposite party No.1 filed an application under section 96 of the Slate Acquisition and Tenancy Act against the present petitioners and others to pre-empt the case land as co-sharer of the case holding. The case was resisted by the pre-emptee petitioners denying the material allegations made in the petition and contending, inter alia that the pre-emptor opposite party NO.1 is not a co-sharer. 

 4. Mr Abu Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioners, urges only one poit before this court. His only submission is that the case land is a homestead land although situated in the rural area and, as such, it is not an agricultural land but a non-agricultural land and, as such, an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act) is misconceived and not maintainable in law but both the courts below overlooking this legal aspect of the case allowed the case illegally and the same has caused an. error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention the learned Advocate refers to the following decisions namely, 20 DLR 562 and 1197 and 21 DLR 633. To fortify his contention he submits that the pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land is governed by section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act whereas a pre-emption in respect of agricultural land is governed by section 96 of the Act irrespective of the location of the land. 

 5. Mr Hasan Foiz Siddiqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor opposite party, on the other hand, submits that it is now well settled that a homestead land situated in the rural area is governed by the provisions of section 96 of the Act and not by section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported 1 MLR (H.C.) 1996 page 70 wherein it has been held that homestead situated in the rural area is an agricultural land and section 96 of the Act is attracted in pre-empting such land. 

 6. In the instant case unfortunately, the point which has been urged by the pre-emptee petitioner before this Court was neither taken in the written objection before the trial Court nor the same was argued before the appellate Court below. Be that as it may, it is an important question of law and, as such, I allowed the learned Advocate to agitate the point before me. His only submission is that since the case land is homestead land it is not agricultural land and it must be governed by the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the pre-emption application ought to have been filed under section 24 of that Act and not under section 96 of the Act 

 7. Thus the question falling to be determined in this case is whether the homestead land situated in rural area is an agricultural land within the meaning of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter called the Act) or is a non-agricultural land within the meaning of section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 8. Here it should also be remembered that the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act came into operation when Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 was in force and governed the agricultural land and that is why homesteads which were within the ambit of section 182 of, the BT Act were kept outside the ambit of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Such a homestead land is not a non-agricultural land as defined in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Thereafter came the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 10. After the promulgation of the Act the question arose as to which of the laws will govern the right of pre-emption in respect of homestead lands in the villages: is it section 96 of the Act or section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act? The question came up before the Pakistan Supreme Court for consideration in Civil Appeal No.47-D of 1963 dated 22-1-1965. In that case the question involved was as to whether an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the SAT Act could be entertained in respect of Non-Agricultural land, The Supreme Court, proceeding on the admitted basis that the dispute was as to non-agricultural homestead land within the municipality, observed and found as under: 

 11. Section 96, in clear terms, lays down that this right of pre-emption will be available only in respect of a 'holding. In view of the definition of 'holding' as given in section 2(13) of the Act, it can not be said that the right of pre-emption can be exercised in respect of non-agricultural land. Here it may be mentioned that there is specific provision for pre-emption of non-agricultural land in the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (XXIII of 1949). Under that Act a contiguous owner can not claim a right of pre-emption. After review of relevant provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act we think that section 96 is confined to agricultural land and therefore, a right of pre-emption under this section can not be claimed in respect of homestead land within a Municipality. 

 12. This interpretation of section 96 has been followed by the then Dacca High Court in the case reported in 20 DLR 562 and 21 DLR 633. But these decisions were given when the original section 81 was in force and section 81-A was not added to the Act. But subsequently, by amending the Act sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 81 was omitted and a new section 81A was inserted by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1967 and after the amendment of 1967 difference of opinion arose as to whether the law enunciated by the Pakistani Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No.47-D of 1963 is still good law. In Noor Jahan Begum vs. Md Tabarak Ali (Civil Revision No.639 of 1969) a Single Bench of the High Court Division held as follows: 

 "By the new provisions, the entire part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has been made applicable to a holder of non-agricultural land. The simple test is as to whether the holder of non-agricultural land has become a tenant under the Provincial Government is respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior rights in such land. If the holder of non-agricultural land has become a tenant directly under the Provincial Government his rights and liabilities will be governed by the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act subject to the provisions contained in Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It comes to this that for the purpose of pre-emption relating to non-agricultural land if the holder of the holding has become tenant directly under the government by virtue of acquisition of the superior rights in such land, section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act will be applicable in preference to section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 81-A(2) makes provision for other non-agricultural tenants." 

 13. After the pronouncement of the said judgment the same law came up for consideration in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.15 of 1975 and a Division Bench of the High Court Division after considering the provisions of law containing in the two Acts, observed that "Under section 24, only the co-sharer tenants of non-agricultural land, which is the subject of the transfer, can make an application. This distinction has been maintained in the two Acts even after the omission of sub-sections (2) and (3) from section 81 and insertion of section 81A to the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thus, we find that insofar as an application for pre-emption is concerned section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will have their application in their respective areas, namely, section 96 shall be applicable to agricultural lands beyond the Municipal area whereas section 24 will be applicable to all classes of lands within the Municipal area and this view that we have taken is supported by the said unreported decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Civil Appeal No.47-D of 1963". 

 14. This divergence of judicial opinion has been finally resolved by the Appellate Division in the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323. In that case the Appellate Division after considering the relevant provisions of both the Acts and the conflicting decisions finally came to the decision that in spite of the omission of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 81 and insertion of section 81 A., section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has not been rendered ineffective nor impliedly repealed so as to compel the owner of any land falling within the Municipal area to prefer an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thus, the law is now well settled that section 96 of the Act shall be applicable to agricultural lands beyond the Municipal area and section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act will be attracted to all classes of lands within the Municipal area. 

 15. Now the pertinent question that calls for determination in the instant Rule is, as to whether the homestead land situated in rural area is an agricultural land or non-agricultural land. Non-Agricultural land has not been defined in the Act but it has been defined in the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act reads as under: 

 section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 (V1lI of 1885) apply Section 182 of the BT Act reads as follows: 

 "Where a raiyat or an under-raiyat holds his homestead otherwise than as part of his holding within the same village or any village contiguous to that village, his status in respect of his homestead shall be that of a raiyat or an under-raiyat according to the status of the landlord of the homestead, and the incidents of his tenancy of such homestead shall be governed by the provisions of this Act applicable to raiyats or under-raiyats, as the case may be." 

 16. The term home stead is not used in that section as a generic term descriptive of a particular kind of land, but was intended to denote any, land used by the raiyat of under-raiyat for residential purposes, The scheme of that section was to divide homestead lands into two classes, (1) those comprised in the raiyati-holding, and (2) those outside the raiyat holding. Thus a homestead land held by a raiyat otherwise than as a raiyati holding and the homestead land held by a raiyat were governed by that section and those homestead lands were kept outside the definition of Non-Agricultural land as contained in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. At the time of enactment of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act the BT Act was in operation and the homestead lands governed by the BT Act were kept outside the ambit of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. In 1950 the parliament passed the East Bengal Estate Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and from the date of coming into force of the whole of Part V in any area, the BT Act stands repealed in that area. By 1964 the Part V was enforced throughout country so, BT Act stands repealed entirely in Bangladesh from that period. Even after the repeal of BT Act by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there has been no corresponding change in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act although the provisions of BT Act have been repealed and replaced by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Thus in interpreting section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act today one must read section 2(4)(a) as a homestead to which the provisions of section 182 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, (VIII of 1985) would have applied instead of the word 'apply'. Thus, from the scheme and  definition of 'non-agricultural land' as given in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, it is crystal clear that homestead land outside the raiyati-holding Situated in the village are not non-agricultural land ie they are agricultural land or land of raiyati holding. So, a transfer of homestead land by a raiyat beyond the Municipality is attracted by section 96 of the Act and not by section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land can be claimed only under the provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and pre-emption in respect of raiyati holding ie agricultural land can only be claimed under section 96 of the Act. The view taken by me gets support from the decision reported in 30 DLR 75, wherein it has been held that homestead being part of the holding of a raiyat is not excluded from the operation of section 96 of the Act. Similarly, in a recent decision reported in 1 MLR 72, another Single Bench of this Division has held that suit holding being homestead situated in the rural area is an agricultural land and section 96 of the Act is only available. It thus, appears that the correct legal position is that a homestead situated in a village shall be governed by the provisions of section 96 of the Act, be it held by a raiyat as a raiyati-holding or independently of a raiyati holding whereas section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will be applicable to all classes of lands within the Municipal areas. In the instant case there is no dispute that the case land although a homestead is situated in a village and, as such, is a raiyati land within a village and so section 96 of the Act is attracted.

parties:
Abdul Aziz ----- Defendant-Appellant
Vs
Abdul Majid ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The case of the plaintiff-respondent is that, defendant-appellant was inducted as a periodical lessee in the suit premises for a period of 11 months beginning from 1st day of December, 1983 to October, 1984 at a monthly rental of Taka 800.00 per month by a written agreement on 1.12.83. According to the plaintiff, there was an option of renewal of the tenancy with the lessor. After the expiry of the period of 11 months the plaintiff filed the suit for eviction of the defendant. 

 4. The learned SCC Judge decreed the suit and passed the order of eviction of the defendant from the suit premises on the finding that no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was necessary prior to the institution of the suit as the tenancy of the defendant was terminated by efflux of time. 

 7. Although the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division held that no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is required as the tenancy expired by efflux of time, but the main question for consideration is, whether the tenant is liable to be ejected solely on this ground of expiry of the period of lease without specifying any other valid grounds as provided in the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. 

 9. Admittedly in this case no notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served upon the defendant determining the tenancy and as grounds of eviction neither default nor bonafide requirement`s have been pleaded. The Courts below held that such a notice is not required to be served as the tenancy expired by efflux of time without at all considering sub-section (2) of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. 

 "18. No order for ejectment ordinarily to be made if rent paid at allowable rate—(I) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or the Contract Act, 1872, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and performs the conditions of the tenancy (Relevant portion quoted). 

 11. The non-obstante clause of sub-section (1) of section 18 shows that the provision of Transfer of Property Act and the Contract Act will not apply in respect of this section. In the present case neither default/bonafide requirement nor any of the clauses (a) to (e) of the Proviso to sub-section (1) of section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance have been pleaded as a ground for eviction other than expiry of the period of lease as per agreement. Tenant has been defined in section 2(Uma) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, which also says that a person continuing in possession after termination of a tenancy in his favour is also a tenant. It is on record that after the expiry of the period of lease the tenant is continuing in possession and is paying rent in the House Rent Control Case No. 367 of 1984 regularly. In that view of the matter, defendant is a tenant under the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and in that sense he is a statutory tenant. Rent Control legislation is a special law which gives a greater protection to a tenant against eviction so long he pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and performs the conditions of the tenancy. Further, reading section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance it appears that a tenant shall not be liable to eviction except on one or more of the grounds laid down in this section. As per section 18 of the Ordinance on the ground of default, bonafide requirements and on other clauses mentioned in (a) to (e) of the proviso to sub-section (I) of section 18 a tenant can be evicted. 

 Thus, it appears that the expiry of the period of lease or that the interest of the landlord in the premises has been transferred shall not by itself be a satisfactory ground within the meaning of clause (e) of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 18 to evict a tenant. Hence, the expiry of the period of lease as argued by Mr. Nurul Huq cannot by itself be a valid ground for termination of tenancy in the present case. It has been already referred herein above, that no valid ground for ejectment of the monthly tenant as contemplated in the provisions of section 18 of the Ordinance has been set up as ground for eviction. Hence, the argument of the learned Advocate for the respondents cannot be accepted. 

 13. Lease of immoveable property is created under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act and as such statutory notice must be given under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act for termination of tenancy. The landlord should comply both with the provisions of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act and also with the provisions of the special enactment. The provisions of the Rent Control Ordinance are in addition to this section of notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. There is nothing in the Ordinance which also absolves the landlord to serve a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. Unless the tenancy is determined by giving a notice as contemplated under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act no suit for ejectment of a monthly tenant can be filed. 

 14. It further appears that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division mis-appreciated the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD)1. That was a case where the main question was whether a monthly tenancy is heritable and in that decision it was held after review of our judgment in 32 DLR (AD)171, that a monthly tenancy is heritable. In that decision it was also observed that section 18 of the Ordinance shall prevail notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and of the Contract. Act, 1872 and as long as the tenant pays rent in full regularly and performs all other conditions of the tenancy he shall not be evicted. In that decision at paragraph 8, section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act was referred to show how a lease of an immovable property is determined by various ways and grounds and in that section "death" was not mentioned as a ground for determination of lease. The reported decision is a ease relating to a contractual tenant and not with regard to a tenant who is a statutory tenant being a person dispossession and paying the rent to the landlord. This distinction having been overlooked an error has crept in the judgment of the High Court Division. Thus, 44 DLR (AD)1 has not been correctly appreciated by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division. 

 ATM Afzal, J.: I have perused the judgments prepared by my learned brothers, Mustafa Kamal, J. and Latifur Rahman, J. I agree that the appeal should be allowed. As for the reasons, however, I find myself more in agreement with those in the judgment of Mustafa Kamal J. I do not think that there is anything useful which I may add in support of our ultimate conclusion that a tenant like the defendant is not liable to be evicted merely on the ground that the tenancy has terminated by efflux of time. 

 19. The trial Court held that with the expiry of the term of lease on 31.10.84 and in the absence of a fresh agreement of lease, the relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties had come to an end and the appellant had no legal right to stay in the demised premises. Discussing the evidence on record the trial Court held that the second notice dated 18.10.84 was validly served upon the appellant, but it was not a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, as the landlord merely wanted the tenant to quit and vacate on the expiry of the term of lease. The trial Court then held that in any view of the matter no notice to quit is necessary where the action of ejectment is brought after the term of the lease has expired and the tenancy has come to an end by efflux of time and the landlord has not accepted the rent from the tenant after the expiry of the term. No notice was taken to the appellant's unchallenged assertion that after the expiry of the tenancy he has been depositing rent regularly and without default to the House Rent Controller. 

 20. The High Court Division on a mistaken appreciation of our judgment in the case of Pradhip Das @ Shambhu Vs. Kazal Das Sarma, 44 DLR (AD) 1 (para 8) and quoting out of context from para 11 thereof that "the tenancy in this case is a contractual tenancy, Right in such a tenancy is ordinarily heritable, though this right is limited "to enjoy" and occupy the property only, and the tenant is liable to be so ejected either on the expiration of the fixed period, if any, or by notice to quit", concurred with the views of the trial Court. No consideration was given to section 18(2) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance, 1963, now section 18(2) of “বাড়ীভাড়া নিয়ন্ত্রণ অধ্যাদেশ, ১৯৯১, although the appellant specifically pleaded it. 

 23. The reason is simple. All leases are created under the Transfer of Property Act and the Contract Act. If the Premises Rent Control Ordinance was not there, a tenancy terminates with the expiry of the period of lease because section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act expressly provides that "a lease of immovable property determines (a) by efflux of time limited thereby". But to give a protection to the tenants, section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance makes a significant departure from the Transfer of Property Act. Sub-section (1) of section 18 protects a tenant from eviction "as long as the tenant pays rent to the full extent allowable by this Ordinance and performs the conditions of the tenancy". This protection is given "notwithstanding anything contained in the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, or the Contract Act, i872". The protection is not available if he is a defaulter and/or in the contingencies mentioned in clauses(a)-(c) of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 18, namely. 

 There may be a host of other circumstances provided for in the Transfer of Property Act and in the contract of tenancy itself which render a tenant liable for eviction, but the causes of eviction under the premises Rent Control Ordinance are limited to the causes of default in the payment of rent and/or any of the circumstances mentioned in clauses (a) to (e) of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 18. To that extent the Transfer of Property Act and the Contract Act are excluded. 

 26. There is another important difference between the Transfer of Property Act and the Ordinance in respect of a tenancy which has expired with efflux of time. Under the Transfer of Property Act, the tenant can "hold over" after expiry of lease and the effect of "holding over" is provided for in section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act as follows: 

 27. The point to note here is that under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, the option is with the landlord to accept or not to accept rent from the lessee or under-lessee after the determination of the lease with efflux of time. If the landlord refuses to accept rent, that will be, the end of the tenancy, there is no "holding over" and the tenant renders himself liable to eviction. But under the Ordinance it is the tenant who exercises the option. If he wishes to continue as a tenant it is he who has to be ready and willing to pay rent to the full extent allowable by the Ordinance. If he sent the rent after expiry of lease by money order and the landlord refuses to accept, and if he makes a timely deposit of the same to the House Rent Controller and continues to do so, he will be protected from eviction. His continuance of the tenancy does not depend upon the landlord's acceptance of the rent, as in the Transfer of Property Act. This position is also in full accord with the definition of the word 'tenant' in section 2(8), at present section 2(Uma), of the Ordinance. 

 28. It is, therefore, not correct to say that a tenant who continues in possession after expiry of tenancy with efflux of time by regularly paying rent either to the landlord or on his refusal to accept rent to the House Rent Controller is a tenant "holding over". The words "holding over" are not mentioned in the Ordinance. A tenant "holding over" is a creature of the Transfer of Property Act and the acceptance of his position as a tenant "holding over" depends upon the sweet will of the landlord. Under the Ordinance, such tenants have not been described by any name and in the absence of a statutory name they are designated by the Courts to be "statutory tenants". This concept was made clear by us, when we mentioned another circumstance under which a "statutory tenant" may be created, when we said (in the case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 1 at para 11), "A tenancy may be created under a statute also: such as, on legal termination of a tenancy, a person continuing in possession and paying rent to the landlord, who accepts it, becomes a statutory tenant." (page 6). 

 29. The fallacy of the High Court Division was that it has made a confusion between a statutory tenant and a contractual tenant and treated the present tenant-appellant as a contractual tenant. It ignored sub-section (2) of section 18 and did not consider the appellant's unrefuted case that after expiry of the tenancy he has been regularly depositing rent with the House Rent Controller. The appellant is a statutory tenant and he can only be evicted by a statutory notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on the ground of default in the payment of rent and/or any of the circumstances mentioned in clauses (a) to (e) of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 18, and not on any other ground whatsoever. The sole ground of expiry of tenancy with efflux of time is simply not available to the respondent, notice or no notice. It is immaterial in this appeal whether any notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served or not. If the respondent has no available ground for eviction, a valid notice will not save his suit. 

 A notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is mandatory in all cases of eviction under the Ordinance as well, because a tenancy is created under the Transfer of Property Act and Contract Act and those two Acts are not entirely excluded by the provisions of the Ordinance. The Ordinance has not excluded the operation of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act either expressly or by implication. That is the basic reason why a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is mandatory in a case of eviction under the Ordinance.

parties:
Bangladesh ----- Appellant
Vs.
Tobarak Ali Mia and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Facts necessary for the disposal of the appeal are that the suit lands are 22.82 acres of char land at village Majichar, known as Underchar at Noakhali. Plaintiffs, thirteen in number, contended that late Priyanath Das and others had taken a pattani howla of the suit land from the Bhulua Zamindars, owners of 11 annas and 5 annas interest in the same. Priyanath Das and others sold the entire pattani howla in 1928 to Fazar Ali and others, predecessors-in-interest of some plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 2-15. On 20.11.1931 Jatindra Kumar Basu and Basanta Kumar Basu auction purchased the entire pattani howla which was put to sale by the Bhulua Zamindars for arrears of rent. The auction purchasers took delivery of possession and transferred their pattani interest to five persons by five kabalas Exts. 2-2(d), all dated 1st Chaitra, 1338 BS. Some of the plaintiffs are transferees from some of those five persons and some of the plaintiffs are successors to the rest. Thus all the plaintiffs combinedly acquired 16 annas interest in the pattani howla. While in possession on payment of rent the suit lands were diluviated by the river Meghna in between 1351 BS to 1353 BS and were reformed in 1361-1362 BS. The plaintiffs however continued to pay rent for 2/3 years after diluvion and even paid rent for the first six months of 1356 BS. They had the reformed lands surveyed and demarcated in 1362 BS and went into possession by constructing huts and grazing cattle. When the suit lands became fit for cultivation in 1366 BS they started cultivation of paddy therein and are in continuous possession thereof ever since. The defendant-Government acquired the interest of the Bhulua Zamindars in 1951 under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiffs went to the local Tahsildar in Baisakh, 1368 BS for payment of rent, but the Tahsildar refused to accept any rent on the ground that the suit lands were auction sold and purchased in 1950 for arrears of rent of the last six months of 1356 BS by the Bhulua Zamindars. The plaintiffs contended that the sale, if any, was of no effect as no rent was payable while the suit lands were completely under water, apparently relying upon section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act. They also alleged material irregularities in the conduct of the sale. The plaintiffs prayed for two declarations, (a) that they have got absolute pattani howla interest or raiyati interest in the suit land and (b) that the sale of the pattani howla in 1950 is void, inoperative, fraudulent, ultra vires and without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs and the suit land. 

 3. It was the contention of the defendant-Government as defendant No. 1 that the Bhulua Zamindars had put to auction sale both the 11 annas and 5 annas pattani howla for arrears of rent of the last six months of 1356 BS on 18.5.50 and the sales were confirmed on 4.7.50. The Zamindars took delivery of possession. The lands diluviated thereafter in the last part of 1357 BS and reformed in 1364 BS. Government is in possession. The auction sale was held in due conformity with the provisions of the Patni Regulations. Moreover the principle of abatement of rent as provided in section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act is not applicable in the case of Patni Taluk. The suit is barred by limitation. 

 5. The trial Court negatived the claim of defendant Nos. 2-15 to the suit land upon discussion of evidence on record but dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs admitted in their application dated 1.12.1955 to the District Manager, Acquired Estate that the pattani had been sold for non-payment of rent. It held further that there were no material irregularities in the conduct of the sale. The plaintiffs, however, are in possession of the lands. There was no finding on limitation, although an issue was framed thereon. There was also no finding when the suit lands were diluviated and reformed and as to whether section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act was applicable or not. 

 6. The High Court Division found on the plaintiffs' appeal that their application dated 1.12.1955 did not constitute an admission that the suit lands were diluviated after 1356 BS. It held on evidence that the suit lands were under water in 1356 BS. The rent of the pattani lands abated in view of the provisions of section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act. No rent being due from the pattani holders the howla could not be sold under section 8 read with section 11 of Patni Regulation of 1819. As the auction sale was made illegally it was void and illegal and did not affect the rights and interests of the plaintiffs in the suit lands. The High Court Division confirmed the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit lands and decreed the suit. 

 7. The learned Additional Attorney-General, Counsel for the defendant-Government-appellant, submits that the provisions of section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act arc not applicable to the Patni Taluks Regulation. He contends that no abatement of rent being available to the plaintiffs the sale was only voidable and not void. Article 12(d) of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act provides that a suit to set aside the sale of a patni taluk sold for current arrears of rent must be instituted within one year from the date when the sale would become final and conclusive had no such suit been brought. The sale took place on 18.5.50 and was confirmed on 4.7.50. A patni sale does not need confirmation. It becomes final and conclusive on payment by the purchaser of the full amount of the purchase money. Hence the suit should have been filed within one year from 18.5.50. The suit having been filed on 7.9.1962 is clearly barred by limitation. Moreover, Article 120 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act provides that a suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in the First Schedule must be instituted within six years from the date when the right to sue accrues. On their own admission the plaintiffs knew about the auction sale at least on 1.12.55 when they filed an application before the District Manager, Acquired Estate. They should have alternatively filed the suit within 6 years from 1.12.55, but the suit having been filed on 7.9.62 is also barred under Article 120. 

 9. The questions are, what briefly is a patni taluk or howla and what are the patni laws ? Do the patni laws contain any provision for setting aside sale and does the present suit come within any special provision of any patni law ? Is section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act applicable to patni laws, if so why? What effect has the application of section 86A to the question of limitation ? If it applies, does the suit become void or voidable ? Is Article 12(d) applicable to a void or voidable sale ? Finally, is Article 120 applicable to the suit and if so is the suit within. time under Article 120 ? 

 15. Before deciding whether this suit comes within the provisions of section 14, it is necessary to decide whether section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act is applicable to patni law. The High Court Division has answered the question in the affirmative without giving any reason whatsoever and the learned Additional Attorney-General has also assailed this finding without advancing any argument as to why it is not applicable. 

 16. Section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides that if the lands of a tenure or holding or a portion of such lands are lost by diluvion, the rent of the tenure or holding shall be abated by an amount which bears the same proportion to the rent of the whole tenancy, as the area lost bears to that of the whole tenancy. Section 2 of the Bengal Patni Taluks Regulation, 1819 clearly recognises taluks held by talukdars under Zamindars as "tenures". It says, "It is hereby declared that any leases or engagements for the fixing of rent now in existence that may ha, been granted or concluded for a term of years or in perpetuity by a proprietor under engagements with the Crown, or other person competent to grant the same, shall be deemed good and valid tenures " Section 5(1) of the Bengal Tenancy Act defines "tenure-holder" thus : "Tenure-holder means primarily a person who has acquired from a proprietor or from another tenure-holder a right to hold land for the purpose of collecting rents or bringing it under cultivation by establishing tenants on it, and also includes the successors-in-interest of persons who have acquired such a right." Hence, a talukdar holds a tenure under a Zamindar, a darpatnidar holds a tenure under a talukdar and so on. The same goes for a howladar and a nim-howladar and so on. Prima facie, therefore, the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act relating to tenures are applicable to Patni Laws. 

 17. But the following provision of section 195(e) of the Bengal Tenancy Act may be looked into 195. Nothing in this Act shall affect- 

 18. Thus, clause (e) simply says that the Bengal Tenancy Act shall not apply to enactment relating to patni-tenures "in so far as they relate to those tenures".
