The legal consequence of this saving clause is that with regard to patni-tenures the special patni law is to apply in the first place and in matters not covered by the special patni laws i.e. when patni laws are silent, the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act will apply, simply by way of supplementing the same, subject to the paramount consideration that the land must have been let out for agricultural purposes, because if the patni lease was a lease for horticultural purposes, it would come within the purview of the Transfer of Property Act. In so far as the relative rights of Zamindars and patni talukdars are concerned, established by Bengal Regulation VIII of 1819, the Bengal Tenancy Act cannot vary or alter the same, but if there are provisions in the Bengal Tenancy Act which are in the nature of supplementing the relationship without in any way being in conflict with the Patni laws, the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act will apply even in respect of Patni tenures. 

 19. Thus section 52 of the Bengal Tenancy Act provides for alteration of rent where there is alteration in area. The patni laws do not contain any such provision. In the case of Maharaja Ranjit Sinha Vs. Abdul Rahim Khan Chowdhury, 45 IC 190, the Patnidar filed a suit for abatement of rent. The Courts below granted the abatement of rent and the Calcutta High Court dismissing the appeal of the Zamindar observed : 

 "The learned Judges in the lower Courts have proceeded under the provisions of section 52 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and on the principles there defined. Section 52 says that every tenant shall be entitled to apply. A patnidar is a tenant and so prima facie he is entitled to make an application under section 52. It is said, however, that section 195 of the Act prevents section 52 from applying to the case of a patnidar on the ground that clause (e) of that section says that nothing contained in the Bengal Tenancy Act shall affect any enactment relating to patni-tenures in so far as it relates to those tenures. Section 52 does not affect any enactment relating to patni-tenures. It is quite clear, in my view, that the conclusion arrived at by the learned District Judge is right." 

 20. Similarly, under section 61 of the Bengal Tenancy Act a tenant can deposit rent in Court under certain circumstances, as in case of doubt as to who is entitled to receive it. In Bata Krishna Rana Vs. Janaki Nath Panday, 18 CWN 916=ILR 41 Cal. 1000, it was observed: 

 "It is also not seriously contested, and upon the facts stated it cannot be contested, that in the events which have happened, the tenant may entertain a bonafide doubt as to who is entitled to receive rent from him. Sec. 61 is, consequently, prima facie applicable. But reliance is placed, on behalf of the defendant, upon cl. (e) of sec. 195, which provides that nothing in the Bengal Tenancy Act shall affect any enactment relating to putni tenures in so far as it relates to those tenures. The question, consequently, arises whether sec. 61 does in any way affect an enactment relating to putni tenures. We invited the learned Vakil for the defendant to specify the particular provision of Reg. VIII of 1819 which is affected by sec. 61 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, but he was constrained to admit that he could not point out any such section. On the other hand, an examination of the provisions of Reg. VIII of 1819 indicates that there is no section which corresponds to sec. 54 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. If the Patni Regulation had contained a provision as to the time and place for payment of putni rent, it might have been plausibly argued that sec. 61 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, if applied to putni tenures, would affect the provisions of the Patni Regulation. On these grounds, we hold that sec. 61 is applicable to a patnidar and it was open to the plaintiff to deposit in Court the putni rent in the manner he did." 

 21. Section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act is in no way in conflict with the Patni laws nor do the Patni laws contain any provision similar or analogous to section 86A. No provision of patni laws is affected by section 86A in any way. We, therefore, hold that the provisions of section 86A apply to patni taluks as a supplemental provision of the Patni laws.

caseno: Civil Appeal No. 108 of 1977 from Civil Rule No. 419 of 1974.
parties:
Abdus Sattar & ors ----- Appellants.
Vs.
Suresh Chandra Das & ors ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, C.J- in this appeal a question of law of public importance is involved in that whether a monthly tenancy created under the provision of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act is heritable upon the death of the tenant. The other question of law involved will be dealt with at its appropriate place. 

 2. Facts, in brief, are that the appellants as plaintiff landlords instituted a Small Cause Courts suit for ejectment of Respondents. Their case for ejectment is that Balaram, father of Respondents, was monthly tenant at the premises in 1968 and from April, 1969, Suresh, the first Respondent took the tenancy in his name, and he having defaulted in payment of rent was liable to ejectment. The second Respondent, brother of Suresh, was added as a party to the suit on the objection of Respondent as he was also residing in the premises and was said to be in permissive possession. Plaintiffs asserted that both were liable to ejectment. The defence, in substance, apart from other grounds not relevant for this appeal, was that the tenancy was in favour of Balaram, and on his death it has devolved upon both the respondents as his heirs and so the notice to quit u/s 106 of the first Respondent was insufficient. 

 3. The trial Court on consideration of evidence, both oral and documentary, accepted the plaint case that Balaram was the first tenant, thereafter from 1969 first Respondent became tenant as evidenced by Ext. 3 series and he did not make payment after October, 1969 and was a defaulter. The second Respondent was in possession as the brother of Suresh but not as a tenant. He, therefore, decreed the suit for ejectment. On revision by the Respondents, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division reversed the findings of the trial Court, and held that the tenancy was only in favour of Balaram and on his death it devolved on his sons, the Respondents and so the notice to quit on Suresh was insufficient. He made the rule absolute and set aside the decree of the trial Court. 

 1.	Whether the High Court Division was well founded in law in holding that a monthly tenancy under the Transfer of Property Act is heritable. 

 2.	Whether upon a correct principle of law the learned Single Judge reversed the finding of fact u/s 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act as to the creation of tenancy in favour of first Respondent. 

 6. Since the question will not take as long, we propose to deal with it first. It is now well settled that a revision under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act lies if there is an error of law involved in the decision or the trial Court. A revision is available with a wider scope than that under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. They are now well settled and require no further elaboration. What is to be seen is whether the learned Judge of the High Court provision has applied the correct principle in interfering with the decision of the trial Court under section 25 of the said Act. First of all, he is to come to a finding the decision of the Court below suffers from an error of law, and then to see whether the error of law has vitiated its decision, and on so finding, he can proceed to reverse the decision of the trial Court. Keeping this principle in view, we are to judge the finding of the learned Single Judge regarding the reversal of the finding of the trial Court on the question of creation of tenancy in favour of Respondent 1. It is to be remembered that both the Courts below have accepted the creation of tenancy in 1968 in favour of Balaram, the father of the Respondents. Where the two Courts differed is on the creation of tenancy in favour of Respondent 1. According to the trial Court, tenancy was created in his favour in 1969 and this he based on a reference to Ext. 3 series the rent receipts. This finding was reversed by the learned Single Judge making a bare observation that it was clear from the pleadings of the parties and the evidence that the tenancy of Balaram was created on 1.1.68 and that the tenancy devolved upon his death on his heirs. The question is whether this finding is in accordance with the provisions of section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act. Plainly it is not. The learned Judge has not shown what was the error in the appreciation of evidence by the trial Court in its finding which could be termed as an error of law.which would give the High Court Division an authority under the Act to interfere. The approach of the learned Judge was as if he was dealing with a first appeal on fact and not a revision under section 25 of the said Act. No error of law was pointed out by him, nor do we find any such error in the finding of the trial Court. The trial Court from evidence drew a conclusion of fact which the learned Judge reversed without pointing out any error of law. He merely drew a second conclusion of fact which section 25 of the said Act does not authorize him to do. In this view of the matter the reversal of finding of fact by the learned Judge on this point cannot be sustained and must be set aside. The finding of the trial Court that a tenancy was created in favour of Respondent 1 on the death of Balaram, his father, must be upheld. In view of this finding, the first question loses much of its importance but since a question of law of public importance is involved, we proceed to deal with it. 

 7. From the facts on record we find that there was no written contract between the plaintiff's on the one hand and Balaram or Respondent 1 on the other, and the tenancy was created on the mere payment of rent between the landlord and tenant. A tenancy of this nature is legal and valid in terms of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. It has been termed to be a lease or tenancy from month to month terminable on the part of either party by fifteen days notice expiring at the end of a month of the tenancy. The section also refers to certain agricultural and manufacturing leases, but we are not concerned with them in this appeal. 

 8. It is further to be remembered that this monthly tenancy is also the subject of Bangladesh Premises Rent Control Ordinance, where, notwithstanding the provisions of Transfer of Property Act and Contract Act, wide-ranging provisions have been introduced encroaching upon the rights of the parties. But, in view of the question of law involved in this appeal, a detailed discussion of the Rent Control Ordinance need not be looked into as the Ordinance chiefly deals with the protection of the tenant from ejectment so long as he pays rent in terms of the Ordinance and with some other incidents of the tenancy but does not deal with the heritability of the tenancy. We only want to refer to the definition of 'tenant' given in the Ordinance. The Ordinance says, a tenant means a person by whom, or on whose account, rent is payable for any premises, and includes a legal representative as defined in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and a person continuing in possession after the termination of a tenancy in his favour. A glance at the definition along with the definition of 'landlord', which is noting but the counterpart of the tenant, indicates that the definition was inserted in the Ordinance only to emphasize the tenant's liability to pay rent and nothing more, and this meaning becomes clear when we advert to the second half of the definition of 'tenant,' which says that it also includes a person continuing in possession after the termination of his tenancy. In this view of the matter, we are not called upon to dilate on this Ordinance any further. 

 9. At the outset, it is to be observed that learned arguments have been advanced from the Bar on the English rule of the tenancy-at-will which is created where lands or tenements are let out by one man to another to have and to hold to him at the will of the lessor, by force of which lease, the lessee is in possession. A tenancy-at-will is determinable at the will of either landlord or tenant and is a personal relation between the original landlord and the tenant and is determined by the death of either of them. Whereas, the relationship between the landlord and tenant created under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act has been termed a lease from month to month, terminable on the part of either party by fifteen day's notice expiring at the end of a month of tenancy. The section, in a restricted sense, describes the tenancy as a lease. The difference between the two is also patently manifest that no fruitful purpose will be served in discussing the subject any further. 

 10. In order to grasp the problem before us, we are to see the character of tenancy that created under the provisions of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. This section is specie of a rider to the principle section which is section 105, and which defines what a lease is, section 105 says that a lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property. made for a certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised, or of money, as hare of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically for or on specified occasions to the transferor by the transferee who accepts the transfer on such term. Now if we analyze the essential elements constituting a lease, we find the following elements : (a) the right must be one as to immovable property ; (b) the right must be that of enjoyment of immovable property ; (c) there must be a transfer of such right ; (d) the right of transfer is an interest in property ; (e) the transfer be made for a certain time express or implied, or in perpetuity ; (f) the transfer must be one for consideration : (g) the consideration must be of the particular kind mentioned in the section, namely, premium or rent, as defined by the section, either or both of them. 

 12. Under section 106 of the Act, the lease contemplated, among others, is a lease or tenancy from month to month and is terminable by either party giving fifteen days notice expiring at the end of a month of the tenancy. A glance at the elements constituting lease under section 105 set out above reveals that all they are not present in a lease under section 106, nevertheless, it has been termed to be a lease under this section. An analysis of the elements constituting a lease along with a comparison of the two sections indicates that the lease coming under section 106 cannot be treated as a lease under section 105 having all its incidents. 

 13. Let us, therefore, consider what interest is created by the lease under section 106. The section says that the lease will be from month to month. No doubt this lease is for the occupation of the premises by the tenant which is terminable at the option of either party on giving fifteen days notice expiring at the end of a month of the tenancy. The termination of the tenancy, of course, cannot take effect unless the notice to quit under this section has been served by one or the other, and the statutory period had expired. Analyzing in this way, we find that a relationship is created under this section between the landlord and the Cannot which is of a personal nature. The right of occupation of the premises has been given and this right of occupation from month to month from its very nature cannot but be personal and so cannot create an interest in the land as a lease under section 105 does. The right of occupation remains personal with the tenant. The right being personal it ceases with the death of either party or so on the death of the tenant. the tenancy ceases and hence it is not heritable. 

 14. Since some interest is created, even though personal, by the monthly tenancy. This may not be, to borrow an English concept, an estate in favour of the tenant, nevertheless the heirs or successors-in-interest of a tenant in occupation of the premises on his death do not become trespassers, because neither their predecessor nor they entered the premises wrongfully, and so their continuance in the premises will be that of a tenant by sufferance. to borrow again another English concept. It is to be noted that tenancy by sufferance arises by implication of law and cannot be created by a contract between the parties. Such interest cannot be assigned or conveyed and is in fact a mere invention of law to prevent the continuance of possession acting as a trespass. Such a tenant may be ejected at any time without demand of possession. If, however, the landlord assents or receives rent, he becomes a tenant in terms of section 106, as his predecessor was, with all the incidents of a tenancy under that section. 

 15. In our view, the construction we have given on section 106 of the Act will obviate serious complications which would otherwise originate if we treat a monthly tenancy under section 106 as full fledged lease of property and so heritable. To illustrate, if it is heritable, then, according to the personal law of the tenant, it will be inherited by the whole group of heirs contemplated therein sons, daughters wife, other kinds etc. and all of them becoming tenants some of them may not be occupying the premises at all. Nonetheless, they will become liable to future rent and will be entitled to receive the notice to quit. Likewise, the landlord will be faced with an insurmountable problem of ejecting those innumerable "tenants by inheritance" many of whom might not be known to him. He would also be faced with the immense difficulty of serving the notice to quit on all of them. 

 16. Then again, under what principle this right is made available to the heirs? The original tenant himself did not enjoy more than a mere right of occupation on payment of rent was liable to be ejected on fifteen days notice. How this uncertain, if not precarious right of occupation, can become an estate to be inherited by persons who have never occupied the premises? It is a proposition which is untenable. In that event the tenant having the bare right of occupation will leave after his death a higher right to his heirs in the tenancy, which he never had. The heirs will become tenants without occupying or using the premises. This cannot be contemplated because in that event heirs will inherit a right higher than that of their predecessor. 

 17. The view we have taken is in accord with the true intent or section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. In this view, the decision in the case of Gouribala Pal vs Kunjalai Saha (1960) 12 DLR 37 where a Single Judge of the Dacca High Court has, relying on an earlier Calcutta decision in the case of Anwarali Bepari vs. Jamini Lal Ray Chowdhury 43 CWN 197, held that upon the death of an original tenant in respect of an immovable property, the tenancy being one from month to month, does not cease to exist and the heirs and legal representatives of the original tenant do not become trespassers but having continued in possession as heirs, they become tenants by holding over, cannot be sustained. The view taken in the Calcutta decision was that there was no reason why a tenant from month to month should not be heritable. For the reasons we have already given, we find it difficult to concur with the view expressed in this decision. 

 18. We therefore, conclude that on the death of the tenant a tenancy from month to month does not become heritable. The finding of the learned Judge of the High Court Division that upon the death of Balaram, the tenancy was inherited by his two son’s cannot, therefore, be sustained. For the reasons we set aside the decision of the High Court Division and restore that of the trial Court.

parties:
Md. Abdur Rouf and others -------- Appellants
Vs.
Ahmuda Khatun and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Appellant Abdur Rouf filed an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in the Third Court of the Sub-ordinate Judge Dacca. His case was that the 'A' schedule property originally belonged to one Samru Goala in whose name C.S. record stood on February 28, 1927. The property was sold by him to Snehalata and Jiban Ranjan Nath on December 23, 1936. Jiban Ranjan Nath sold a portion of his share to Anukul Chandra Majumder. Subsequently, Snehalata, Anukul and Jiban sold the entire plot to Abdus Sultan Wali Bhai who, in his turn, sold the entire 'A' schedule property with standing structures thereon to Mrs. Fatema Begum on January 8, 1955. Since then she was in possession of the property until she transferred 1½ kathas of land along with standing structures as shown in schedule, 'B' to one Sakina Bai by a sale deed dated May 11, 1966. 

 4. The application for pre-emption was resisted by Keramat Ali on the ground, among others, that the 'B' schedule lands, buildings, and structures which bear Municipal holding No. 49/2, Purana Paltan Line, Dacca, was previously held by Sakina Bai on her purchase from Fatema Begum. She possessed the same on amicable partition with Fatema and mutated her name in the records of the Municipality. On receiving the consideration of Tk. 25,000/- from Keramat Ali, Sakina Bai executed the same deed in his favour on October 30, 1972. The appellants are not entitled to pre-emption as they are not co-sharers in respect of schedule property. Furthermore, the application under section 24 of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not maintainable and the same is barred under section 8 (2) of the same Act. The appellants should have filed an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Moreover, he has, since his purchase improved the schedule property by additions and alterations in the existing structures at a cost of Tk. 15,600/- without depositing which amount the appellants were not entitled to any relief. 

 1. Whether, in view of the provision of section 85 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, application for pre-emption of non-agricultural land under section 24 of the Act was maintainable. 

 2. Whether, having regard to the amended provisions of section 81 and insertion of section 81(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the application for pre-emption, whether of agricultural land or non-agricultural land was to be made under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 6. Since, as the learned Judge of the High Court found that the case of Akhtaruzzaman vs. Jadu Nath Pal, (1965) 17 DLR 384 (FB) PLD 1967 Dacca 546, decided by a Full Bench of the High Court has already settled the point involved in the first question they application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was competent. 

 7. As regards the second question, the learned Judges after consideration the diver-gent views of the different Benches held that the provisions of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act would apply to agricultural land lying outside the municipal areas and section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act would be applicable to all classes of land, whether agricultural or non-agricultural within the municipal areas. 

 9. The second question regarding which conflicting decisions exist requires the consideration of the provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act as well as section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act both which confer the right of pre-emption. Their application in a particular case would depend on the nature of land, the person who holds such land and the relationship between him and the person who claims to pre-empt the land transferred by the former. Since the two laws, namely, Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the State Acquisition Act dealt with two kinds of land, i. e., non-agricultural land and agricultural land, the right of pre-emption in respect of the former could be claimed under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and in respect of agricultural land right of pre-emption could be claimed under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This position is stated by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in deciding the question whether in respect of non-agricultural land pre-emption could be claimed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The dispute before the Supreme Court related to non-agricultural homestead, land within the municipality. The Supreme Court observed as follows:— 

 "Because section 96 occurs in Chapter XIII the trial Court held that the right of pre-emption can be claimed in respect of non-agricultural land. The court, however, overlooked the fact that this Chapter, which regulates the right and liabilities of a raiyat was made applicable to tenants of non-agricultural land but it does not enlarge the content of the right as given in section 96 or introduce any change in the incidents  of the right. In other words, it does not materially affect the character of the land in respect of which the right of pre-emption can be claimed. Section 96 in clear terms lays down that this right of pre-emption will be available only in respect of a 'holding'. In view of the definition of 'holding' as given in section 2(13) of the Act it cannot be said that the right of pre-emption can be exercised in respect of non-agricultural land. Here it may be mentioned that there is specific provision for pre-emption of non-agricultural land in the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act (XXIII) of 1949. Under that Act a contiguous owner cannot claim a right of pre-emption. After review of relevant provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act we think that section 96 is confined to agricultural land and, therefore, a right of pre-emption under this section cannot be claimed in respect of homestead land within a municipality'. 

 10. Had there been no amendment of certain provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the law stated by the Supreme Court of Pakistan would perhaps have remained unquestioned, but the omission of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 81 and the insertion of section 81-A by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1967 were claimed to have changed this otherwise unassailable position. The provisions of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 81 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the aforesaid amendment were as follows: 

 11. The newly inserted section 81-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides as follows :- 

 "81-A(I) Except as otherwise provided in this part, the right and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under the Provincial Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such land under the provisions of this Act shall, where the provisions of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, applied to such land, at the time of such Acquisition, be regulated by the provisions of that Act. 

 Provided that, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant shall sub-let the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms and conditions whatsoever, and if any tenancy or any part of a tenancy is sublet in contravention of this provision, the interest of the non-agricultural tenant in the tenancy or in that part of the tenancy, as the case may be, shall be extinguished, and the tenancy or the part of the tenancy shall vest in the Provincial Government from the date of such subletting free from all encumbrances". 

 12. The effect of these amendments on the applicability of the provisions of section 96 of the State Acquisition and tenancy Act to non-agricultural land was considered in Mst. Noor Jahan Begum vs. Md. Tobarak Ali decided by a Single Bench of the High Court Division (Civil Revision No. 639 of 1969). Referring to the aforesaid amendments and their effect on the question the learned Judge observed as follows: 

 "By the new provisions, the entire Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has been made applicable to a holder of non-agricultural land. The simple test is as to whether the holder of non-agricultural land has become a tenant under the Provincial Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior rights in such land. If the holder of non-agricultural land has become a tenant directly under the Provincial Government his rights and liabilities will be governed by the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act subject to the provisions contained in Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It comes to this that for the purpose of pre-emption relating to non-agricultural land if the holder of the holding has be, come tenant directly under the Government by virtue of acquisition of the superior rights in such land, section 96 of the State Acquisition Act will be applicable in preference to section 24 of the East Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 81-A(2) makes provision for other non-agricultural tenants." 

 13. After considering the provisions of law contained in the two Acts. the amendments to the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and other provisions defining the expressions 'holding', 'raiyat', 'land' agricultural land', 'non, agricultural tenancy' and the decisions quoted above, the learned Judges of the High Court Division in this instant case expressed their agreement with the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. They observed as follows: 

 Under section 24, only the co-sharer tenants of non-agricultural land, which is the subject of the transfer, can make an application. This distinction has been maintained in the two Acts even after the omission of sub-sections (2) and (3) from section 81 and insertion of section 81-A to the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thus, we find that insofar as an application for pre-emption is concerned section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and section 24 or the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act will have their applications in their respective areas, namely, section 96 shall be applicable to agricultural lands beyond the Municipal area whereas section 25 will be applicable to all classes of lands within the Municipal area and this view that we have taken is supported by the said un-reported decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Civil Appeal No. 47-D of 1963." 

 14. The views expressed above are no doubt correct, since even after the insertion of section 81-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which proceeded to regulate certain rights and liabilities of a bolder of non-agricultural land who has become a tenant under the Government as a result of the acquisition of the superior right in such land, the distinction between the rights of a holder of non-agricultural land and those holding agricultural land was not entirely done away with. For, as it appears from the very provisions of sub-section (1) of section 81-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the rights and liabilities of a holder of non-agricultural land, insofar as they were sought to be not affected by this section, were to be still governed by the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. There is no ambiguity in this respect and the relative positions of the holders of non-agricultural land and agricultural land concerning the right of pre-emption exercisable by them under the, two different Acts have not been disturbed by any express provision in that part of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which contains the aforesaid section 'as might have been supposed by the opening words of sub-section (1) of section 81-A, "except as otherwise provided in this part". 

 Neither in sub-section (2) of this section which deals with the rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants, that is, those who did not come under sub-section (1), nor in any other provision in Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is there any provision which has obliterated the distinction. Moreover, the ingredients of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and of Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are different. Some of these distinctions are that while section 96 confers right of pre-emption on the holder of land contiguous to the land transferred, no such holder of land can exercise the right of pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which merely confers the right of pre-emption on a non-agricultural tenant in respect of non-agricultural land. Moreover, as observed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan which has been referred to above, the use of the expression 'holding' in section 96 which is not to be found in section 24 also makes for a meaningful distinction. 

 15. We, therefore, hold that in spite of the omission of section 81A, section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has not been rendered ineffective nor impliedly repealed so as to compel the owner of any land falling within the municipal area to prefer an application under section 96 of that State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 17. The position does not seem to be what has been stated here. If the mutation itself has not been according to the provisions of law the co-sharers cannot be said to have loft their interest in the tenancy. The provisions for subdivision of tenancy which are contained in section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are as follows: 

 c) for the purpose of subdivision of joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such sub-division of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent if any as he may consider fair and equitable : Provided that no such order shall be passed unless reasonable notice is given to the parties concerned to appear and be heard in the matter : Provided further that where an order under clause (c) is passed, and distribution of rent, by reason thereof, results in bringing the rent of a portion of the tenancy below one, a fraction of one shall be rounded off into one 

 18. These provisions correspond-roughly with those contained in section 88A of the Bengal Tenancy Act. From the first provision to clause (c) of section 117 it will appear that no order for the sub-division of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants shall be passed unless reasonable notice has been served upon all of them to appear and are heard in the matter. Mr. M.H. Khondker, Counsel for the respondents, submitted that the word 'shall' used in the, proviso is directory and not mandatory. Therefore, even if no notice has been given to the appellants of the application of the respondents to sub-divide the tenancy who did not, therefore, appear before the Revenue Officer when he passed the order for splitting up of the jama, such order cannot be said to have been vitiated by such non-service of notice upon the appellants. Furthermore, even though no such notice has been served upon him, it was open to the appellants to take recourse to the remedy provided in the Act to rectify their grievances with the time provided therein. Since they have not done so, the matter is concluded and the Court cannot while hearing the application for pre-emption entertain an objection regarding the non-service of notice during the mutation proceedings. In support of his submission that the word 'shall' is mandatory and not directory, he quoted the decisions re-ported in (1895) 1 QB 724 at 729 and 47 CWN 323. 

 19. On the other hand, Mr. T.H. Khan, Counsel for the appellants, submitted that the word 'shall' is mandatory and not directory in the absence of notice, as provided in section 117(1)(c), upon the co-sharer tenants, the order of sub-division of the tenancy will be bad and not be binding on the non-notified co-sharer tenants. In support, Mr. Khan, relied on Begum Asia Rahman Vs. Abdul Basir Bhuiyan (1974) 26 DLR (SC) 58. Here, the provisions of section 88A of the Bengal Tenancy Act which corresponds to section 117 (1)(c) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, were being considered. In saying that the sub-division of the holding could not create a bar for the exercise of, the right of pre-emption by the respondent when no service of notice under section 88A was served upon him, the Court observed as follows: 

 20. In the present case before us the respondents produced exhibits F & G, the record of right and rent receipts respectively, in order to establish that during the pendency of the application for pre-emption the record of right was changed in the name of Sakina Bai. As a result of the mutation so effected by the respondents the appellants ceased to have any subsisting interest in the disputed land. Had this mutation been effected with a notice to the appellants, it might be argued that the mutation was binding upon the appellants but the non-service of notice of the mutation case has not only resulted in the violation of the principles of natural justice so far as the appellants are concerned but is in direct violation of the statutory requirement laid down in section 117 (1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The words used therein are both positive and clear and the requirement of notice being in respect of rights to property the word 'shall' used therein in mandatory and not directory. There is no vagueness or ambiguity about the intention of the legislature in imposing the duty of serving notice upon the co-sharers when one of them wants to divide the holding. The respondents have failed to show the fulfillment of the requirement provided under the aforesaid section. They have no doubt been able to produce the order of sub-division of the holding but such sub-division which is an exparte order in substance having been obtained without notifying the appellants cannot be binding on them. As a consequence their interest in the holding subsisted and the intended effect of the document contained in exhibits F & G which might have otherwise taken away such interest has not been produced. The principles laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the decision reported in (1967) 19 DLR (SC) 36 is not, therefore, applicable to the facts of the present case and right of pre-emption claimed by the appellants is not accordingly affected by the order of sub-division of the holding. 

 22. Mr. Khondker, Counsel for the, respondents, vehemently argued that the mutation which had been affected by the respondents under the provisions of section 117 (1) (c) does neither come under the word 'transferred' or the word 'otherwise dealt with' and cannot therefore, be questioned by the respondents as affecting his rights to property. What the word 'transferred' means is not vague or unclear. It means such transfers as are contemplated by the Transfer of Property Act, such as, sales, gifts, mortgages, leases and exchanges but there is some scope for doubt as the meaning of the word 'otherwise dealt with'. Whatever other transactions may be included by them the questions is, as has been raised by the learned Counsel for the respondents, whether they include mutation as a result of an order of sub-division of a tenancy effected under section 117 (1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He submitted that the expression 'otherwise dealt with' ejusdem generis with the word 'transfer' and therefore, the transaction which may be included under former expression must partake of the same nature as that of a 'transfer. Since the order of sub-division under section 117 (1) (c) cannot be viewed as 'transfer' mutation effected thereunder is not hit by the principle of lis pendens. On the other hand, the learned Counsel for the appellant made contrary submissions. According to him, the expression 'otherwise dealt with' does not bring ejusdem generis rule into play. In support, he relied upon the decision reported in AIR 1958 SC 838; 1943 AC 166.

full_judgment:
2. Late Eklas Hossain Khan predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 made an application under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the case land measuring 0.0206 acre of C.S. and S.A. plot No. 565 appertaining to S. A. Khatian No. 612 and Mutation Khatian No. 474/18. The case of the pre-emptor, in short, is that the case land along with other lands originally belonged to Jogesh Chandra Majumder and others and the C.S. record of rights was accordingly prepared and published in their names. Golam Mortuza Khan, father of the pre-emptor and opposite party Nos. 3-11 purchased 5 kathas of land by registered deed of sale from the said tenants and lived there by constructing dwelling house and on payment of rents on mutation in his own name. Thereafter Golam Mortuza Khan died leaving pre-emptor and opposite party Nos. 3-5 as four sons and opposite party Nos. 6-11 as six daughters and the said heirs possessed the lands jointly by way of inheritance. Opposite party No. 4 by registered deed of sale dated 18.02.88 transferred his share to his brother opposite party No. 3 and delivered possession. Opposite party No. 3 transferred the said land by a deed of sale executed on the same date to the petitioner and the deed of sale was registered on 13.08.88. In spite of the fact that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the joint tenancy no notice was served upon him. The pre-emptor was in possession in the house constructed by him. 

 6. On the pleadings issues framed are whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy, whether the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation, whether there was any improvement made by the purchase and what relief or reliefs the pre-emptor is entitled to. 

 8. On consideration of the evidence on record the trial court held that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer of the tenancy, that the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation and that there is a proof of development of the case land by purchaser. Upon such view, the trial court dismissed the application for pre-emption. 

 10. Mr. N. H. Khondker appearing for the purchaser submits that in view of provision of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appellate court failed to take into consideration the findings of the trial court and reasons given for those and without considering the evidence on record held that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the tenancy and the application for pre-emption is not barred by limitation. In support of his submission he also cited the cases reported in 5 BLD (AD) 54, 15 BLD (AD) 91, 16 BLD (AD) 197 and 17 BLD (AD) 47. 

 11. The learned Advocate also submits that the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters were separated by amicable partition among them and had been enjoying separate jama since then and the Municipal holding also shows that the pre-emptor was enjoying his share separately in separate holding number. The Court of appeal below therefore, committed serious error of law in riot considering those facts incoming to its decision. I-le further submits that after purchase he also got his purchased land mutated and he has been paying rent through his mutated Khatian since purchase and also staying there after constructing a semi-pucca house and installing all modern utility services, namely, electricity, gas, WASA etc. Even after such independent and separate enjoyment of the purchased land, the finding of the appellate court that tenancy was riot separated is totally misconceived and not sanctioned by any law. 

 13. Mr. Abdul Barek Chowdhury appearing for the opposite Party Nos. 1 and 2, submits that only two questions are involved in the case as to limitation and whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy out of which that land was sold. On limitation, he submits that the impugned kabala was finally registered on 13.08.88 and application was filed on 25.09.88 so it cannot be said that application for pre-emption was beyond the time, no matter the certified copy of the application was obtained on 16.03.88. On the issue of locus standi as co-sharer, he submits that as no order of any competent authority could be adduced by the purchaser to show that the tenancy was ever sub-divided and the rents were distributed amongst the co-sharers of the tenancy and as such, no amount of testimony or amicable partition can be taken into consideration to find the joint tenancy was sub-divided and jama was separated and thereby, the pre-emptor ceased to be a co-sharer in the tenancy. 

 15. It is true, out of the issues framed by the trial court the issues with regard to limitation and whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy out of which the land was sold are raised as the most issues before me. No other issues was pressed for, so let me see whether the judgment and order of the court of appeal below are well founded in law as well as on facts. 

 17. Now, with regard to the locus standi of the petitioner. I have gone through the written objection filed by the purchaser. He has claimed that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the tenancy on three counts. Firstly after the death of Golam Mortuza Khan the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters amicably partitioned their inherited land and properties and they have been possessing their specific share independently and separately since then. Secondly, the land sold belongs to a separate Municipal holding than that of the holding where the petitioner has been living in and thirdly O.P.W. No. 5 wife of opposite party No. 3 Moslemuddin Khan admitted that after the death of her father-in-law the properties were separated amicably and now the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters staying in their separate and independent shares. The purchaser also adduced a D.C.R. Ext. Uma dated 29.02.88 issued by Assistant Tahsilder in respect of a Khatian No. 474/17/1. I have also seen the rent receipts marked as Ext. Uma (1) and Uma (2) showing payment of rents on 17.03.88 and 14.04.90. I have also perused a tax receipt Ext. Uma (3) issued by Dhaka Municipal Corporation showing payment of tax for the year 1988/89 and 1989/90 against holding No. 18/6/C in the name of Harunur Rashid. The purchaser examined himself as O.P.W. No. 1 and he testified that after the death of Golam Mortuza Khan the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters in 1974 amicably partitioned their inherited lands and properties. He also claimed to have got his purchased lands mutated in his name. In cross-examination, he testified that he could not remember whether he got the land mutated before the making of the application for pre-emption. But he was very categorical in deposing that he did not serve any notice upon the pre-emptor or his brothers and sisters because they were living in separate holdings. 

 18. There is no dispute, the property was originally owned and possessed by Golam Mortuza Khan. After his death the petitioner and his three brothers and six sisters opposite parties 3-11 inherited. They are living separately. Now, the question is whether in view of the above facts and the evidence on record can it be said, there was sub-division of the tenancy held by Golam Mortuza Khan and rents were distributed in accordance with law and thereby, the petitioners ceased to be a co-sharer in the joint tenancy and thereby, lost his right of pre-emption. 

 19. Section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950 has provided for sub-division of a holding and/or a joint tenancy and distribution of rents. Section 117 reads- 

 (c) for the purpose of subdivision of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing such subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any, he may consider fair and equitable: 

 This provision is applicable for subdivision and distribution of rents in respect of all sorts of lands, agricultural and non-agricultural. Under the above provision, Revenue officer is given the power to subdivide a joint tenancy for the purpose of distribution of rents. Such jurisdiction can only be exercised upon an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants and after service of reasonable notice to the parties concerned to appear, and after hearing them. Following the provisions of the Section, the Revenue officer by an order in writing may direct subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer-tenants and distribution of rents thereof amongst them. 

 No such order of Revenue officer directing subdivision of the joint tenancy held by Golam Mortuza Khan and distributing the rents amongst the co-sharers i.e. the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters has been adduced in this case. The purchaser have categorically stated that before his getting the purchased land mutated, he did not serve any notice upon any heirs of said Golam Mortuza Khan Because, they are living in separate holding. Here, it must be noted that such authority for subdivision of a joint tenancy and the distribution of rents has not been given to any other authority including the Dhaka Municipal Corporation. Mutation of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation to be valid must be based on an order in writing of the Revenue officer concerned making the joint tenancy subdivided and rents distributed. It cannot be other way round. Separate holding number given by a Municipal Corporation cannot replace an order under Section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, so, the heirs of Golam Mortuza Khan must be held to be still enjoying the joint tenancy left by him. Similarly, no amicable partition among the co-sharers even if reached in writing nor even a decree passed in a partition suit allotting different shares to the co-sharers can substitute the order as mentioned in Section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In such view of the legal position as well as the factual position, the court of appeal below was perfectly justified in holding that the joint tenancy of Golam Murtoza Khan was never subdivided and the rents were never distributed amongst his heirs, pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters in accordance with law, and thereby, the pre-emptor did not cease to be a co-sharer in the Joint tenancy left by him. Accordingly, the pre-emptor, Eklas Hossain Khan is a co-sharer in the joint tenancy left by Golam Mortuza Khan. 

 20. In the case of M.A. Rouf Vs. Ahmuda Khatun, 33 DLR (AD) 323, it was clearly held, any subdivision without notice upon co-sharer of a joint tenancy would not affect the right of pre-emption. Moreover, even if a mutation or subdivision is obtained lawfully during the pendency of a proceeding for pre-emption that must be hit by the doctrine of lies pendent under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. In this case, the purchaser did not adduce any evidence to show when the purchaser got the purchased land mutated in his name. But, Exts Uma series clearly show, those were issued during the pendency of the proceeding for pre-emption. If it is so, such mutation or subdivision is not based on any lawful order of a Revenue officer. Because, the order admittedly obtained without service of notice upon the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters, must be also hit by the doctrine of lies pendent under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. In the case of Begum Aisa Rahman Vs. Abdul Basir Bhuiyan, 26 DLR (SC) 58 it was held, subdivision of a holding without notice, on a co-sharer, does not defeat the right of a co-sharer of pre-emption. In the case of Begum Khodeja Akter Vs. Hareza Khatun, 37 DLR (AD) 212 as referred by Mr. N. H. Khondker for the purchaser, the case was remanded by the Appellate Division to the trial court to determine whether the jama was separated or not as none of the courts below held that a joint holding was subdivided or the rents were distributed. In the case of Sunil Krishna Banik Vs. Kailash Chandra Saha (1984) 4 BLD (AD) 320 the Appellate Division held that if an original co-sharer ceases to be a co-sharer of the joint tenancy he cannot apply for pre-emption. The person making the application for pre-emption must have a subsisting interest in the joint tenancy and such interest must continue au through the proceeding of pre-emption in order to be successful to get an order for pre-emption. 

 23. In the result, the Rule is discharged. No order as to costs. The judgment and order of the court of appeal below reversing those of the trial court are confirmed. The application pre-emption made by the predecessor of opposite party No. 1 and 2 under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the impugned deed No. 617 executed on 18.02.88 and registered on 13.03.88 is allowed.

Shaher Khatun & ors  ------ Petitioners

State and others  ------ Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
2. Complainant-opposite Party No.1 made a complaint before, the court of Magistrate, Tangail against accused petitioners alleging, inter alia, that they in collusion with each other created a forged order purported to be made by then Munsif, 3rd Court, Tangail in Miscellaneous Case No.337 of 1973 under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, shortly the Act, for correction of the record of right in respect of the case land, that subsequently the petitioners filed the said forged order before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Mirzapur for correcting the record of rights in their favour, that pursuant thereto, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) issued notice upon the complainant who on enquiry ascertained that petitioners filed a forged copy of the order of the learned Munsif and thereupon filed an application before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) for attaching the said forged order of the learned Munsif for drawing up a proceeding under section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) refused to make any complaint and directed the complainant to file case against the accused and accordingly, complaint was made. 

 8. Now the question is a Revenue Officer, in the instant case Assistant Commissioner (Land), dealing with a Mutation proceeding is a Revenue Court within the meaning of sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure shortly the Code. In the Code, no definition of the "Revenue Court" has been given. Since there is no definition of Revenue Court in the Code, let us examine other Laws as to the meaning of the term 'Revenue Court. In the Tenancy Law i.e. the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there is no definition of Revenue Court." The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act only speaks of "Revenue Officer" includes "any officer whom the government may appoint to discharge all or any of the functions of a Revenue officer under this Act or any rules made thereunder". Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954 provide the procedure of preparation of the records of rights by the Revenue officer. Sub- section 9(a) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act defines the term "Chief Revenue Officer" means the National Board of Revenue constituted under the National Board of Revenue Order 1972, (president's Order 76 of 1972). Since there is no definition of "Revenue Court" in the Code of Criminal Procedure, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the General Clauses Act let us examine the meaning of the term "Court." Section 6 of the Code describes classes of criminal Courts, namely: 

 12. As pointed out earlier, the term revenue court has not been defined in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The said .Act only speaks of Revenue Officer. A Revenue Officer initiates a Mutation Proceeding in exercise of powers under section 143 of the State Acquisition .and Tenancy Act 1950 and the Rules framed thereunder. Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, provides: 

 For carrying out purposes of the Act, the Government promulgated the Tenancy Rules 1954 in exercise of powers conferred under section 152 of the Act. In the said Rules, Rules 22 and 23 provide the procedures and the manner in which the record of rights referred to In section 143 shall be maintained. The relevant portions of Rules 22 and 23 are reproduced below- 

 13. These Rules clearly provide that when Tahsilder primarily responsible for. report to the Revenue Officer apparently makes clerical mistake in record-of-rights, changes of ownership, etc., the Revenue Officer shall direct correction of such clerical mistakes and making such inquiries as he "may consider necessary direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act being a ministerial act shall not be open to appeal. A Revenue Officer holding an inquiry in a mutation proceeding, in the premises, does not become a court as he does not really adjudicate a right and he does not give a decision which is binding on the parties. He merely corrects apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of-rights and directs correction of such clerical mistakes. If he is vested with necessary powers, incorporates necessary changes in the record-of-rights mutating the names when mutation is asked for as a result of inheritance on the report of Tahsilder under Rule 22 and also when mutation is asked for as a result of transfer, his acts being ministerial acts, shall not be open to appeal as provided in Rule 23 sub-rule (4) of the Tenancy Rules, 1954. He certainly exercises no judicial function. The functions are much more in the nature of a fiscal enquiry for the purpose of ascertaining which of the several claimants for the occupation of certain denominations of immovable property may be put into occupation of it with greater confidence than the revenue for which will be paid. Inquiry in mutation proceedings, therefore, being a fiscal inquiry conducted by agents of the State, for their own purposes, it could by no means be described as judicial proceeding. Therefore, a Revenue Officer when dealing with a mutation proceedings does not constitute a "Revenue Court" within the wider meaning of section 195(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 "We are in full agreement with the view expressed in the aforesaid decisions. We are, therefore, of the opinion that a Revenue Officer dealing with a mutation proceeding under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Rules framed thereunder does not constitute a court. Since we have found that a Revenue Officer acting under Rule 23 of the Tenancy Rules is not a Court, it is needless for us to dilate on the question whether he is a civil, criminal or Revenue Court." 

 "We respectfully disagree with the above views of the Division Bench which held that Revenue Officer doing mutation matter is not a Revenue Court. Tenancy Rules 30 and 31 deal with preparation of record-of-rights and Tenancy Rules 20-24 deal with correction of records of right by way of Mutation. Both the matters are dealt with by the Revenue Officers and regarding Mutation matter there is a provision for review to the Revenue Officer. Weare of the view that the principle applicable to preparation of record of right also be applicable to the mutation of name in the record of rights inasmuch as both relate to preparation, modification, addition or alteration of record of rights. Relying upon the principles as laid down by the Appellate Division in above decision reported in BCR 1987 (AD) 152, we hold that the Revenue Officer dealing in Mutation of the name in the record of rights is also a Revenue Court. As we are holding this view relying upon the above decision of the Appellate Division, we need not refer this matter to a Full Bench for our disagreement with another Division Bench." 

 16. The said decision of the Division Bench in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarker was mainly based upon the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Nur Ahmed (Supra) holding that since the Appellate Division has settled the point, the learned Judge felt it not necessary to refer the matter to a Full Bench for settling the point. Let us now examine the case of Nur Ahmed (Supra) and if the decision of the Appellate Division is exactly on the point, then certainly the said decision is binding on us and we are bound to follow that decision. In the Appellate Division's case, a complaint was lodged by a care-taker of Kodam Mobarak and Adam Rasul Waqf Estate before the Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong to the effect that he received a notice from the Objection Officer of Settlement Department and pursuant thereto, on query came to learn that accused had filed an objection case alleging that he has purchased the land in dispute and filed the deed before the objection officer, which was a forged deed. The complainant brought to the notice of the Objection Officer about the said forgery whereupon the Objection Officer seized the kabala. Accordingly, the learned Magistrate issued process upon the accused persons under sections 467/468/109 of the Penal Code. In the said case the Appellate Division upon consideration of Rules 30, 31 and 39 of the Tenancy Rules, 1954 held that: 

 "Reading the provisions of Rules 30 and 39 ,of the Tenancy Rules 1954, there could be no difficulty in holding that Mr Golam Mostafa, the Objection Officer was functioning as a Revenue Court while the alleged document was placed before him in connection with proceeding under Rule 30 of the said Tenancy Rules and as such, section 195(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is clearly attracted which puts an embargo on taking cognizance of the alleged offence under sections 467 and 468 of the Penal Code in the absence of a complaint from the court concerned". 

 17. In the Appellate Division's case the issue was whether an Objection Officer having power of an Assistant Settlement Officer in deciding Objection Petition is a Revenue Court or not. The Appellate Division upon consideration of Rules 30, 31 and 39 of the Tenancy Rules 1954 held that a Revenue Officer having additional powers of Settlement Officer while hearing objection case shall have all powers exercisable by a civil court in a trial of suits under Civil Procedure Code and decides ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land and therefore, the objection officer is functioning as a "Revenue Court". These Rules were framed for carrying out the purpose and the manner in which revision of the record-of-rights can be prepared under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 144 provides: 

 These rules are included in chapter VII of the Tenancy Rules 1954 under the heading "Revision of record of rights under section 144 of the Act." This chapter deals with the particulars to be recorded at the stages of the work, procedure of work up to attestation, publication of draft record of rights, objection, appeal, publication of final records, certificate of final publication, presumption as to correctness of record of rights, powers of Revenue Officers, etc. while revising the record-of-rights under section 144 of the Act. After such revision of the record-of-rights at the instance of the Government of any district, part of a district or local area by the Revenue Officer appointed for the purpose who shall have either with or without the additional designation of "Settlement Officer", or "Assistant Settlement Officer", such Revenue Officer shall publish a draft record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection at such convenient place as he may determine and a proclamation be published informing the tenants/maliks for filing objections. After hearing the objections, if any, he shall proceed to frame the final record-of-rights. Similarly, in case of an appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision. The provisions of Act and the Rules clearly show that the revision of the record-of-rights made under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has' presumptive value, but any order of mutation of the record made under section 143 of the Act has no such presumptive value. A Revenue Officer appointed with the power of Settlement Officer shall have all powers exercisable by a Civil Court in the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure. These Rules and the rules framed by the Governor in Council of Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 are closely akin Rule 36 of the Tenancy Rules 1954 is similar to Rule 41 of the Bengal Rules. Similarly, Rules 39 and 40 are equivalent to Rules 44 and 45 of Bengal Rules. The Bengal Government Rules were framed for carrying out the purpose of chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It is settled that the record of rights prepared in chapter I of the Bengal Tenancy Act i.e. under sections 101-104 of the Bengal Tenancy Act have the presumptive value as in section 144 of the Act but such presumption is not available in section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the Appellate Division's case no argument was made as to whether a Revenue Officer dealing with Mutation proceeding is a Revenue Court or not and naturally the Appellate Division has not decided the said issue. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Nur Ahmed is quite distinguishable from the facts of the case of Idris Ali (38 DLR 270) and the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar (44 DLR 533). The Appellate Division case was decided upon consideration of the Rules contained in Chapter VII and VIII of the Tenancy Rules 1954 which were framed in exercise of section 152(2)(2b) of the Act, for carrying out the purposes for all or any of the provisions of section 144 of the Act which the facts in the case of Idris Ali (Supra) and that of Ajit Kumar Sarkar(Supra) are similar to the present case, which relate to mutation proceedings under section 143 of the Act and Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954 framed in exercise of section 152 (2)(2a) of the Act. In the premises aforesaid, we are in respectful agreement with the views taken by the Division of the High Court Division in the case of Idris Ali (Supra). For the reasons discussed above and the provisions of law quoted herein before, with due respect to the learned Judges of the High Court Division, we are unable to endorse the views taken by them in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar (Supra). 

 20. It has been pointed out earlier that the High Court Division, in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarker and others (Supra) based its decision relying upon the case of the Appellate Division, the facts of which are quite distinguishable from the case of the case reported in the case of Noor Ahmed and the High Court Division without examining the relevant provisions of law i.e. section 143 of the Act and chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954, held that a "Revenue Officer" dealing with mutation proceeding is a "Revenue Court." Therefore, we are unable to approve the views taken in that case and consequently, we are of the opinion that the matter need not be referred for decision to a larger Bench since there is earlier decision of a Division bench over the said issue, with whom we are in full agreement. Accordingly, we approve the decision of the Division Bench in the case of Idris Ali. Our view is that a Revenue Officer when dealing with a Mutation Proceeding does not constitute a Revenue Court within the meaning of section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore, a Criminal Court can take cognizance of any offence described in sections 463 and 471, 475 and 476 of the Penal Code on the basis of complaint filed by any aggrieved party when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any Mutation proceeding in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding. Accordingly, we find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.

parties:
Shamser Ali alias Mobassar Ali being dead his heirs 1(A). Ashik Tara Begum ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Toimus Ali and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The opposite party No. 1 filed an application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for preemption of the case land against the purchaser-petitioner. The case of the opposite party No. 1, in short, is that the land mentioned in the application for pre-emption under section 96 was sold by the petitioner's husband Mobassar Ali by a registered kabala and after knowing the same the opposite party No.1 filed the application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption including the petitioner-purchaser on the ground that the opposite party No.1 is a contiguous owner and accordingly, he prayed for pre-emption of the case land. The said Miscellaneous Case No. 197 of 1970 was allowed by his judgment and order dated 12-12-81 ex parte when the present petitioner was found to be absent on repeated calls at the time of hearing of the case. 

 3. Against the aforesaid ex-parte order dated 12-12-81 passed by the Court of Assistant Judge, Chhatak, Sunamganj in Miscellaneous Case No. 197 of 1970 the husband of the petitioner filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1982 which was subsequently renumbered as 69 of 1984 under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte order dated 12-12-81 but on a subsequent date the said Miscellaneous Case No.69 of 1984 was transferred to newly created upazila Chhatak. The said Misc. Case 69 of 1984 was also dismissed for default on 17-12-86. The opposite party No.1 subsequently filed an application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 on 15-2-90 for getting delivery of possession of the pre-empted land on the ground, amongst others, that the pre-emption case was allowed on 12-12-81 by ex parte order and after ex parte order there was a Miscellaneous Case under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the ex parte order dated 12-12-81 but the same was also dismissed for default on 17-2-86 and as such, the opposite party No. 1 herein prayed for recovery of khas possession of the pre-empted land. 

 6. Mr AKM Faiz, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the purchaser-petitioner, submits that the said Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 1990 ought to have been filed within three years from the date of cause of action in as much within three years from the date when the Miscellaneous Case filed by the present petitioner was dismissed ex parte on 17-2-86. The learned Advocate submits that no period of limitation is provided in section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for filing application for possession. Therefore, residuary Article 181 of the Limitation Act would apply. Accordingly, the opposite party No.1 should have filed the Miscellaneous Case for possession of the pre-empted land within three years from 17-2-86 as per Article 181 of the Limitation Act. The opposite party No. 1 herein having not filed the application for possession of the pre-empted land within three from 17-2-86 the application, numbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 6/90, is ex facie barred by limitation. The learned Advocate further submits that where residuary Article 181 applies section 5 of the Limitation Act would not apply. Therefore, the learned Assistant Judge has committed an error of law in condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act and allowing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 7. The opposite party No. 1 by filing counter-affidavit has denied the material allegations made in the petition and, contended, mainly that section 5 of the Limitation Act is applicable in an application filed under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 8. Mr JN Deb, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1, submits that section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is very clear and has provided that sections 6, 7, 8, and 9 and sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 (Act IX of 1908) shall not and, subject to the provisions of part V of this Act, the remaining provisions of the Limitation Act shall, so far as applicable, apply to all suits, appeals and applications arising under the said part. Application of sections 6, 7, 8 and 9 and sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act has been excluded, other provisions including section 5 of the Limitation Act have been made applicable under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The learned Advocate further submits that opposite party No.1 filed as many as 9 medical certificates showing that he was a TB patient and the delay for filing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the said Act has been explained sufficiently. The Court having been satisfied with the explanation has condoned the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act and allowed the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Therefore, no error of law has been committed in condoning the delay in preferring the application under section 96(9) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 9. I have heard the learned Advocates of the respective parties, perused the judgment passed by the courts below as well as relevant provisions of law. It appears. that section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is very clear in as much as section 5 of the Limitation Act has been made applicable in a proceedings under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 including the proceeding under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. For convenience the relevant portion of section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is quoted as under: 

 Therefore, it appears that the application of section 5 of the Limitation Act in a proceeding under section 96(9)(c) State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 has been made applicable. Whereas applications of sections 6, 7, 8 & 9 and sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 have been clearly made not applicable in a proceeding under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Mr. JN Deb, the learned Advocate on this point has submitted that in a proceedings under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act section 5 of the Limitation Act has been made applicable in the case of Abdul Hamid Kazi vs. Abdul Jabbar Jamadar and others reported in 26 DLR (SC) 68. 

 10. Mr AKM Faiz, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, on the other hand, has submitted that when residuary Article 181 of the Limitation Act has been applied in this particular case, there is hardly any scope for application of section 5 of the Limitation Act and therefore he submits that the learned court has committed an error of law in condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act and allowing the application. The proceeding under section 96(9) (c) of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act is identical to that of the proceedings for execution of decree and the period of limitation is three years and the learned Court having not followed the aforesaid principles of law he has committed an error of law in condoning the delay in a proceeding under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 11. It appears that section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act clearly provides that "(c) the Court on further application of such applicant or applicants may place him or them, as the case may be, in possession of the property vested in him or them "but no period for making such application has been provided in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, the residuary Article 181 of the Limitation Act shall apply. To this the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 also concedes that Article 181 is applicable in the case of application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but relying on section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 has submitted that section 5 of the Limitation Act has not been ousted from application or filing application under section 96(9) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The opposite party No.1 having successfully shown that he was suffering from TB for a long time and he has adduced as many as 9 medical certificates that he was prevented by sufficient cause for not being able to file the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act within prescribed period of 3 years, the trial Court in his discretion has condoned the delay in filing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner though has vehemently argued that once residuary Article 181 of the Limitation Act has been applied, there is no scope for application of section 5 of the Limitation Act but he has failed to cite any decision in support of his arguments. Mr JN Deb, the learned Advocate, on the other hand, has cited a decision reported in 26 DLR (SC) 68 wherein section 5 of the Limitation Act has been made applicable in a proceeding under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, I am of the view that application of section 5 of the Limitation Act in a proceedings under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has not been barred where residuary Article 181 of Limitation Act has been made applicable. The Court may in his discretion condone the delay in preferring an application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provided the condition of section 5 of the Limitation Act is fulfilled. 

 12. In this particular case the trial Court has considered the facts and circumstances of the case in as much as the applicant was suffering from TB for a long time and the opposite party produced as many as 9 medical certificates, and the court has believed the same and for that cause he has condoned the delay in preferring the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Under the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case and position of law as enumerated in section 151 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, I find hardly any reasons to interfere with the same. 

 13. In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and order dated 9-3-91 passed by the Assistant Judge, Chhatak in Miscellaneous Case No.6 of 1990, allowing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act after condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act in filing the application under section 96(9)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, is hereby affirmed.
