full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam J.- This appeal by special leave which arises out of a pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The respondents filed application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the auction sale on 24-10-1973 in Certificate Case No 408 of 1967-1968 held by the Certificate Officer, Chittagong, for arrear rent dues from H E Percival, the recorded tenant, transferring land of P.S. Plot No. 108 of P.S. Khatian No. 14. The respondents claimed to be co-sharers of the Certificate Debtor by purchase of 1 kani 10 gondas of land of plot Nos. 107 and 87 appertaining to said Khatian No. 14, from H.E. Percival by registered kabala dated 29-12-1965 and their names were duly mutated in Khatian No. 14, which has been described in Schedule No. 2, which is part of Schedule 1 containing P.S. Khatians Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 owned by H.E. Percival in Mouza Kashim Bazar, P.S. Kotwali Chittagong, Their further case is that in the Oerti6cate Sale it was wrongly shown that P.S. Plot No. 108 appertained to P.S. Khatian No. 18 created after amalgamation and consolidation of the holdings held by H.E. Percival, because, such ambulation was done without giving any notice to the co-sharers. The pre-emption case was contested by the pre-emptee contending inter alia that the pre-emptors though were co sharers of the P.S. Khatian No. 14, but they ceased to be co-sharers after the lands in different plots in Kbatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24 in Mouza Kashim Bazar still owned and possessed by H.E. Percival were amalgamated and consolidated in one Khatian, namely Khatian No. 18 and the auction sale was held on the basis of the new Khatian No. 18, wherein they were not co-sharers of the Certificate Debtor. 

 2. The pre-emption case was dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge and on appeal the learned District Judge. Chittagong allowed the pre-emption case in part and remanded the case to the trial Court for assessment of the cost of improvement in the case land. The appellant unsuccessfully moved the High Court Division in revision and thereafter obtained leave from this Court. Leave was granted to examine the question whether after creation of a new tenancy by amalgamation and consolidation of holdings the respondent pre-emptors could rightly claim to be co-sharers of the recorded tenant H.E. Percival. Leave was also granted to consider the question whether a person claiming to be co-sharer in the holding, and not in the land transferred, could validly, maintain an application for pre- emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. 

 4. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdbury, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant submitted that amalgamation and consolidation of holdings having been made by the Revenue Officer in due course of his official duties, it should be presumed that it was validly done and in accordance with law, besides it is not correct to say that a new tenancy in P.S Khatian No. 18 in the name of H.E. Percival as the sole owner was made in the absence of any written application by the recorded tenant H.E. Percival in this regard; and the order was made without giving any notice to the co-sharers of H.E, Percival. With reference to different documents on record the learned Counsel submitted that the record would show that the amalgamation proceeding was initiated at the instance of H. E. Percival. When Certificate Case No. 408/67-68 and six other Certificate Cases were started against H.E. Percival by the Certificate Officer Chittagong for realization or arrear rents, on 12-3-69, the certificate debtor filed an application under section 9 of the Public Demands Recovery Act. in the aforesaid 7 Certificate Cases denying his liability for the huge arrear revenue dues on the grounds, inter alia that the lands of some of the khatians had been acquired by the Government and some of the lands bad been transferred by him to different persons; and praying for permission to pay the proportionate amount of the rent dues for him existing land in different khatians. On this application an order was passed by the Certificate Officer on 21-6-1973 directing the Tahsilder concerned for filing revised certificate on fresh assessment of correct rental dues, after amalgamation and consolidation of the lands in deferent khatians still in the possessions of H.E. Percival. The learned Counsel submitted that a regular case under Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was started by the Revenue Officer concerned and as a result new khatian No. 18 solely in the name of H.E. Percival was created, and on the basis of this khatian revised certificate was filed. The learned Counsel further submitted that auction was held on the basis of this amalgamated newly created khatian No. 18 wherein the respondents not being co- sharer are not entitled to pre-empt the certificate sale 

 5. On perusal of the material on record it appears that admittedly the land of khatian No. 18 was sold in auction for arrears of rent and the pre-emptors were not co- sharers in the said khatian. H.E. Percival was a recorded tenant in respect of khatian Nos. 14, 18, 20 and 24, and for recovery of a huge arrear of rent in respect of those khatians Certificate Case Nos. 408, 109, 411, 412, 413 and 414 of 1967-68 were started. H.E. Percival filed an application under section 9 of Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 on 12-3-69 stating inter alia that he was not liable for the entire arrear rent dues, because some of the lands had been acquired by the Government and some of the lands had been transferred by him to different persons. He stated therein that he was prepared to pay the proportionate rent for the lands still in his possession. This application was duly signed by H.E. Percival. On this application, it appears from the order sheet that the relevant Revenue authority took certain actions on the direction of the Circle Officer (Revenue) and a proposal for consolidation and amalgamation of several holdings of H.E. Percival was submitted, and on the basis of this recommendation for amalgamation and consolidation the relevant Revenue Officer passed the order. From the Circular of the Board of Revenue dated 26-6-69 it appears that the district authorities were instructed to the effect that the work of amalgamation of holdings should be started in all the circles in the month of July and complete by the end of October, 1969. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, rightly pointed out with reference to the Circular that the amalgamation of the lands belonging to H E. Percival was not a solitary case, because, the process of amalgamation and consolidation had already been started in the district There is no doubt the action was taken at the instance of H.E. Percival, and it was taken up in this background Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for amalgamation, sub-division and consolidation of holdings. Section 116 provides that where various parcels of land are held by One tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject of separate tenancies, such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue- officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. Section 117 provides the at notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this part, the Revenue-officer may.- 

 (c)for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co- sharer tenants..................’' 

 Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for maintenance and revision of the record- of fights. Section 143 of the Act provides that the Collector shall maintain up-to-date, in the prescribed manner, the record-of rights prepared or revised under Part IV or under this Chapter by correcting clerical mistakes and by incorporating therein the changes on account of- 

 6. With reference to section 117 of the Act Khondkarm Mahbubuddin Ahmed submitted that the entire proceedings and the purported amalgamation and consolidation of holdings as claimed by the appellant being not in accordance with Jaw, was illegal, and as such the new khatian 18 having no legal basis, it should be presumed that the khatians 14, 18, 20 and 24 continued to be the existing khatians and khatian 14 to which Plot No. 108 appertained, the respondents continued to be co-sharers of H.E. Percival in the said, holding, and it is not correct to say that H.E. Percival was the sole owner of Plot No. 108 without any co-sharer, He also argued that the purported amalgamation and consolidation of holdings under section 116 of the Act was done without giving any notice to the co-sharers. In the absence of any notice upon the co-sharers the alleged amalgamation and consolidation of holding is not tenable in law. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, however submitted by pointing out from the record that the noting in the order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73 (under Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act) sufficiently showed that amalgamation and consolidation of holdings of HE. Percival was made after the service of notice on all the parties concerned as per provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 8. In view of the circumstances as noted above, it would not be correct to say that the proceeding for amalgamation and consolidation of holdings under sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was initiated suo motu without having any basis. In the auction sale P.S. Plot No. 108 as appearing appertained to new P.S. Khatian No. 18 was sold. It is admitted that plot No. 108 previously appertained to khatian No. 14, and in its 16 annas belonged to H.E. Percival. So separation of plot No.108 from khatian No. 14 and its amalgamation in khatian No. 18, could not prejudice the pre-emptors who claimed to be a co- sharer in khatian No. 14 on the basis of their purchase from H.E. Percival. Apart from that there is a presumption under the law that all official acts are presumed to have been rightly and regularly done. 

 9. Chapter XV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act deals with "Amalgamation Sub-division and Consolidation of holdings." Section 116 provides for amalgamation of holding of a tenant in the same village. This section requires that where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject of separate tenancies such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue-officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. This section however provides that if the tenant concerned has any objection thereto which appears to such officer to be reasonable and sufficient no such amalgamation shall be ordered by the Revenue-officer. Section 116 read with section 117(1) (a) provides that amalgamation and consolidation can be taken by the Revenue-officer, either on his own motion or on an application made to him, in that behalf Section 17(1)(c) contains the provision for sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof subject to the conditions indicated therein. On examining sections 116 and 117 Hind that the learned Judge of the High Court Division is completely in error in taking the view that it is a case of sub-division of a joint tenancy as provided under section 117(1)(c) for which an application was required to be filed; and in the absence of an application by the parties the Revenue officer had no authority of his own motion to sub-divide a joint tenancy. He was however conscious that "Amalgamation and consolidation as have been referred in the section may begin for the purpose of collection of revenue and for that purpose the Revenue-officer may on his own motion exercise jurisdiction." The relevant finding of the learned' Judge is quoted below: 

 "So I am of the view that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application must be filed by the tenant concerned. In the instant case the typed copy of the application dated 12.3.69 in the certificate case before the Certificate Officer at Chittagong under section 9 of the P.D.R. Act for dismissing the certificate cases could not be suo motu brought in the Miscellaneous case No. 89/72-73 by the Revenue Officer" 

 10. Khondkar	Mahbubuddin	Ahmed only faintly argued that as a matter of fact this was a case of sub-division of a joint tenancy. He however failed to give sufficient reasons in support of this view. Prior to amalgamation Khatian No. 14 contained plot Nos. 108, 107, 87 and 124; Khatian No. 20 contained Plot No. 116; and Kbatian No. 24 contained plots 117 and 121. By the process of amalgamation and consolidation Plot 108 of Khatian 14, plot 119 of khatian 18, plot 16 of khatian 20 and plots 117 and 121 of khatian 24 were amalgamated and consolidated into one khatian, that is khatian 18. This sufficiently shows that it was a case of amalgamation and consolidation as contemplated under section 116 read with section 117(1)(a) and not a case of sub-division of a tenancy recorded in kbatian 14, as provided in section 1l7(1)(c). The order of the Certificate officer who was also the Revenue Officer, shows that the action for amalgamation and consolidation was taken at the instance of the tenant when it was considered necessary for the purpose of collection of revenue. Plot 108 solely owned and possessed by H. E. Percival was amalgamated with Plot No. 119 of khatian 18 plot No. 116 of Khatian No. 20 and plot Nos. 117 and 121 of khatian 24 and thereby new khatian 18 was brought into being and a new jama was fixed for the amalgamated and consolidated khatian. Endorsement on khatian 14 filed by the respondents itself shows that separation of plot No. 108 from that khatian and its amalgamation to khatian 18 was noted on it. Payment of rent at the old rate even after the amalgamation and consolidation as claimed by the respondents cannot set at naught the process and the order of amalgamation and consolidation which was duly made and acted upon. The learned Subordinate Judge took the correct view on this question saying:- 

 “As there was no short payment it was accepted when the petitioners paid rent at the old rate. This payment of rent at the previous rate itself does not show that the amalgamation and separation of tenancy was not given effect to." 

 11. There is another point to be discussed which is that the learned District Judge as wen as the learned Judge of the High Court Division took the view that the so called amalgamation and consolidation of holdings suo motu and that too after death of H.E. Percival cannot be said to have any legal sanction and must be treated as a void one and need not be avoided. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury In support of his submissions that the order of amalgamation and consolidation was made in accordance with law, further submitted that when such an order has been passed by the competent authority and in accordance with law, its validity cannot be challenged in the pre-emption proceeding. In support of this proposition he relied upon a decision of this Court in the case of Md. Jabed Ali Vs. Pakhal Chandra Mondal, 33 DLR (AD) 309. This is a case of separation of jam a under section 117(1) (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and not a case of amalgamation and consolidation, but the principle laid down therein provides the necessary guidance. In that case it has been held as follows:- 

 14. The land under pre-emption is plot No. 108 of Khatian No. 14 which belonged to one Percival. Khatian No. 14 consisted of three plots, Nos. 87, 107 and 108 and this Khatian, it is needless to say, constituted a non-agricultural holding under Percival. Respondent, pre-emptor purchased Plots Nos. 87 and 107 by a registered kabala dated 29 December 1965 and thereby became a co-sharer in the holding and in due course his name was mutated as Percival's co-sharer under a joint Jarna of Rs.4 and annas 7. Percival also held many other parcels of land such as in Khatians Nos. 18, 20 and 24, but the Respondent is not interested in those lands as he is not a co-sharer there. A Certificate Case being C.C. No. 408 of 1967-68 along with other such cases was filed against Percival for recovery of money due asarrear of rent under the Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 and this case was pending when he die in August, 1971. Two years five months after his death that is, on 24 December 1973, the appellant-pre-emptee, a stranger, auction purchased Plot No 108 along with other lands of Percival in connection with that Certificate Case. Respondent filed the pre-emption case on 15 April 1976, under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act alleging that he had come to know of the sale for the first time on 3 January 1976. He further alleged in his application that by an inquiry be had ascertained that, for the purpose of avoiding pre-emption, the pre-emptee had, by collusion with the Revenue Officer, got a Mutation case, being Miscellaneous Case No. 89 of 1972-73, started and thereby made a show of separation of Plot No. 108 from the joint tenancy under Khatian No. 14 and amalgamation of the separted hare with the other lands of late Percival, which were shown constipated as a new tenancy under Khatian N.18. Separation of this plot from the original holding having been made in total disregard of mandatory provisions of section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the pre-emptor alleged, the separation is void and not binding upon him and that he continued to be a co-sharer of the holding in Khatian No. 14. 

 15. The application for pre-emption was resisted on grounds of limitation and maintainability, particularly the latter. It was contended that "the separation and amalgamation" was effected by the Revenue Officer in accordance with law and that the Revenue Officer's order could not be challenged in a collateral proceeding like the pre-emption case. The trial Court accepted both the grounds and refused pre-emption holding the pre-emptor ceased to be a co. sharer in the holding since 24 April 1973 when plot No. 108 of Percival was validly separated from the original holding. But on appeal the learned District Judge reversed the findings on both the points and allowed the pre-eruption subject to payment of compensation for improvement of the land the amount of which was to be determined on remand after arriving at the findings that the Revenue Officer's order for separation of Percival's share was void in that the said order was passed by the Revenue Officer "on his own motion's and not upon any application from a co-sharer and that no notice of the 'Separation' was served upon the other co-sharer and further that the order was also acted upon as rent of the joint tenancy continued to be paid at the old rate. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division did not find anything to interfere with the District Judge's order in revision. 

 16. Leave was granted on both the grounds, limitation and maintainability, but the ground as to the limitation was not pressed. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, learned Counsel for the appellants directed his arguments on the question of maintainability of the application for pre-emption contending that the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer in the holding since the separation of Percival's share and creation of a new tenancy comprising the separated portion and other lands of Percival. Mr. Chowdhury next contends that when the Record of the Revenue Officer prima facie shows the separation and amalgamation according to law, his order cannot be challenged in a collateral proceeding like the instant one. Yes, if the original holding under Khatian No.14 were subdivided and plot No. 108 were separated therefrom according to law, then the pre-emptor got no case, as on sub-division of an original holding the former co-sharers cease to remain co-sharers with right to pre-emption. This is a settled law; reference. if at all necessary, may be made to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Begum Asia Rahman, 26 D.L.R, (S.C ) 58, and the decision of this Court in the case of Mofizuddin Patwary; 33 D.L.R. (AD) 305. But the question is whether the alleged separation of Plot No. 108 from Khatian No. 14 was made in conformity with law and to determine this question to what extent a civil court can go into the matter in a collateral proceeding such as the one at hand. 

 17. It appears that some confusion has crept in during the bearing of this appeal because of using, in a loose sense, the terms "separation" and "amalgamation" of holdings. These are quite distinct things each having specific meaning and implication; and as such, these terms should be understood in their proper perspective. For this purpose section 116 and 117(a), 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, which are relevant in this case, are quoted below: 

 "116. Where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subjects to separate tenancies such parcels of land shall under the orders of the Revenue Officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy." 

 (c) for the purpose of subdivision of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any as he may consider fair and equitable: 

 18. It appears clearly that 'amalgamation' means joining of various parcels of lands held by only one tenant so as to constitute one tenancy; and as such it is that tenant's problem alone. No other person, such as his co-sharer, is interested in it and that is why it may be ordered by the Revenue Officer either on his own motion or on an application made to him by the tenant; no notice of the amalgamation is required to be served upon anybody. Sub-division on the other hand, means physical division of a joint-tenancy as well as distribution of the rent thereof among the co-sharer tenants. Sub-division can be made by the Revenue Officer only on an "application made to him by one or" more co-sharer tenants". It shall not be ordered by the Revenue Officer "on his own motion". Secondly, notice of the sub-division shall be served upon all other co-sharers. Non-fulfillment either of these two requirements shall render the order of sub-division void. The term 'separation' is not a legal term like "amalgamation" or "sub-division"; it is not used in section 116 or 117, but nevertheless it denotes in general sense, separation of a share from a joint tenancy and as such 'separation' necessarily means subdivision of a joint tenancy and falls under, and is governed by clause (c) of section 117 Effect of separation of a share from the joint holding falls upon all co-sharers who, after separation, cease to be co-sharers of the original holding. A co-sharer after getting his share separated may get his portion constituted into a new tenancy or he may tag this share with his other land, if any, and if he does so, his case may be referred to as a case of 'separation and ‘amalgamation' for the sake of convenience though the two terms are quite different. His former co-sharers are not interested in such amalgamation. But whether amalgamation or not, for separation of a share from a joint tenancy the two mandatory provisions of clause (c) of section 117 must be first complied with. These provisions cannot be avoided or bypassed by saying that it is not a case of subdivision but it is 'separation and amalgamation'. An undivided share in a joint tenancy cannot be amalgamated with other independent holdings of a co-sharer without first getting his undivided share separated from the joint tenancy. This procedure shall apply even if he has applied for both in the same application. 'Amalgamation' cannot precede 'separation' as cart cannot be put before horse. It is the very case of the appellant that the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer in Khatian 14 from 24 April 1973 when plot 108 was" taken out and constituted into a new tenancy along with his other lands. If the original tenancy was not subdivided how the respondent ceased to be a co-sharer as the appellant claims? Revenue Officer's order shows that the original jama was also divided, out of Tk. 4.45 respondents jama was re-fixed at Tk. 2 55 and that of Percival at Tk. 1.90, which thereafter was added to the jama of the other holdings making his total jam a at Tk. 18.60 for the newly created separate tenancy under Khatian No. 18. This is subdivision pure and simple of the original holding under Khatian No.14. Again, whether a case attracts clause (c) depends upon its nature and implication and not upon how it has been described or designated by the Revenue Officer, The Revenue Officer took this case as 'separation and amalgamation'; but separation as shown above resulted necessarily in subdivision of the old tenancy. 'Separation' is synonymous with 'subdivision' under clause (c) of section 117 The argument that the original holding was not subdivided but was separated and amalgamated is self-defeating and self-contradictory. 

 20. 00 24 April 1973 the Circle Officer (Revenue) passed the final order on receipt of the Tahshilder's report allowing 'separation and amalgamation on the basis of his (Percival's' petition' The trial Court treated the carbon copy of the Certificate Debtor's objection petition as an application for separation of his share in the joint tenancy; but the lower Appellate Court and the High Court Division held that the unsigned carbon copy of an objection petition denying liability in a certificate proceeding under the Public Demands Recovery Act can, under no circumstances. be treated as an application for subdivision or separation of a joint tenancy under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In that objection petition, the Certificate debtor did not pray for 'separation or amalgamation' but expressed his readiness to pay the proportionate rent; the objection was filed in 1969 by Percival but he died in August 1971. This objection petition could not have been treated as an application for separation of his share in the joint holding two years after his death. Even if it is taken that Percival while filing the objection petition also intended the petition to be an application for separation of his share in his joint tenancies it abated on his death in 1971 whereupon his legal, representatives were not substituted. In the Certificate proceedings however his legal representatives were brought on record. From the proposal submitted by the Dealing Assistant and the order of the Revenue Officer starting the proceeding for separation and amalgamation, it is crystal clear that the Revenue Officer, whatever might have prompted him, had initiated the matter on his own motion. Had it been the case of mere amalgamation under clause (a) it would have been perfectly lawful. But this being a case of separation first, it comes well within the mischief of clause (c), and the 'separation' not having been made on an application it is void. 

 21. As to the contention about non service of notice-another mandatory provision for separation of the share-it is only the order-sheet of the Mutation case, which shows "notice duly served" Khandker Mahbubuddio Ahmed con- tends that the Record does not contain the. Service Return nor the name and address of Percival's co-sharer were stated in the carbon copy petition nor in any other document or paper of the Record and the Firisti of documents forming the record does not show any paper missing either. In these circumstances, the learned Counsel contends that prima facie this mandatory provision was not complied with by serving notice upon the respondent, The learned Counsel has in this connection relied upon a decision of this Court in the case Abdur Rouf Vs. Amuda Khatun, 33 D.L. R. (A D) 323, wherein if was held that the splitting,up of a joint tenancy effected behind the bat of a co-sharer was void. Mr. Harnidul Huq Chowdhury however, contends that the entry in the order-sheet of the Mutation Case made in usual course of official business is sufficient proof of prima facie service of notice and that in the proceeding for pre-emption the Court is not competent to go further into the matter to ascertain whether the notice the actually served in support of this contention the learned Counsel has referred to another decision of this Court in the case of Md. Jabed Ali Vs. Rakhal Chandra Mondal 33 D.L.R. (A.D.) 309. The purport of that decision is that when an order is passed by a competent Revenue Officer under section 117 of the Act and the order is inconformity with the statutory requirements and the order has been given effect to by the co-sharer tenants of the holding the holding stands separated under law and.................the civil court is not competent to ignore the order on the ground of finding some irregularity in the same as a court of appeal while dealing with the application under section 96 of the Act for pre-emption", I do not find any conflict between these two decisions. The questions raised there related to prima facie compliance of mandatory provisions as to splitting up of a joint tenancy by a competent Revenue Officer and the scope of enquiry in a collateral proceeding. In one case the order for splitting up was found prima facie valid and in the other the order was not so found. These cases were decided on their respective facts and circumstances. In the instant case apart from the question of compliance with the two statutory requirements, there is the question of giving effect to the order for splitting up of joint jam a of Khatian No.14. Though Plot No. 108 was separated and constituted into a new tenancy with effect from 24 April 1973 as alleged by the appellant, the record or right was not amended accordingly until two years after the filing of this pre-emption case. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdbury relies upon Ext. R which is purportedly the amended Khatian No. 14 showing the splitting up of the joint tenancy between Percival and the respondent by an order of the Revenue Officer dated "28-1-67". But it also shows that this splitting up of the original jama was made on the basis of the Mutation Case. No. 89 of 1972-73. How the amendment was made six years before the filing of the Mutation Case its basis? Obviously, Ext. R bas been created for the purpose of this instant case and as such is not reliable. As to its rent it continued to be paid at the old rate of Tk. 4.45 till 1978. Tile trial Court is of course right in its observation that mere non-payment of rent at the new rate will not affect the splitting up; but this omission is a factor which must be considered when the question is whether the splitting up order was given effect to as against the consistent claim of the respondent that everything was done behind his knowledge in the Dame of a dead co-sharer. Facts of this case attract Abdur Rouf Vs. Amuda Khatunand not "Jabed Ali Vs. Rakhal Chandra Mondal:" The order of Revenue Officer splitting up a joint-tenancy whichever way it may be designated if it serves the old relationship of its co-sharers and thereby destroys a co-sharer's statutory right of pre-emption, must be examined by the Court in a pre- emption proceeding in order to be satisfied that prima facie the order was passed in accordance with law, that is to say the mandatory provisions of section 117(c) were complied with on the face of the record. The scope of this examination cannot be so limited as to ask the Court to keep its eyes closed and to accept without hesitation whatever order is placed before it simply because the order was passed by a competent Revenue Officer. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has submitted that the scope of enquiry in a case for pre-emption is wide enough to include the question of benami transaction in certain cases placing his reliance upon the case of Balai Chandra Mondal Vs. Nibaran Chandra Das 51 C.W.N. 644. In that case two long lines of cases, one line reo presenting the view that question of benami was outside the scope of s. 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the other line representing the contrary view were elaborately discussed and considered and it was held that the question of benami transaction fell within the scope of s. 26F only in two classes of cases. In one class, the transfer is made to a co-sharer tenant in the benami of a stranger, and in the other class no transfer at all takes place but a show of transfer is made as in the case of plaintiff Nibaran. The suit was decreed and the order of pre-emption was declared void. 

 22. In the instant case it has been argued, the aggrieved co-sharer got proper remedy against the Revenue Officer's order by appeal. But his case is that the whole matter was manipulated after Percival's death and behind his knowledge and as such he got no opportunity to seek remedy by appeal. Be that as it may, on perusal of the records of the Miscellaneous case I find no difficulty to bold that the proceeding for separation of Plot No. 108 from Kbatian No. 14 was void ab initio as it was taken suo motu by the Revenue Officer and behind the co-sharer's knowledge and consequently the joint tenancy was Dot divided but it still continues and this being the position the pre-emption is a co-sharer in the holding having right to pre-emption. I find nothing to interfere with the order of the High Court Division which rightly confirmed that of the lower appellate Court. I would therefore dismiss the appeal' with costs.

parties:
Md. Khairullah Bhuiyan -------- Petitioners. 
VS
Amena Khatun and others -------- Opp. Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. The learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong dismissed the application for pre-emption. On appeal the learned District Judge, Chittagong, set aside the Judgment of the trial Court and allowed the application for pre-emption in part. 

 3. The case of the preempted-petitioner in brief, was that, he purchased the case land in said certificate case on 24.10.73 for Tk. 9000/-. The petitioner got delivery of possession on 11.2.74 through court. After getting possession the petitioner constructed C.I. huts on the hills and another but at the bottom of the hill in March and April. 1974. The petitioner after the auction purchase paid an amount of Tk. 80,000/- to the servant Mofizullah and to the relation of H.E. Percival for the price of the structures standing on the case land. According to the petitioner he also made payment of Tk. 10,000/- to Mofizullah at the request of the son of H.E. Percival. The petitioner spent about 20,000/-. for improvement of the case land after auction purchase. The pre-emptee has denied the date of knowledge of the preempted from 3.1.76. According to the pre-emptee, the pre-emptor knew about the sale from before. According to the present petitioner, the pre-emptors are not co-sharers in P.S. khatian No 14 which was auction purchased by the petitioner for arrears of rent as the remaining land of khatian No. 14 was separated by Misc. case No. 89/72-73. According to the pre-emptee, the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer in old khatian No. 14 as the old khatian No. 14 merged into P.S. khatian No. 18 and this khatian was put to auction sale and the pre-emptor did not remain a co-sharer. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record dismissed the application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. On appeal the learned District Judge allowed the application for pre-emption in part and remanded the case to the trial court for assessment of the costs of improvement in the case. Mr. S. R. Pal, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioner has submitted mainly two grounds for my consideration. Firstly, the learned Advocate or the petitioner has submitted that the learned lower appellate Court acted illegally and with material irregularity in holding in a summary jurisdiction that the amalgamation and separation of Tenancy in Misc. Case No. 89/72-73 is illegal, null and void and without jurisdiction and further committing illegality in holding that the pre-emptor continued to remain a co-sharer in Khatian No. 24. Secondly, he has contended that the application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not maintainable in view of the bar under section 85 (2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 1 will proceed to consider the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner hereinafter. 

 5. Thus, in the background of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant findings of fact on the question of notice in the proceeding in separation and amalgamation, the relevant laws on the subject are to he carefully considered in this proceeding. Section 116 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as follows :— 

 "116—Amalgamation of holding of a Tenant in the same village. Where various parcels of land are held by one tenant within one village, and such parcels of land or some of them are the subject to separate tenancies, such parcels of land shall, under the orders of the Revenue Officer, be amalgamated into one tenancy. 

 Section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy read as follows :— 

 (c) for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to hint by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing, such sub-division of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any as he may consider fair and equitable : 

 6. Thus, from the reading of the relevant provisions of sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is clear that a Revenue Officer is competent to start with the proceeding of amalgamation, consolidation and subdivision of a tenancy but for this purpose namely, for amalgamation and consolidation the proceeding may be started either on the own motion of the Revenue Officer or on an application made in that behalf by one or more co-sharer tenants. But clause (c) of section 117 says that for sub-division of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent an application a to be made by one or more co-sharer-tenants and on this application by the tenants concerned the Revenue Officer by order in writing direct such sub-division of a joint tenancy as he may consider fair and equitable. Thus it is clear that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application is to be made by the parties and the Revenue Officer has got no authority on his own motion to sub-division a joint tenancy. The amalgamation and consolidation as have been referred in the section may begin for the purpose of consolidation and amalgamation of holding for the purpose of collection on revenue and for that purpose the Revenue Officer may on his own motion exercise jurisdiction. This power has been given under sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act but for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy the legislature though it lit and proper that such a sub-division is only permissible on the application of one of more co-sharer tenants as the interests of the tenants are primary concerned in the scheme of sub-division of a joint tenancy. Thus, it is clear that the legislature provided that the sub-division of a holding may be made when notice has been given to the parties concerned for appearance and being heard in the matter. That it is clear that the legislature intended that when any co-sharer tenant wants division of a holding such a proceeding can be taken. So, I am of the view that for the purpose of sub-division of a joint tenancy an application must be filed by the tenant concerned. In the instant case the typed copy of the application dated 12.3.69 in the certificate caws before the Certificate Officer at Chittagong Under section 9 of the P.D.R. Act for dismissing the certificate cases could not be roe wale brought in the Misc. Case No. 89/72-73 by the Revenue Officer. I have held earlier that there was in fact no application by H.E. Percival for amalgamation and separation of his holding. The courts below were also of the view that this power was exercised suo-motu by the Revenue Officer in this Misc. proceeding for amalgamation and separation. I may point out here that the application of H. E. Percival denying his liability In respect of the certificate cases was dated 12.3.69 and this proceeding for amalgamation and separation started on 17.3.73 after about 4 years and the admitted position being that H. E. Percival died in August, 1971, the question of filing this application by H.E. Percival thus, in fact, does not arise. Thus, this was a suo-motu exercise of power by the concerned Revenue Officer in this behalf. A reference to the provision of section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shows that no order shall be passed unless a notice is given the parties concerned and the matter is heard. This proviso clearly indicates that notice is a must to the partied concerned in cases of amalgamation, consolidation and sub-division without service of notice on the parties concerned no final order can be passed in the matter of amalgamation, consolidation and sub-division. Thus, after careful consideration of the relevant provisions of sections 116 and 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act I am of the opinion that no proceeding for sub-division of a joint tenancy can be taken without any application by a tenant and in that proceeding notices must be served on the parties concerned. I have indicated earlier that in the instant case there was no application for amalgamation and separation by the tenants and the Lower Appellate Court has correctly come to a finding from the perusal of the records of the Misc. proceeding No. 89/72-73 that no notices were served on the parties concerned and consequently the lower appellate court rightly held that the proceeding taken under amalgamation and separation of the holding was null and void and the same is liable to be set aside. 

 7. Thus after a careful consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant provisions of law as discussed above I had no substance in the first point raised by S.R. Pal in this behalf. Incidentally, I may point out here that proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for pre-emption is no doubt a summary proceeding but since the question of amalgamation and separation in the proceeding as mentioned above is relevant for the purpose of determination of the fact whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in khatian No. 14 or not, the courts below very rightly proceeded to see whether the tenancy has been separated in accordance with law thereby the pre-emptor remained a re-sharer or ceased to be a co-sharer. Thus the contention of Mr. S. R. Pal that in a summary proceeding in the courts below should not have gone to determine the legality or otherwise of amalgamation and separation of tenancy is without any substance. 

 8. Thus I hold that the pre-emptor continued to remain a co-sharer in the Malian No. 14 as if there was no separation under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such the pre-emptor was competent to file an application for pre-emption and the lower appellate court has correctly decided this point by holding that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer and he had locus stanch to file this application for pre-emption. 

 9. Now coming to the second point raised by Mr. S. R. Pal that an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not maintainable in view of the Bar under section 85(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, it will be seen that section 85(2) does not bar an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Section 85(2) of the Act reads as follows "nothing 'in this act shall apply to any non-agricultural land held by a tenant under the Central or Provincial Government :— 

 10. In the connection a reference may be made to the case of Haji Aktaruzzaman Vs. Jadunath Pal and another reported in 17 D.L.R. 384. A Full Bench of the Dacca High Court considered section 80(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and in paragraph 16 of that reported decision as follows: 

 In the light of the proviso to section 85(3) of the Act a tenant in respect of non-agricultural land would not be deprived of a right reposed in him by the provisions of Act on the only ground of acquisition of superior tight in the land by Government. The right vested in a tenancy by the provisions of the Act in the right to take advantage of the provisions of the Act, including a right which is immediately enforceable and also a right which is enforceable in future, on the happening of a contingency. The aforesaid answer will also apply in respect of an application under section 24 of the Act. We hold that section 85(2) of the Act does not bee the application filed by the opposite parties under section 24 of the Act. We also hold that the case reported in 16 D.L.R. 77, in which it held that such an application under section 24 was competent, was correctly decided although we have come to the same conclusion by a somewhat different process of reasoning."

parties:
Chandpur Tea Company Ltd. ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Joint Secretary & ors. ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
SM Hussain J: Chandpur Tea Company Ltd. being the petitioner in Writ petition No. 427 of 1977 has challenged the legality of certain Certificate cases allegedly on the ground that in view of the provisions of section 142 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the recovery of arrear rents dues therein was barred by limitation. The Certificate cases arose out of non-payment of the balance dues of rent after the final publication of the records of right. The petitioner was assessed provisionally under sub-section (1) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The petitioner bad was paying such provisional rent till such time when such rent was finally determined under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. After adjustment of rent with the previous years the petitioner was served with a demand notice to pay the balance dues being the determining enhanced rent. The petitioner having failed to pay the balance dues of rent the impugned certificate cases were instituted by the Revenue Authority against which the petitioner moved this Court and obtained this Rule under disposal. 

 2. So far as the impugned certificate cases are concerned they relate to certain Tea gar-dens situated in the district of Sylhet. In such circumstances, the limitation for the recovery of arrear rent dues is governed by the provisions of section 142 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with sub-section (4a) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 142 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides that the period of limitation for the recovery of arrear rent shall be three years running from last day of the year in which the arrear fell due. Sub-section (4a) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act further provides that in computing the period of limitation for the recovery of any arrear of rent in the district of Sylhet, a period of twenty-four months that is two years shall be excluded on and from the date of acquisition of the rent receiving interest to which such arrear relate. Reading the aforesaid provisions of section 142 and sub-section (4a) of section 3 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act together it clearly appears that the period of limitation for the purpose of recovery of arrear rent with regard to any land in the district of Sylhet extended up to a period of five years from the last day of the year in which such arrear fell due. 

 3. In this connection reference may be made to the provisions of clause (ff) of subsection (4) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which provides for the obligation of every owner of any land to pay rent to the Government at the enhanced rate, if any, after the final determination of the rent under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and in such case the tenant in question shall be liable to pay the balance with retrospective effect from the notified date that is the date of final publication of the records of right under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thus it will appear that once the rate of rent is finally determined and published in the final records of right under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, any balance dues there under can be recoverable with retrospective effect from the date of such final publication of the records of right under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. So for the purpose of prospective realisation of rent at the final rate the time for limitation shall run from notified date that is, the date of final publication of the records of right under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. That being so inevitably the aforesaid period of limitation as provided under section 142 read with sub-section (4a) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shall normally be a period of five years with regard to any land situated in the district of Sylhet from the date of the final publication of the records of right of that area under sub-section (3) of section 19 of the State Acquisition. and Tenancy Act. 

 4. The only question now remaining for consideration is whether such period of limitation of five years as aforesaid from the date of the final publication of the records of right is an absolute period or is subject to any extension under section 19 of the Limitation Act. In this connection reference may be made to the provision of section 151(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act wherein it has been provided that apart from sections 6, 7, 8 and 9 and sub-section (2) of section 19 of the Limitation Act all the remaining provisions of the Limitation Act shall apply as far as possible to all suits, appeals and applications arising under Part V of the said State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, but subject to the provisions of the said Part V of the said State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. From the aforesaid provisions of section 151(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it clearly appears that the provisions of section 19 will be applicable in any application arising under Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Therefore, unless it is found that the provisions of section 19 of the Limitation Act is repugnant to any of the provisions of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the said provisions of section 19 of the Limitation Act shall be applicable in any application arising under Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The present proceeding admittedly having taken place under Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, section 19 of the Limitation Act applied in the present case in full force. 

 5. Section 19(1) of Limitation Act provides that where before the expiration of the period prescribed for an application in respect of any right, an acknowledgement of liability in respect of such right has been made in writing by the parties against whom such right is claimed, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgement was so made. In the present case since the draft publication of the records of right and the provisional determination of the fate of rent, the petitioner had all along paid the provisional rent to the Revenue Authority of the Government periodical and successively every year and such payment of provisional rent continued even after the publication of the records of right and final determination of the rate of rent. Such payment of provisional rent every year by way of a "treasury chalan" signed by the petitioner in favour of the Government bore an acknowledgement on the part of the petitioner its liability to pay the enhanced rate finally from time to time. This has created a legal obligation on the petitioner to pay the enhanced rate of part of the rent as finally determined and published in the record of right under sub-section (3) of Section 19 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This payment from year to year is a clear acknowledgement on the part of the petitioner about its liability to pay the enhanced rate of rent when so finally determined and by making such payment every year the period of limitation was extended from year to year by way of an acknowledgement as contemplated under section 19 of the Limitation Act. That being so for the purpose of computing the period of limitation in the present case, it shall run from the date of the last payment of provisional dues, by the petitioner in favour of the Government by way of "treasury chalan" and shall continue till the completion of five years from such date where after any recovery of arrear rent shall be barred."

lawyer:
Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court (Mahbubey Alam, Advocate, Supreme Court, with him), instructed by Syed Sakhawat Ali, Advocate on Record -----For the Appellant,
M.H. Khondker, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, instructed by S R. Karmakar, Advocate on Record -----For the Respondent No. 1.
parties:
S.M. Basiruddin ----- Appellant
Vs. 
Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam J.—This appeal by special leave arises from an application under section 14 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 filed by respondent No. l in respect of certain land with the Dacca City. The sale under pre-emption was effected by Ayesha Khatun respondent No. 2 in favour of the appellant by a kabala dated 10-9-73 which was registered on 5-4-76. The case land appertained to a permanent tenure recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 214 under Mouza Shahar Dacca, owned by Akshoy Kumar SahaBanik, and Rangubala Choudhurani. Akshoy Kumar SahaBanik instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca for partition and by the decree passed in the suit Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik got 1/3rd share and Ran-gubala got the remaining rd share. One Nafisa Khatun by purchasing the interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik by a registered deed of sale dated 19-7-52 became co-sharer of Rangubala. Rangubala created a lease in respect of her 2/3rd share for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 in favour of Ayesha Khatun, respondent No. 2 Nafisa Khatun sold her interest to respondent No. 1 by a registered sale deed dated 18-4-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered sale deed dated 10-9-73. Against this sale respondent No. 1 filed the application for pre-emption. The appellant contested the case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 was not a co-sharer in the tenancy, because the land of the tenure was partitioned by the decree in Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 between Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani ; and that a separate tenancy was created in favour of Ayesha Khatun by Rangubala by granting permanent lease for 99 years, reserving for herself annual rent of Tk. 1/-; and that Ayesha Khatun paid rent of Tk. 1/- to the lessor Rangubala till the rent receiving interest was acquired by the Government; and that S.A. Khatian was not correctly prepared because neither respondent No. 1 nor his vendor was co-sharer of Ayesha Khatun. He further claimed that after his purchase he applied for mutation of his name and accordingly his name was mutated in the S A. Khatian and jama was separated. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed pre-emption case against the appellant and the appeal was dismissed. Thereafter the appellant moved the High Court Division in revision under section 115(1)1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and being unsuccessful moved this Court and obtained leave from this Court to appeal from the judgment of the High Court Division. 

 2. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division was correct in making no distinction between the expression 'holding' as occurring in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the expression 'non-agricultural land' as occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. At the hearing of the appeal the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant made two points out of the leave order. Firstly, he argued that upgradation of an under tenant to the status of a tenant under the Government on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest over the tenant by the notification in April, 1956 did not have the effect of merging the two distinct interests, that is, of Akshoy and Rangubala on one side and that of Ayesha Khatun on the other hand; and, according to the learned Advocate, Ayesha Khatun attained the status of full tenant on up gradation and ceased to be a co-sharer-tenant of successor-in-interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik. In this context, he alternatively argued that the shares of Akshoy Kumar and Rangubala having been partitioned by the decree of the civil court in partition suit, resulting in the creation of two separate holdings under the Municipality. Akshoy Kumar and Rangubala ceased to be co-sharer in the tenancy. Secondly he argued that the expression 'non-agricultural land' as occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act not being expression 'holding' as occurring in section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the learned Judge of the High Court Division fell into an error in treating the successors-in interest of Akshoy Kumar Saba Banik as co-sharer of Ayesha Khatun, and allowing the pre-emption case. In this connection the learned Advocate submitted that the decision relied upon by the High Court Division in the case of Brindaban Chandra Chowdhury v. Mosammat Rezia Begum, (l964) 16 DLR 77 has not laid down the law on correct interpretation of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. 

 3. Now let me examine the first point argued by Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant The learned Advocate strenuously argued in support of the proposition that on the elimination of the rent-receiving interest the under raiyati interest of Ayesha Khatun by operation of law became upgraded and attained the independent status of raiyat under the Government. On careful consideration of the argument of the learned Advocate I find it difficult to accept his proposition. Chapter IV of Part IV of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 provides for "preparation of record-of-rights." This chapter contains the provision of preparation of record of rights with a view to assessment of compensation regarding interests of all rent-receivers which are liable to be acquired and which have already been acquired under Chapter II of the Act. Section 17 empowers the Government to make an order for preparation of record-of-rights. Section 18 provides that the Revenue-officers are to record certain particulars in the record of rights. Section 19 provides that they are to prepare the draft as well as final publication of such records. Section 20 prescribed the quantum of land 'which can be retained' by a person in his possession. Sections 21 and 22 provide that all lands are subject to payment of fair and equitable rent, as determined by the Revenue-officer in accordance with the provisions of Chapter IV and the rent so determined shall be entered in the record-of-rights. Sections 23 to 28 require the Revenue-officers to assess fair and equitable rents for different classes of tenants. Section 29 provides that the rents entered in the record-of-rights shall be deemed to have been correctly determined and to be fair and equitable. Preparation of record-of-rights in a district, part of a district or local area as provided in section 17 was intended to- 

 (i) the use by tenants, of water for agricultural purposes, whether obtained from a river, jhil, tank or well or any other source of supply, and 

 (k) the special conditions and incidents, if any, of the tenancy; 

 4. According to section 18 the Revenue-officer is required to prepare or revise the record-of-rights in pursuance of the order passed under section 17, and in preparing or revising the record-of-eights the Revenue- officer has been directed to record such particulars as may be prescribed under the Rules. Rule 18 quoted above shows that the nature of the particulars to be recorded as provided in clause (b) of rule 18 the Revenue officer is required to record the class or the classes to which each tenant or occupant belongs, whether the tenant is a proprietor, tenure holder, raiyat holding at fixed rates, settled raiyar, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy raiyat, under raiyat, with or without a right of occupancy, or a non-agricultural tenant, and if he is a tenure-holder, whether be is a permanent tenure-bolder or not, and whether his rent is liable to enhancement during the continuance of his tenure, Clause (f) requires that rent payable at the time the record-of-rights is being prepared as well as the rents determined as fair and equitable according to rules 28 to 30 to be mentioned. Rule 24 provides for preparation of preliminary record-of-rights which is also known as draft record-or-rights. According to this rule, the draft record shall consist of statements of rights which are styled as the khatians. This rule further directs that ordinarily there shall be a separate khatian for each person interested, or each group of persons jointly interested, in the land, whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyar, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant and each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons. Statutory provisions clearly show sections 18 and 19 and the rules 18, 19 and 24 do not support the proposition canvassed by the learned Advocate on the elimination of the rent receiving interests all under-raiyats became raiyats under the Government and their status having thus been upgraded, the Revenue-officer while preparing the record-ofrights was required to record the under-raiyat as a raiyat in separate khatian, fixing fair and equitable rent for such upgraded tenant. It has already been stated above that the preparation of record of rights as provided in section 17 was with a view to assessment of compensation payable for all such interests liable to be acquired under the Act. Rule 24 provides for preparation of statements of rights which is styled as the khatian. According to this rule ordinarily there shall be a separate khatian for each person interested or each group of persons jointly interested in the land whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant and each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons, according to particulars mentioned in rule 18. The rules neither authorize nor require the Revenue-officer to prepare separate khatians for the individual raiyats and under-raysts, but, on the other hand, it provides that each group of person jointly interested in the land, whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant ordinarily are to be shown in separate khatian, and it further provides that each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons, recording the particulars as indicated in rule 18. In support of the proposition that the under raiyat was upgraded to the status of raiyat, on the elimination of rent receiving interest, support was sought from the doctrine of merger as provide in section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which provides that when the raiyati disappears the under-raiyat cannot any longer remain as such. Section 22 as it stands after amendment of 1907 merely provides that 08 the transfer of the occupancy right to a person jointly interested in the land as proprietor or permanent tenure-holder, such person shall have no right to hold the land as the raiyat but shall hold it as a proprietor or permanent tenure-holder as the case may be. By the amendment of 1907 the principle of merger as contemplated in section 22 was altered. The most important incident of merger under sub-section (1) of section 22 is that the landlord does not hold the land upon merger as a raiyat but holds it only as a proprietor or a permanent tenure-holder. It necessarily follows that the under-raiyats are automatically promoted to the status of raiyats. This view received judicial recognition in Ram Charan Sutradhar Vs. SM. Makhan, 38 CWN 1976, and it was followed by a Division Bench in the case of Pramatha Nath Shikder Vs. Jitendra Nath Roy. 43 CWN 1102. Upon acquisition of the rent receiving interests all under-raiyats by operation of law became raiyats under the Government is not in controversy, but the doctrine of merger as provided in section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act has no application to the conversion of all tenants holding land as proprietor, tenure holder raiyat, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant, as raiyats or maliks under the Government.

On carefully examining the different sections of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder, I am of the opinion that it is not correct to say that on the publication of the Notifications under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act existing classification and gradation of tenants as provided under the Bengal Tenancy Act disappeared and there was only one class of tenants with effect from April 14, 1956. It is correct that with from that date all tenants irrespective of their status under the Bengal Tenancy Act became liable to pay rent direct to the Government end for that purpose alone they were treated as raiyats under the Government, but for all other purposes the tenancies continued to be regulated by the Bengal Tenancy Act, that is why the Bengal Tenancy Act was kept in force till Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into operation on the publication of the Notification under section 79 of the Act and Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed by operation of section 80 of the Act. In the case of Mobasher Ali V. Md. Makbul Hossain, the conclusions arrived at by learned Judges are not based on correct appreciation of the different provisions of the statute. The learned Judges applied the doctrine of merger as provided is section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which in my opinion is not applicable in the case of acquisition of rent receiving interests under section 3 of the Act. And on this wrong premise the learned Judges held that on the elimination of rent receiving interests an under-raiyat stood upgraded to the status of raiyat. It is by operation of section 3(4)(e) all tenants became tenant. directly under the Government, and as such all tenants became tenants under the Government not by a process of up gradation in consequence of merger as provided under section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Government by several Notifications acquired the interests of some of the rent- receivers as shown in the Notifications; and then by a general Notification dated the 2nd April, 1956 under section 3, acquired all the interests of the remaining rent-receivers with effect from 14th April, 1956. According to clause (e) of sub-section (4) of section 3 all tenants holding lands in such estatestaluks tenures, holdings or tenancies directly under the rent-receiver specified in Notification under sub-section (1) shall become tenants directly under the Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate, in respect of the rent-paying lands so held by them to the Government and not to anybody else provided that in cases where no notification was issued under sub-section (2) of section 43 before commencement of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1957, declaring that Compensation Assessment-roll in respect of the interest of any such rent-receiver in any such estate, taluk, tenure, holding or tenancy directly under such rent-receiver, shall as the tenants under the Government, be liable to pay rents in respect of lands so held by them except rent-free lands, at the rates determined in the record of rights finally published under sub-section (3) of section 19 subject to modification under section 53. Sub-section (4), clause e) of section 3 clearly shows that purpose of this provision is to ensure collection of rent by the Government from all the tenants who were liable to pay rent to the rent- receivers before the Notification. So the mandate is that on the vesting of the receiving interests in the Government, all tenants under the rent- receivers shall be liable to pay rent direct to the Government and not to anybody else. The statutory provisions sufficiently indicate that only for the purpose of collection of rent the existing tenants became one class, that is, 'raiyats' under the Government. However, the classification and gradation of different tenancies, for all other purposes, such as, identification and determinant of their status and their rights and other liabilities, continued till the notification under sub- section (21 of section 43 was issued. The scheme of the Act as shown from the different chapters does not provide that on the publication of the Notification under section 3 all rent-receivers were eliminated and all raiyats, under raiyats non-agricultural tenants, etc. existing in the estates acquired stood upgraded and along with it classification of tenants as provided under the Bengal Tenancy Act disappeared. What as a matter of fact happened is that with the publication of the Notification under section 3 all the rent receiving interests no doubts stood acquired, and the raiyats, under raiyats, non- agricultural tenants, for the purpose of payment of rent to the Government, became 'raiyats' under the Government, but the existing classification of tenants as contemplated under the Bengal Tenancy Act, and record-of-rights prepared under the Bengal Tenancy Act continued until publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll under section 43; and the consequences as provided under section 44 ensued, namely, acquisition and vesting of the interests of proprietors, tenure-holders and other rent-receivers, absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances subject to the rights of such proprietors tenure-holders and other relit receivers specified in clause (2) of section 44. In view of the position in law is obtaining due to both the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Bengal Tenancy Act bolding the same field, an under ralyat, no doubt, on the elimination of the rent-receiver (raiyat who created the under raiyat) attained the status of raiyat directly under the Government, as the Government by operation of law became the owner, and the under raiyat became liable to pay rent direct to the Government and to no other agency unless specifically authorized by the Government in this behalf. Hassan and Sekandar Ali J.J. differed on this question. According to Hasan, J. the words non-agricultural land means a 'piece' of land in joint possession and enjoyment without partition which may form a tenancy or a portion of a tenancy.
