Therefore, unless the other parties of the suit wish to be separated, only the plaintiff’s properly would be separated by the Court’s final decree. 

 43. Let me now deal with the question as to when/why and how a partition can be done. In order to get a clearer answer, one must know what is the meaning of the expressions ‘tenant’, ‘tenancy’, ‘joint tenancy’, ‘co-owner’, ‘tenancy-in-common’ and ‘hotchpotch’. 

 44. In the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the definition of the word ‘tenancy’ has not been provided directly; but the word ‘tenant’ has been defined in Section 2(27) of the aforesaid Act describing the ‘tenant’ as the holder of the land paying rent to the Government. Black’s Law Dictionary defines ‘tenancy’ as ‘(1) The possession or occupancy of land under a lease; a leasehold interest in real estate, (2) The period of such possession or occupancy and (3) The possession of real or personal property by right or title, esp. under a conveying instrument such as a deed or will’. Black’s Law Dictionary also provides the meaning of joint tenancy, which is extracted below: Joint Tenancy: A tenancy with two or more co-owners who are not spouse on the date of acquisition and have identical interests in a property with the same right of possession. A joint tenancy differs from a tenancy in common because each joint tenant has a right of survivorship to the other’s share (in some states, this right must be clearly expressed in the conveyance- otherwise, the tenancy will be presumed to be a tenancy in common). 

 45. A.C. Freeman, in his treatise Cotenancy and Partition 71 (2d ed. 1886) describes joint tenancy in the following words: As joint-tenancy was a favorite of the common law, no special words or limitations were necessary to call it into being. On the other hand, words or circumstances of negation were indispensable to avoid it. Whenever it was shown that property had vested in two or more persons, by the same joint purchase, there arose at once, both in law and in equity, the presumption that it vested as an estate in joint-tenancy. This presumption is liable to be overthrown in equity by proof of circumstances from which the Court may infer that the parties intended a several rather than a joint estate. 

 46. Thomas F. Bergin & Paul G. Haskell, in his authoritative book Preface to Estates in Land and Future Interests 55 (2d ed. 1984), states about the joint tenancy in the following language: The rules for creation of a joint tenancy are these: The joint tenants must get their interests at the same time. They must become entitled to possession at the same time. The interests must be physically undivided interest, and each undivided interest must be an equal fraction of the whole- e.g., a one-third undivided interest to each of three joint tenants. The joint tenants must get their interests by the same instrument- e.g., the same deed or will. The joint tenants must get the same kinds of estates- e.g., in fee simple, for life, and so on. 47. Black’s Law Dictionary also provides the meaning of ‘tenancy-in-common’. The meaning is given below: Tenancy-in-common: A tenancy by two or more persons, in equal or unequal undivided shares, each person having an equal right to possess the whole property but no right of survivorship. 

 48. A. C. Freeman, in his book Cotenancy and Partition 67 (2d ed. 1886), states about the tenancy-in-common in the following language. If there be a doubt whether an estate was, at its creation, a joint-tenancy or a tenancy in common; or if, conceding the estate to have been a joint-tenancy at its creation, there be a doubt whether there has not been a subsequent severance of the jointure – in all such cases equity will resolve the doubt in favor of tenancy in common. 

 49. Thomas F. Bergin & Paul G. Haskell, in writing about tenancy-in-common in his treatise Preface to Estates in Land and Future Interests 54 (2d ed. 1984) makes the following opinion: The central characteristic of a tenancy in common is simply that each tenant is deemed to own by himself, with most of the attributes of independent ownership, a physically undivided part of the entire parcel. 

 50. Let me now be acquainted with the terminology ‘hotchpotch’. When various properties are put together or blended for the purpose of achieving the portion of property to be distributed among the beneficiaries or legal heirs as per the laws of the concerned country; in other words, in order to divide the properties, which are presently enjoyed by the different individuals by virtue of inheriting or purchasing from a single person/source, ‘hotchpotch’ is the process of combining and assimilating of the said properties. Although the terminology may seem to be a jargon to the commoners, however, it is widely used in legal parlance in the suits for partition in all over the common-law jurisdiction. 

 51. After knowing about the meanings of the aforesaid terms of ‘tenant’, ‘tenancy’, ‘joint tenancy’, ‘co-ownership’, ‘tenancy-in-common’ and ‘hotchpotch’ as well as having been acquainted with the term ‘partition’, on which a brief discussion has been made hereinbefore, it has now become easier for this Court to state as to when/why and how a partition can be done. 

 55. From my extensive research on the case-laws regarding suit for partition of our jurisdiction and that of the Privy Council, Indian jurisdiction and Pakistani jurisdiction, it appears to me that, on the issue of inclusion of the entire properties of the joint tenants or co-owners or co-tenants in a suit for partition, the followings are the well-settled principles: (1) there is no existence of joint tenancy in the Mohammedan Law/Muslim Law; only Hindu coparceners are joint in estate. Mohammedans are only co-owners or tenants-in-common; (2) there is substantially no difference in respect of the subject-matter of a suit for partition amongst Muslim co-owners or Hindu co-owners, where they hold property as tenants-in-common; (3) a suit for partition of even one item of such property is maintainable as Section 44 of the TP Act heralds that an undivided share in immovable property can be transferred, provided that the partition can be effected without much inconvenience to the other co-owners or co-tenants. In other words, in the case of tenants-in-common, whether such tenants are Muslims or Hindus, one of them is not obliged to sue for the partition of all the items of the property in which they are interested, inasmuch as each of them is entitled to his definite share in every item of the property, unless the partition sought for results in inconvenience to the other tenants-in-common; (4) as per the provisions of the Mahomedan Law, although all the legal heirs of a Muslim deceased do not inherit the property of equal share, for example, deceased’s each daughter gets half of the share of each son and so on, however, as the co-owners, each of them, having notionally held their respective portions under the Shariah Law till a division/partition is done by metes and bounds, are competent to sell their respective portion of definite share from each of the plot; (5) a co-owner is legally not barred to transfer his/her entire share from one plot or one item of the properties left by the deceased if the rest of the co-owners consent to such transfer, either by standing as witness/es of the transfer-deed or by executing a registered deed announcing and confirming their consents; (6) if one of the co-owners transfers a quantum of land from a plot without the consent/s of other co-owners and, subsequently, it is revealed that the transferred-land is more in quantum than what s/he is entitled to inherit in the said plot, then, a scenario of application of hotchpotch rule arises to find out (i) what was the total quantum of land of the deceased, (ii) the quantum of land inherited by each of the legal-heirs, (iii) whether any heir has already transferred more land in measurement than s/he is entitled to inherit, (iv) whether there was any verbal arrangement among the co-owners to waive his/her due share in a particular plot, either in lieu of another land in other plot/s or in exchange of monetary transaction or by taking any other type of benefit and (v) how to mitigate the scenario; (7) the rule that the suit for partition must cover the entire property held jointly by the parties is merely a rule of equity and convenience and (8) a suit for partition must embrace only the property/properties in which the parties have community of interest and unity of possession. 

 57. It is evident from the facts of the suit that the parties of this suit are not the members of Hindu family and, thus, the principle regarding joint tenancy is not applicable here in this suit. Also, the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1 (the only contesting defendant in the suit) are not the descendants of Saifa Bibi and, hence, they cannot be seen as the direct co-owners. By virtue of being purchasers of land from the legal heirs of Saifa Bibi in the single plot i.e. in the same tenancy, the nature of relationship between the plaintiffs and the respondent No. 1 is of co-tenancy and, that is why, they are co-tenants/tenants-in-common. Also, since there is no issue as to separation/division of any property which is being used jointly (such as dwelling house, ponds, wall etc), this suit is not going to yield any botheration for other co-tenants. So, according to the principle laid down hereinbefore, the parties of the suit being co-tenants they are very much competent to approach the Court for partition and separation of a single plot of Saifa Bibi and, on this count, it is held that this suit is very much maintainable. 

 72. Now, given that the present plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1 would be in a position to claim themselves to be the co-tenants in this tenancy having stepped into the footings/shoes/status of the co-owners, only when the title and shares of Saifa Bibi’s four sons/their legal heirs and the title and shares of Saifa Bibi’s daughters would be adjudicated, and since the four sons of Saifa Bibi have sold 0.1025 acres of land each, which apparently is suggestive from the above-mentioned evidence that Saifa Bibi’s two daughters might have been allotted a quantum of land in other lands, therefore, the said other lands are required to be tracked down in order to see whether Saifa Bibi’s two daughters (Aymona Bibi & Momina Bibi) had received their due 10 shares from the remaining other plots and, therefore, in order to be properly enabled to arrive at the sound and proper findings on the issue as to whether the descendants of the two daughters of Saifa Bibi have sold more land in quantum than what the two daughters of Saifa Bibi are entitled to inherit from Saifa Bibi, in other words, for the purpose of determining whether these three groups have their title and shares in the suit land, the entire properties of Saifa Bibi which have been inherited by her four sons and two daughters are needed to be presented before the trial Court/appellate Court. 

 75. However, taking into consideration the prevalent phenomenon in most of the learned Judges of the lower appellate Courts to remand back the suits for partition on this or that plea by shrugging off their own responsibility of disposing of the suits on merit, this Court, as part of its constitutional duty under Article 109 of the Constitution in tandem with its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 of the CPC, proclaims that the appellate Court, in an appropriate suit if required, is not only empowered to take additional evidence, which would not amount to filling up lacuna caused due to the negligence/failure of any party to the suit, but also competent to call for necessary documents and persons by invoking the Court’s power under Section 165 of the Evidence Act read with Sections 30, 31, 32 and Order 19 of the CPC. Under the above constitutional duty of superintendence in addition to being invested with the revisional power by the CPC, this Court notifies that when the learned Judges of the subordinate Courts perform their functions as the trial Court’s Judge or the appellate Court’s Judge, they should not hesitate to resort to the provisions of Section 165 of the Evidence Act, 1872, Sections 30, 31, 32 and Order 19 of the CPC in an appropriate case for the purpose of fair and effective adjudication of a suit. The trial Courts and appellate Courts, under the above provisions of laws, possess ample powers to summon and, if the situation warrants, then, to compel the appearance of any person in the Court and to produce the necessary relevant papers to the Court and take their deposition as Court Witness/es (CW/s), as has been held in the case of STS Educational Group Vs Bangladesh 18 BLC 806 (Para – 41 to 42). In this suit, the appellate Court’s duty should be to collect the relevant papers regarding inheritance of Saifa Bibi’s entire estate from all the known sources and, upon poring over and scanning through all the documents in connection with the entire property of Saifa Bibi with an aim to assess the ownership of the sellers/vendors of the land sold to the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1, if the appellate Court considers that in the interest of a fair and final disposal of the suit, some relevant persons should clarify their respective position, the Court shall be competent to ask them to appear before the Court and depose as Court Witness/es (CW/s) and, thereafter, pass appropriate Judgment and Decree commensurate with the findings to be arrived at on the basis of examination of all the papers connected with Saifa Bibi’s estate devolved upon her four sons and two daughters. 

 77. It is evident from the written statements that the defendant No. 1 did not make any specific averments as to claiming title in the suit land on the basis of adverse possession, nor is there an alternative prayer by the defendant No. 1 for obtaining a declaration of title based on adverse possession. Furthermore, the defendant No. 1 also did not ask the trial Court to frame an issue on the point of adverse possession and, more so, no evidence was led by the defense in an endeavour to make out a case of adverse possession and, thus, there is hardly any scope for the Court to take a view that although specific prayer is not made, but from the evidence, substance to that effect is present in the suit. Above all, there is always a legal presumption that the co-owners are in constructive possession of the property by virtue of inheriting from the same deceased person and, for that reason, in a suit for partition if adverse possession is claimed, it must be established by the claimant that the other party was totally ousted in assertion of the claimant’s hostile title, but in the four corners of the written statements no such assertion was made by the defendant No. 1. Therefore, the findings of the appellate Court on the points of adverse possession are liable to be set aside. 78. In drawing up the conclusion, this Court pronounces that (i) since from the examination of the evidence, it appears that the claim made by the three groups of descendants of Saifa Bibi’s two daughters in the suit land after around 21 (twenty one) years, as to having shares of their predecessors (Aymona Bibi and Momina Bibi), - has not been proved on a balance of probabilities, let alone conclusively; (ii) since by simply remanding back this suit for proper evaluation of the much-discussed two pieces of documentary evidence, there shall not be an effective adjudication of the suit; (iii) since the status of both the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1 are tenants under the tenancy-in-common and their title and shares in the suit land are dependent on the title and shares of the four sons and the two daughters of Saifa Bibi, (iv) since the findings and observations made by the appellate Court on the issue of adverse possession are not compatible with the laws regulating that field, therefore, this suit is remanded back to the appellate Court, namely, Second Joint District Judge Court, Sylhet upon setting aside the appellate Court’s Judgment and Decree dated 10.04.2006 passed in Title Appeal No. 9 of 2002, so far as it relates to the findings on the issue of adverse possession, and upon staying the operation of the trial Court’s Judgment and Decree dated 30.10.2001 passed in TS No. 61 of 2000 decreeing the suit in part till the time of the disposal of the appeal by the appellate Court, with the following Orders and Directions: (i) The appellate Court shall direct the plaintiffs, defendant No. 1, the four sons of Saifa Bibi (defendant Nos. 23, 24, 25 and legal heirs of the late son Abdul Qaium) and the descendents through Saifa Bibi’s two daughters (Aymona Bibi and Momina Bibi) to submit all the papers and documents together with their descriptions of the entire properties left by Saifa Bibi at the time of her death. (ii) After receiving all the schedules of the entire land of Saifa Bibi, the appellate Court shall heedfully scrutinize the papers. (iii) If it appears to the appellate Court that further papers are required for the purpose of effective disposal of the suit, it shall not hesitate to issue summon upon the officials of the concerned land office, sub-register’s office, settlement office or any other public office to furnish the requisite papers. (iv) Upon receiving all the documents of Saifa Bibi’s entire properties and, thereafter, by fastidiously carrying out necessary scrutiny of the same, if it appears to the appellate Court that any relevant person should explain his/her position with regard to identification and distribution of Saifa Bibi’s properties among her four sons and two daughters, in that event, the appellate Court shall issue summons upon the said person to appear before the Court as Court Witness/es (CW/s). (v) The appellate Court shall not deal with issue of adverse possession or any other issue, except concentrating on the issue as to whether the two daughters of Saifa Bibi (Aymona and Momina) were given any property from Saifa Bibi’s other land in exchange for their due shares in the suit land. (vi) If it is revealed that Saifa Bibi’s two daughters were not given any extra land in other properties in lieu of their due shares in the suit land, in that event, the decree passed by the trial Court shall stand valid and, accordingly, the appellate Court, upon affirming the trial Court’s decree, shall remit the LCR to the trial Court with a direction upon the trial Court to proceed with the accomplishment of the remaining tasks in the suit, without waiting for receiving any formal application for passing Final Decree, but by simply notifying both the parties in writing to that effect. (vii) If it surfaces that Saifa Bibi’s two daughters had received their due shares in other plots upon waiving their respective shares in the suit land, in that scenario, the appellate Court shall pass a fresh Judgment and Decree pronouncing the appropriate declaration of the title and shares of the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1 with reference to the title and shares of their respective vendors. (viii) It is to be borne in mind by the learned Judge of the appellate Court that only the suit land of 0.041 acres of land shall be partitioned and separated among the four sons and two daughters of Saifa Bibi. The other lands having not been asked for partition by the co-owners (Saifa Bibi’s four sons/their legal heirs and two daughters/their descendants), there shall not be any Judgment and Decree for partition of the same. The other lands are being brought into scene simply for the purpose of assessing as to whether Safia Bibi’s Daughters have been allotted larger shares therein in exchange for their due shares in the suit land. 

 79. Before parting with this Judgment, I consider it pertinent to observe here that in the context of prevailing incoherent practice in the sub-ordinate Courts in the different Districts of this country as to naming a ‘suit for partition’, that is to say, when in some Districts it is marked as a Partition Suit, in some Districts it is characterized as a Title Suit and in some Districts it is branded as a Other Class Suit, ‘The Rules Committee of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh’ should either recommend the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs to undertake a project for updating the CRO towards setting out appropriate rules therein or, in the alternative, the said committee should issue a ‘Practice Direction’ (PD) with a proper instructions upon the sub-ordinate Courts as to naming of the suits in different names or to use only ‘Civil Suit’ for all the types of civil suits and ‘Civil Miscellaneous Case’ for the various proceedings which are known as civil proceedings. Secondly, in course of dealing with suits for partition, I have noticed in a significant number of suits that the trial Courts oftentimes become fallible in arriving at an apparent correct decision due to not being familiar with the following terminologies; ‘tenancy’ ‘joint tenants’, ‘co-owners’, ‘co-tenants’ ‘hotchpotch’ and proper application of the afore-said terminologies in a given situation. Therefore, in my humble opinion, the judiciary would be benefitted if the Judicial Administration Training Institute (JATI) includes the relevant useful topics in their courses, so that the tasks of the learned Judges of the trial Courts and appellate Courts become painless and joyous to deal with the suits for partition.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Muhammad Khurshid Alam Sarkar

lawyer:
AJ Mohammad Ali with JN Deb and Md Ekramul Haque, Advocates---For the Petitioners. 
Promila Biswas, Advocate---For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Mridul Kanti Sarder alias Mridul Sarder and others   ----- Petitioners
Vs
Krishna Charan Sarder and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule are that one Krishna Charan Sarder instituted the Other Suit No. 16 of 1990 on 20-1-1990 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Patiya, Chittagong against Mridul Sarder and 6 others, praying for a decree for declaration of title and confirmation of possession of the suit land, measuring an area of 4 sataks, i-e, 2 gandas of land in RS Plot No. 1377 under the RS Khatian No. 418, in Mouza-Dengapara, together with a decree for declaration of the BS Khatian recorded in respect of the suit property, is void, baseless and wrongly recorded, stating, inter alia, that one Uma Charan Sarder was in the right, title and possession of the suit land and the RS Khatian stood recorded in his name and after his death, Mathura inherited the right, title, possession and interest in the suit land. Mathura died leaving behind his daughter Khemlata and Khemlata with her son, Arun Sarder, inherited the same. Both Khemlata and Arun Sarder sold out the suit property to the plaintiff and handed over its possession. The defehdants have no right, title and possession in the suit land, but they are threatening the plaintiff of dispossession. The suit land is contiguous land to the homestead of the plaintiff and the BS Khatian has wrongly been recorded in the names of the defendants. 

 3. The defendant Nos. 1 to 6 have contested the suit by filing written statements, stating that Uma Charan had his 'Chakran' interest in the suit land and on his death, the suit property was restored to the Zamindar Sita Sundari Dutta and while she was in her khas possession, settled the suit land with Hirendra Lal Sarder, the predecessor of the defendants on 22-8-1956 under a registered Patta and handed over possession thereof and Hirendra Lal Sarder made a cowshed upon the suit land as the same is contiguous to his homestead and upon his death, the defendants have inherited it as his heirs and are in continuous possession in the suit land. The BS Khatian has rightly been recorded in the name of their predecessor and the purchase deed of the plaintiff has not been acted upon nor has he acquired any right, title and possession in the suit land by virtue of that deed, Since the plaintiffs vendor had no right, title, possession and interest in the suit land, the plaintiff too, has not acquired any such interest. The dispute being a long standing dispute, a local Shalish took place on 28-9-1980 between the plaintiff and the predecessor of the defendants and all the Arbitrators made an unanimous award in this respect and, according to the award, the plaintiff had no interest in the suit land. 

 4. After conclusion of the trial, the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Patiya, has been pleased to dismiss the suit on his findings that the plaintiff has not disputed the registered Patta of the predecessor of the defendants and nothing has been mentioned about the Patta in the plaint and thus, the plaintiff has admitted the said Patta. The Patta was executed and registered on 22-8-1956 and the plaintiff claimed that it was not acted upon, and thereby also admitted that his vendors had no right, title and interest in the suit land and if, at all, the Patta made after 14-4-1956 was ineffective, in that case, the suit property will be khas land of the Government and, as such, the plaintiffs purchase is also not effective. The PW 1 has admitted in cross-examination that the BS record has rightly been prepared, which is Annexure-C, in the suit and, as such, the possession of the defendants has been proved in the suit land. Though the plaintiff claimed that he is in possession of the suit land from 8-9-1980, but could not mention the plot number of the suit land which is waste land and the PW 2 claimed possession of the plaintiff for 4/5 years, whereas the defendants claimed that they are possessing the same since the time of their predecessor having a cowshed and the Advocate Commissioner was examined in the suit as DW 2, who stated that he saw a cowshed in the suit land during his inspection made more than 7/8 years ago and from the Arbitration Award, Exhibit -F(1) also it appears that the defendants are in possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs with a view to prove his possession exhibited two rent-receipts, vide Exhibit-3-3(a) which are of much later time of the institution of the instant suit i-e, the suit was instituted on 20-1-1990 and the rent paid under these Dakhilas on 28-6-1990 and 10-6-1991 respectively and the defendants exhibited 6(six) rent-receipts vide Exhibit-E-E(5) and Chowkidari receipt, vide Exhibit-D in respect of the suit land showing that the defendants are paying rent right from 19-4-1974 and in view of the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 217 the rent-receipts are evidence of the possession, also may be used as a collateral evidence of title, thereby proving that the defendants are in exclusive possession of the suit land and, for argument's sake, if the Patta is not considered, still the possession of the defendants is for more than 12 years, and thereby creating possessory rights in favour of the defendants. In view of the case reported in 3 DLR 484 that if any person possesses any lane for 12 years is vested with the title of it and the person in possession became an owner' and that the plaintiff without instituting a suit for recovery of possession, cannot maintain his suit in its present form. The possession of the plaintiff in the suit land has not been proved and the BS Khatian has rightly been recorded. 

 5. On the other hand, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Patiya, Chittagong has been pleased to allow the Other Appeal No. 555 of 1991, preferred by the plaintiff against the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge in Other Suit No. 16 of 1990 setting aside the said judgment and decree and also to decree the suit declaring the right, title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land holding that at the time of hearing, the plaintiff appellant has produced the PS Khatian on 4-5-1993, which has also been considered in the appeal and the genealogy of Uma Charan given by the plaintiff has been proved and the plaintiff's purchase from Uma Charan's descendants, namely Khemlata and Arun Sarder, by a Saf-Kabala dated 8-9-1980 (Exhibit-2), is also proved, holding further, that since Uma Charan had his Chakran interest during the RS operation and subsequent PS record has also been recorded in the name of Uma Charan showing his Chakran interest, it is thus established, beyond reasonable doubt, that by operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, Uma Charan acquired his tenancy right under section 11 of the Act, since he was in possession of the suit land at the time when the said Act came into force and thus, became a tenant under the Government and the learned Assistant Judge has failed to consider this legal aspect of the case. The learned Appellate Court also held that the learned Advocates appearing for the defendants-respondents had admitted that the Patta in question has never been acted upon, since it was registered after 14-4-1956 and has argued on the right of the defendants by adverse possession, on the ground of possessing the suit land for more than 12 years. But the DW 3 Manindra Sarder has admitted the possession of the vendors of the plaintiff in his evidence admitting also that after the death of Mathura Sarder, Krishna Sarder is possessing the suit land and Krishna Sarder was the original plaintiff of this suit and since, the DW 3 himself admitted the possession of the plaintiff, the adverse possession of the defendants could not be held. 

 6. The defendants-respondents have thereafter preferred this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule with an order of maintaining status quo in respect of the suit property, on the grounds that the learned Appellate Court has committed a grave error of law in deciding the question of possession relying upon the confused statements of the DW 3 without noticing his clear evidence on record and the learned Appellate Court has wrongly construed the section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in view of the fact that Mathura died in 1943 and the Chakran interest was not heritable. The learned Appellate Court has erred in law in not holding that Khemlata and Arun Sarder did not acquire Chakran interest and also by relying upon the PS Khatian which was not filed and proved in accordance with law before the learned trial Court and the learned appellate Court has also committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiff has failed to prove his title and possession in the suit land. 

 8. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate, appearing with Mr JN Deb and Mr Md Ekramul Hoque, the learned Advocates for the petitioners, by placing his reliance upon the case of Sakina Bibi vs Matra Bibi, reported in 1985 BCR (AD) 37 submitted that since Chakran interest is not heritable, Khemlata or her son Arun cannot be treated as in possession of the disputed land in the capacity of Chakran interest after the death of Uma Charan and that section 11 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act gives protection only to those persons who are in possession of the lands in the capacity of Chakran interest at the time of operation. The learned Advocate thus submitted that the RS record tenant Uma Charan had his interest in the suit land as Chakran and so also in the unproved PS Khatian and since, according to law, the Chakran interest is not heritable, Khemlata and Arun Sarder have not inherited the interest of Uma Charan and, as such, they acquired no right, title interest and possession in the suit land to transfer it to the plaintiff. 

 11. From the RS Khatian No. 418, it appears that Uma Charan, son of Joyman Hori, got tenancy of 4 sataks of land under Chandra Mohan Dutta and Ramoni Mohan Dutta and others as “দখল কার চাকরান বাধ্যকর” and from the PS Khatian, produced before the learned Appellate Court, it also appears that 4 sataks of land was recorded in the name of Uma Charan, son of Joyman Hori, as his Chakran interest. 

 13. From Exhibit-B of the defendants, it appears that the Patta No. 4844 was registered on 22-8-1956 in respect of these 4 sataks of land by Sreemati Sita Sundari Dutta for settlement of land with Sree Khirendra Lal Sarder and the BS Khatian No. 736 (Exhibit-C) stood recorded in the name of Khirendra Lal Sarder in respect of these 4 sataks of land, and Exhibits-D and E series are the rent-receipts, showing rent paid by Khirendra also in the name of Uma Charan from the decade of seventies and the Exhibit-F is the Arbitration Award, where it was held that the vendors of the plaintiff had no possession of the suit land and also that the first party Krishna Kumar Sarder (plaintiff) had no possession in the land of dispute. The plaintiff produced 3 witnesses, including himself (Lalu Sarder, son of Krishna Sarder) and the stated, in gist that after the death of Uma Charan his son Mathura Sarder inherited the property and after the death of Mathura, Khemlata and her son Arungot it and the Amanat Kha stated that the plaintiffs father would possess the suit land and now the plaintiff is possessing it and the defendants have no possession in the suit land. The PW 3 is Khemlata, daughter of Mathura Sarder, stating that she had no brother and she along with her son Arun sold the suit property to the plaintiff and delivered its possession and they were in possession in the suit land. 

 14. DW 1 is Mridul Kanti Sarder who supported their Patta got through their father from Zamindar Sita Sundari also supporting the BS Khatian and the Award asserting their possession in the suit land. DW 2 is Md Ishaque who held the local inspection and proved his report stating that he found a cowshed in the suit land. The DW 3 is Monindra Sarder stating that there is a cowshed in the suit property and plaintiff or his vendors have never possessed the suit land and he saw the suit land in possession of Krishna Sarder after death of Mathura. Khemlata is his daughter and Arun grandson. After Mathura, Khemlata did not possess it. He did not know that Khemlata sold it to Krishna Sarder. It is not a fact that the plaintiff is in possession in the suit land. 

 24. Under the RS Khatian No. 418, Uma, son of Joyman Hori, had the Chakran interest in respect of the suit land. 

 26. In this portion, the vendor stated that at the time of death of Uma Charan, he had no other heir except the vendor No. 2, Khemlata and she was the granddaughter of Uma Charan. It also appears from the statement above, that her father Mathura Charan died some time before her grandfather, Uma Charan. Now if Uma Charan was alive on 16-5-1951, he acquired his right of occupancy in the land, recorded in the RS Khatian, If Uma Charan acquired the tenancy right, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, only after then, the sale deed of Khemlata and her son Arun Sardar may be operative. 

 33. Exhibit-F(1) is the Arbitration Award given by the 13 No. Shu-Chakradandi Union Parishad on 28-9-1980 holding the possession of Khirendra Sardar and finding no possession of Krishan Kumar Sardar. The BS Khatian No. 736 was recorded in the name of Khirendra Lal Sardar evidencing his possession, Khirendra Lal Sardar paid rent in the name of Uma Charan from the year 1974, vide Exhibit-E (series) and Lalu Sardar also paid rent in the name of Uma Charan for the years 1990 and 1991, vide Exhibit-3. 

 35. But there cannot be any adverse possession against the Government, in law. The land in question has been vested in the Government by operation of law on 2-4-1956. The possession could be adverse against Khemlata and her vendee. The Government has admitted possession of the defendants by receiving rent and by publishing the BS Khatian. 

 37. This collateral evidence may be taken with the BS Khatian for consideration. 

 38. In the case of Abdul Hamid vs Abul Hossain Mir, reported in 35 DLR 295 his Lordship held that "Presumption of Khatian loses its weight with the passage of time and that the entries in the subsequent khatian would be more acceptable to a Court than the entries in the earlier Khatian."

parties:
Abdul Mannan and others  ------ Appellants.
Vs.
Kulada Ranjan Mowali and others  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.-This appeal is against a judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division, discharging a Rule issued on an application made by the appellants under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against an order or the Subordinate Judge, Patuakhali, recording abatement of a suit, instituted by the appellants, under section 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972. 

 3. According to the plaintiff's case, as made out in the plaint, the disputed lends appertained to the Estate of Bishweshwar Roy Choudhury, which were diluviated and after the said lands had reappeared as reformation in stu and had become fit for possession. Babu Rajeswar Choudhury, the then executor of the -10/- annas share of the Estate of late Bishweshwar Roy Choudhury settled the said lands with the predecessors of plaintiffs 1 to 42 and plaintiff No. 45 at an annual rent of Tk. 250/- on the basis of a Karsha Kabuliyat dated 1st Jaistha, 1331 B.S. corresponding to May, 1924.  The proprietors of 6/- annas share of the said Estate settled their 6/- annas share of the said lands with some of the defendants at an annual rent of 7k. 75/- on the basis of another Kabuliyat of the sane date, namely, 1st Jaistha, 1331 B.S. which were ultimately sold, and purchased in auction by the landlords, in execution of a decree for rent obtained by them and were then settled in 1344-45 13.S. with the predecessors of some of the plaintiffs on the basis of a Kabuliyat at a rental of Tk. 75. After the rent receiving interests of the previous landlords had been acquired under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the Government has stepped into the shoes of the previous landlords and the plaintiffs have become tenants directly under the Government, in respect of the said lands, some of which had been wrongly recorded in the name of the Government. The Government, however, have had no right, title and interest in the said lands nor any right to dispossess the plaintiffs from any part thereof, which are the lands of their tenancy. 

 5. After the amendment of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 the contesting defendants filed an application for abatement of the suit under the said amended provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. While disposing of the said application by his order dated 24.3.73. the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have gone into the question of the truth or otherwise of the allegations made in the plaint and having held, on the basis of certain papers, that the story of reformation in situ and the induction of the plaintiffs as tenants could not be believed, recorded an order of abatement of the suit in respect of the lands in suit on The basis of the amended provisions of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 7. The High Court Division was moved under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure on behalf of the plaintiffs against the order of abatement made by the learned Subordinate Judge but the learned Judges of the High Court Division affirmed the decision of the Subordinate Judge on holding that the suit had been rightly held to have abated in view of President's Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 amending the provisions of Sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

 8. Special Leave to appeal was granted by the Appellant Division to consider whether the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as amended by the Presidential Orders No. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 could be applied in respect of the lands in the instant suit. This appeal, thus, raises an important question as to the interpretation of the amended provisions of the aforesaid two sections of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 10. It should be pointed out at the out-set that the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Judges of the High Court Division were not correct in going into the question as to the truth of the allegations made in the plaint before any evidence had been adduced in deciding the question of abatement of the suit as a preliminary issue. To decide the question of abatement of the suit in the light of the provisions of the newly enacted sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act., the proper procedure which should have been followed was to take the allegations made in the plaint as such and then to see if the relevant provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act were attracted to them. 

 11. The plaint of the suit, out of which the appeal arises, if properly read, would show that the claim of the plaintiffs is based upon an allegation of settlement of the tenancy right in respect of the disputed lauds in their favour by the former proprietors of the estate to which the disputed lands appertained. The said proprietors are alleged to have acquired right to the said lands when they reappeared after division by virtue of their right to reformation in situ and there appears to be no allegation in the plaint relating to accrual of any right of accretion at any stage, requiring the application of section 87 as amended by President's Order Nos. 72 and 137 of 1972 but as the trial Court held that the suit abated in view of the amended section 87, and the learned Judges of the High Court expressed the view that the suit had abated in view of the provisions of both the sections, namely sections 86 and 87, as amended the Appellate Division granted special leave to consider the meaning and scope of both the said two sections amended by the relevant Presidential Orders. 

 The lands gained from the river is or sea by the means above mentioned are a frequent source of contention and affray, and although the law and custom of the country have established rules applicable to such cases, these rules not being generally known, the Court of Justice have sometimes found it default to determine the rights of litigant parties claiming chars or other lands gained in the manner above described. 

 19. The former tenancy law, as incorporated in sections 17 and 18 of the Rent Act 1859, recognized the principle that a tenant was liable to enhancement of rent in case of increment of the area of the land of his tenancy by allusion or otherwise and that similarly a tenant was entitled to abatement of rent in case of diminution of the area of the land of his tenancy by dilution or otherwise. On diluvion a tenant was entitled to reduction of rent in respect of the diluviated property under section 17 of the Act but his title to such property was not affected in any way by such dilution and whenever they said property reappeared he could take back the property in his own right, however long the period of submergence might be. On the repeal of the Rent Act 1859, by the enactment of Bengal Tenancy Act 1885, similar provisions as to abatement and enhancement of rent were made in section 52 of the Act. There were no specific provisions relating to the right of accretion or right to reformation in sue either in the Rent Act of 1889 or The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885. Such matters were regulated by e provisions of Alluvion and diluvion Regulation of 1825 and the principles laid down by the judicial authorities. Some change was effected in 1929 when section 86A was inserted in the Bengal Act by an amendment introduced by Bengal Act IV of 1928, which provided that the tenants' right in the diluviated lands, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, would be deemed to have been surrendered and would be extinguished, if the tenant obtained any abatement in respect of such dilution. This extinction of the right in respect of reformation in situ was dependent on the tenant's obtaining an abatement of rent of such land which was to be deemed, according to the amendment, an act or surrender on his part. It was, however, clearly provided in sub section (2) of this newly inserted section that such extinction of right would not affect the accrual of his right of accretion in respect of the said land if it was available to him under any other law. In 1938 a new section 86A was substituted in place of the aforesaid provision, enlarging the rights of the tenants in certain respects. This new provision provided for automatic abatement of rent in case of the loss of land by delusion, and also ensured the subsistence of the right title and interest of the tenant in the lands lost by such diluvion for a period of 20 years, notwithstanding the abatement of rent of such lands. 

 20. After the partition of the country a big change was effected in 1951 in the land tenure system of the country by the enactment of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 where under all grades of rent-receivers intervening between the Government and the actual occupants of the soil were abolished and such occupants became tenants directly under the Government, subject to a ceiling as to the maximum area of land which a tenant can hold. No substantial change in regard to the law as to accretion or reformation in situ was, however, brought about by this enactment excepting that a specific provision incorporating the law of accretion, which was so long regulated by the provisions of Bengal Regulation XXI of 1825 was made in section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The provisions relating to abatement of rent due to diluvion of some land of the tenancy and subsistence of the tenants' title in respect o such land, similar to those contained in section 86A of the Bengal Tenancy Act, were incorporated in section 86 of the new Act, Part V of the Act which contains sections 86 and 87 came into force on different dates in different areas of the country on the publication of the Notifications as prescribed under section 79 of the Act and, according to the provisions of section 80 of the Act, on and from the date of coming into force of the said Part in a particular area the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed in the said area. 

 21. On June 28, 1972 the riparian owner's right of accretion which was recognized by the usage and custom of the country, as referred to in the preamble of the Bengal Regulation XI of 1815 and which had enjoyed the sanction of positive legislation for about a century and a half was abrogated by President's Order No. 72 of 1972, which substituted, in place of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, a new Section 87 which is to the following effect; 

 "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being enforce, when any land has been gained by gradual accession, whether from the recess of a river or of the sea, it shall not be considered as an increment to the holding or tenancy to which it may be thus annexed, but shall vest absolutely in the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and shall be at their disposal." 

 22. The aim and object of this amending legislation has not been spelt out in the Presidential Order nor there do any reference in the order to any possible mischief which this legislation intended to remedy. It has been stated in a very brief preamble, as is usual in modern legislation, that "it is expedient to amend the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950" "for the purposes appearing" in the enacting provisions. When the law of accretion was given a legislative shape in Bengal Regulation XI of 1825 the law-making authority explained in a very detailed and comprehensive preamble, which may have been prolix in certain respects but sufficiently expressive of the considerations which weighed with the said authority in making the said legislation. This preamble has been quoted above for the proper appreciation of the nature and background of the right created by the said regulation and the principle underlying it. 

 "(2) The provision of sub-section (1) shall apply to all land so gained whether before or after the 28th June, 1972, but shall not apply to any land so gained before the said date if the right of a Malik to hold such land as an increment to his holding was finally recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Sixth Amendment) Order 1972 	(P.O. No. 137 of 1972), under the law then in force. 

 27. The effect of making the provision of sub-section (1) of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act applicable to any land which may have been gained by accession by the recess of a river or the sea before 28.6.72, as it purported to have been done under President's Order No. 137 of 1972 appears to do away with, in the literal sense of the words used in the amending Presidential Order/ the right which had been acquired by the riparian owner under Bengal Regulation XI of 1825 and, if such accession took place after Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act had come into force, also under section 87 of the Act, as it stood before the enactment of the President's Order No. 72 of 1972. 

 31. The provision of sub-section (1) of section 87 that the land gained by accession shall not be considered as an increment to the holding or tenancy makes it abundantly clear that the said provision is applicable only to the land which has been added to the land of a raiyat or any other tenant and it is not attracted to the case of the land which has been added to the khas land of a proprietor or a tenure-holder. If for the applicability of the aforesaid provision the Legislature conceived of a situation where there were the lands of a tenant as well as those of a proprietor or a tenure-holder, there appears to be absolutely no good reason to exclude the khas land of a proprietor or a tenure-holder from the operation of the said provision and thus to discriminate against those who were not so. The inference seems to be irresistible that, for the application of the said provision, the Legislature was conceiving of a situation where there were no proprietors nor tenure holders but were only tenants and such a situation arose when all the rent receiving interests were acquired by the Government under the provisions of The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 24. According to the aforesaid provisions on and from the date specified in the notifications all tenants in respect of the lands of their tenancies, and the rent receivers in respect of their khas lands, became tenants directly under the Government in respect of the said lands. If any land had accreted to the land of the tenants or the khas land of the rent-receivers before the date specified in the said notifications, the said accreted land became a part of their tenancies or khas land, as the case may be, under the law then in force and they became tenants, by virtue of the provisions of clauses (e) and (f) of sub-section (4) of Section 3 of the Act, directly under the Government in respect of the said lands. The right of accretion accruing to the tenants or the rent-receivers in respect of the lands, accreting to the lands of their tenancies of khas lands, was given a new statutory force by the said legislative & provisions and the right so acquired became indefeasible in the sense that it was not dependent for its enforceability on any further recognition or declaration by any authority or court. Since the State Acquisition an Tenancy Act had come into force on 16.5.51, the notifications under section 3 of the Act were issued in respect of certain big rent receivers from time to time as a special measure for acquisition of their interests on or about the 2nd April, 1956 several omnibus notifications under section 3 of the Act purporting to acquire the entire interest of the whole body of the rent-receivers within the province of East Bengle with effect from 14.4.56 were issued, and since 14th April, 1956 all accreted lands, if any, adjoining those of the tenants or rent receivers became parts of their tenancies by virtue of the aforesaid provisions of The State Acquisition on and Tenancy Act. Having regard to the legal consequences flowing from the notifications under section 3 of the Act, as referred to above, no retrospective effect can be given to the provision of sub-section (2) of Section 87 of the Act, in any view of the matter, in most of the cases beyond 14.4.56, as the said provision read with that of sub-section (1) does not purport to extinguish or nullify any right which has been created under the provision of this very statute, of which this newly enacted section 87 is a part. It is significant that in the introductory clause of sub-section (1) of section 87, namely, "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force" there is reference only to ''any other law", but there is no reference to the law as contained in the present Act. It is, therefore, reasonable to conclude that there was never any intention on the part of the legislative authority to extend the retrospectively of section 87 beyond 14.4.56 or such other date as may have been specified in any earlier notifications under section 3(1) of the Act. 

 (2) Each proprietor, tenure holder and other rent receiver, whose interests in any estate, tenure or holding or tenancy or in any part of any estate, tenure or holding or tenancy as the case may be, within the area to which such roll relates, are acquired under this Act, shall with effect from the first day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of such notification in the Official Gazette, be entitled to retain possession of this Act, as a tenant. under the Provincial Government all lands of which he is entitled to retain possession of and holy, subject to the provision of this to, as a to cant, under Provincial Government all lands of which he is entitled to retain possession under Chapter IV and he hall.; to pay rent for such lands to the Provincial Government ; 

 37. There appears to be another limitation to the retrospectively of section 87 of the Act. This section is contained in Part V of the Act, which includes sections 9 to 152 of the Act. We have already noticed that section 79 provides for commencement of the provisions contained in Part V of the Act in different areas on different dates and section 80 provides for repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act along with some other Statutes in the said areas on the commencement of the sad Part therein. It is pertinent to quote section 79 in this connection, which is as follows; 

 "unless (Sic) the right of a Malik to hold such land as an increment to his holding was finally recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (6th Amendment) Order 1972 (President's Order No. 137 of 1972) under the law then in force. 

 40. The use of the term 'Malik" in sub section (2) is also significant. Such term can be used in place of the term 'raiyat' or tenant only after Part V of the Act has come into operation. Section 81 (1) of the Act provides that on and from the date of coming into force of the whole of Part V in any area, there shall be within that area one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, Maliks' and the rights and liabilities of every such land holder shall be regulated by the provisions of this Part, and clause (8) of section 82, which is an interpretation section also provides that on and from the date of coming into force of the whole of this Part in any area, the word 'Malik' shall be deemed to have been substituted for the word 'rayiat' or 'tenant'. The use of the word malik in place of the word 'raiyat' or tenant' in sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act to denote a person whose right to hold the newly added land as accretion to his holding or tenancy might be recognized or declared by a competent authority or Court before the commencement of President's Order No. 137 of 1972 unmistakably points out that the legislative authority was contemplating a situation in subsection (I) and sub-section (2) of Section 87 Which could arise only after the coming into force of Part V of the Act in the area in which the accreting lands are situated. The retrospectively of the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act cannot therefore be pushed beyond the date of the commencement of Part V of Act in the area where the accretion in question had taken place and it is only such accretion as took place after the coming into force of Part V of the Act to which sub-section (1) read with sub-section (2) of section 87, may apply. The date of the commencement of Part V of the Act in any area must necessarily be a date later than that of the publication of the notification under Section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act in that area. 

 44. We have noticed that all accretions, which took place before the notification under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act, have been statutorily recognized to be the lands appertaining to the tenancies of the riparian owners and the provisions of clause (e) and (f) of Sections 3(4) or items (2) and (4) of section 44 of the Act have clearly conferred the right of tenancy upon the riparian owner in respect of such accredited lands. Any suit etc. which may be brought in respect of such land is not obviously a suit in which the assertion of the claim of right is on the basis of the riparian owner's right of accretion. Such a suit is really on the basis of the statutory right as has been conferred by clauses (e) and (0 of sections 3 (4) or items (2) and (4) of sect ion 44 of the Act and is, there-fore, clearly outside the purview of sub-section (3) of section 37 of the Act. As regards the accretions, which took place after the publication of the notifications under section 3 or section 43(2) of the Act but before the coming into force of Part V of the Act, they are also, we have noticed above, beyond the scope of sub-sections (1) and (2) of sections 87 and as such, the rights which accrued to the riparian owners in respect of such accretions have not been affected in any way by the said provisions of section 87. There seems to be no conceivable reason why the legislative authority, while preserving the right of a riparian owner in respect of such accretions under sub-section (1) and (2) would deprive, by sub-section (3) the said owner of the remedy to enforce the said right. Such reading of sub-section (3) would undoubtedly lead to injustice and some absurd consequences, which cannot be the intention of the legislative authority. Sub-section (3) should be read harmoniously with sub-sections (1) and (2) and the land gained or alleged to have been gained from the recess of a river or the sea, as have been contemplated in subsection (3) must be such lands as are within the purview of sub sections (1) and (2) of section 87. It will necessarily be those accredited lands which have appeared as hard soil only after the coming into force of Part V of the Act and the provision as to the and abatement of suits etc. as made in sub-section (3) are attracted in case of those suits etc. where a claim of the right is asserted in respect of such lands. 

 (2) "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successors in interest shall be extinguished in such lands or a portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by dilution took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972 lands or portion thereof within twenty years of their loss by dilution, and be liable to pay the arrears of rent without interest or damage in respect of the land, which has re-appeared, for the period during which it was lost or four years whichever is less; 

 Explanation:-For the purpose of this section, the word "family" shall have the same meaning as in clause (a) of section 151 J, as amended by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order 1972". 

 46. It will appear that the provision of subsection (1) of this new section, which latest to abatement of rent in respect of the land lost by dilution did not bring about any great charge in the law then in force, as this provision is similar to sub-section (I) of the old section as amended by East Pakistan Ordinance No. XXI of 1969 which dispensed with the filing of an application by the tenant to the Revenue Officer for abatement of rent, as was required under the former provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act. This provision is clearly prospective and refers to land which is still subject to delusion. The provision of sub-section (2) which purports to extinguish the title of the tenant to the land which has been lost by delusion, whether before or after the commencement of the President's Order No. 135 of 1972, is also clearly prospective and there is no difficulty as to the construction of the said provision. But the construction of subsection (3) which purports to confer title upon the Government in respect of the lands which were lost by delusion under sub-section (2) but re-appeared before the date of commencement of the Order seems to be fraught with some difficulty, in so far as its real import is concerned. The plain meaning of the said provision seems to be that the lands which were lost by diluvion but have reappeared before the commencement of the Order and also the lands so lost by diluvion which may re-appear on or after the said date shall vest in the Government and shall be at the disposal. So far as the second part of the subsection is concerned, there is no difficulty, but the first part of the sub-section which provides for accrual of right in favour of the Government in respect of the lands which were lost by diluvion but have re appeared before the commencement of the President's Order No. 135 of 1972 does not appear to be consistent with the provision of subsection (2) of the section, which purports to extinguished the title of the tenant to such land as has been lost by diluvion. Subsection (2) does not appear to contemplate a case where the lands which were lost by diluvion before the commencement of the order but have also re-appeared before such commencement does on the other hand, mean that the title of the tenant to the land which is lost to him by diluvion at the time of the commencement of the Order shall be extinguished on such commencement, although the diluvion took place before such commencement. If the diluvion and the loss in consequence thereof have ceased, and the land reappeared before the commencement of the Order there was no discontinuance of his right and it subsisted with all its force. But the first part of subsection (3) which purports to vest such lands on the Government seems to be incongruous to a certain extent, because, by such vesting, the tenant is also correspondingly divested of all his rights by necessary implication, although under sub-section (2) which provides for the extinguishment of the tenants' right, such divestment is not contemplated. However, if sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 86 are read together, it appears that the legislative authority wanted to give a kind of retrospective effect to the provision of subsection (2) although such intention has not been properly expressed in the language used in the said subsection (3) is clear so far as it Oaks to divest, though in-directly a tenant of his title to the land which was once lost by diluvion but reappeared before the commencement of the Order, unless his right to repos session was recognized or declared by a competent authority or court. But the question is, as it was the case of sub-sections (I) and (2) of section 87 whether the lawmaker intended to give the full or limited retrospective effect to the provision of sub-section (3) of section 85 of the Act. 

 50. Now, the provisions of sections 86 and 87 as have been enacted by President's Order Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 are clearly inapplicable to the facts of the suit out of which this appeal arises, inasmuch as there is no assertion in the plaint of the suit of a claim of the right of accretion or reformation in situ in respect of the lands in suit. The allegations made in the plaint are that the lands in suit which formerly appertained to the estate of Bishweswar Roy Chowdhury were lost by diluvion, that the said lands having re-appeared as firm land and become fit for cultivation, the 10/-annas share of the said lands was settled with the predecessors of plaintiffs No. 1 to 42 and plaintiff No. 45 by the proprietors of the said share on the 1st Jaistha, 1331 B S. that is, middle of May, 1924 and the remaining 6/4 as share in the said lands was also settled with some of the plaintiffs and the predecessors of some other plaintiffs in 1345 B.S. i.e. 1938/39. The basis of some of plaintiffs' claim in respect of the 10/- as share of the lands is the settlement granted by the landlords of the said share in May, 1924 and that of some other plaintiffs in respect of the remaining 6/- as share is the settlement granted to the said plaintiff by the landlords of the 6/- as share in 1938/39. There is no recital in the plaint as to accretion in respect of any part of the lands in suit. There are, no doubt, some allegations in the plaint as to diluvion of the land in suit aid subsequent reformation of the said lands but they happened, according to the said allegations, long ago i.e., prior to May 1924. The plaintiffs have prayed in the suit for a declaration of their title which accrued, according to the averment made in the plaints, from the settlement granted by the proprietors, partly in May 1924 and partly in 193 8/39. After the promulgation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in 1961 the rent receiving interests of the plaintiffs' landlords were acquired by the Government on publication of the notification under section 3 and section 43(2) of the Act and the plaintiffs have become tenants directly under the Government by virtue of the provisions of clause (e) and (f) of sub-section (4) of section (3) and items (2) and (4) of section 44 of the Act slur then. The immediate basis of the plaintiffs' claim in the suit, therefore, is the statutory right conferred upon them by section 3(4)(e) and (f) and there-after, under items (2) and (4) of section 44 and the remote basis of the claim may be said to be the settlement granted by the superior land-lords partly in 1924 and partly in 1938-39. But the basis of the plaintiffs' in respect of the lands  in their site after they had been lost by diluvion, and, as such, the present suit cannot be said, in any view of the matter, to be a suit for a claim to repossession of any land lost by diluvion which has re-appeared or is alleged to have reappeared.
