3. Both the civil appeals by leave are directed against the judgment and order dated 14.12.2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos.2332 and 2333 of 2007 discharging the Rules. 4. Facts, relevant for disposal of the civil appeals, are that the petitioner herein as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No.25 of 2001 on 16.04.2001 under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet, for pre-emption of 1.67 acres of land appertaining to khatian no.530 and 167 respectively as co-sharer by inheritance stating, interalia, that the case land belonged to one Arjan Ullah who died leaving Abdul Motlib, Abul Hashem and Abdul Kader as successive heirs who subsequently sold out 53 decimals of land from plot no.1311 by registered sale deed dated 10.03.1964 to one Ishaque Mia.; Abdul. Motlib, Abul Hasheni sold out 30 decimals of land from plot no.1321 to the said Ishaque Mia by another registered sale deed dated 22.03.1963; Said Abdul Motlib also sold out another 15 decimals of sale deed dated 16.05.1963; Thus, Ishaque Mia became the owner of 53 decimals of land in plot no.1311 and 45 decimals in plot no.1321 who subsequently transferred the same to Mossammat Khairunnessa, step mother of the petitioner, by registered sale deed dated 27.06.1970 and thus, Mossammat Khairunnessa became the co-sharer in the respective khatians; Abdul Motlib and Abdul Kader died leaving pre-emptee-opposite-party nos.6-11 and 12-15 as the successive heirs; Mossammat Khairunnessa also claimed to have purchased 30 decimals of land from one Tayaibullah by registered sale deed dated 28.11.1964; She claimed to have purchased other properties in the said vicinity; Mossammat Khairunnessa died leaving one son, one daughter, husband Haji Jahir Box and pre-emptee nos.36-44; Said Haji Jahir Box died leaving wife preemptee no.20, 7 (seven) sons Md. Azad Box, Md. Afroz Box, pre-emptor no. l and pre-emptee opposite party nos.36-38, 6 daughters pre-emptee opposite party nos.39-44 and 2 daughters of a deceaseds daughter pre-emptee opposite nos.45 and 46; Pre-emptee opposite party nos.36-44 transferred their shares in plot no.1311 and 1321 to Azad Box and others and pre-emptee opposite no.31 by registered sale deed dated 0107.1989; The pre-emptor became the co-sharers in the case land by inheritance and also by purchase; The pre-emptor mutated his name in Mutation Case No.209 of 1 994/9 5; Cause of action arose in the middle of March 2001, when the pre-emptee opposite party no.2 disclosed that he and pre-emptee opposite party no.1 had purchased the case land from pre-emptee opposite party nos. -17; Having came to know about the same, the pre-emptor procured the certified copy of the sale deed dated 12.03.2001 wherefrom he had the definite knowledge that the pre-emptee opposite party nos.3-17 transferred the case land to pre-emptee opposite party nos.1 and 2 at a consideration of Tk.1,00,000/-; No notice was served upon the pre-emptor under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act; The case land is necessary to the pre-emptor for convenient and effective enjoyment of his existing land; if he knew about the said transfer, he would have purchased the same; Pre-emptee opposite party nos.1 and 2 are strangers to the case holding; The pre-emptor has made statutory deposit with the application for pre-emption. 

 "Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the co-petitioners did not file the pre-emption case within the stipulated time as prescribed under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and sought pre-emption under section 96(4) of the Act. As they failed to discharge their burden of not having knowledge of the transfer till receipt of the notice under section 96(4) of the said Act, they are not entitled to get preemption and their claim for pre-emption is not maintainable. But the High Court Division though found that the co- petitioners failed to prove their knowledge of the alleged transfer, discharged the Rules in order to give benefit to the co-petitioners and as such the judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. He further submits that in sub-section 6 of section 96 of the SAT Act the phrase "whichever is earlier" is used in place. of the phrase "whichever is later" used in section 26F(4) (a) of the Bengal Tenancy Act,1885 and which goes to suggest that the pre-emption case has to be filed within 4 months of the knowledge of transfer of the land in question which was made on 12.03.2001 and the co-petitioner applied for impleading them as co-petitioners and claimed pre-emption on 07.07.2003 without stating anything about their knowledge of trans-fer and, therefore, in view of the phrase "whichever is earlier" used in section 96(4) of the SAT. Act, their claim for pre-emption is hopelessly barred by limitation. But the High Court Division misconstrued the provision of law and erroneously discharged the Rules. The learned Advocate also submits that the High Court Division committed an error in holding that section 96 (4) of the SAT Act excludes the prescribed period of limitation given in section 96(1) of the said Act in order to give benefit to the co-petitioner inasmuch as the right of pre-emption is a statutory right and unless one comes within strict compliance of law, he is not entitled to claim such right and there is no scope for giving benefit against the law and as such the judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. He lastly submits that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that cross objection is maintainable against the order passed in a pre-emption case. Order 41 Rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure pro-vides for filing of cross objection, only against decree, and order passed in pre-emption case is not a decree and it is only an appealable order in view of section 96(3) of the SAT Act and, therefore cross objection against an order passed in pre-emption case is not at all maintain-able. As such the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set aside." 

 12. Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the appellant in both the appeals at the very outset submits that he does not want to press the last submission of the leave granting order. Mr. Probir Neogi in line with the leave granting order submits that the co-petitioners sought pre-emption under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act beyond the timeframe without disclosing their source of knowledge regarding transfer of the land in question and without considering this legal and factual aspect the High Court Division as well as the Courts below committed illegality which occasioned failure of justice. He also submits that the High Court Division committed an error of law in not considering that co-petitioners did not comply the provision of compulsory deposit enunciated in clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. 

 13. On the other hand, Mr. A. F. Masan Ariff, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondent no. 1 in C.A. No.148 of 2015 and respondent nos.1-4 in CA. No.149 of 2015 submits that section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act prescribe the timeframe regarding knowledge of the transfer when application is made under subsection (1) of section 96 but sub-section (4) of section 96 clearly stipulates that 'within two months of the date of service of the notice of the application under Clause (b) of sub-section (3)' which is applicable in the case in hand inasmuch as the co-petitioners were not served notice under section 89 and they were notified about the transfer through court when the pre-emtor impleaded them as party as co-sharer by inheritance in the case holding and as such disclosing knowledge of transfer under section 96(1) of the Act is not applicable for the co-petitioners. He also submits that both the Courts below as well as the High Court. Division on perusal of the record came to a clear finding that the co-petitioners appeared in the miscellaneous case within two months of the date of service of notice of the application under Clause (b) of sub-section (3) and the question of limitation being a mixed question of facts and law the same is addressed by the Courts below on perusal of the materials on record. He further submits that the provision of clauses (a)(b) of sub-section 6 of section 96 the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act requires to be read together which makes it clear that on determination by the court the co-petitioners under sub-section (4) shall deposit the amount. 

 15. Three questions of law are involved in these appeals, (i) Whether the co-petitioners are bound to file their application under Sub-section(4) of section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act with-in the timeframe mentioned in sub-section(1) of section 96 of the Act, (ii) Whether the co-petitioners are bound to deposit the consideration money alongwith interest at the time of application under sub-section 0) of section 96 of the SAT Act, (iii) whether this Division under Article 103 of the Constitution can take a diverge finding on point of limitation, a mixed question of law and fact, differing concurrent findings of fact of the Courts below based on record concurred by the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 17. From the above quoted provisions of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, it is clear that section 96 contemplates two distinct applications, one application under sub-section (1) and another application by the co-petitioner under sub-section (4) to join with the original application under sub-section (1) within the period of limitation as provided in sub-section (4) of section 96 of the Act. The right to purchase the land transferred as contemplated under section 96 is a statutory right and this right can be exercised by two ways: one is under sub-section (1) and another under subsection (4) of section 96. Under sub-section (1) this right is to be exercised within four months of the service of the notice given under section 89, or if no notice has been served under section 89, within four months of the date of knowledge of the transfer. Again, sub-section (4) provides the period of limitation for the remaining co-sharer tenants or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred, to join in the pre-emption proceedings, under sub-section (4) this right is to be exercised within the period referred to in sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act or within two months of the date of the service of the notice of the application under clause (b) of sub-section (3), whichever is earlier. 

 18. It is admitted that notice under section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was not served upon the pre-emptor as well as the opposite party nos. 54-57 i.e. co-petitioners, It appears that the co-petitioners i.e. opposite party nos.54-57 were impleaded as a party by the pre-emptor by way of amendment of the application filed under section 96 of the Act. Thus, on perusal of the provisions of section 96 of the SAT Act, it is apparent that the period of limitation for the co-petitioners for filing application under sub-section (4) is two months from the service of the notice under clause (b) of sub-section (3) of section 96 i.e. the application for pre-emption. 

 "Thus reading these various provisions of section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it is clear that section 96 contemplates to distinct applications, one application under subsection (1) of section 96 and another application by the co-applicant or applicants under sub section(4) of section 96 for joining with the original application under sub-section(1) within the period of limitation as provided in sub-section(4) of section 96 of the Act. Application under sub-section (1) of section 96 speaks of a deposit under clause (a) of sub-section (3) of the Act which is mandatory and without the deposit the application shall be dismissed. But in the case of joining with the original application by the co-applicant or applicants under sub-section (4) of section 96 such deposit is not mandatory Sub-section (4) of section 96 of the Act does not speak of any deposit alongwith the application of the co-applicant or applicants. The provision of clause, (a) (b) of sub-section (6) makes it clear that on determination by the court the co-applicant under sub-section (4) shall deposit the amount. Thus, it is abundantly clear from the plain language of the provision of the relevant sub-section as mentioned herein above that in an application under subsection (4) of section 96 the period of such deposit is left with the discretion of the court and the order having been made by the court such deposit is to be made. Thus, have no hesitation in holding that a deposit as required under the law is mandatory under sub-section (1) of section 96 whereas the deposit under sub-section(4) of section 96 of the Act is not mandatory and the same can be deposited subsequently as contemplated in clauses (a) (b) of sub-section(6) of section 96 of the Act." 

 35. Facts leading to filing of this civil appeals, in short, are that the petitioner as preemptor filed Miscellaneous Case No.25 of 2001 on 16.4.2001 under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 in short, SAT Act), 1950 before the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Syihet for pre-emption of 1.67 acres of land appertaining to Khatian Nos.530 and 167 respectively as co-sharer by inheritance stating, inter alias that the case land originally belonged to one Arjan Ullah, who died leaving behind Abdul Motlib, Abdul Hashem and Abdul Kadir as heirs who subsequently sold out 53 decimals of land of plot No.1311 by executing registered sale deed dated 10.03.1964 to one Ishaquc Mia. Accordingly, Ishaque Mia became the owner of 53 decimals of land of plot No.1311 and 45 decimals of land of plot No.1321. Subsequently, he transferred the same to one Mosammat Khairunnessa, the step mother of the petitioner vide sale deed dated 27.6.1970. As such, Mosammat Khairunnessa became the co-sharer in the respective khatians. The .Abdul Motlib and Abdul Kader died leaving behind pre-emptee Nos. 6-11, 12-16 as heirs. Mosammat Khairunnessa also claimed to have purchased 30 decimals of land from one Tayaibullah vide registered sale deed dated 2811.1964 and she claimed to have purchased other proper-ties in the said vicinity. While Mosammat Khairunnessa was enjoying 83 decimals of land of plot No.111, and 45 decimals of land of plot No.1321, she died leaving behind a son, a daughter, her husband Hazi Zahir Bakth and the pre-emptee Nos.36-44. That Hazi Zahir Bakth died leaving behind one wife, the pre-emptee No. 20, seven sons, Md Azad Bakth, Md. That pre-emptee Nos.36-44 transferred their respective shares of plot Nos.1311 and 1321 to Azad Bakth and others, including the pre-emptor and premptee No.31, vide registered sale deed dated 03.07.1989. Hence, the pre-emptors became the co-sharers in the case land by inheritance and also by purchase. The pre-emptors mutated their names vide Mutation Case No.209 of 1994-95. The cause of action arose in the middle part of March, 2001 when the pre-emptee No.2 disclosed in the locality that the pre-emptee No.1 and he purchased the case land from pre-emptee Nos.3-17. Having come to know about the alleged transfer, the preemptors obtained the certified copy of the sale deed dated 12.03.2001 wherefrom it was disclosed that the pre-emptee Nos.3-17 transferred the case land to pre-emptee Nos.1-2 for consideration of taka one lac. 6. The prosecution case, in brief, is that, the Anti-Corruption Commission (shortly, the "Commission") received an information that the accused-appellant Mir Mohammad Nasir Uddin, former State Minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism himself and in the name of the members of his family was in possession of property disproportionate to his known source of income. Anti-Corruption Commission thus issued a notice dated 18-2-2007 under section 26(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 (briefly, the ACC Act, 2004) directing him to submit his statement of wealth along with the statement of wealth of his wife and other dependents within 72 hours from receipt of the said notice. At that time the appellant was in Bogra Jail under an order of detention. He, however, submitted the statement of wealth to the Commission through his representative Advocate Mohammad Mezbah Uddin (PW 4) wherein, on inquiry, ACC, found that he has concealed wealth of Taka 3,22,11,637 (three crore twenty two lacs eleven thousand six hundred thirty seven) only. 

 7. The Commission, on inquiry, has further found that as per Income-tax returns up to 2006, total income of Mir Mohammad Nasir Uddin along with his wife Dalia Naznin (now dead) and son Barrister Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin stand at Taka 1,60,60,000 (one crore sixty lac sixty thousand) only, their total expenditure stand at Taka 27,70,000 (twenty seven lac seventy thousand) only and their total savings stand at Taka 1,32,90,000 (one crore thirty two lac ninety thousand) only. Further prosecution case is that co-accused Mir Mohammad Nasir Uddin opened income-tax file in 1984 while his wife Dalia Naznin opened her Income Tax file in 1996 and his son Barrister Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin opened income tax file in 2006. In that way, their total savings, as shown in the income-tax returns, stand at Taka 1,32,90,000 (One crore thirty two lac ninety thousand) only but Mir Mohammad Nasir Uddin declared Taka 22,50,06,999 in their wealth statement submitted before the Commission. On inquiry it was further found of Taka 3,22,11,637 was concealed and thereby Mir Mohammad Nasir Uddin himself, in the names of his wife and son, had amassed wealth of Taka 22,50,06,499 + 3,22,11,637 = Taka 25,72,18,136 out of which Taka 1,32,90,000.00 was found legal. Thus rest Taka (25,72,18,136 — 1,32,90,000 = Taka 24,39,28,136 (twenty four crore thirty nine lac twenty eight thousand one hundred thirty six) only which is disproportionate to his legal and known source of income. From the aforesaid, it transpires that while he was holding the post of Mayor, (1991-94) Ambassador (1995-96) and State Minister (2001-05) he acquired wealth by abusing his official position and power by illegal means which is disproportionate to his legal and known source of income. Not only that during inquiry, she found that Dalia Naznin, by exercising husband's power and influence, acquired wealth through improper means and she is the beneficiary of said wealth. Barrister Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin is the beneficiary of his father's wealth acquired through improper means. The material particulars of the allegations against each of the accused were specifically described and annexed with the FIR. It was further found that immediately after arrest of Mir Mohammad Nasir Uddin, his son Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin transferred Taka 2,08,33,195 to unknown place which kept in different Banks in his name and in joint account to conceal the illegal income of his father.  "78. In respect of Criminal Appeal Nos. 16- 18 of 2013 we are required to examine whether for initiating a proceeding under section 27(1) of the ACC Act, 2004 a prior notice is necessary and whether a proceeding under section 27(1) of the ACC Act, 2004 is liable to be struck down for service of unlawful notice. To answer the aforesaid question we have to decide firstly, whether the notice dated 19-5-2007 or 3-7-2007 under section 26(1) of the ACC Act is lawful or not and Secondly, whether section 27 is independent of the notice served under section 26(1) of the ACC Act and whether the proceedings under section 27(1) have any nexus with the notices dated 3-7-2007 or 29-5-2007 issued by the Commission under section 26(1) of the Act demanding statement of assets and liabilities of the appellants in Criminal Appeal Nos. l6 and 18 of 2013 and the respondent No. 1 in Criminal Appeal No. 17 of 2013. As regards the 1st option in the foregoing discussions we have formed the opinion that order/notice under section 26(1) of the ACC Act is very much in accordance with the provisions of law. Regarding the 2nd option it is to be noted that section 26(1) of the ACC Act contemplates that if the Commission on the basis of any information and after holding necessary inquiry is satisfied that a person or any other persons on his behalf acquired or possessed property disproportionate to his known source of income, then the Commission may by an order in writing direct him to submit the statement of assets and liabilities and any other information as pointed out in the said order in the prescribed manner. Sub-section (2) of section 26 provides for imposition of sentence for a term not exceeding 3 years or with fine or with both on a person who fails to submit written statement or information in respect of assts and liabilities or supplies false or baseless information and documents in violation of the order pursuant to section 26(1) of the ACC Act. Whereas section 27 of the ACC Act provides for maximum Sentence of 10 years and minimum 3 years imprisonment for acquiring/amassing property beyond known source of income and the property in question be confiscated if he fails to explain satisfactorily to the court in the trial in respect of acquisition or amassing of the property. Generally, no notice is required to be served upon a person before instituting a criminal proceeding against him. Moreover, section 27 does not envisage any notice to be served upon the person before initiation of a criminal proceeding under the section. In other words, there is nothing in section 27 requiring service of any prior notice before initiation of a criminal proceeding. Therefore, section 27 is independent of the notice served under section 26(1) of the ACC Act and the proceedings under section 27(1) have no nexus with the notice served by the ACC under section 26(1) of the ACC Act demanding statement of assets and liabilities of the accused appellants in Criminal Appeal Nos. 16 and 18 of 2013 and the accused respondent No. 1 in Criminal Appeal No. 17 of 2013. The established principle of law is that if the law enforcing agency knows that a person has committed an offence or there are sufficient reasons to believe that the person has committed an office, then the law enforcing agency is empowered to institute a criminal proceeding against him and no notice is required to be served upon him before initiation of the same against him. This view has been aptly expressed in the decision of this Division in the case of ACC vs lqbal Hawn Mahmud, reported in 66 DLR (AD) 185 wherein we observed as under: 

 "Section 27 is an independent provision and for initiation of a proceeding against any person under the said provision no notice is required to be served. If the prosecution can establish that any person has acquired or amassed wealth which is beyond his known source of income, he may be prosecuted and convicted under section 27(1)." 

 79. We have already discussed the purpose, intendment and scheme of the ACC Act, 2004. From the scheme and contents of the Act it appears that section 26 and section 27 of the ACC Act are independent from each other and there is no nexus between these two sections. Section 27 being an independent section provides that if there are sufficient reasons to think that a person has acquired or amassed property illegally which is beyond his known source of income then he may be sentenced to suffer imprisonment for a term not more than 10 years and not less than 3 years and to pay fine and the property in question is liable to be confiscated. Therefore, there is no difficulty to say that before issuance of any notice under section 26 of the ACC Act upon a person the Commission must have knowledge that the said person has acquired property beyond known source of income. In other words, the fact of acquiring property beyond some one's known source of income was within the knowledge of the Commission long before the issuance of the order/notice under section 26 of the Act. Section 27 of the ACC Act is independent of the notice served under section 26(1) of the ACC Act. Therefore, in the instant cases the proceedings under section 27(1) have no nexus with the notices dated 3-7-2007 or 29-5-2007 issued under section 26(1) of the ACC Act."

Learned advocate for the appellant further submits that secretary of the commission issued notice under section 26 of the ACC Act which served upon Mir Mohammad Nasir on 20-2-2007 while he was in jail. It is on record that all the commissioners resigned from the commission on 7-2-2007 and commission was re-constituted on 24-2-2007. On the date of issuance of Notice commission was not properly constituted as per section 5 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act though the commission was in existence as an institution under the provisions of sections 3 and 4 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004. In order to issue notice under section 26(1) of the ACC Act, the commission is required to be satisfied that a person possesses or has acquired ownership of property disproportionate to his assets known source of income through illegal means then the commission may by an order in writing direct the said person to submit the statement of his assets and liabilities or any other information as directed by the said order. In the case of the appellant the order/notice was issued by the secretary of the commission without having obtained any satisfaction by or decision of the commission. In that view of the matter the notice dated 18-2-2007 was defective for not having obtained satisfaction decision from the commission. To fill up the lacuna section 18 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 was amended by inserting sub-section (2) in section 18 of the Act on 18-4-2007 by the amending ordinance No. VII of 2007 which provides for ex-post facto ratification of the acts done by the officers of the Commission during the period from 7-2-2007-24-2-2007 when the commission was not properly constituted as per provision of section 5 of the Act. In support of his submission learned Advocate relied on paragraphs 42 and 43 of the decision of 62 DLR (AD) 290. But on this issue their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the latest decision in the case of Moudud Ahmed vs State reported in 68 DLR (AD) 118; in unequivocal terms declared that the view expressed by this Division regarding effect of section 18(2) of the Act, granting ex-post facto approval of any act done or power exercised by an officer of the commission during the period when the commission was not properly constituted as per provisions of section 5 of the Act does not reflect the correct principle of law. Having regard to the aforesaid decision of 68 DLR (AD) 118 it cannot be said that the notice under section 26(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act was defective. Moreover, in this case no issue with regard to ex-post facto approval was framed, deliberated upon and decided in view of the provision of section 18(2) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act. So, ex-post facto approval to the issuance of notice dated 18-2-2007 (Exhibit-1) by the secretary of the commission is very much legal in pursuant to the provisions of section 18(2) of the Act. In view of the forgoing discussions and the principles enunciated in 68 DLR (AD) 118 we are of the view that the initiation and the conviction based on such notice is legal and inconformity with the purposes, objectives and functions of the commission.

Therefore, we can easily conclude that the aforesaid money Taka 2,90,49,265 was transferred by Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin with dishonest purpose to conceal their illegal money which is disproportionate to known source of income of his father Mir Nasir Uddin to the satisfaction of the court. So, we do not find any reason to disagree with the findings of the Special Judge in giving conviction and punishment of the appellant Mir Mohammad Helal Uddin for abetment under section 27(1) of Anti-Corruption Commission Act, read with section 109 of the Penal Code. 

 (e) if he or any of his dependents is in possession, for which the public servant cannot reasonably account, of pecuniary resources or of property disproportionate to his known sources of income. 

 (2) Any public servant who commits or attempts to commit criminal misconduct shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both and the pecuniary resources or property to which the criminal misconduct relates may also be confiscated to the state. 

 (3) In any trial of an offence punishable under sub-section (2) the fact that the accused person or any other person on his behalf is in possession, for which the accused person cannot satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income may be proved, and on such proof the Court shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, that the accused person is guilty of criminal misconduct and his conviction there for shall not be invalid by reason only that it is based solely on such presumption  

 172. Considering the evidence, the prosecution conclusively proved that the appellant Mir Mohammad Nasir Uddin by abusing his different positions as public servant obtained pecuniary advantage for himself and other dependents by concealing wealth and also of the property disproportionate to his known source of income thereby committed offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(1)(d)(e) punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.

3. In the writ petition, it was stated, inter-alia, that the property scheduled for auction in the auction sale notice published in the 'Daily Amardesh' dated 18.08.2006 and in schedule-`Kha' to the plaint of Artha Rin Suit No. 9 of 1991 of the Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Joypurhat (hereinafter referred to as the property in question) was leased out. by the then Dacca Improvement Trust (DIT) now Rajdhani Unnayan ' Kartipakkha (RAJUK) to one Qazi Mesbahuzzaman for 99 years by registered deed of lease being No. 10973 dated `1 30.07.1963. Qazi Mesbahuzzaman sold the property in question to one A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed by registered deed No. 7392 dated 24.09.1971 and his name was mutated with DIT as evidenced by Memo No. DIT/EO/1489 dated 26.11.1971. A.B. M. Shafiquddin Ahmed gifted the property in question to his wife, Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed orally and her name was duly mutated with Da vide Memo No. DIT/EO/729 dated 05.07.1972. Later on, Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed generally gifted the property in question to her two sons, Abrar Atric Ahmed and Esrar Abin Ahmed and their names were mutated with RAJUK vide Memo No.  RAJUK/ESTATE/141 dated 16.01.1992. Abrar Atric Ahmed and Esrar Abin Ahmed appointed their father, A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed as their duly constituted attorney by registered power of attorney being No. 22 dated 03.01.1994 giving him power to manage and transfer the property in question, which was duly  accepted/approved by RAJUK vide Memo No.  RAJUK/ESTATE/31781 dated 01.08.1994. Abrar Atric Ahmed and Esrar Abin Ahmed, through their attorney, A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed, sold the property in question to Green Garden Housing Limited (hereinafter referred to as Green Housing) by registered deed No. 2923 dated 28.02.1995 upon obtaining k RAJUK's permission by Memo No.  RAJUK/ESTATE/542 dated 16.02.1995. The property in question was mutated in the name of Green Housing vide Mutation Case No. 12952 of 1996. Green Housing constructed a 6-storied building on the property in question with 20 apartments as per the plan approved by RAJUK. Of the above 20 apartments,  Green Housing sold 12 apartments to the petitioners along with proportionate undivided and undemarcated shares in the I property by registered deed being Nos. 7207, 7208, 7204, 7210, 7209, 7206, 7205, 7202, 7201, 7212 and 7211 dated 05.06.2003 and 13041 dated 08.10.2004. The particulars of the flats purchased by each of the petitioners were shown in the cause title of the writ petition against their names. The said transfers took place upon payment of transfer fee to RAJUK and upon obtaining permission from it by Memos dated 05.05.2003 and 01.01.2003. The names of the petitioners have been duly mutated as owners of the flats and co-owners of the property in question by separate Memos dated 28.09.2003, 29.09.2003 and 15.06.2004 issued by RAJUK. Since purchase of the said flats along with proportionate undivided and undemarcated share in the property in question as bonafide purchasers for value without notice of any adverse inters of encumbrance, the petitioners have been peacefully occupying their respective flats populating their names as owners with the revenue authorities and on payment of all applicable rents and levies. The petitioners were shocked to come across the impugned auction sale notice dated 

 4. Thereafter, the petitioners on inquiry/inquires learnt that respondent No. 3, Agrani Bank (the bank) instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 9 of 1991 on 16.03.1991 in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) and Artha Rin Adalat Joypurhat (respondent No. 2) impleading Northern Distilleries Limited and 13 others as defendants for recovery of TK. 9,94,76,565.15. The petitioners were not parties to the suit, so they had no knowledge about the suit. A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed was impleaded as defendant No. 9 in the suit. From the plaint of the said suit, it is apparent that it was filed for recovery of loans outstanding against certain credit facilities extended to Northern Distilleries Limited since 1985. In paragraph 5 of the plaint, it was averred that defendant No. 9 mortgaged the property in question in favour of the bank to secure the said credit facilities. No particulars of such mortgage were averred in the plaint However, it was stated that defendant No. 9 had deposited a certified copy of the title deed of the property in question with the Bank but despite several requests, never submitted the original of the title deed. 

 6. The suit was decreed by the Artha Rin Adalat by judgment and decree dated 24.11.1998 against the defendants except defendant Nos. 4, 5 and 10. The defendants were directed to pay the decretal amount within 60 days of the decree, failing which the bank could realise the amount by sale of the mortgaged properties which purported to include the property in question co-owned by the writ petitioners. In the judgment and decree, the Artha Rin Adalat did not give any finding whether defendant No. 9 i.e. A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed in fact mortgaged the property in question in favour of the bank as alleged. Decree was passed to realize the decretal amount by sale of, inter-alia, the property in question  as described in schedule-Kha: In execution of the judgment and decree dated 24.11.1998, the bank as decree holder, levied Money Execution Case No. 01 of 1999 on 05.02.1999 before the: Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Joypurhat. The said case was subsequently renumbered as Artha Jari Case No. 223 of 2005. The Artha Jari case was then transferred to Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka where it was registered on 12.09.2005 as Artha Jari Case No. 603 of 2005. The bank on 16.07.2006 filed an application under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 in the said jari case to amend the schedule of the property of the execution case to include the description of the property in question as given in the auction sale notice subsequently This application was allowed by the Adalat vide impugned order No. 8 dated 16.07.2006. Artha Jari Case No. 603 of 2005 was originally filed on 05.02.1999 as Money Execution Case No. 01 of 1999 in the Artha Rin Adalat, Joypurhat which was constituted under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990(the Ain, 1990). Section 60(1) of the Ain, 2003 repealed the Ain, 1990. Section 60(3) of the Ain, 2003 provides that notwithstanding the repeal of the AM, 1990 all the suits which were under adjudication (Bicharadhin shokol mamla) in Courts constituted under the Ain, 1990 shall be transferred for further proceedings to Courts constituted under the Ain, 2003. An execution case is not a suit under adjudication, i.e. it is not a "bicharadhin mamla". Section 60(3) of the Ain, 2003 does not operate to transfer execution cases filed in Courts constituted under the Ain, 1990, to Courts constituted under the Ain, 2003. As such, the transfer, A registration and proceedings of Artha Jari Case No. 603 of 2005 were without lawful authority and were of no legal effect. 

 10. The Rule was opposed by the bank by filing an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter-alia, that it as mortgagee of the property in question was entitled to satisfy its decree by sale of the mortgaged property and as such, there was no illegality in publishing the notice for auction sale of the mortgaged property. The petitioners' claim over the property in question is subject to the mortgage in favour of the Bank. In the writ petition it was stated that the property in question was sold to the Green Housing on 28.02.1995 by registered deed No. 2933, whereas the same was mortgaged to the Bank in 1986 i.e. long before the alleged transfer to the Green Housing. So, the purchase was subject to the mortgage in favour of the Bank. Once the property was mortgaged then who ever purchases the same the right of the mortgagee shall remain attached to the property. The copies of the deed of equitable mortgage, power of attorney executed by Mahbub Husain Khan to the Bank, Foreign Exchange Branch and a forwarding letter sent by Mahbub Hussain Khan (executive Director of Northern Distilleries Limited) have already been annexed to the application for vacating the order of stay. The petitioners neither being judgment debtors in the decree passed in the suit nor parties to the execution case had any locus standi to challenge various orders passed in Artha Jari Case No. 603 of 2005 and their only remedy to claim the property as third party claimant was by filing an application under section 32 of the Ain 2003 and in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure before the executing Adalat. The petitioners without availing the said remedies filed the writ petition. The alleged right, title to and interest of the petitioners in the property in question cannot he adjudicated in writ jurisdiction. It has already been decided in Writ Petition No. 4716 of 2004 that the provision of section 37 of the Ain, 2003 is not mandatory but directory. The petitioners filed the writ petition only to delay the recovery of outstanding dues of the Bank. The writ petition being not maintainable the Rule was liable to be discharged. 

 11. The Bank filed a supplementary affidavit dated 10.02.2009 stating that earlier it had filed an application for vacating the order of stay on 06.05.2007 which was duly recorded in the order book on 06.05.2007, but at the time of hearing on 04.02.2008 the same was not found with original record of the case and therefore, it filed a copy of the said application for vacating the order of stay annexing the documents contained in that application. The Bank also filed another supplementary affidavit dated 13.02.2008 stating that the facts and circumstances of the instant case was covered by the judgment and order passed in the case of Aroj Ali Khan-vs-Agrani Bank and others vide Writ Petition No. 4190 of 2004 on 05.02.2007. 

 14. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order of by the High Court Division, the writ petitioner-appellants filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 949 of 2008 before this Division and leave was granted on 15.10.2009 to consider the submissions made on behalf of the petitioners, (1) the petitioners, who are the bonafide purchasers for value without notice, had come forward for enforcement of fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 31 and 42 of the Constitution and in that view of the matter the High Court Division ought to have suspended the hearing of the writ petition till the withdrawal of the Emergency, (ii) the High Court Division wrongly discharged the Rule as not being maintainable for non-exhaustion of efficacious remedy inasmuch as the petitioners having sought to enforce fundamental rights involved in the case under article 102(1) of the Constitution, exhaustion of efficacious remedy was not necessary, (iii) the writ petition having been involved pure question of law and demonstrating patent error of law, could not he dismissed on the ground of non-maintainability, (iv) the property in question could not be auction sold as it was not mortgaged by production of original title deed and furthermore it could not be mortgaged by the borrower as neither the borrower nor his principal was the owner of the same and this fact could not be properly appreciated by the High Court Division, (v) the High Court Division failed to notice that it would have disastrous consequences if equitable mortgage can he created by deposit of certified copy of the title document, (vi) admittedly the property described in `Kha' schedule to the plaint was mortgaged to the respondent No. 3 Bank by submitting certified copy of the deed of the said property without the original deed and as per Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act the said property was not at all mortgaged property and the same being free from any sorts of encumbrances the respondent No. 3 had no right to claim the said property as mortgaged property but the High Court Division; without considering those aspect of dial case committed error of law in holding that the petitioners have enough scope to file an application under section 32 of the Ain, 2003 and without considering that alternative remedy always does not bar to file writ petition under article 102 of the Constitution, (vii) `Kha.' scheduled property to the plaint of Artha Rin Suit having not been included in the power of attorney, the attorney had no authority to mortgage the same to the respondent No. 3 and in the facts and circumstances of the case of the petitioner the High Court Division ought to have declared that inclusion of the said property in the plaint was without law fid authority in spite of having alternative remedy under Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, but the High Court Division without considering so fell into an error in discharging the Rule and (viii) the High Court Division was wrong in discharging the Rule when there was no mortgage to be enforced as could be seen from paragraph 5 of the plaint which showed that the borrowers provided alternative property when they could not produce original deed of the Gulshan property. 

 21. In spite of coming to the above findings, the High Court Division considered the claim of the writ-petitioners to the property in question on merit and held that whether A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed who became the owner of the property in question by purchase from the original allottee transferred the same by way of oral gift to his wife Hosne Maksuda Hena Ahmed in 1972 and whether in 1986 A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed had any interest therein are complicated questions and to decide those, the question of title to the properly has to be determined and that would require evidence, both oral and documentary. The High Court Division further observed that oral and documentary evidence will also be necessary Co-determine whether there was any valid gift in favour of the wife under the Mohamedan law; oral gift is valid provided offer, acceptance and delivery of possession in favour of the done by the donor is proved; here, the donor and the done being husband and wife, physical delivery of possession may not be necessity), and the alleged oral gift having been made in London physical possession of the property situated in Dhaka was not possible at time of making the oral gift. However, there must be some other acts to show that the gift was acted upon but there is nothing to show that the house was mutated in the name of the wife in the Government records (revenue authority) for the purpose of paying Municipal Taxes; unless there is such evidence, it cannot be said that the gift in favor of the wife by A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed was acted upon and if it was not acted upon, the gift will not be valid and all subsequent gift or transfers will become questionable. The learned Judges further observed that though mutation was done in the records of RAJUK, but there was nothing to show that the 'house' was mutated in the name of the wife in the records of the revenue authority or in the Municipal records. The learned Judges went on to observe 

 22. The High Court Division further found that according to the plaint, the original title deed of the mortgaged property was not deposited with the Bank as required in case of equitable mortgage and the Bank should have taken in its custody the original title deed before granting any loan to the defendants to the suit. The High Court Division noticed that the irrevocable power of attorney executed by A.B. Shafiquddin Ahmed appointing Mahbub Husain Khan as his constituted attorney to sell, mortgage etc do not contain "any schedule of properties". The properties owned by A.B. Shafiquddin Ahmed have not at all been described in the document. The High Court Division observed "We fail to understand why the Bank accepted the mortgage of the property from Mahbub Hussain Khan without bothering to verify this power of attorney executed by A.B. Shafiquddin Ahmed which is not also a registered one." Finally, the High Court Division opined that "even if the petitioners may have a good arguable case" but the same must be decided on merits by the executing Adalat or by a civil Court in accordance with law by taking proper evidence and if so advised, the petitioners may ventilate their grievance in the appropriate forum. 

 28. From the admitted facts as stated in paragraph 5 of the plaint of the Artha Rin ,suit, it appears that the property in question was mortgaged with the respondent-basic by one Mahbub Husain Khan as the Managing Director (Executive Director) of the loance company Northern Distilleries Limited on the basis of power of attorney given by A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed by depositing the certified copy of the title deed. And when the Bank gave repeated tagid to said Mahbub Husain Khan to deposit the original title deed, he deposited the original title deeds of two other properties of the two Directors of the -company. We consider it beneficial to quote the relevant portion of the said paragraph of the plaint: 

 "Mortgage by deposit of title-deeds—(f) Where a person in the town of Dacca, Narayangonj and Chittagong and in any other town which the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, specify in this behalf, delivers to a creditor or his agent documents of title to immovable property, with intent to create a security thereon, the transaction is called a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds." 

 30. A reading of section 58(f) of the Act shows that in order to create mortgage in respect of a property delivery of the documents of title of such property to the creditor, here the Bank is a must. And the documents of title definitely mean the original one and not the certified copy. The Bank knew much about the said requirement of delivery of original title document when in the plaint it said that it gave repeated tagid to Mahbub Husain Khan to file the original title document of the property in question but he did not, even then it created the mortgage accepting the certified copy of the title deed of the property in question. And yet another shocking aspect of the case is that the power of attorney allegedly given by A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed to Mr. Mahabub Husain Khan to mortgage the property in question did not contain any schedule of property. There was also no mention of any property whatsoever   in the body of the power of attorney. We fail to understand in the absence of original documents of title of the property   in question and non-mentioning of any property of A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed in the power of attorney how the Bank could accept the mortgage and gave loan to the defendant company. Thus, we find substance in the submission of Mr. Mahmudul Islam that there was no mortgage at all of the property in question in the eye of law. The High Court Division after considering paragraph 5 of the plaint rightly observed that "Therefore, it appears that according to the plaint the original title deed of the mortgaged property was not deposited with the Bank as required in case of equitable mortgage which is also supported by the decision reported in AIR 1935 Lahore 721". So, the so-called mortgage created by Mahbub Husain Khan, in 1986 on the basis of power of attorney given by A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed did not encumber the property in question in any way. We have gone through the judgment and decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. The Artha Rin Adalat neither framed any issue as to whether the mortgage created by Mahbub Husain Khan without depositing the document of title was a valid mortgage of the property in question or gave any finding in that respect. The judgment further shows that the Artha Rin Adalat did not consider the admitted broad fact that the power of attorney given by A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed in favour of Mahbub Husain Khan did not contain any schedule of the property in question in respect of which he was appointed the attorney. The Artha Rin Adalat also failed to consider that the power of attorney was not even registered and it passed the decree in a very casual manner. Therefore, the case of the Bank that since the property in question was mortgaged with it, in 1986, the purchase of Green Housing from Abrar Atric Ahmed and Esrar Abin Ahmed through their attorney was subject to mortgage is not factually and legally acceptable and consequently the same cannot be the subject of sale in execution of the decree passed in the Money Suit No. 9 of 1991. 

 31. Admittedly A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed became the owner of the property in question by way of purchase from the original lessee Qazi Mesbahuzzman by registered deed being No. 7392 dated 24.09.1971. His name was mutated by DIT by Memo No. DIT/EO/1489 dated 26.11.1971. Appellants' case is that A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed orally gifted the property in question to his wife, Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed on 01.01.1972. The name of Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed was mutated by DIT which fact was intimated to her by Memo No. DIT/EO/729 dated 08.07.1972. Subsequently, Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed orally gifted the property to her two sons namely, Abrar Atric Ahmed and Esrar Abin Ahmed and the property was also mutated in the names of the latter by Rajuk vide Memo No.  RAJUK/ ESTATE/141 dated 16.01.1992. Abrar Atric Ahmed and Esrar Abin Ahmed appointed their father, A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed as their duly constituted attorney by a registered power of attorney being No. 22 dated 03.01.1994 giving him authority to manage and transfer the property in question; the power of attorney was accepted/approved by RAJUK by its Memo No.  RAJUK/ ESTATE /31781 dated 01.08.1994. Abrar Atric Ahmed and Esrar Abin Ahmed, through their attorney, A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed sold the property to Green Housing by registered deed No. 2923 dated 28.02.1995 upon obtaining permission from RAJUK by Memo No.  RAJUK/ ESTATE/542 dated; 16.02.1995. The property was then mutated in the name of the Green Housing in Mutation Case No. 12952 of 1996. Thereupon, the Green Housing constructed a 6 storied building on the property in question with 20 apartments as per approved plan of RAJUK. Out of the said 20 apartments, the Green Housing sold 12 apartments to the appellants along with proportionate undivided and undemarcated shares in the property by various deeds dated 05.06.2003 and 08.10.2004. The transfers took place upon payment of transfer fees to RAJUK and upon obtaining permission from it vide Memos dated 05.05.2003 and 01.01.2003. The names of the appellants have been mutated as owners of the apartments and co-owners of the property in question by separate Memos dated 28.09.2003, 29.09.2003 and 15.06.2004. The true copies of the appellants' deeds of purchase of the apartments from Green Housing and the Memos issued by RAJUK, mutating their names, were annexed to the writ petition as annexure -'C' C-11' and C-12' to C-22' respectively. Thus, the claim of title of the appellants to the property in question proportionate to their undivided and under interacted share starts from the oral gift made by A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed to his wife Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed on 01.01.1972. And if it is found that A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed gifted the property in question to his wife Hosna Maksoda Hena Ahmed on 01.01.1972 and if the same was acted upon then on and from 01.01.1972 the right, title and interest therein absolutely vested upon her and conversely on and from the said date A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed ceased to have any right, title and interest whatsoever therein. In this regard, it may be stated that on or before is July 2005, there was no necessity of registration of declaration of heba by a Mohamedan under the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat). Amendment to the above effect was brought in section 17 of the Registration Act by inserting clause (aa) therein making registration of such declaration compulsory by Act No. XXV of 2004 giving effect from 1st July 2005. 

 32. The ingredients of a valid oral gill as per Mohamedan Law is proposal by the donor to the done, acceptance of the proposal by the done followed by delivery of possession of the gifted property. In the case in hand the donor ABM Shafiquddin Ahmed is the husband of the donee Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed. The specific case of the appellants is that the donee accepted the gift and the donor also delivered the possession of the properly in question to the donee and thus the gift was complete. In the writ petition, it was specifically stated that after the gift, the name of Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed was mutated by DIT as lessee in place of ABM Shafiquddin Ahmed which fact was communicated to her vide Memo. DIT/EO/729 dated 05.07.1972. Although with the writ petition the Memo of DIT showing mutation of the name of Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed was not annexed, by filing a supplementary affidavit, the writ-petitioner-appellants annexed the said letter issued by DIT as annexure-'H1'. The said letter issued by DIT clearly shows that the oral gift was accepted by it and accordingly, mutated the name of Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed as lessee in place of A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed. In annexure-'XI' it has been clearly stated that "and henceforth you would be recognized lessee of the same". The respondent bank did not dispute this document. The very mutation of the name of Hosna 'Maksuda Hena Ahmed by the DIT, lessor, as lessee of the property in question, Prima-facie, shows that she accepted the gift made by her husband, A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed and the same was acted upon. It is true that at the time of making the gift, both the donor and donee were in London and therefore, it was not possible to take physical delivery of possession   of the property in question. The donor and the donee being husband and wife, it was sufficient to show some overt-act on the part of the donor to indicate the delivery of possession to the donee and when the name of the donee was mutated with DIT as a lessee in place of the donor, A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed it constituted sufficient indication of the overt-act of the donor. In this regard, it may further be stated that the respondent has failed to show any subsequent conduct by the donor to disown the oral gift made by him on 01.01.1972 in favour of his wife, the donee. And with the acting upon of the gift made by ABM Shafiquddin Ahmed, be divested himself of all his right, title and interest in the property in question, so he could not have any right to give power of attorney to Mahbub Husain Khan to mortgage the same in 1986. The learned Judges of the high Court Division were absolutely in error in terming the gift made by ABM Shafiquddin Ahmed as "alleged" and also in observing that "So, the pertinent question is whether A.B.M. Shafiquddin had any interest in the property in the year, 1986 when he appointed Mr. Mahbub Husain Khan as attorney. To decide this question, the question of title to the property is to be determined which is a very complicated question and requires evidence, both oral and documentary. Oral and documentary evidence will be necessary to determine whether there was any valid gift in favour of the wife". The learned judges also failed to consider that after the property in question was transferred by A.B.M. Shafiquddin to his wife Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed by way of oral gift which was already acted upon, she became the absolute owner thereof and had every right to deal with it in any lawful manner she liked and thus there was nothing wrong to transfer the same by way of oral gift to her two sons and when the sons became the owners of the property there was nothing wrong in appointing their father as their attorney to manage and transfer the same and the Green Housing rightly purchased the same with prior permission of RAJUK. It is also noteworthy that after purchasing the property in question Green Housing mutated its name with RAJUK and constructed at storied building with 20 flats/apartments therein after obtaining plan from RAJUK and the appellants purchased the 12 flats/apartments with proportionate undivided and undemarcated shares in the property in question by various deeds with permission from RAJUK on payment of transfer fees to it and their names were also mutated as owners of the respective apartments and co-owners of the property in question. What more is necessary to show that there had been subsequent devolution of interest in the property in question upto the appellants since Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed became its owner through the oral gift made by her husband A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed? 

 33. The High Court Division found fault with the title of Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed in the property in question on the basis of the oral gift made by A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed on the ground that her name was mutated only with RAJUK and not "in the Government records (revenue authority) for the purpose of paying rents and in the Municipal records for the purpose   of paying municipal taxes" totally forgetting that it is the RAJUK which is the lessor of the same. And non recording, of her name with the two other authorities in no way would disprove her title which she had already acquired from her husband through the gift made in her favour as back as on 01.01.1972, whereas the alleged mortgage was created only in 1986 on the basis of an alleged unregistered power of attorney and that too without mentioning of any property whatsoever of the principal. 

 35. This Division refused to accept the case of the respondent of becoming the owner of the property on the basis of the deed of gift dated 26.02.1965 on the ground that she failed to produce the original deed of gift and no paper was filed showing mutation of her name with DIT and any authority including the municipality or any document from which it could be found that she got implied possession of the property or that there was acceptance of the gift. The facts of the instant case are quite differentiable from the said reported case. In the instant case as already discussed hereinbefore after the gift, the name of Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed was mutated with the lessor, namely, DIT now RAJUK and then the name of the successive transferees who stepped into her shoes were mutated with RAJUK which facts, prima-facie, suggest that the gift made by A.B.M. Shafiquddin Ahmed in favour of Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed was acted upon. 

 (a) The oral gift of the property in question made by ABM Shafiquddin Ahmed on 01.01.1972 in favour of his wife Hosna Maksuda Hena Ahmed was acted upon and since that date, she became its absolute owner. A.B.M. Siddique had  no title in the; property in question in 1986 to execute any power of attorney in favour of Mahbub Husain Khan to mortgage the same with the defendant-bank. 

 (b) The property in question was not legally mortgaged in favour of the respondent-bank since the original title deed of the same was not admittedly deposited with it as required to create an equitable mortgage under section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act. 

 36. Taking into account the admitted factual and legal aspect of the case as noted down hereinbefore, we are of the view that the, appellants have got prima-facie, valid right, title and interest in the properly in question proportionate to their undivided and under marketed share therein and their rights need be protected; it shall cause more miseries and harassment if they are pushed back to the executing Court to avail of the forum provided in section 32 of the Ain, 2003. And in the context; we consider it a fit case where the power of doing complete justice as given to this Division under article 104 of the Constitution should be exercised. And in exercise of such power, we are inclined to interfere with the judgment and decree UP passed by the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Joypurhat in Money, Suit No. 9 of 1991 and the auction sale notice as published in the 'Daily Amar Desh' dated 18.08.2006 pursuant to the order passed by Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Dhaka in Artha Jari Case No. 603 of 2005 for selling the properties as mentioned? Therein co-owned by the appellants. However, we approve the observations made by the High Court Division that "the Bank must take appropriate action against those officials and others involved in the loan granting process in accordance with law."

parties:
Ganesh Mohanto & ors ------ Petitioners 
vs
Md Abdul Hakim and ors ------ Opposite Parities
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiffs-respondents-petitioners instituted a suit for permanent injunction and the short fact of the case is that the suit land has originally belonged to Aminuddin Pramanik and Shaharon Mai Bibi and the CS Khatian was duly recorded in their name. While Amiruddin and Shaharon Mia were in peaceful possession of the suit land by purchase they wanted to sell the land for necessity of money, then Shibran Mohanto, the predecessor of the plaintiff purchased the suit land on 14-11-1942 by a registered deed and became the owner and possessor of the suit land. Subsequently SA Khatian was duly prepared in the name of Shibran Mohanto who died leaving behind his two sons namely, Mohabir and Shukdeb. Thereafter on the death of Shukdeb the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 became his heirs and after the death of Mohabir the plaintiff No. 3 became his heir. They have been possessing the suit land on payment of rent and in some portion of Plot No. 613/1080 they constructed homestead and in Plot No. 614 they planted fruit trees such as mango, jack-fruit, lichi trees, etc. They have been enjoying the property for 55/56 years. On the other hand, the defendants have got no right, title and possession in the suit land. On 12-7-1997 AD the defendants threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs forcibly from the suit land and thereafter on 25-7-1997 they tried to erect some huts in some portion of the suit land but due to strong resistance of the plaintiff they could not erect any hut. The defendant is threatening the plaintiff continuously to dispossess him from the suit land hence the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit. 

 3. On the other hand, the defendants-opposite parties contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that Shahar Mai Bibi was the tenant under the original landlord Najargpat Singh and others. Subsequently, Shahar Mai Bibi sold the suit land to Amiruddin Paramanik, the predecessor of the defendants in CS record. That out of 3.28 decimals of land 2.02 decimal was in khas possession of Amiruddin and he made pattani settlement of the remaining land and it was recorded in CS Khatian Nos. 87, 88, 91, 92 and 93 respectively. That Shibran Mohanto, predecessor of the plaintiff, was a borgadar under Amiruddin Paramanik and thereafter SA khatian was wrongly prepared in the name of Amiruddin Paramanik and Shibran Mohanto which Amiruddin did not know in his life time. Since Shibran Mohanto did not give the borga crops regularly, so Amiruddin Paramanik returned back the land in his own possession. Thereafter, when settlement operation for preparing SA record was started the fake right of Shibran Mohanto was cancelled. 

 4. Thereafter, Amiruddin died leaving behind his widow Shaharon alias Shahar Mai and three daughters namely, Asia Mai, Asron Mai and Nais Mai and one son Sarafuddin. Then Sarafuddin died leaving behind two sons, namely, Aftabuddin and Abu Taleh. Then Asaron Mai died leaving behind two sons Afsar Ali Mondal and Asgar Ali Mondal and a daughter Kandiri Mai. Then Afsar Ali Mondal died leaving behind five sons namely, Mosharraf Hossain, Ashraf, Wares, Golam Moula and Ziauddin and six daughters namely, Amena Khatun, Asma Khatun, Jahanara, Sufia, Shefali and Ayesha Khatun. Thus they remained in ejmali possession of the suit land. Thereafter Alauddin, Abdul Hakim and Halima Khatun sold 80 decimal of land on 7-7-1997 and Wares All sold 10 decimal of land And Azahar Ali sold 5 decimal of land on 17-7-1997 to Alikur Rahman, the defendant No. 3. That the defendant No. 3 got the property by purchase and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 got the property by way of inheritance and they have erected tin shed and have been living in the suit land and the remaining portion they are possessing by cultivation. The predecessors of the plaintiff have got no title and possession in the suit land and that deed dated 24-11-1942 in favour of the plaintiffs are forged, false and collusive. The plaintiffs have got no possession in the suit land and the suit brought for permanent injunction is liable to be dismissed. 

 8. Mr Alauddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondents-petitioners, submits that the plaintiff has been able to prove the case successfully by producing the original title deed dated 24-11-1942 and the certified copy of the CS Khatian, SA Khatian, rent receipts and other connected papers which were proved and exhibited as Exhibit-1, 2, 3, 4 and rent receipts as Exhibits series 5. 

 9. The plaintiff examined as many as 4 witnesses to prove the possession of the suit land. The plaintiff Ganesh Mohanto was examined as PW 1 who categorically stated in his evidence that the entire case of the plaint was proved and exhibited the original registered deed of the year 1942 as Exhibit 1 and CS Khatian Exhibit 2, SA Khatian Exhibit 3, BCR Exhibit 4 and rent receipts Exhibits 5 series. The PW 2 Abdus Sobhan, PW 3 Sharifuddin and PW 4 Mominuddin were examined to prove and corroborate the PW 1 with regard to the possession of the plaintiff in the suit property. Next, he submits that the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur did not at all apply his judicial mind in assessment of the evidence of the PWs, particularly the evidence of PW 1 plaintiff and also did not consider the original registered title deed over 55 years old, CS Khatian, SA Khatian, DS Khatian and rent receipts. The observation made by the lower appellate Court that in the CS Khatian the name of Shahar Mai Bibi should not be published along with the name of Amiruddin, because she transferred her share to her husband Amiruddin before publication of CS Khatian. The learned Counsel further submits that this finding of the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur is manifestly perverse, because it is neither the case of the plaintiff nor the case of the defendant and he has made out a third case of transfer without any basis and no such transferred deed or document was produced before the Court by any parties. Finally, the learned Counsel submits that the cardinal principle of law followed in reversing the finding of the trial Court, the lower appellate Court should reverse the finding with reference to the evidence on record assigning the cogent ground. But the lower appellate Court without applying his judicial mind and without considering the evidence on record and Exhibits i.e. 55 years old original registered title deed, original CS, DS, RS Khatian and series of rent receipts, disbelieved the case of the plaintiff without assigning any cogent reason occasioning failure of justice which is liable to be interfered by this Court. In support of his contention the learned Counsel referred the decision in the case of Shishir Kanti Pal and others vs Noor Muhammad and others reported in 55 DLR (AD) 39 wherein it is stated: 

 10. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr KZ Alam with Mr Md Firoz Shah, appearing on behalf of the defendants-appellants-opposite parties, submits that the finding of the lower appellate Court is final unless and until it appears to be manifestly perverse. The learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur is absolutely correct and justified in reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court because the plaintiff miserably failed to prove his possession in the suit land. The defendant examined as many as 5 witnesses to prove his possession and as well as produced and exhibited 3 registered title deeds executed by Azizur Rahman, Asgar Ali and Wares Ali, the grandson of Amiruddin Promanik in the name of Atiqur Rahman, the defendant No. 3 who was examined as DW 3. The learned Counsel next submits that the defendants purchased the suit land measuring 95 decimals of land from the heirs of Amiruddin Promanik by 3 registered deeds dated 3-7-1997, 7-7-1997 and 17-7-1997. The DW 2 proved and exhibited the registered deeds and stated in his evidence that since the purchase i.e. from 1997 the defendants have been in possession of the suit land. The learned Counsel further submits that there was no misreading, non-reading and non-consideration of any material evidence by the learned Additional District Judge, Rangpur and he did not commit any error of law in allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The learned Counsel next submits that in a suit for permanent injunction the factum of possession is a main consideration of the Court and the question of title is a secondary matter. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel referred the decision in the case of Md Kamal and others vs AKM Mohsin and others reported in 10 MLR (AD) 100 wherein it has been held that: 

 "In a suit for permanent injunction plaintiff must prove his exclusive possession. Court can incidentally, look into the prima facie title. 

 It is well-settled that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is required to prove his exclusive possession of the suit land and prima facie title thereto. Court cannot decide title in a simple suit for injunction." 

 12. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, documents, khatian, rent receipts and judgment of both the Courts below and other connected paper, it transpires that the trial Court discussed the evidence and also perused the documents, exhibits and also considered the material evidence on record and made his clear observation in decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff. The lower appellate Court without applying his judicial mind gave much importance in determining the title of the suit land without considering the prime factor of possession. In the instant case, the plaintiff examined 4 witnesses to prove his title in the suit land and also to prove his possession and all the 4 witnesses categorically stated in their evidence that the plaintiff has been living in the suit land since the purchase of the suit land in the year 1942 i.e. about 55 years. On the other hand, the defendant claimed that they purchased the same suit land in the year 1997 and since then they have been in possession of the suit land but the defendant could not prove any act of possession by adducing cogent evidence. Moreover, it appears from the title deed of the plaintiff that Amiruddin Promanik and his wife Shahar Mai Bibi purchased the suit land by a registered deed on 24-11-1942 and the original document was produced and exhibited by the plaintiff and three other PWs stated in their evidence that the plaintiff has been living in the suit land since long, as such, the plaintiff is in consistent possession of the suit land since purchase. Therefore, the plaintiff has been able to prove his title and possession over the suit land by producing original title deed and by adducing oral evidence proved his possession in the suit land. In this connection, I like to refer the decision in the case of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) vs Md Reazuddin PK and others reported in 5 BLC (AD) 76 section 90 Evidence Act wherein it has been held: 

 "Once such a document more than 30 years old is produced from proper custody section 30 of the Evidence Act entitles the Court to presume that it is a genuine document." 

 14. From impugned judgment of the trial Court it transpires that in arriving at its finding the said Court carefully considered the material facts and circumstances of the case and also the material evidence on record, the documents, exhibits, the legal position, and also the act of possession in the suit land. The learned trial Court did not commit any error of law and illegality in arriving at its finding because the plaintiff could be able to prove his title as well as the possession in the suit land by adducing oral and documentary evidence. The lower appellate Court, on the other hand, committed an error of law and came to a wrong and erroneous finding occasioning failure of justice in not believing the 55 years original title deed and the possession of the plaintiff over the suit land which was a prime factor of the suit for a permanent injunction and, as such, committed an error of the law which is liable to be interfered by this Court. In this connection, I like to rely on the case of Hussain Ahmed Chowhdhury alias Ahmed Hussain Chowdhury vs Nurul Amin reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 wherein it has been held:
