So it cannot be believed that Mainuddin, who was 45 in 1987, was the only son and heir of Zainul Abedin. The suit property was initially listed as an abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972. As the defendant number 1 had a greedy eye on the property, he had influenced over the matter and managed to misplace all the relevant documents. As a result the suit property could not be subsequently enlisted and published in the official gazette as an abandoned property. As a part of his plan, defendant number 1 set the fictitious Mainuddin and did all the mischiefs to get the property registered in his name. It is a settled principle of law that fraud vitiates everything. So, whatever decree defendant number 1 got in his favour, it would not help him when the fraud has been proved subsequently. 

 22. Mr Munsur Habib further submits that the plaintiffs stated that the summons in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 were suppressed and not served upon the defendants, but it appears from the ex-parte judgment passed in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 that the present plaintiffs as defendants appeared in the previous suit and prayed for time repeatedly, but ultimately did not contest the suit. There is no scope to say that the summons were not served upon the defendants in the previous suit. After rejection of the Miscellaneous Case and failure of the Government/Police. to set-aside the decree up to the Appellate Division, when defendant number 1 filed the execution case and a writ of possession was issued, the plaintiffs instituted the present suit which is hopelessly barred by limitation as well as by the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. Despite service of summons upon the defendants and making their appearance in the previous suit, they did not contest the suit by raising any claim over the suit property. The instant suit is, therefore, barred by res-judicata. 

 23. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocates and carefully gone through the evidence and other materials on record. The plaintiff-appellants filed the application for additional evidence annexing the photocopies of some documents starting from serial number 9! Of them the first one (Annexure-9!) is a letter dated 27-6-1972 issued by the Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development informing the Inspector General of Police that the attached list of houses (it includes the suit property) would be allotted for accommodation of Police Units, Police Out-Posts, Police Officers and Staff in the Dacca City provided the houses were abandoned houses within the meaning of PO 16 of 1972. It is thus clear from the language of this letter that the suit property was yet to allot and the Government was not very sure whether it was an abandoned house. In the said letter, it was also mentioned that the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca was requested to take possession of the houses. It does mean that the Police had no independent possession over the suit property at the time of issuance of the said letter. It helps the defendant number l's case that the Police was a tenant under the original lessee since before 1972. 

 24. Annexure-10 to the application is a notice dated 7-8-1969, by which the Government asked the original allotee Zainul Abedin to pay the arrear installments with an intimation that in case of his failure to pay the arrear, it would be recovered under the Public Demand Recovery Act. When the suit property was leased out by a registered instrument on receipt of salami and possession was handed over to the allotee, who already paid two installments out of four, and constructed a building thereon taking permission from the Government, the registered deed of conveyance would not be invalidated for non-payment of two installments. The Government would be entitled only to realize the arrear. As a consequence of such non-payment, the lease would not be cancelled, nor would the property be treated abandoned. So, this piece of document would not develop the plaintiffs' case. 

 27. All the annexed documents are photo-copies, but there is no explanation wherefrom the plaintiffs collected these photocopies when they specifically pleaded that the office record in respect of the suit property was lost. No statement regarding payment of land development tax (vide Annexure 11 series) and the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit Number 260 of 2003 (vide Anexure-14/B) have been made in the plaint. These documents being out of pleadings are not admissible in evidence. Similarly, the plaint in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 (Annexure-13) has been annexed to be adduced as an additional evidence, but has not been explained why it was relevant to prove what contention of the plaintiffs. In this regard, it is pointed out that the factum of institution of the said suit has not been disputed by the adversary. 

 28. Moreover, Annexures: 13-15 are photo-copies of certified copies of plaint, decree, judgment, judicial order etcetera. When a certified copy itself is the secondary evidence as defined in section 63 of the Evidence Act, photocopy of certified copy of any judicial record is not ac:missible as secondary evidence where the originals are lying with judicial record and certified copy thereof can easily be obtained by any person. It is not explained in the application, why the plaintiff-appellants failed to obtain the certified copies of these documents. There was no scope to adduce any of these documents in evidence during trial of the suit. In such a position, we do not find any reason to allow the application for additional evidence at appellate stage and, as such, it is rejected. 

 31. In the previous suit, decree was passed in favour of the plaintiff (defendant number 1 herein) for eviction of the Police in presence of the Government-plaintiffs. The Police filed Miscellaneous Case Number 65 of 1996 for setting aside the ex-parte decree which was rejected for default by order dated 3-10-1997. Thereafter the Police filed a time-barred first miscellaneous appeal before the High Court Division that was summarily rejected by order dated 24-8-2000. The Appellate Division by its order dated 30-3-2003 also dismissed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Number 1364 of 2002. The Government though appeared in the title suit, did not contest the same or challenge the decree in any forum. The ex-parte judgement and decree dated 8-9-1996 passed in Title Suit Number 219 of 1994 thus reached finality. 

 33. On the other hand, if we go through the evidence of defendant number 1, his title on the basis of a registered sale deed with prior permission of the Government, successive mutation in the name of Mainuddin and Abu Muzaffor Ahmed (defendant number 1), full payment of lease money, issuance of clearance certificate by the Government, repayment of outstanding loan to HBFC and return back of the original title documents, payment of rent and municipal tax, WASA bill etcetera and production of original title documents by defendant number 1 have been proved in support of the defendant's case. The Ministry of Home issued letter and reminders to the Police for vacating the suit property. In cross-examination, PW 1 could not reply whether the Police rented the house in 1967 from its original lessee Zainul Abedin. It proves that before getting allotment in 1972, the Police was in possession of the suit property. In this background, a duty is cast upon the plaintiffs to explain how the Police went into the possession of the suit property, if it was not let out to them by the original lessee. In view of the above, we think that the defendant number 1 has been able to prove his better title. 

 35. Learned Additional Attorney-General for the plaintiff-appellants heavily relied upon Exhibits-1 and 3 and tried to impress upon us that the original lessee Zainul Abedin had seven minor children. So attaining 45 years age on the part of Mainuddin in 1987 was a false statement. We have critically examined both the documents, which were photocopies. Nowhere in those photocopies, the age of Mainuddin was mentioned, but in the affidavit (Exhibit 3) Zainul Abedin was described as a man of 45 years of age. PW 1 adduced those photocopies in evidence without producing the originals, but stated that he was holding the same. There was no endorsement of the learned trial Judge that the plaintiffs ever produced those original documents before the Court, or that the learned Judge himself examined the originals. In paragraph 2 of the plaint, it was stated that the original record of the suit property was lost. In such a position, without producing the originals or any explanation about missing of the same and disclosing the source of photocopies, how the photocopies could be adduced in evidence. Even if the application dated 10-1-1963 (Exhibit 1) is taken to be a replica of the original, it is best known to Zainul Abedin why he stated like that. May be for the purpose of drawing sympathy in his favour, but without any explanation offered by Zainul Abedin, it is difficult to arrive at a ready conclusion on such a doubtful document. 

 36. In order to appreciate the identity of Mainuddin, we have critically examined the original copy of the letter of guarantee dated 16-7-1964 (Exhibit Ga), registered mortgage deed dated 20-7-1964 (Exhibit Bha) and the sale deed dated 18-8-1988 (Exhibit Chha). In all the documents, the signatures of Mainuddin appear to be of the same hand. His father's name in Exhibits-Ga and Chha is written "Md Zainul Abedin". In the letter of guarantee and mortgage deed, the address of Md Zainul Abedin and that of Mainuddin on the first page of the letter of guarantee are same, i.e. "81, Dania Angul Lane, Dacca". If these three documents, of which two are older than 50 years and undisputed, are considered with the citizenship certificate (Exhibit Cha) and oral evidence of DW1, there are reasons to arrive at the finding of fact that Maiduddin was the son of Zainul Abedin.
